Abraham's covenant.background:
The story of Abraham is told in the Book of Genesis, the first book of the Torah. He is first called Abram, son of Terah, and grows up in Ur of the Chaldees, a wealthy city in southern Mesopotamia (today's Iraq). The family later moves north to Haran, in what is now south-eastern Turkey.

Historians debate whether Abraham was a real person or a figure of memory and tradition, and the date of around 1800 BCE is a traditional estimate. What is clear is that the stories reflect a world of herders moving between the great river cultures of Mesopotamia and Egypt.
Abraham's covenant.happened:
According to Genesis 12, God tells Abram to leave his land, his birthplace and his father's house and go to a land he will be shown. He sets out at the age of 75 with his wife Sarai, his nephew Lot and their household, and reaches Canaan, stopping at Shechem and Bethel. Later chapters describe a covenant, or binding agreement, made in a vision in which animals are cut in half and a flame passes between them.

In Genesis 17, when Abram is 99, God renames him Abraham, meaning "father of many nations", and renames Sarai as Sarah. Every male in the household is to be circumcised as a sign of the covenant. Sarah, long childless, gives birth to Isaac at a great age. Abraham also has a son, Ishmael, with Sarah's servant Hagar. Abraham buys the Cave of Machpelah in Hebron as a family tomb.
Abraham's covenant.matters:
Jews call Abraham "Avraham Avinu", our father Abraham, and see him as the first person to commit fully to one God. The ceremony of circumcision on the eighth day after birth, called brit milah (covenant of circumcision), is still performed today, and converts to Judaism are traditionally called "son" or "daughter of Abraham and Sarah".

The Cave of the Patriarchs in Hebron, where tradition says Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebecca, Jacob and Leah are buried, remains a holy site. Abraham is also honoured in Christianity and Islam, which is why the three faiths are often called the Abrahamic religions. His journey from Mesopotamia to Canaan sits at the start of the story of the Jewish people and its link to the land.

Binding of Isaac.background:
After many years of waiting, Abraham and Sarah have a son, Isaac, whose name comes from the Hebrew word for laughter, because Sarah laughed at the idea of giving birth in old age. Isaac is the child through whom the covenant is meant to continue. In the ancient Near East, offering children to gods was not unknown, which gives the story its sharp edge.

The account is found in Genesis 22. Like the other patriarchal stories, it cannot be dated or confirmed by outside evidence, and the date given here follows traditional reckoning.
Binding of Isaac.happened:
God tells Abraham to take his beloved son to the land of Moriah and offer him there. Abraham rises early, saddles his donkey and sets out with Isaac and two young servants. On the third day he sees the place from afar. Isaac carries the wood and asks his father where the lamb is, and Abraham answers that God will provide it.

Abraham builds an altar, binds Isaac and lifts the knife. An angel calls out to stop him, and Abraham sees a ram caught by its horns in a thicket, which he offers instead. He names the place with words meaning "the Lord will see" or "provide". The Hebrew name of the episode, Akedah, means "binding". Later rabbinic tradition, the midrash, imagines that Isaac was a grown man of 37 who went willingly.
Binding of Isaac.matters:
The Book of Chronicles says Solomon built the Temple on Mount Moriah, so tradition links the Akedah to the Temple Mount in Jerusalem. The rock beneath the Dome of the Rock is associated by many with the spot.

The story is read in synagogue on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, and many Jews recite it in their daily morning prayers. The shofar, a ram's horn blown on Rosh Hashanah, recalls the ram that took Isaac's place, and prayers ask God to remember Abraham's faithfulness. Thinkers from the rabbis to the philosopher Søren Kierkegaard have wrestled with its meaning. It also features in Christianity and in Islam, where many traditions name Ishmael as the son. It has been painted by artists from Caravaggio to Rembrandt.

Jacob becomes Israel.background:
Jacob is the younger twin son of Isaac and Rebecca. According to Genesis, he buys the birthright from his brother Esau for a bowl of lentil stew, then, with his mother's help, disguises himself to receive his blind father's blessing. Fearing Esau's anger, he flees to his uncle Laban in Haran. On the way, at a place he names Bethel ("house of God"), he dreams of a ladder or stairway with angels going up and down.

In Haran he works seven years to marry Rachel, is tricked into marrying her sister Leah first, and works seven more. With Leah, Rachel and their servants Bilhah and Zilpah he has twelve sons and a daughter, Dinah. After twenty years he heads home, frightened to meet Esau, who is coming with 400 men.
Jacob becomes Israel.happened:
Genesis 32 says that Jacob sends his family across the ford of the Jabbok river, a tributary of the Jordan, and is left alone. A man wrestles with him until dawn. Unable to win, the stranger touches Jacob's hip and puts it out of joint, but Jacob refuses to let go without a blessing. The stranger gives him the name Israel and Jacob calls the place Peniel, meaning "face of God", because he has seen God face to face and survived.

The next morning Jacob, limping, meets Esau, bows to him seven times, and the brothers embrace and weep. Jewish interpreters have understood the stranger in different ways: as an angel, as Esau's guardian angel, or as Jacob struggling with himself.
Jacob becomes Israel.matters:
The name Israel became the name of the whole people, the "Children of Israel" (Bnei Yisrael), of the land, and in 1948 of the modern state. The idea of a people defined by wrestling with God, and not giving up, has inspired Jewish thought for centuries.

The Torah says that because of the injury, the Children of Israel do not eat the sciatic nerve (in Hebrew gid hanasheh) of an animal, a rule still kept in kosher butchery today. Jacob's ladder has become a common image in art and literature, and his twelve sons gave their names to the twelve tribes.

Jacob's family goes to Egypt.background:
Joseph is Jacob's favourite son, the first child of his beloved Rachel. Jacob gives him a special coat, often called the coat of many colours, and Joseph tells his brothers of dreams in which they bow to him. Genesis says the jealous brothers throw him into a pit and sell him to traders travelling to Egypt, telling their father he was killed by a wild animal.

In Egypt Joseph serves an official named Potiphar, is falsely accused and jailed, and gains a reputation for interpreting dreams. Pharaoh dreams of seven fat cows eaten by seven thin ones, and Joseph explains that seven years of plenty will be followed by seven years of famine. Pharaoh puts him in charge of storing grain and gives him an Egyptian name and a wife, Asenath.
Jacob's family goes to Egypt.happened:
When famine reaches Canaan, ten of Joseph's brothers go to Egypt to buy grain and bow before the governor without recognising him. Joseph tests them, holding one brother and demanding that they bring the youngest, Benjamin. When his silver cup is found in Benjamin's sack, Judah offers himself as a slave in Benjamin's place. Moved, Joseph reveals himself and forgives them, saying their act was part of a larger plan to save lives.

Jacob, now old, travels down with his family, which Genesis counts as seventy people. Pharaoh lets them settle in Goshen, good grazing land in the eastern Nile Delta. Before dying, Jacob blesses each of his sons and Joseph's two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, and asks to be buried in the family tomb in Hebron.
Jacob's family goes to Egypt.matters:
This move explains how the Israelites came to be in Egypt, setting the scene for slavery and the Exodus. There is no direct Egyptian record of Joseph, and historians debate the story's origins. However, archaeology shows that people from Canaan did settle in the eastern Delta in this era, especially at Avaris (Tell el-Dab'a).

The story's themes of jealousy, forgiveness and reconciliation remain powerful. On Friday nights many Jewish parents bless their sons with the words "May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh". The tale has inspired many retellings, including Thomas Mann's novel Joseph and His Brothers and the stage musical Joseph and the Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat.

Death of Joseph.background:
After Jacob's family settles in Goshen, Joseph continues to serve as Pharaoh's chief official. When Jacob dies, Joseph has him embalmed in the Egyptian manner and leads a great funeral procession back to Canaan to bury him in the Cave of Machpelah. Afterwards, his brothers fear he will now take revenge, but Joseph reassures them that what they meant for harm, God meant for good.

Joseph lives to see his great-grandchildren. The age of 110 given in Genesis was considered the ideal lifespan in ancient Egyptian texts, a detail scholars often point to.
Death of Joseph.happened:
The Book of Genesis ends with Joseph's death. Before dying he tells his brothers that God will surely remember them and bring them up out of Egypt to the land promised to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and he makes them swear to carry his bones with them. He is embalmed and placed in a coffin in Egypt.

The Book of Exodus (13:19) records that Moses took Joseph's bones when the Israelites left. The Talmud adds a legend that Moses did not know where the coffin was, and that Serah, daughter of Asher, an old woman who remembered, showed him it had been sunk in the Nile. According to Joshua 24, the bones were buried at Shechem, in the plot of land Jacob had bought there for a hundred pieces of silver.
Death of Joseph.matters:
Jewish tradition calls Joseph "Yosef HaTzaddik", Joseph the righteous, for resisting temptation and forgiving his brothers. Moses carrying his bones through the desert is seen as a model of keeping promises across generations, and the story has given comfort to Jews who wished to be buried in the Land of Israel.

The site known as Joseph's Tomb lies on the edge of Nablus. It has been visited by Jews, Samaritans, Christians and Muslims, and Muslim tradition has also linked it to a local sheikh. In modern times it has become a point of tension, and Jewish visits are arranged under security escort. Joseph's two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, became tribes in their own right.

Hyksos driven from Egypt.background:
From around 1650 BCE, Egypt was divided. The north was ruled by foreign kings known as the Hyksos, a Greek form of an Egyptian phrase meaning "rulers of foreign lands". They formed Egypt's Fifteenth Dynasty and governed from Avaris in the eastern Nile Delta. Excavations there, at Tell el-Dab'a, led for decades by the Austrian archaeologist Manfred Bietak, revealed houses, tombs and pottery in a Canaanite style.

The Hyksos are credited with spreading the horse-drawn chariot and new weapons in Egypt. Native Egyptian kings ruled the south from Thebes and resented the foreign rulers.
Hyksos driven from Egypt.happened:
The Theban king Seqenenre Tao seems to have fought the Hyksos, and his mummy shows terrible head wounds. His son Kamose carried on the war. Kamose's brother Ahmose I finished the job around 1550 BCE, though exact dates are debated. A soldier called Ahmose son of Ebana recorded his own part in the campaign on the walls of his tomb at El Kab, describing the capture of Avaris and the pursuit of the enemy to Sharuhen in southern Canaan, which fell after a three-year siege.

Ahmose reunited Egypt and founded the Eighteenth Dynasty, the start of the New Kingdom. Under his successors, Egypt pushed deep into Canaan and Syria and controlled the region for centuries.
Hyksos driven from Egypt.matters:
The Egyptian priest Manetho, writing in Greek in the third century BCE, described the Hyksos, and the Jewish historian Josephus, quoting him in his work Against Apion, linked them to the ancestors of the Jews. Most modern historians do not identify the Hyksos with the Israelites, but some see a distant memory of Canaanites living in, and leaving, Egypt in the Exodus story.

The expulsion also matters because it began Egypt's long rule over Canaan. Egyptian forts, letters and inscriptions from the following centuries, such as the Amarna letters, are key sources for the world in which ancient Israel later emerged.

Slavery begins.background:
The Book of Exodus opens by listing the sons of Jacob who came to Egypt and noting that Joseph and his whole generation died. The Israelites, it says, were fruitful and filled the land. Then a new king arose who did not know Joseph. Rabbis later debated whether he was truly new or simply chose to forget what Joseph had done.

The Torah says the Israelites lived in Egypt for 430 years, while rabbinic tradition counts 210 years from Jacob's arrival. The date here follows one traditional reckoning based on 1 Kings 6:1, but historians debate the chronology, and there is no Egyptian record of Israelite slaves.
Slavery begins.happened:
Pharaoh tells his people that the Israelites have become too many and might side with Egypt's enemies. Taskmasters are set over them and they are forced to build the store cities of Pithom and Raamses. When this fails to reduce their numbers, Pharaoh orders two Hebrew midwives, named in the Torah as Shiphrah and Puah, to kill newborn boys. The midwives refuse, and Pharaoh then orders all his people to throw every Hebrew baby boy into the Nile.

Egyptian evidence gives a sense of the setting. The tomb of the official Rekhmire at Thebes, from the fifteenth century BCE, shows foreign workers making mud bricks. The city of Pi-Ramesses, built by Ramesses II in the Delta, is often linked with the biblical Raamses, which leads many scholars to favour a later date.
Slavery begins.matters:
Slavery in Egypt is the starting point of the Passover story. At the Seder, the festive meal on the first night of Passover, Jews eat maror, bitter herbs, to taste the bitterness of slavery, and charoset, a sweet paste said to look like the mortar the slaves used. Salt water recalls their tears. The Haggadah, the book read at the Seder, begins its answer to the children's questions with the words "We were slaves to Pharaoh in Egypt".

The Torah repeatedly tells Israel to treat the stranger kindly, because they were strangers in Egypt. The midwives' refusal is often cited as one of the earliest recorded acts of civil disobedience.

Birth of Moses.background:
Pharaoh's decree that every Hebrew baby boy be thrown into the Nile sets the scene. According to Exodus 2, a man and woman of the tribe of Levi, named elsewhere as Amram and Jochebed, have a son. They already have a daughter, Miriam, and a son, Aaron, who will both become leaders.

As with the rest of the Exodus story, there is no outside evidence for Moses's life, and historians debate when and whether these events took place. Some point out that a similar birth legend was told about Sargon of Akkad, a Mesopotamian king.
Birth of Moses.happened:
His mother hides the baby for three months. When she can hide him no longer, she places him in a basket of papyrus sealed with tar and sets it among the reeds of the Nile. The Hebrew word for the basket, tevah, is the same word used for Noah's ark. Pharaoh's daughter comes to bathe, finds the crying child and takes pity on him. Miriam steps forward and offers to find a Hebrew nurse, and brings his own mother. Pharaoh's daughter names him Moses, explained in the text as "I drew him out of the water", though the name also resembles the Egyptian word for "son", seen in names like Thutmose.

Grown up, Moses sees an Egyptian beating a Hebrew and kills him. He flees to Midian, marries Zipporah, daughter of the priest Jethro, and becomes a shepherd. At Mount Horeb he sees a bush that burns but is not consumed and hears God call him to free his people.
Birth of Moses.matters:
Moses, known in Jewish tradition as Moshe Rabbeinu, "Moses our teacher", is seen as the greatest of the prophets. He leads the Exodus, receives the Torah at Sinai and guides the people for forty years.

Tradition holds that he was born and died on the seventh day of the month of Adar, which some communities mark as a day honouring burial societies. The Torah says he died at 120, the source of the Jewish birthday wish "until 120". Rabbinic tradition names Pharaoh's daughter Bitya and praises her courage. Moses is also a central figure in Christianity and Islam, where he is known as Musa.

The Exodus.background:
After years of slavery, the Israelites cry out and God remembers the covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Moses and his brother Aaron go before Pharaoh with the demand that he let the people go to worship in the wilderness. Pharaoh refuses and makes their work harder, ordering them to gather their own straw for bricks.

The Exodus is the central story of the Torah, but historians debate it widely. There is no direct Egyptian or archaeological record of it, and scholars disagree on whether it reflects a large migration, a smaller group's memory, or a later national story. Suggested dates range from the fifteenth to the thirteenth century BCE.
The Exodus.happened:
The Book of Exodus describes ten plagues: the Nile turning to blood, frogs, lice, swarms of wild animals, disease among livestock, boils, hail, locusts, darkness and finally the death of every Egyptian firstborn. Before the last plague, each Israelite family slaughters a lamb and marks its doorposts with the blood so that death will pass over their homes, the origin of the name Passover. In their haste to leave they have no time for their bread to rise.

The Torah says about 600,000 men on foot, plus women and children, set out. Pharaoh changes his mind and chases them with chariots. At the Yam Suf, often translated as the Red Sea but literally the Sea of Reeds, Moses lifts his staff, the waters divide and the Israelites cross on dry land. The waters return over the Egyptian army. Moses and the people sing the Song of the Sea, and Miriam leads the women with drums and dancing.
The Exodus.matters:
Passover (Pesach) is celebrated for seven days in Israel and eight elsewhere, beginning on the 15th of the Hebrew month of Nisan. Families hold a Seder, eat matzah (unleavened bread) and remove all leavened food from their homes. The Exodus is also recalled every day in prayer, in the Friday night Kiddush blessing and in the Song of the Sea recited in morning services.

The story has inspired movements for freedom far beyond Judaism. Enslaved African Americans drew on it in their spirituals, and civil rights leaders used its language. Its message, that a people can move from slavery to freedom, remains one of the most retold stories in the world.

Torah given at Sinai.background:
After crossing the sea, the Israelites travel through the wilderness, complaining of thirst and hunger. The Torah says they are fed with manna, a bread-like food that appears each morning, and fight off an attack by Amalek. In the third month after leaving Egypt they arrive at the wilderness of Sinai and camp before the mountain.

The location of Mount Sinai is unknown and debated. Christian tradition since the fourth century has identified it with Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai Peninsula, where St Catherine's Monastery stands, but other sites in Sinai, the Negev and Arabia have been proposed.
Torah given at Sinai.happened:
Exodus 19 describes three days of preparation. On the third day there is thunder, lightning, a thick cloud, the loud blast of a shofar and smoke rising from the mountain as it trembles. God speaks the Ten Commandments to the whole people, who are so afraid that they ask Moses to speak to them instead. The people answer, in the Torah's words, "we will do and we will hear", which the rabbis praised as a promise to obey even before understanding.

Moses then spends forty days and nights on the mountain. While he is gone the people make a golden calf, and Moses breaks the first tablets on seeing it. Tradition dates this to the 17th of Tammuz and says he came down with the second tablets on Yom Kippur. The tablets were later kept in the Ark of the Covenant. The rabbis counted 613 commandments in the Torah.
Torah given at Sinai.matters:
Jewish tradition holds that Moses received both the Written Torah and the Oral Torah, the explanations later written down in the Mishnah and Talmud. The covenant at Sinai is seen as the moment Israel became a people with a shared law and purpose.

Shavuot, the Feast of Weeks, falls fifty days after Passover, at the end of seven weeks of counting called the Omer. Customs include staying up all night to study Torah, decorating synagogues with greenery, eating dairy foods and reading the Ten Commandments and the Book of Ruth. The Ten Commandments have also shaped Christian teaching and Western ideas of law and ethics.

Merneptah Stele.background:
Merneptah was the thirteenth son and successor of Ramesses II, one of Egypt's most famous pharaohs. He came to the throne already old, around 1213 BCE, at a time when Egypt still controlled Canaan but faced threats on its borders, especially from Libyan tribes allied with the so-called Sea Peoples.

Pharaohs often recorded their victories on large stone slabs called stelae, placed in temples so that both gods and people would see them.
Merneptah Stele.happened:
The stele is a slab of black granite about three metres tall. It was not new: Merneptah's scribes reused the back of a stone first carved for the earlier pharaoh Amenhotep III. Most of its 28 lines celebrate Merneptah's defeat of the Libyans in the fifth year of his reign. Only the last lines turn to Canaan, listing Ashkelon, Gezer and Yenoam as conquered, followed by the line about Israel.

The British archaeologist Flinders Petrie found it in 1896 in the ruins of Merneptah's funerary temple at Thebes, in Upper Egypt. In the hieroglyphs, the names of the cities are marked with a sign meaning a city or land, but Israel is marked with the sign for a people. Many scholars take this to mean Israel was then a group of people in Canaan rather than a settled kingdom.
Merneptah Stele.matters:
The stele is sometimes called the Israel Stele. It is the earliest known mention of Israel outside the Bible and the only one known from ancient Egypt. It shows that a group called Israel existed in Canaan by the late thirteenth century BCE, which is important for debates on the origins of ancient Israel and the date of the Exodus and settlement.

Some scholars, notably Frank Yurco, have argued that battle reliefs at the Karnak temple show the same campaign, possibly including Israelites, though this remains debated. The stele is displayed in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo, and copies appear in museums and textbooks around the world.

Joshua enters Canaan.background:
Joshua son of Nun, from the tribe of Ephraim, served as Moses's assistant for forty years. He was one of the twelve spies sent into Canaan, and with Caleb he was the only one to bring back a hopeful report. Because the people lost faith, the Torah says, they wandered for forty years until a new generation grew up.

Deuteronomy 34 tells how Moses climbs Mount Nebo in Moab, sees the land and dies there aged 120. No one knows where he is buried. Before his death he lays his hands on Joshua and appoints him leader.
Joshua enters Canaan.happened:
The Book of Joshua describes two spies hidden in Jericho by Rahab, who is saved by a red cord in her window. On the 10th of Nisan the people cross the Jordan, which stops flowing as the priests carrying the Ark step in. Twelve stones, one for each tribe, are set up at Gilgal. There the men are circumcised and the first Passover in the land is held.

At Jericho the Israelites march round the city once a day for six days and seven times on the seventh. The priests blow shofars, the people shout and the walls collapse. Battles follow at Ai, Gibeon and in the north. The land is then divided by lot among the tribes, with Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh settling east of the Jordan, while the Levites receive cities rather than territory. Joshua ends his life by gathering the tribes at Shechem to renew the covenant.
Joshua enters Canaan.matters:
Archaeology has complicated the picture. Kathleen Kenyon's excavations at Jericho in the 1950s suggested that its walls fell long before Joshua's likely date, and that the site was small or empty in the thirteenth century BCE. Many historians now think Israel emerged more gradually, pointing to hundreds of new hill-country villages that appear around 1200 BCE. Others defend a version of the conquest. The debate continues.

Jewish tradition credits Joshua with the Aleinu prayer said at the end of services. The Book of Joshua begins the section of the Bible called the Prophets, and the image of Jericho's falling walls has become one of the best-known scenes in the Bible.

Deborah the judge.background:
After Joshua, the tribes had no central government. The Book of Judges describes a repeated cycle: the people turn away from God, an enemy oppresses them, they cry out, and a leader called a judge (shofet) rises to save them. Judges were mostly military heroes rather than courtroom figures.

In Deborah's time, the Bible says, Jabin, a Canaanite king ruling at Hazor in the north, had oppressed Israel for twenty years. His army commander, Sisera, based at Harosheth-haggoyim, had 900 iron chariots, which gave him great power on flat ground.
Deborah the judge.happened:
Judges 4 says Deborah, wife of Lappidoth, sat under a palm tree between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim, where people came to her for judgement. She summoned Barak son of Abinoam from Kedesh in Naphtali and told him to gather 10,000 men from Naphtali and Zebulun on Mount Tabor. Barak agreed only if she came too, and she warned that the glory would then go to a woman.

Sisera's chariots gathered by the Kishon river. The Song of Deborah suggests that a storm turned the river into a torrent and the chariots were trapped. Sisera fled on foot to the tent of Yael, wife of Heber the Kenite. She gave him milk, covered him, and as he slept she drove a tent peg through his temple. The Song in Judges 5 praises the tribes who came, scolds those who stayed home and pictures Sisera's mother waiting at her window for a son who will not return.
Deborah the judge.matters:
Deborah is the only woman in the Bible described as a judge, and the Talmud lists her among the seven prophetesses of Israel. She has become a symbol of women's leadership, and the name Devorah, meaning "bee", remains popular.

The Song of Deborah is considered by many scholars to be one of the oldest passages in the Hebrew Bible, perhaps close in date to the events it describes. In many communities, together with the prose story, it is read in synagogue as the haftarah (reading from the Prophets) on Shabbat Shirah, the Sabbath of Song, alongside the Song of the Sea. The Bible says the land then had rest for forty years.

The story of Ruth.background:
The Book of Ruth opens "in the days when the judges ruled". A famine strikes Judah, and a man from Bethlehem named Elimelech moves with his wife Naomi and their sons Mahlon and Chilion to Moab, a neighbouring kingdom east of the Dead Sea. The sons marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth. Then Elimelech and both sons die, leaving three widows.

Relations between Israel and Moab were often hostile, and Deuteronomy says a Moabite may not enter the congregation of Israel. This makes Ruth's story all the more striking. Scholars debate when the book was written, with suggestions ranging from the time of the kings to after the Babylonian exile.
The story of Ruth.happened:
Naomi decides to return to Bethlehem and urges her daughters-in-law to go back to their families. Orpah tearfully agrees, but Ruth clings to Naomi and pledges to follow her people and her God, and to be buried where she is buried. They arrive at the start of the barley harvest.

Ruth goes to glean, gathering the stalks left behind by reapers, as the Torah requires farmers to leave for the poor and the stranger. She ends up in the field of Boaz, a wealthy relative of Elimelech, who treats her kindly. On Naomi's advice, Ruth goes to the threshing floor at night and asks Boaz to act as a goel, a redeemer, the relative responsible for protecting a family's land and name. A closer relative declines, removing his sandal before ten elders at the town gate to seal the deal. Boaz marries Ruth and they have a son, Obed, the father of Jesse and grandfather of David.
The story of Ruth.matters:
Ruth is honoured as the model convert, someone who joins the Jewish people out of love and loyalty. The rabbis explained that the ban on Moabites applied only to men, which allowed her place in David's line. Many women who convert to Judaism choose the Hebrew name Ruth.

The book is one of the five Megillot, or scrolls, read on festivals, and is read on Shavuot. Reasons given include its harvest setting, the tradition that David was born and died on Shavuot, and the idea that Ruth's acceptance of the Torah mirrors Israel's at Sinai.

Philistines capture the Ark.background:
The Philistines were one of the Sea Peoples, groups who arrived on the coast of Canaan from the Aegean world around 1175 BCE. They settled in five main cities: Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron and Gath. Excavations at these sites have found pottery, cooking habits and buildings with Aegean roots.

By the eleventh century BCE the Philistines were pressing inland into the hill country where the Israelite tribes lived. At this time the Ark of the Covenant, the gold-covered chest holding the tablets of the Ten Commandments, was kept at the shrine of Shiloh, served by the elderly priest Eli and his sons Hophni and Phinehas.
Philistines capture the Ark.happened:
According to 1 Samuel 4, the Israelites camp at Eben-Ezer and the Philistines at Aphek. In the first battle about 4,000 Israelites are killed. The elders send for the Ark, hoping it will bring victory, and Eli's sons bring it from Shiloh. The Philistines are frightened but fight harder, and Israel is crushed, with 30,000 dead. Hophni and Phinehas are killed and the Ark is captured. When a messenger brings the news, Eli, aged 98, falls backwards from his seat and breaks his neck. Phinehas's wife gives birth and names her son Ichabod, meaning "the glory has departed".

The Philistines place the Ark in the temple of their god Dagon at Ashdod. The statue of Dagon is found fallen before it, and the people of Ashdod, then Gath and Ekron, are struck with tumours. After seven months they send the Ark back on a new cart drawn by two cows, with golden offerings shaped like tumours and mice. It reaches Beth Shemesh and is later kept at Kiriath-jearim for twenty years.
Philistines capture the Ark.matters:
The defeat marked a low point. Shiloh appears to have been destroyed, and the prophet Jeremiah later used its ruin as a warning. The judge and prophet Samuel led a revival, and when the Philistines were later beaten, he set up a stone he called Eben-Ezer, "stone of help". Pressure from the Philistines, together with the failure of Samuel's own sons as judges, led the people to demand a king.

The word Ebenezer later became a popular name for chapels and people in the English-speaking world. The name Palestine also comes, through Greek and Latin, from the Philistines' land.

Saul, the first king.background:
Samuel had led Israel as prophet and judge, travelling between Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpah. In his old age, the Bible says, his sons took bribes, and the elders asked for a king to judge them and lead them in war. Samuel was displeased and warned that a king would take their sons for his chariots, their daughters as servants and a tenth of their crops and flocks. The people insisted.

The tribes were loosely united and under constant pressure from the Philistines in the west and the Ammonites in the east. The traditional date of about 1050 BCE is approximate, and historians debate how large Saul's kingdom really was.
Saul, the first king.happened:
1 Samuel 9 tells how Saul, son of Kish, from the tribe of Benjamin, goes looking for his father's lost donkeys and meets Samuel, who secretly anoints him with oil. Saul is described as a head taller than anyone else. He is later chosen by lot at Mizpah and proves himself by rescuing the town of Jabesh-Gilead from the Ammonite king Nahash. He rules from his home town of Gibeah.

Saul twice falls out with Samuel: once for offering a sacrifice without waiting for the prophet, and once for sparing Agag, king of the Amalekites, and the best of the livestock against God's command. Samuel tells him the kingdom will be taken from him. Saul is troubled by dark moods, soothed by the young harpist David, whose fame after killing Goliath fills Saul with jealousy. He hunts David for years. Before his last battle he consults a medium at Endor. On Mount Gilboa the Philistines kill Jonathan and two other sons, and the wounded Saul falls on his own sword.
Saul, the first king.matters:
The Philistines hang the bodies on the walls of Beth Shan, but the men of Jabesh-Gilead, remembering Saul's rescue, travel through the night to recover and bury them. David's lament for Saul and Jonathan in 2 Samuel 1, with its refrain "how the mighty have fallen", is one of the most moving poems in the Bible.

Saul is remembered as a tragic figure: brave and humble at first, but unable to cope with power. His story begins the age of kings in Israel and raised questions about kingship and prophecy that echo through the Bible.

David takes Jerusalem.background:
David, the youngest son of Jesse of Bethlehem and great-grandson of Ruth, was anointed by Samuel while still a shepherd boy. After Saul's death he became king of Judah, ruling from Hebron for seven and a half years, while Saul's son Ish-bosheth ruled the northern tribes. After Ish-bosheth was murdered, the elders of all Israel came to Hebron and anointed David as king over the whole nation.

Jerusalem at the time was held by the Jebusites, a Canaanite people. It sat on a ridge between the territories of Judah and Benjamin, belonged to neither tribe, and was guarded by steep valleys and a reliable water supply, the Gihon Spring.
David takes Jerusalem.happened:
2 Samuel 5 says the Jebusites mocked David, claiming that even the blind and lame could keep him out. David took the fortress of Zion, apparently by sending men up a water channel, and 1 Chronicles says his commander Joab was the first to climb up. He renamed it the City of David and Hiram, king of Tyre, sent cedar and craftsmen to build him a palace. David then ruled for 33 years in Jerusalem.

He brought the Ark of the Covenant from Kiriath-jearim. On the first attempt a man named Uzzah was struck dead for touching it, and it stayed three months at the house of Obed-edom. When it was finally carried in, David danced before it with all his might. He wanted to build a temple, but the prophet Nathan told him that his son would build it, while God would establish David's dynasty for ever.
David takes Jerusalem.matters:
Jerusalem became the political and spiritual centre of the Jewish people and has remained so. Jews pray facing it, and its name appears again and again in daily prayers. The promise to David's line is the root of the Jewish hope for a Messiah, an anointed king descended from David, and many psalms are traditionally attributed to him.

Archaeologists continue to dig in the City of David, south of today's Old City walls. Eilat Mazar argued in 2005 that she had found David's palace, but this is debated, and scholars disagree about how large Jerusalem was in his time. The Tel Dan inscription of the ninth century BCE mentions the "House of David", supporting his existence as founder of a dynasty.

First Temple built.background:
David had wanted to build a house for the Ark but, according to the Bible, was told that his son would do it. He bought a threshing floor from Araunah the Jebusite on the hill north of the City of David and gathered materials. Solomon, son of David and Bathsheba, became king around 970 BCE and was famed for his wisdom and wealth.

Solomon made an agreement with Hiram, king of Tyre, the great Phoenician port. Cedar and cypress logs from Lebanon were floated down the coast on rafts in exchange for wheat and olive oil. 1 Kings says Solomon drafted 30,000 Israelites to work in Lebanon in shifts, along with 70,000 carriers and 80,000 stonecutters.
First Temple built.happened:
1 Kings 6 says building began in the fourth year of Solomon's reign, 480 years after the Exodus, and took seven years. The stones were cut at the quarry so that no hammer or iron tool was heard on site. The building was 60 cubits long, 20 wide and 30 high, roughly 27 by 9 by 13.5 metres, and was lined with cedar and gold. In front stood two great bronze pillars named Jachin and Boaz, and a huge bronze basin called the Sea, resting on twelve bronze oxen.

The innermost room, the Holy of Holies, held the Ark, guarded by two cherubim of olive wood covered in gold. Solomon dedicated the Temple at the autumn festival of Sukkot with a long prayer asking God to hear the prayers of all who turned towards this house, including foreigners. The date of 957 BCE follows one common reckoning; others differ, and rabbinic tradition places it later.
First Temple built.matters:
The Temple became the heart of worship. Only the High Priest could enter the Holy of Holies, and only on Yom Kippur. Israelites made pilgrimage there at the three festivals of Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot.

No remains of Solomon's Temple have been excavated, as digging on the Temple Mount is not possible for religious and political reasons. The Temple Mount remains the holiest place in Judaism, and is also sacred to Muslims as the Haram al-Sharif. Synagogues face Jerusalem, and the cabinet holding the Torah scrolls, called the ark, echoes the Ark of the Covenant.

The kingdom splits.background:
Solomon's reign was remembered as a golden age, but his grand projects, including the Temple, his palace and fortified cities such as Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer, required heavy taxes and forced labour. The Bible also says his many foreign wives led him to build shrines to other gods. Discontent grew, especially among the northern tribes.

One of Solomon's officials, Jeroboam son of Nebat of the tribe of Ephraim, had been in charge of forced labour from the northern tribes. The prophet Ahijah of Shiloh met him, tore his own new cloak into twelve pieces and gave him ten, saying he would rule ten tribes. Jeroboam fled to Egypt, to Pharaoh Shishak, until Solomon died.
The kingdom splits.happened:
1 Kings 12 says Solomon's son Rehoboam went to Shechem to be crowned. The people, with Jeroboam as their spokesman, asked him to lighten their burden. The elders advised him to agree, but the young men he had grown up with told him to be harsher still. Rehoboam told the people his father had punished them with whips, but he would use scorpions. The northern tribes rejected the house of David. When Rehoboam sent his chief of forced labour, Adoram, they stoned him to death, and Rehoboam fled to Jerusalem.

Jeroboam became king of Israel. To stop his people going to Jerusalem's Temple, he set up golden calves at Dan and Bethel. His capital moved from Shechem to Penuel and Tirzah, and later King Omri built Samaria. In Rehoboam's fifth year, Shishak invaded and took the Temple's treasures.
The kingdom splits.matters:
The northern Kingdom of Israel was the larger and richer, but it was unstable, with nine dynasties and several kings murdered in coups. Judah kept David's line throughout its history. The English word "Jew" comes, through Latin and Greek, from Yehudi, someone from Judah, because it was Judah's people who survived as a nation.

The split shaped the rest of biblical history and the writings of the prophets, several of whom dreamed of the two kingdoms being joined again, as in Ezekiel's vision of two sticks becoming one. The Samaritans, a small community still living near Nablus and in Holon, trace their roots to the northern tribes.

Elijah the prophet.background:
In the northern Kingdom of Israel, King Omri founded a strong dynasty and built a new capital at Samaria. His son Ahab married Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Phoenician city of Sidon. Jezebel promoted the worship of Baal, the Phoenician storm god, and Ahab built a temple to Baal in Samaria.

Into this setting steps Elijah the Tishbite, from Gilead east of the Jordan, who appears suddenly in 1 Kings 17 to announce a drought.
Elijah the prophet.happened:
During the drought Elijah hides by the brook of Cherith, where ravens bring him food, then lives with a widow in Zarephath whose flour and oil never run out, and he revives her dead son. In the third year he summons the people and the prophets of Baal and Asherah to Mount Carmel. Each side prepares a bull on an altar and calls on its god to send fire. Baal's prophets cry out all day with no answer. Elijah drenches his altar with water three times, prays, and fire falls and consumes everything. The people fall on their faces and cry out that the Lord is God. Rain soon follows.

Jezebel threatens his life, and Elijah flees to Mount Horeb, where God is not in the wind, earthquake or fire, but in a still, small voice. He appoints Elisha as his successor, and 2 Kings 2 describes how a chariot and horses of fire part the two men and Elijah goes up to heaven in a whirlwind.
Elijah the prophet.matters:
Because the Bible does not record his death, and the prophet Malachi says God will send Elijah before the great day of the Lord, Jewish tradition sees him as the herald of the Messiah. At the Passover Seder a special cup of wine is filled for him and the door is opened to welcome him. At a circumcision, a chair called the Chair of Elijah is set out, and songs about him are sung at Havdalah, the ceremony ending the Sabbath.

The cry from Mount Carmel, "The Lord is God", is repeated seven times at the very end of Yom Kippur. He is also honoured in Christianity and Islam, and a Carmelite monastery stands on Mount Carmel at the traditional site of the contest.

Tel Dan Stele.background:
In the ninth century BCE, the Kingdom of Israel's main rival to the north-east was Aram, with its capital at Damascus. The two kingdoms fought repeatedly over land in Gilead and the Golan. Dan, at the foot of Mount Hermon near the sources of the Jordan, was Israel's northern border city and the site of one of Jeroboam's royal shrines.

Kings of the region often celebrated victories with inscriptions. Few have survived, which makes the ones that do especially valuable for checking the Bible's account.
Tel Dan Stele.happened:
In July 1993, Gila Cook, a surveyor on Avraham Biran's excavation at Tel Dan, spotted a fragment of basalt with writing reused in a later wall. Two more pieces were found in 1994. The inscription is in Aramaic, and the king who set it up is not named in the surviving text, though most scholars think it was Hazael of Damascus. He claims to have killed Joram, son of Ahab, king of Israel, and Ahaziah, son of Jehoram, of the "House of David", though parts of the names are restored. The Bible (2 Kings 9) credits the deaths of the same two kings to the Israelite rebel Jehu, a difference scholars still discuss.

The Mesha Stele, also called the Moabite Stone, was found at Dhiban in Jordan in 1868. Its 34 lines tell how Mesha, king of Moab, threw off the rule of Israel after Omri and his son had oppressed Moab for many years, matching a revolt described in 2 Kings 3. It was broken up before it could be taken away, but a paper impression made beforehand allowed it to be pieced together.
Tel Dan Stele.matters:
The phrase "House of David" was the name of a ruling dynasty, which suggests that people a century and a half after David's time remembered him as its founder. Before 1993 some scholars doubted that David had existed at all, so the find had a major effect on the debate. Some scholars have also proposed reading "House of David" on the Mesha Stele, though this is uncertain.

The Tel Dan Stele is displayed at the Israel Museum in Jerusalem, and the Mesha Stele at the Louvre in Paris.

Amos and Hosea.background:
In the first half of the eighth century BCE, the northern Kingdom of Israel enjoyed a long period of power and wealth under King Jeroboam II, who ruled for about four decades. Assyria and Aram were temporarily weak, trade flourished and the borders expanded. Archaeologists have found carved ivory panels in the ruins of Samaria, a sign of the luxury the prophets condemned.

But wealth was unevenly shared. Small farmers fell into debt and lost their land, and the courts favoured the rich. At the same time, shrines at Bethel and elsewhere were busy with sacrifices.
Amos and Hosea.happened:
Amos was not a professional prophet. The book says he came from Tekoa in Judah and was a herdsman and a dresser of sycamore figs. He travelled north to Bethel, the royal shrine, and denounced those who sold the poor for a pair of sandals and wealthy women he called "cows of Bashan". He warned that God took no pleasure in festivals and offerings without justice. Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, told him to go back to Judah. The book dates his words to two years before a great earthquake, and geologists and archaeologists have found evidence of a strong earthquake around 760 BCE.

Hosea, a northerner, used his own painful marriage as a message. He married Gomer, who was unfaithful, and gave their children names meaning "not pitied" and "not my people", to show Israel's betrayal of God. Yet he also described God's love as stronger than betrayal and promised that the people would be taken back.
Amos and Hosea.matters:
Within a few decades of their warnings, Assyria destroyed the northern kingdom. Their books are part of the Twelve Minor Prophets, called "minor" only because they are short. Amos's call for justice to roll down like waters was quoted by Martin Luther King Jr. and is carved on the Civil Rights Memorial in Montgomery, Alabama.

Hosea's words are part of daily Jewish life. When men wind the strap of tefillin (small leather boxes worn for prayer) around the finger, they recite Hosea's verses about God betrothing Israel for ever. His closing call to "return, O Israel" is read on Shabbat Shuvah, the Sabbath between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.

Isaiah's prophecies.background:
By the middle of the eighth century BCE, Assyria was rebuilding its empire under Tiglath-pileser III, and the small kingdoms of the Levant had to decide whether to submit, resist or seek help from Egypt. Judah faced pressure from its neighbours too. When Aram and Israel attacked Judah to force it into an anti-Assyrian alliance, King Ahaz turned to Assyria for help.

Isaiah son of Amoz lived in Jerusalem and had access to the royal court. The book bearing his name dates his work to the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah.
Isaiah's prophecies.happened:
Isaiah 6 describes his call. In the year King Uzziah died, he sees God on a throne in the Temple, surrounded by fiery beings called seraphim, who call to each other "Holy, holy, holy". A seraph touches his lips with a burning coal, and he answers "Here am I, send me". He advises Ahaz to trust God rather than Assyria and gives him the sign of a child called Immanuel, "God is with us". Later, during Sennacherib's siege of 701 BCE, he assures Hezekiah that Jerusalem will not fall.

His vision of the "end of days" in chapter 2, which also appears in the Book of Micah, foresees nations streaming to Jerusalem to learn God's ways and no longer learning war. Chapter 11 pictures a king from the line of Jesse ruling with justice, when the wolf will live with the lamb. Many scholars think chapters 40 to 66 were added later by prophets during and after the Babylonian exile, often called Second Isaiah, beginning with the words "Comfort, comfort my people".
Isaiah's prophecies.matters:
Isaiah's words appear constantly in Jewish worship. The seraphim's cry forms the Kedushah, a high point of the Amidah prayer. More haftarot (readings from the Prophets) come from Isaiah than from any other book, including the seven readings of comfort after Tisha B'Av.

The Great Isaiah Scroll, found at Qumran in 1947, is about 7.3 metres long and dates to around the second century BCE. It is one of the oldest complete biblical books ever found and is displayed in the Shrine of the Book in Jerusalem. The vision of swords into ploughshares is carved on a wall opposite the United Nations in New York, and Christians read several of his passages as prophecies of Jesus.

Assyria destroys Israel.background:
Assyria, centred in what is now northern Iraq, was the strongest empire the region had yet seen. In 733 to 732 BCE Tiglath-pileser III took Galilee and Gilead from Israel and deported many of their people. Israel was reduced to the area around Samaria and paid heavy tribute.

Its last king, Hoshea, stopped paying and sought help from Egypt, which never came. The Bible says King Shalmaneser V of Assyria arrested him and laid siege to Samaria. The prophets Amos and Hosea had warned for years that Israel's injustice and idolatry would lead to disaster.
Assyria destroys Israel.happened:
2 Kings 17 says the siege of Samaria lasted three years before the city fell. Shalmaneser died around this time, and his successor Sargon II claimed the victory in his inscriptions at his palace at Khorsabad, stating that he carried off 27,290 people. The Bible says the Israelites were settled in Halah, by the Habor river in Gozan and in the cities of the Medes, in what are now northern Mesopotamia and Iran.

In their place, the Assyrians brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Hamath and other places, as was their policy to break national resistance. The Bible links these settlers, mixed with the Israelites who remained, to the origins of the Samaritans, though the Samaritans tell their own history differently. Archaeology shows that Jerusalem grew rapidly in the late eighth century, and many think refugees from the north fled south to Judah.
Assyria destroys Israel.matters:
The fall of Samaria ended the northern kingdom after about two centuries. The exiles gradually merged into the peoples around them and became known as the Ten Lost Tribes. Legends grew up about them, such as a mysterious river called the Sambatyon that rests on the Sabbath, and the ninth-century traveller Eldad ha-Dani, who claimed to come from the tribe of Dan.

Over the centuries many groups have been linked to the lost tribes. The Beta Israel of Ethiopia were recognised by Israel's Sephardi Chief Rabbi in 1973 as descendants of Dan, and the Bnei Menashe of north-east India claim descent from Manasseh. In the 1650s, the Dutch rabbi Menasseh ben Israel cited the lost tribes in his appeal to Oliver Cromwell to readmit Jews to England.

Siege of Jerusalem.background:
After the fall of Samaria, Judah survived as a vassal of Assyria, paying tribute. King Hezekiah, who came to the throne in the late eighth century BCE, carried out religious reforms and, when the Assyrian king Sargon II died in 705 BCE, joined a revolt with other local kingdoms and with Egyptian support.

Knowing Assyria would respond, Hezekiah strengthened Jerusalem. Archaeologists have found the Broad Wall, a massive seven-metre-thick wall built through existing houses, and thousands of storage jar handles stamped with the words "belonging to the king". He also secured the city's water supply, which lay outside the walls at the Gihon Spring.
Siege of Jerusalem.happened:
Hezekiah's workers dug a tunnel from the Gihon Spring to the Pool of Siloam inside the city, starting from both ends at once. An inscription found inside it in 1880 describes the moment the two teams heard each other's voices through the rock and broke through. The original is now in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums.

In 701 BCE Sennacherib invaded. His own annals, on clay prisms such as the Taylor Prism in the British Museum, claim he took 46 walled cities, carried off 200,150 people and shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem "like a bird in a cage". He besieged Lachish, Judah's second city, and his commander, the Rabshakeh, stood outside Jerusalem's walls and called on the people in Hebrew to surrender. Hezekiah paid a huge tribute, and the prophet Isaiah urged him not to give in. 2 Kings 19 says an angel struck down 185,000 Assyrians in one night, and Sennacherib went home. Notably, his annals do not claim to have captured Jerusalem.
Siege of Jerusalem.matters:
Jerusalem's survival, when so many cities fell, strengthened the belief that God protected Zion. Sennacherib's palace at Nineveh had a room lined with carved panels showing the siege and fall of Lachish, discovered by Austen Henry Layard in the 1840s and now in the British Museum. The Assyrian siege ramp can still be seen at Lachish.

Today visitors can wade through Hezekiah's Tunnel in the City of David, a rare chance to walk through a structure described in the Bible. The Greek historian Herodotus told a different story of mice gnawing through the bowstrings of Sennacherib's army, and Lord Byron's poem The Destruction of Sennacherib retold the biblical account.

King Manasseh.background:
Hezekiah had survived the Assyrian invasion of 701 BCE, but Judah was left smaller and weaker, and still a vassal of Assyria. When he died, his son Manasseh came to the throne at the age of twelve, around 697 BCE. Assyria under Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal was at the height of its power.

Manasseh chose to remain loyal. Assyrian records support this: Esarhaddon lists "Manasseh, king of Judah" among 22 western kings who sent building materials to Nineveh, and Ashurbanipal names him among kings who supported his campaign against Egypt.
King Manasseh.happened:
2 Kings 21 describes Manasseh's reign of 55 years as a complete reversal of his father's reforms. He rebuilt the local shrines called "high places", set up altars to Baal, placed an image of the goddess Asherah in the Temple, worshipped the stars, practised sorcery and made his son "pass through the fire", a phrase understood to mean child sacrifice. He is also said to have filled Jerusalem with innocent blood.

The Book of Chronicles adds a different ending. It says Assyrian commanders took Manasseh in chains to Babylon, where he humbled himself and prayed. God restored him to Jerusalem, and he removed the foreign gods. A short prayer attributed to him, the Prayer of Manasseh, appears in some Christian Bibles. The Talmud tells that Isaiah hid from him inside a cedar tree and was killed when the tree was sawn in two. Some archaeologists think this long, peaceful period under Assyria brought Judah economic recovery.
King Manasseh.matters:
The Book of Kings blames Manasseh's sins for the destruction of Jerusalem that came about fifty years after his death, and the prophet Jeremiah says the same. This makes him a key figure in how the Bible explains the exile.

In rabbinic tradition he is a symbol of both great wickedness and the power of teshuvah, meaning repentance or return. The Mishnah lists him among kings who have no share in the World to Come, but one sage disagrees, pointing to his repentance in Chronicles. The Talmud uses his story to teach that the door to repentance is never fully closed.

Josiah's reforms.background:
Manasseh's son Amon ruled for only two years before being assassinated by his own officials around 640 BCE. The people of the land killed the plotters and crowned Amon's eight-year-old son, Josiah. As he grew up, Assyria was declining fast, giving Judah new room to act on its own.

2 Chronicles says that at sixteen Josiah began to seek the God of David, and at twenty he started removing idols. The major turning point came in the eighteenth year of his reign, around 622 BCE.
Josiah's reforms.happened:
While money was being collected to repair the Temple, the High Priest Hilkiah found a "book of the law" and gave it to the royal scribe Shaphan, who read it to the king. Josiah tore his clothes and sent officials to consult Huldah, a prophetess, who said disaster would come on Judah, but not in his lifetime. Josiah gathered the people at the Temple, read the scroll aloud and made a covenant to keep it.

He removed objects made for Baal and Asherah from the Temple, ended the shrines where children were sacrificed in the Valley of Hinnom, and destroyed the local shrines across Judah and the altar at Bethel in the former northern kingdom. Worship was centred in Jerusalem, and he held a Passover there unlike any since the days of the judges. In 609 BCE Josiah was killed at Megiddo trying to stop Pharaoh Necho II, who was marching north to help the Assyrians. Jeremiah lamented him.
Josiah's reforms.matters:
Many scholars believe the scroll was an early form of Deuteronomy, which stresses worship in one chosen place, and that the historical books from Deuteronomy to Kings were shaped in this period. Archaeologists have found a seal impression naming Gemaryahu son of Shaphan, a family known from the Bible, in the City of David.

Josiah's early death was a shock and seemed to end hopes of revival, and within 25 years Jerusalem fell. Yet his reform made the Torah scroll the authority over religious life, an idea that later became central to Judaism. The Huldah Gates on the southern side of the Temple Mount are named after the prophetess, and Megiddo, where he died, gave its name to Armageddon.

First exile to Babylon.background:
After Josiah's death, Egypt controlled Judah briefly, but in 605 BCE the Babylonian crown prince Nebuchadnezzar crushed the Egyptians at Carchemish and became king. Judah's king Jehoiakim submitted to Babylon, but after three years he rebelled, relying on Egypt. The prophet Jeremiah warned that this was a mistake.

Jehoiakim died in late 598 BCE, and his eighteen-year-old son Jehoiachin, also called Jeconiah, became king just as the Babylonian army arrived.
First exile to Babylon.happened:
The Babylonian Chronicle, a clay tablet in the British Museum, records that in his seventh year Nebuchadnezzar marched to the west, besieged "the city of Judah", and on the second day of the month of Adar seized it, captured its king, appointed a king of his choosing and took heavy tribute. This date corresponds to March 597 BCE, one of the most precisely dated events in biblical history.

After a reign of three months, Jehoiachin surrendered with his mother, officials and servants. 2 Kings 24 says 10,000 people were deported, including all the craftsmen and smiths, and the Temple treasures were taken. Jeremiah gives a figure of 3,023. Among the exiles was the priest Ezekiel, who later saw visions by the Chebar canal in Babylonia. Nebuchadnezzar made Jehoiachin's uncle Mattaniah king, renaming him Zedekiah.
First exile to Babylon.matters:
Jehoiachin lived on in Babylon. Clay tablets found near the Ishtar Gate list oil rations for "Jehoiachin, king of Judah" and his sons. 2 Kings ends with his release from prison by Nebuchadnezzar's successor, a small sign of hope. The leaders of Babylonian Jewry, called exilarchs, later claimed descent from him.

Jeremiah wrote to the exiles telling them to build houses, plant gardens and seek the welfare of the city where they lived. This advice helped shape Jewish life in the diaspora. Tablets from a Babylonian town called Al-Yahudu, "Judah town", show Judean families living there for generations. The Jewish community of Babylon, later Iraq, lasted around 2,500 years.

First Temple destroyed.background:
Zedekiah ruled Judah as a vassal of Babylon, but court officials pushed for revolt with Egyptian support. The prophet Jeremiah urged surrender and was imprisoned as a traitor. Around 589 BCE Zedekiah rebelled, and Nebuchadnezzar's army returned.

The siege of Jerusalem began on the tenth day of the month of Tevet. Other towns fell one by one. Pottery letters found at Lachish in 1935, the Lachish Letters, include a message from an officer saying they are watching for the fire signals of Lachish because they can no longer see Azekah, matching Jeremiah's note that these were the last fortified cities left.
First Temple destroyed.happened:
The siege lasted about eighteen months, and famine gripped the city. On the ninth of Tammuz the walls were breached. Zedekiah fled by night towards Jericho but was caught and brought before Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah in Syria. His sons were killed in front of him, then he was blinded and taken to Babylon in chains. A month later Nebuzaradan, commander of the guard, burned the Temple, the palace and the houses of Jerusalem and tore down its walls. Many people were exiled, while the poorest were left to work the land.

Nebuchadnezzar appointed Gedaliah son of Ahikam as governor at Mizpah, but he was murdered by Ishmael son of Nethaniah, a member of the royal family, and many of the remaining Judeans fled to Egypt, taking Jeremiah with them. Archaeologists in the City of David have found burnt buildings, arrowheads and clay seal impressions from this destruction.
First Temple destroyed.matters:
The fall of Jerusalem and the Temple was a catastrophe that forced the Jewish people to find new ways to worship and survive without a land or Temple. Many scholars think this period, during the exile, saw much of the Bible take its final shape.

Tisha B'Av, the ninth of Av, is the main day of mourning, when Jews fast and read the Book of Lamentations, traditionally linked to Jeremiah. The Tenth of Tevet marks the start of the siege, the Seventeenth of Tammuz the breaching of the walls, and the Fast of Gedaliah his murder. Customs such as breaking a glass at weddings recall the destruction. The fate of the Ark remains a mystery, with legends saying it was hidden beneath the Temple Mount or on Mount Nebo.

Cyrus lets the exiles return.background:
In Babylon the exiles kept their identity alive. Prophets such as Ezekiel, and the later chapters of Isaiah, promised a return. Meanwhile the Babylonian Empire weakened after Nebuchadnezzar's death. To the east, Cyrus II, king of a small Persian kingdom, conquered the Medes, then Lydia in Asia Minor.

In 539 BCE Cyrus defeated the Babylonian army and his forces entered Babylon without a fight. The last Babylonian king, Nabonidus, had made enemies of the priests of the god Marduk, and Cyrus presented himself as a liberator.
Cyrus lets the exiles return.happened:
The Book of Ezra opens with a decree from Cyrus in his first year, telling the Jews to go up to Jerusalem and rebuild the house of God, and asking their neighbours to help with silver, gold and goods. The same decree closes 2 Chronicles, the last book of the Hebrew Bible. Cyrus returned the Temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken, which Ezra numbers at 5,400, and gave them to Sheshbazzar, called the prince of Judah.

Ezra 2 lists the returnees family by family and gives a total of 42,360, plus 7,337 servants. They rebuilt the altar and laid the Temple's foundations, but local opposition soon halted the work. The Cyrus Cylinder, found in Babylon in 1879 and now in the British Museum, describes Cyrus returning gods and deported peoples to their homes. It does not mention the Jews, but it matches the policy the Bible describes.
Cyrus lets the exiles return.matters:
Isaiah 45 calls Cyrus God's anointed, using the Hebrew word mashiach, the only time a non-Jew is given this title in the Bible. He is remembered with great respect in Jewish tradition. Most Jews stayed in Babylon, and that community later produced the Babylonian Talmud.

The return began the Second Temple period and the rebuilding of Jewish life in the land, now a small province called Yehud. The Cyrus Cylinder has sometimes been described as an early charter of human rights, though historians see it mainly as royal propaganda. A replica is displayed at the United Nations headquarters in New York.

Second Temple dedicated.background:
The returnees had laid the Temple's foundations soon after 538 BCE, but neighbours, described in Ezra as "adversaries of Judah and Benjamin", hired advisers to frustrate the work and wrote to the Persian kings, and building stopped for about sixteen years. People were struggling with poor harvests and building their own homes.

In 522 BCE Darius I took the Persian throne after a period of turmoil. In his second year, 520 BCE, the prophets Haggai and Zechariah urged the people to resume work, with Zerubbabel, a descendant of King David and the governor, and Joshua son of Jehozadak, the High Priest.
Second Temple dedicated.happened:
Haggai challenged the people for living in panelled houses while God's house lay in ruins. When Tattenai, governor of the Persian province Beyond the River, asked who had given permission to build, the elders cited Cyrus's decree. Ezra 6 says Darius had the archives searched and the decree was found at Ecbatana, so he ordered that the building be paid for from royal taxes.

The Temple was finished on the third of Adar in the sixth year of Darius, in 516 or 515 BCE. At the dedication the people offered 100 bulls, 200 rams, 400 lambs and twelve goats, one for each tribe of Israel, and then celebrated Passover. The Talmud lists five things missing from the Second Temple that the First had, including the Ark and the oracle of the priests, the Urim and Thummim.
Second Temple dedicated.matters:
Haggai promised that the glory of this latter house would be greater than the former, and centuries later King Herod rebuilt it on a huge scale. The Second Temple stood until the Romans destroyed it in 70 CE. The Western Wall in Jerusalem is part of the retaining wall Herod built around its platform.

Zechariah's vision of a golden lampstand, with the message "not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit", is read on the Sabbath of Hanukkah, and the menorah with olive branches from this vision became the emblem of the State of Israel. Historians use the term "Second Temple period" for Jewish history from about 516 BCE to 70 CE.

The story of Esther.background:
After Cyrus's decree, many Jews stayed in Persia and lived across its vast empire. The Book of Esther is set at the court of King Ahasuerus in Shushan, the Hebrew name for Susa, one of the Persian capitals, in today's south-western Iran. Ahasuerus is usually identified with Xerxes I, who ruled from 486 to 465 BCE.

Historians debate whether the story is historical. No Persian source mentions Esther or Mordecai, and the Greek historian Herodotus names Xerxes' queen as Amestris. Many scholars see it as a historical novel, though a Persian official called Marduka appears in tablets from Persepolis.
The story of Esther.happened:
The book begins with a six-month feast, after which Queen Vashti refuses the king's summons and is removed. Young women are gathered, and the king chooses Esther, an orphan also called Hadassah, raised by her cousin Mordecai of the tribe of Benjamin. Mordecai uncovers a plot by two guards to kill the king. When Mordecai refuses to bow to the royal minister Haman, Haman persuades the king to issue a decree to destroy all Jews. He casts lots, called pur, and they fall on the 13th of Adar.

Mordecai urges Esther to act, suggesting she may have become queen for this very moment. She asks the Jews of Shushan to fast for three days, then approaches the king and invites him and Haman to two banquets. The sleepless king hears the court records read and honours Mordecai. At the second banquet Esther reveals Haman's plot, and Haman is hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai. A new decree allows the Jews to defend themselves, and on the 13th of Adar they defeat their enemies.
The story of Esther.matters:
Purim, named after the lots, is celebrated on the 14th of Adar, and on the 15th in walled cities such as Jerusalem, called Shushan Purim. Jews hear the Megillah read in the evening and morning, send gifts of food to friends, give gifts to the poor and hold a festive meal. The Fast of Esther is held the day before.

The book is unusual because God's name never appears in it, which the rabbis saw as a lesson that God works in hidden ways. Esther has become a symbol of courage, and a traditional tomb of Esther and Mordecai stands in Hamadan, Iran.

Ezra reads the Torah.background:
Decades after the Second Temple was dedicated, Judah was a small, poor Persian province. Many Jews had married into neighbouring peoples, and knowledge of the Torah was weak. In Babylon, meanwhile, Jewish scholars had kept the tradition alive.

Ezra was a priest descended from Aaron and described as a scribe skilled in the law of Moses. The Bible says he travelled in the seventh year of King Artaxerxes. If this was Artaxerxes I, the date is 458 BCE, but some historians think it was Artaxerxes II, which would place Ezra in 398 BCE, after Nehemiah. The order of the two leaders is still debated.
Ezra reads the Torah.happened:
Ezra 7 preserves a letter from the king allowing Ezra to lead any Jews who wished to go, to bring gifts for the Temple and to appoint judges who knew the law. He set out with about 1,500 men and their families, plus Levites, and the journey took four months. On arrival he was distressed to find many marriages with foreign women, and he led the community in a painful decision to end them.

Nehemiah 8 describes the great reading. On the first day of the seventh month, the day now kept as Rosh Hashanah, the people gathered in the square before the Water Gate. Ezra stood on a wooden platform and read from the Torah from first light until midday, while Levites helped the people understand. Some interpret this as translation into Aramaic, the everyday language. The people wept, but were told to celebrate, and they went on to keep Sukkot by living in booths, as the Torah commands.
Ezra reads the Torah.matters:
Jewish tradition sees Ezra as a second Moses. The Talmud says that if Moses had not come first, the Torah could have been given through Ezra. It credits him with ten enactments, including the reading of the Torah in synagogue on Monday and Thursday mornings and on Sabbath afternoons, customs still kept today. It also says he introduced the square Hebrew script used in Torah scrolls.

The public reading of the Torah, with explanation, became the model for synagogue worship and Jewish learning. The practice of translating the reading led to the Aramaic translations called Targum. A shrine called Ezra's Tomb, on the Tigris in southern Iraq, was long a place of Jewish pilgrimage.

Nehemiah rebuilds the walls.background:
Nearly a century after the first return, Jerusalem was still thinly populated and its walls were in ruins, leaving it open to raids. Nehemiah was a Jew serving at the Persian court in Susa as cupbearer to King Artaxerxes I, a trusted post that gave him close access to the king.

The Book of Nehemiah, much of it written in the first person, says that in the month of Kislev in the king's twentieth year, about 445 BCE, his brother Hanani arrived with news of Jerusalem's state. Nehemiah wept, fasted and prayed.
Nehemiah rebuilds the walls.happened:
Some months later the king noticed Nehemiah's sad face and asked what he wanted. Nehemiah asked to be sent to rebuild the city, and received letters for safe passage and for timber from the royal forest. In Jerusalem he inspected the walls secretly by night, then called the people to build. Chapter 3 lists the families, priests, goldsmiths and perfumers who each repaired a section.

Local leaders opposed him: Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite and Geshem the Arab mocked the work and plotted attacks. Nehemiah had half the men work while the other half stood guard, and the builders wore swords at their sides. The wall was finished on the 25th of Elul after 52 days. He also forced the wealthy to cancel debts and return land taken from the poor, refused the governor's food allowance, and during a second term shut the city gates on the Sabbath to stop traders from selling.
Nehemiah rebuilds the walls.matters:
Nehemiah gave Jerusalem security and new life, and he moved families into the city to repopulate it. Together with Ezra he helped shape a community built around the Torah, Sabbath and Temple. In the Hebrew Bible, Ezra and Nehemiah were originally one book.

Sanballat is mentioned in the Elephantine papyri, letters from a Jewish garrison in Egypt in 407 BCE that refer to his sons and call him governor of Samaria, confirming him as a real figure. In 2007 Eilat Mazar suggested she had found part of Nehemiah's wall in the City of David, though this is debated. The image of building with a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other has been used in modern Israel as a symbol of determination.

Men of the Great Assembly.background:
The Hebrew Bible's last prophets, Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi, were active in the early Persian period. The Book of Malachi ends with a call to remember the Torah of Moses and the promise that God will send Elijah. Jewish tradition holds that prophecy ended with them.

Leadership then passed to sages and scribes who taught and interpreted the Torah. The Mishnah, compiled around 200 CE, opens its tractate Pirkei Avot, "Ethics of the Fathers", by tracing a chain of tradition: Moses received the Torah at Sinai and passed it to Joshua, Joshua to the elders, the elders to the prophets, and the prophets to the Men of the Great Assembly.
Men of the Great Assembly.happened:
In Hebrew they are the Anshei Knesset HaGedolah. The Talmud says the assembly had 120 members, and tradition includes Ezra, Nehemiah, Mordecai and the last prophets among them. The Mishnah records three teachings in their name: be careful in judgement, raise up many students, and make a fence around the Torah, meaning extra safeguards to avoid breaking its laws.

The Talmud credits them with writing down or editing several biblical books, including Ezekiel, the Twelve Minor Prophets, Daniel and Esther, and with forming the Amidah, the central standing prayer of eighteen blessings, as well as the blessings of Kiddush and Havdalah. Historians have little outside evidence about the assembly. Some think it was not a permanent council but a memory of gatherings like the one in Nehemiah 8 to 10, when the people signed a covenant to keep the Torah.
Men of the Great Assembly.matters:
The Great Assembly stands at the start of rabbinic Judaism, linking the prophets to the later sages of the Mishnah and Talmud. Its teaching to raise up many students reflects the central Jewish value of learning passed from teacher to student across generations.

Much of the structure of Jewish prayer still used today is traced to them, especially the Amidah, recited three times a day. Israel's parliament, the Knesset, takes its name from the Great Assembly, and its 120 members match the traditional number of the assembly's sages.

Alexander the Great.background:
For about two centuries Judea was a quiet province of the Persian Empire, governed by its High Priests with Persian approval. In 334 BCE the young king Alexander of Macedon crossed into Asia. He defeated the Persian king Darius III at the Battle of Issus in 333 BCE and marched south along the coast.

Tyre resisted him for seven months and Gaza for two, and both were destroyed. Judea and Samaria passed to Alexander with little fighting. He went on to Egypt, where he founded Alexandria, and then beat Darius again at Gaugamela in 331 BCE.
Alexander the Great.happened:
Josephus, in his Jewish Antiquities, tells a famous story. The High Priest Jaddua led a procession of priests in white to meet Alexander outside Jerusalem. To everyone's surprise Alexander bowed before him, saying he had seen this man in a dream. He then offered sacrifices in the Temple, was shown the Book of Daniel, and granted the Jews the right to live by their laws. The Talmud tells a similar story about Simon the Just, adding that the Samaritans had asked permission to destroy the Temple. Historians doubt the details, but the legends show how Jews remembered Alexander kindly.

In Samaria, people rebelled and burned Alexander's governor. Papyri found in 1962 in a cave at Wadi Daliyeh, near Jericho, belonged to Samaritan refugees who seem to have fled there and been killed. Alexander died in Babylon in 323 BCE at the age of 32.
Alexander the Great.matters:
Alexander's conquest began the Hellenistic age, when Greek culture spread across the Near East. Greek became the common language of trade and government, and Greek-style cities, theatres and gymnasiums appeared. Jews met Greek philosophy and ideas, and Greek words entered Hebrew, such as sanhedrin for a council.

The tension between Jewish tradition and Greek culture led eventually to the Maccabean revolt and the festival of Hanukkah. Many Jewish interpreters link the Book of Daniel's vision of a goat with a great horn to Alexander. Legend says the name Alexander became popular among Jews in his honour, and it remains a common Jewish name.

Ptolemy takes Jerusalem.background:
When Alexander died in 323 BCE with no adult heir, his generals, known as the Diadochi or "successors", divided and fought over his empire for decades. Ptolemy son of Lagus took Egypt and founded a dynasty that ruled there until Cleopatra. Seleucus took Babylonia and later Syria.

Judea lay on the route between Egypt and Syria in a region the Greeks called Coele-Syria, and it changed hands several times. The exact date of Ptolemy's first capture of Jerusalem is uncertain, with historians suggesting 320, 312 or 302 BCE.
Ptolemy takes Jerusalem.happened:
Josephus, quoting the Greek writer Agatharchides of Cnidus, says Ptolemy entered Jerusalem on the Sabbath, pretending to come to offer sacrifice, and took it without a fight because the Jews would not take up arms on their holy day. Agatharchides mocked them for this. Josephus adds that Ptolemy took many captives from Judea and Samaria to Egypt and settled them there, using some as soldiers in his garrisons.

After the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE, Ptolemy held Judea firmly. The Ptolemies ran a highly organised system of taxation, and papyri belonging to an official named Zenon, from around 259 BCE, describe his travels through the region and dealings with local figures, including a Jewish leader called Tobias. The High Priest remained the leader of the Jews in Jerusalem.
Ptolemy takes Jerusalem.matters:
Under the Ptolemies, Alexandria became home to one of the largest Jewish communities in the world, with its own quarter, synagogues and leaders. Its Greek-speaking Jews produced the Septuagint and later the philosopher Philo. Judea remained under Ptolemaic rule for about a century until the Seleucids took it in 200 BCE.

The question of fighting on the Sabbath came back during the Maccabean revolt, when about a thousand Jews were killed rather than defend themselves on the holy day. Their leader Mattathias then ruled that Jews may fight to defend their lives on the Sabbath. This became part of the principle of pikuach nefesh, that saving a life overrides almost every other commandment.

Simon the Just.background:
Under Persian and then Greek rule, the High Priest was the leading figure in Jerusalem, responsible for the Temple and often for dealings with foreign rulers. The office passed down within one priestly family, the descendants of Zadok.
