Two High Priests named Simon are known from this era, and scholars debate which is the famous Simon the Just, in Hebrew Shimon HaTzaddik. Josephus calls Simon I, around 300 BCE, "the Just". But many historians think the title belongs to Simon II, around 200 BCE, who is praised in the Book of Ben Sira for repairing and fortifying the Temple.
Simon the Just.happened:
The Mishnah in Pirkei Avot calls Simon one of the last survivors of the Great Assembly and records his saying about the three things on which the world stands. His student Antigonus of Socho continued the chain of tradition. Ben Sira, chapter 50, gives a vivid picture of Simon in his priestly robes, coming out from the sanctuary on a holy day, shining like the morning star.

The Talmud says that during Simon's forty years as High Priest, special signs showed God's favour: on Yom Kippur the lot for God always came up in his right hand, the red thread tied in the Temple turned white as a sign of forgiveness, and the western lamp of the menorah never went out. It also says that in his last year he told the people he would die, because each Yom Kippur an old man dressed in white had gone with him into the Holy of Holies, but that year the man was dressed in black.
Simon the Just.matters:
Simon the Just is remembered as the model of a righteous priest, and his teaching that the world rests on Torah, worship and kindness is one of the best-known lines in Jewish ethics. It is studied in Pirkei Avot, which many Jews read on summer Sabbath afternoons.

His traditional tomb lies in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood of Jerusalem. Scholars think the burial cave itself dates from Roman times, but it has long been a place of Jewish pilgrimage, especially on Lag BaOmer, when some families bring young boys for their first haircut. In recent years the surrounding neighbourhood has become the subject of legal and political disputes.

The Septuagint.background:
After Alexander's conquests, many Jews lived in Egypt, especially in Alexandria. Within a few generations most of them spoke Greek as their main language and could no longer read Hebrew easily. Alexandria was also home to the great Library, founded by the Ptolemies to gather the world's knowledge.

A Greek translation of the Torah met the needs of Jews who wanted to read and hear it in synagogue, and it also made Jewish scripture available to the wider Greek-speaking world.
The Septuagint.happened:
The main account comes from the Letter of Aristeas, a Greek work probably written in the second century BCE. It says that Demetrius of Phalerum, head of the Library, asked King Ptolemy II Philadelphus to obtain the Jewish law. The king wrote to the High Priest Eleazar in Jerusalem, who sent 72 elders, six from each tribe. They worked on the island of Pharos and finished in 72 days. The philosopher Philo later added that the translations came out identical, and said the Jews of Alexandria held a yearly festival on Pharos to celebrate. The Talmud tells a similar story, in which the elders worked in separate rooms and were all guided to make the same small changes.

Historians agree that the Torah was translated in Alexandria in the third century BCE, and that the other books of the Bible were translated over the following two centuries by various hands.
The Septuagint.matters:
The name Septuagint, from the Latin for seventy, is often shortened to LXX. It was used by Philo, Josephus and the writers of the New Testament, and became the Bible of the early Christian church. It includes books not in the Hebrew Bible, such as Maccabees, Judith and Tobit. The Eastern Orthodox churches still use it as their Old Testament.

Once Christians adopted it, many Jews turned to newer Greek translations such as that of Aquila. Some later rabbinic writings even compared the day of the translation to the day of the golden calf. For scholars, the Septuagint is a vital witness to early forms of the Hebrew text, and some Dead Sea Scrolls agree with it where it differs from the later standard Hebrew text.

Seleucids take Judea.background:
For a century the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Syria fought a series of conflicts called the Syrian Wars over Coele-Syria, the region that included Judea. Antiochus III, known as "the Great", became Seleucid king in 222 BCE and set out to restore his empire. His first attempt to take the region ended in defeat at the Battle of Raphia in 217 BCE.

When the Egyptian king Ptolemy IV died in 204 BCE, leaving a young child as heir, Antiochus saw his chance and invaded again.
Seleucids take Judea.happened:
Around 200 BCE Antiochus defeated the Ptolemaic general Scopas at Panium, a site near the springs of the Jordan at the foot of Mount Hermon, later called Banias. Josephus says the Jews of Jerusalem welcomed Antiochus and helped expel the Egyptian garrison from the citadel.

Josephus preserves a letter in which Antiochus rewarded them. He granted supplies for the Temple sacrifices, timber for repairs, and freedom from certain taxes for the council of elders, the priests and the Temple scribes. He freed Jerusalem's residents from taxes for three years and allowed the Jews to live by their ancestral laws. Another decree banned foreigners from entering the Temple courts. An inscription found near Beit She'an, known as the Hefzibah inscription, records letters between Antiochus and a local governor from this time.
Seleucids take Judea.matters:
Antiochus's generosity did not last for his successors. In 190 BCE he was defeated by Rome at Magnesia, and the peace treaty forced the Seleucids to pay a huge sum to Rome. Short of money, his son Seleucus IV sent his minister Heliodorus to seize the Temple treasury in Jerusalem, according to 2 Maccabees, which says he was stopped by a vision.

The financial pressure and political divisions of this period set the scene for the reign of Antiochus IV, the Maccabean revolt and Hanukkah. The Book of Daniel's account of wars between the "king of the north" and the "king of the south" is widely understood to describe the Seleucids and Ptolemies.

Hellenism comes to Jerusalem.background:
Greek culture had been spreading in the region for 150 years, and many Jews, especially among the wealthy and the priesthood, admired its learning, sport and style. Others saw it as a threat to Jewish law and identity. In 175 BCE Antiochus IV, who called himself Epiphanes, "god made manifest", became Seleucid king. He needed money to pay Rome and to fund his wars.

The High Priest at the time was Onias III, a traditional leader. His brother, whose Hebrew name was Joshua but who used the Greek name Jason, saw an opportunity.
Hellenism comes to Jerusalem.happened:
According to 2 Maccabees, Jason offered Antiochus 440 talents of silver to be made High Priest, plus 150 more for permission to build a gymnasium and to enrol the people of Jerusalem as citizens of Antioch. Onias was pushed out. The gymnasium was built just below the Temple Mount, and young men wore the Greek broad-brimmed hat. 2 Maccabees complains that priests left their duties at the altar to watch the discus throwing. 1 Maccabees says some men had surgery to hide their circumcision, since athletes exercised naked.

Jason's rule did not last. Around 172 BCE a man named Menelaus outbid him for the high priesthood by 300 talents, and Onias III was murdered near Antioch. Fighting broke out in Jerusalem, and in 168 to 167 BCE Antiochus plundered the Temple, banned Sabbath, circumcision and Torah study, and set up a pagan altar in the Temple.
Hellenism comes to Jerusalem.matters:
These events are known mainly from 1 and 2 Maccabees, which are not part of the Hebrew Bible but are included in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, and from Josephus. Historians debate how far the crisis was driven by the king and how far by a struggle between Jewish factions.

The divisions led to the revolt of the priest Mattathias and his sons, the Maccabees, the rededication of the Temple and the festival of Hanukkah. The story has made Hellenism a byword in Jewish thought for the pull of a surrounding culture, and the question of how to engage with that culture while staying faithful remains part of Jewish life today.

Maccabean revolt.background:
After Alexander the Great died, his generals split his empire. Judea was first ruled by the Ptolemies of Egypt, then from about 200 BCE by the Seleucid kings based in Syria. Greek culture, or Hellenism, spread across the region, and some wealthy Jews in Jerusalem embraced it eagerly. The office of High Priest was even bought and sold: first Jason and then Menelaus paid the king for the post.

Antiochus IV, who called himself Epiphanes, 'god made manifest', was humiliated in 168 BCE when Rome forced him to abandon his invasion of Egypt. Unrest in Jerusalem followed, and the king answered with force. According to the First Book of Maccabees, in 167 BCE he outlawed the core practices of Judaism and had an altar to Zeus set up in the Temple, which the book calls the 'abomination of desolation'.
Maccabean revolt.happened:
Royal officers went from town to town ordering Jews to sacrifice to the Greek gods. At Modi'in, in the hills north-west of Jerusalem, the priest Mattathias refused. When another Jew stepped forward to obey, Mattathias killed him and the king's officer, tore down the altar and fled with his sons John, Simon, Judah, Eleazar and Jonathan. Others who wished to keep the Torah joined them, including a pious group called the Hasideans.

Early on, a group of refugees was attacked on the Sabbath and died without resisting. Mattathias and his followers then decided that Jews could defend themselves on the Sabbath. When Mattathias died around 166 BCE, Judah took command. Using surprise and knowledge of the hills, he defeated a string of larger Seleucid forces, including one near Emmaus.
Maccabean revolt.matters:
The revolt is one of the earliest known struggles for religious freedom. It was not only a war against a foreign king but also a conflict among Jews over how far to adopt Greek ways. The Books of Maccabees, preserved in Greek and included in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles though not in the Hebrew Bible, tell the story, along with the historian Josephus.

The revolt led directly to the festival of Hanukkah. Modi'in is today a modern Israeli city, and each Hanukkah a torch is traditionally lit there and carried to other parts of the country. The name Maccabee still stands for Jewish courage, from sports clubs to the Maccabiah Games.

Temple rededicated.background:
In about two years of fighting, Judah Maccabee's guerrilla army had beaten several Seleucid armies. The regent Lysias, who ran the empire while Antiochus IV campaigned in the east, led a large force towards Judea but was turned back near Beth Zur, south of Jerusalem. This opened the road to the city.

The Temple had stood defiled since late 167 BCE. Weeds grew in the courtyards, the gates had been burned, and pagan sacrifices had been offered on the altar. A Seleucid garrison still held the Acra, a fortress overlooking the Temple Mount.
Temple rededicated.happened:
Judah posted soldiers to hold off the Acra garrison while chosen priests cleaned the sanctuary. According to the First Book of Maccabees, they took apart the polluted altar and stored its stones until a prophet could say what to do with them, then built a new altar from uncut stones. They made new holy vessels, including the menorah, the incense altar and the table for the showbread.

On the 25th of the Hebrew month of Kislev, in 164 BCE, exactly three years after the desecration, sacrifices were offered again. The people celebrated for eight days and decided to mark the anniversary every year. The Second Book of Maccabees links the eight days to Sukkot, the autumn festival they had been unable to keep. The story of the single jar of oil lasting eight days is first recorded centuries later in the Babylonian Talmud (Shabbat 21b).
Temple rededicated.matters:
Hanukkah is now one of the best-known Jewish festivals. Each night a candle is added to the hanukkiah, an eight-branched lamp with an extra 'helper' candle, called the shamash. Families place it where it can be seen from outside to 'publicise the miracle'. A prayer called Al HaNissim, 'for the miracles', is added to daily prayers and grace after meals, and foods fried in oil, such as latkes and doughnuts, recall the oil.

The rededication was not the end of the war. Fighting went on for another twenty years before full independence. But it restored Temple worship and made the Hasmonean family the leaders of the nation, setting the stage for the only independent Jewish kingdom between the Babylonian exile and modern times.

Treaty with Rome.background:
After Antiochus IV died in 164 BCE, the Seleucid throne passed through disputes and rivals. In 161 BCE the new king, Demetrius I, sent the general Nicanor to crush the Maccabees. Judah defeated and killed him at Adasa, near Beth Horon, on the 13th of Adar. The day was celebrated for a time as 'Nicanor's Day'.

Rome was by then the rising power of the Mediterranean. It had beaten the Seleucids at Magnesia in 190 BCE and imposed a harsh peace at Apamea in 188 BCE. Rome was happy to support smaller peoples who could weaken its rivals, and Judah knew the Seleucids would soon return in force.
Treaty with Rome.happened:
According to the eighth chapter of the First Book of Maccabees, Judah sent two envoys, Eupolemus son of John and Jason son of Eleazar, on the long journey to Rome. The book describes the Romans admiringly as powerful, loyal to their friends and governed by a council rather than a king.

The Senate agreed to a treaty of friendship and alliance. The text, as quoted in 1 Maccabees, said that each side would help the other if attacked and would not supply the enemy. A copy was reportedly written on bronze tablets and sent to Jerusalem. The Senate is also said to have warned Demetrius to stop oppressing the Jews. Some historians question parts of the account, but most accept that a real diplomatic contact took place. Eupolemus may be the same man known as an early Jewish historian who wrote in Greek.
Treaty with Rome.matters:
The treaty was the first formal link between the Jewish people and Rome. In practice it gave Judah no direct help: Roman legions never came to his aid, and he fell in battle the following year. His brothers Jonathan and Simon renewed the alliance, and it gave the Hasmoneans international standing.

With hindsight, the treaty has an ironic ring. Rome, invited in as a distant protector, became the power that ended Jewish independence when Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BCE, and later destroyed the Temple in 70 CE. Historians often point to it as a lesson in how small states seek protection from great powers, sometimes at a high cost.

Judah Maccabee falls.background:
Judah's victory over Nicanor at Adasa in 161 BCE angered King Demetrius I. He sent his experienced general Bacchides back to Judea with a much larger army. The First Book of Maccabees gives the Seleucid force as 20,000 foot soldiers and 2,000 cavalry.

Judah's position was weaker than it had been. Some of the pious Hasideans had already made peace with the new High Priest, Alcimus, whom the king had appointed. One of Judah's brothers, Eleazar, had been killed a few years earlier at Beth Zechariah, crushed beneath a war elephant he attacked.
Judah Maccabee falls.happened:
Judah camped at Elasa, north of Jerusalem, with about 3,000 men. When they saw the size of the enemy, most deserted, leaving him with around 800, according to 1 Maccabees. His remaining men urged him to withdraw and fight another day. The book has him reply that if their time had come, they should die bravely for their people and leave no stain on their honour.

The battle lasted from morning to evening. Judah attacked the stronger right wing of the Seleucid army, where Bacchides stood, and drove it back, but the left wing closed in behind him. He was killed and his army scattered. His brothers Jonathan and Simon recovered his body and buried him in the family tomb at Modi'in. The book records that all Israel mourned him for many days, comparing him to the heroes of old.
Judah Maccabee falls.matters:
Judah's death seemed for a moment to end the revolt. Bacchides placed garrisons across Judea and the Hellenising party regained power. The surviving fighters chose Jonathan as their leader, and he began a long and patient struggle, mixing warfare with diplomacy, which would eventually achieve far more than battle alone.

Judah became one of the great heroes of Jewish memory. In the modern era he inspired the Zionist movement, sports organisations such as Maccabi and the Maccabiah Games, first held in 1932, as well as Handel's oratorio Judas Maccabaeus of 1747. His readiness to fight against huge odds remains central to how the Hanukkah story is told.

Jonathan becomes High Priest.background:
After Judah's death in 160 BCE, Jonathan led the remaining rebels from the Judean wilderness. Another brother, John, was killed by a desert tribe soon after. For several years Jonathan fought small actions and then made a truce with the general Bacchides, settling at Michmash, north of Jerusalem, where he quietly built up his influence.

The Seleucid kingdom was now torn by rival claims. In 152 BCE a young man named Alexander Balas, claiming to be a son of Antiochus IV, challenged King Demetrius I for the throne. Both men needed allies, and Jonathan was in a position to choose.
Jonathan becomes High Priest.happened:
Demetrius wrote first, allowing Jonathan to raise an army and freeing hostages held in the Acra. Jonathan used this to move into Jerusalem and repair its walls. Alexander Balas then offered more. According to the First Book of Maccabees, he named Jonathan High Priest and a 'Friend of the King', sending him a purple robe and a golden crown. At the festival of Sukkot in 152 BCE, Jonathan put on the sacred vestments.

Jonathan backed Balas, who won the throne. Over the next decade he switched sides skilfully as new rivals appeared, gaining land and titles. In 143 BCE the general Diodotus Tryphon, who feared Jonathan's power, invited him to Ptolemais (Acre) with a small escort. There he was seized, his men were killed, and he was later murdered. His brother Simon buried him at Modi'in.
Jonathan becomes High Priest.matters:
Jonathan's appointment changed the Jewish priesthood. For centuries the High Priests had come from the family of Zadok. The Hasmoneans were priests, but not of that line. Some Jews never accepted them. Many scholars think the 'Wicked Priest' attacked in the Dead Sea Scrolls refers to Jonathan or a later Hasmonean, though this is debated. Onias IV, heir of the old line, had already gone to Egypt and built a rival temple at Leontopolis.

By joining the High Priesthood with military and political leadership, Jonathan set the pattern for Hasmonean rule for the next century. Josephus names his era as the time when the Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes first appear, which suggests that this concentration of power helped split Jewish society into rival schools of thought.

Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes.background:
The Maccabean revolt and the rise of the Hasmoneans raised hard questions. Who should be High Priest? How should the Torah be applied to daily life? How far should Jews adopt Greek ways? Different answers produced distinct groups. Josephus, writing in the first century CE, describes three Jewish 'philosophies', and he first mentions them in his account of Jonathan's time, around 150 BCE.

Our knowledge comes mainly from Josephus, Philo of Alexandria, the Roman writer Pliny the Elder, the New Testament, rabbinic literature and, since 1947, the Dead Sea Scrolls. Each source has its own point of view, so historians piece the picture together carefully.
Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes.happened:
The Pharisees, whose name probably means 'separated ones', believed that God gave Moses an Oral Law alongside the written Torah, explaining how to keep it. They believed in the resurrection of the dead and in reward and punishment after death, and they balanced fate with free will. Josephus says they had great influence with ordinary people.

The Sadducees, whose name probably comes from Zadok, the ancient High Priest, were linked to the priestly and wealthy elite. They rejected the Pharisees' oral traditions and did not believe in resurrection. The Essenes lived in close communities, shared property, practised strict purity and, according to Pliny, had a settlement on the western shore of the Dead Sea. Many scholars link them to Qumran. Josephus says John Hyrcanus broke with the Pharisees and favoured the Sadducees, and the rivalry shaped Hasmonean politics.
Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes.matters:
These groups shaped the future of Judaism. The Sadducees, tied to the Temple, faded after its destruction in 70 CE. The Essenes also disappeared, though their library survived as the Dead Sea Scrolls. The Pharisees' approach, with its focus on study, prayer and the Oral Law, became the basis of rabbinic Judaism, which produced the Mishnah and the Talmud.

The groups also appear in the New Testament, where the Pharisees are often shown in conflict with Jesus. Modern scholars stress that this picture is coloured by later disputes. Today almost all forms of Judaism trace their roots, directly or indirectly, to the Pharisaic tradition.

Independence under Simon.background:
After Jonathan was taken prisoner by Tryphon in 143 BCE, the people turned to Simon, the last of Mattathias's five sons. He was older and known for good judgement. Tryphon, having killed Jonathan, went on to murder the young king Antiochus VI and seize the throne himself.

Simon sided with Tryphon's rival, Demetrius II. In return, Demetrius granted Judea freedom from tribute and taxes. According to the First Book of Maccabees, this happened in the year 170 of the Seleucid era, which is 142 BCE, and the book describes it as the year the yoke of the nations was lifted from Israel.
Independence under Simon.happened:
Simon captured the coastal town of Gezer and secured the port of Joppa (Jaffa), giving Judea access to the sea. In 141 BCE, after a long siege, the Seleucid garrison in the Acra surrendered. Simon entered it with praise, music and palm branches, and the day was later remembered as a festival.

In 140 BCE a great assembly of priests, people and elders met in Jerusalem. They confirmed Simon as High Priest, military commander and ethnarch, or leader of the nation, and said this should last until a true prophet arose. The decree was carved on bronze tablets set up on Mount Zion. Rome renewed its alliance with him. In 134 BCE Simon and two of his sons were murdered at a banquet in the fortress of Dok near Jericho by his son-in-law Ptolemy son of Abubus, who hoped to take power.
Independence under Simon.matters:
Under Simon, Judea became a truly independent state for the first time since the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BCE. The First Book of Maccabees ends with a hymn-like picture of his rule, with old men sitting in the streets and each person under their own vine and fig tree, echoing the prophets.

The assembly's decree also created a hereditary Hasmonean dynasty, combining the religious and political leadership of the nation in one family. Megillat Taanit, an ancient list of days on which fasting was forbidden, includes days linked to these victories, a sign of how they were celebrated. Simon's line ruled Judea until the Roman conquest.

John Hyrcanus expands the kingdom.background:
When Simon was murdered in 134 BCE, his son-in-law Ptolemy also tried to kill Simon's son John, who was based at Gezer. John was warned in time, reached Jerusalem first and was accepted as ruler and High Priest. He is known by the Greek name Hyrcanus.

His early years were difficult. The Seleucid king Antiochus VII Sidetes besieged Jerusalem, and Hyrcanus had to agree to terms, paying money and handing over hostages. Josephus reports that he took silver from the tomb of King David to pay. In 129 BCE Antiochus VII was killed fighting the Parthians, and Seleucid power collapsed for good.
John Hyrcanus expands the kingdom.happened:
Hyrcanus used the Seleucid weakness to expand in every direction. East of the Jordan he took Medeba. To the north he captured Shechem and destroyed the Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim, which archaeologists date to around 111 to 110 BCE. His sons later besieged and destroyed the city of Samaria. To the south he conquered Idumea, the land of the Edomites, including the towns of Adora and Marisa (Maresha), and, according to Josephus, required its people to be circumcised and follow Jewish law if they wished to stay.

He hired foreign soldiers and minted coins with the Hebrew words 'Yehohanan the High Priest and the council of the Jews'. Josephus says that late in his reign he broke with the Pharisees after one of them suggested he give up the High Priesthood, and he turned to the Sadducees instead. He ruled for about thirty years and died in 104 BCE.
John Hyrcanus expands the kingdom.matters:
Hyrcanus turned a small temple state into a regional power. Josephus writes that he was considered worthy of three great gifts: rule of the nation, the High Priesthood and prophecy. His conquests also left lasting legacies. The forced conversion of the Idumeans brought them into the Jewish people, and one Idumean family later produced Herod the Great.

The destruction of the Mount Gerizim temple deepened the long split between Jews and Samaritans, which is still felt in the New Testament story of the 'Good Samaritan'. A small Samaritan community survives today on Mount Gerizim near Nablus and still offers its Passover sacrifice there. Excavations at Maresha and Gerizim have uncovered evidence of these campaigns.

Aristobulus takes the crown.background:
John Hyrcanus had ruled as High Priest and leader, but not as king. According to Josephus, he left the government to his wife and the High Priesthood to his eldest son, Judah Aristobulus, who used the Greek name Aristobulus. His coins call him by his Hebrew name, Yehudah the High Priest.

In the Hellenistic world, kingship was the normal form of rule, and neighbouring rulers wore a royal diadem. The Hasmoneans had grown rich and powerful, and some in the family wanted the title to match.
Aristobulus takes the crown.happened:
Josephus says Aristobulus was the first of his family to put a diadem on his head, about 481 years after the return from Babylon by his reckoning. To secure power he imprisoned his mother and, according to Josephus, let her starve to death in prison. He also jailed three of his brothers. His favourite brother, Antigonus, shared power at first, but palace enemies turned Aristobulus against him, and Antigonus was killed by guards.

Aristobulus was nicknamed 'Philhellene', meaning lover of the Greeks. In his short reign he campaigned against the Itureans in the north, bringing much of the Galilee under Judean control and, says Josephus, requiring the inhabitants to accept circumcision and Jewish law. He fell ill and died in 103 BCE after only about a year on the throne, reportedly tormented by guilt over his brother's death.
Aristobulus takes the crown.matters:
By taking the title of king, Aristobulus changed the nature of the Hasmonean state. In Jewish tradition, kingship belonged to the house of David from the tribe of Judah, while the priests came from the tribe of Levi. Joining the two in one family troubled many. The Psalms of Solomon, written in the first century BCE, criticise rulers who seized the throne of David.

Later Jewish thinkers, such as the medieval scholar Nachmanides, suggested that the Hasmoneans' downfall came partly because priests had taken the crown. The bringing of the Galilee into the Jewish state had long-term effects: within two centuries it would become the centre of Jewish life and learning.

Alexander Jannaeus's civil war.background:
When Aristobulus I died in 103 BCE, his widow, Salome Alexandra, freed his brothers from prison. According to Josephus, she married one of them, Alexander Jannaeus, who became king and High Priest. His Hebrew name was Yehonatan, and his coins bear both 'Yehonatan the king' in Hebrew and 'King Alexander' in Greek.

Jannaeus spent much of his reign at war, attacking the coastal cities, the Nabataeans and the regions east of the Jordan. He destroyed Gaza around 96 BCE. His wars were costly, and his style of rule, much like other Hellenistic kings, angered the Pharisees and many ordinary people.
Alexander Jannaeus's civil war.happened:
At Sukkot, the High Priest poured a water offering on the altar. Josephus says that when Jannaeus stood at the altar, the crowd pelted him with citrons, the etrog fruit carried at the festival, and insulted him. The Talmud tells a similar story about a Sadducee priest who poured the water on his feet instead of the altar. Josephus says Jannaeus's soldiers killed about 6,000 people.

A civil war followed, lasting about six years. The rebels invited the Seleucid king Demetrius III, who defeated Jannaeus near Shechem around 88 BCE. Many Jews then switched back to Jannaeus, fearing foreign rule. Once he regained control, Josephus says, he crucified 800 opponents in Jerusalem while he feasted, and had their wives and children killed before their eyes. Thousands of others fled the country.
Alexander Jannaeus's civil war.matters:
The war shows how deeply the Hasmonean kingdom was divided between rulers and religious leaders. A Dead Sea Scroll known as the Pesher Nahum speaks of a 'Lion of Wrath' who hanged men alive and mentions a king named Demetrius. Most scholars connect it to these events, making it a rare case where the scrolls refer to known history.

Despite the bloodshed, Jannaeus expanded the kingdom to its greatest size, including most of the coast, the Golan and lands across the Jordan. His small bronze coins, decorated with an anchor and a star, are among the most common finds in Israel today. Josephus says that on his deathbed in 76 BCE he advised his wife to make peace with the Pharisees.

Queen Salome Alexandra.background:
Alexander Jannaeus died in 76 BCE while besieging a fortress east of the Jordan. He left the throne not to one of his two sons but to his wife, Salome Alexandra, whose Hebrew name was Shelamzion, meaning 'peace of Zion'. She had already been married to his brother Aristobulus I and had lived through three reigns.

The country was exhausted by years of war and the bitter civil war between Jannaeus and the Pharisees. Josephus says Jannaeus advised her to give the Pharisees a share of power so that the people would accept her rule.
Queen Salome Alexandra.happened:
As a woman, Salome could not serve as High Priest, so she gave the post to her elder son, Hyrcanus II, a quiet man. Her younger son, Aristobulus II, was more ambitious and was given military roles. She brought the Pharisees into government, and they reversed some of the Sadducees' rulings. Josephus also says they took revenge on Jannaeus's former advisers, which caused new tensions.

Rabbinic tradition names the sage Shimon ben Shetach as her brother. He is credited with reforms such as strengthening the ketubah, the marriage contract that protects a wife's rights, and, according to the Jerusalem Talmud, with ordering that children attend school. Salome kept a strong army, doubled the number of soldiers according to Josephus, and used gifts and diplomacy to turn away the Armenian king Tigranes, who threatened from the north.
Queen Salome Alexandra.matters:
Salome Alexandra was the last woman to rule an independent Jewish state, and the only queen regnant in Jewish history apart from the hated Athaliah of the Bible. The Talmud (Taanit 23a) recalls her reign as a golden age, when rain fell at convenient times, on Wednesday and Sabbath nights, and grains of wheat grew as large as kidneys. Her name, Shelamzion, appears in a fragment among the Dead Sea Scrolls.

Her peaceful rule did not last beyond her. As she lay dying in 67 BCE, Aristobulus seized fortresses across the country, and civil war broke out between her sons. Today Shlomzion HaMalka, 'Queen Shlomzion', is the name of a well-known street in central Jerusalem.

Hasmonean civil war.background:
Salome Alexandra had made her elder son, Hyrcanus II, High Priest and her heir. Her younger son, Aristobulus II, was a forceful soldier with the support of the army and of the Sadducee nobles. Before she died in 67 BCE, Aristobulus had already started to take over fortresses around the country.

The wider region was changing. The Seleucid kingdom had all but vanished, and Rome was moving into the east. The Roman general Pompey had defeated King Mithridates of Pontus and was reorganising Asia Minor and Syria.
Hasmonean civil war.happened:
Aristobulus defeated his brother near Jericho, and Hyrcanus agreed to give up the throne and the High Priesthood. But Antipater, an able and ambitious Idumean adviser, persuaded Hyrcanus to fight on. They fled to Petra, capital of the Nabataean king Aretas III, who brought an army to Jerusalem and besieged Aristobulus on the Temple Mount.

Josephus tells of Honi, also called Onias, a holy man famous for praying for rain, who was asked to curse Aristobulus's side. He refused, praying that God would not answer either side against the other, and was stoned to death. The Talmud tells another story from this siege: the defenders lowered money in a basket each day to buy lambs for sacrifice, until one day the besiegers sent up a pig instead. A Roman officer, Scaurus, ordered Aretas to withdraw. In 63 BCE both brothers, and a third delegation asking for no king at all, appeared before Pompey in Damascus.
Hasmonean civil war.matters:
The civil war gave Rome its opening. Within months Pompey marched on Jerusalem, and Judea lost the independence the Maccabees had fought for. Rabbinic tradition saw the quarrel between the brothers as a warning about the cost of internal division.

The war also brought Antipater and his family to the centre of power. His son Herod would later rule Judea as a Roman client king and marry into the Hasmonean family, then destroy it. The story of Honi the Circle-Maker, remembered in the Mishnah and Talmud for drawing a circle and refusing to leave it until rain fell, adds a striking moment of faith to a bitter conflict.

Rome takes Jerusalem.background:
By 63 BCE the Roman general Pompey had brought Syria under Roman rule. When the two feuding Hasmonean brothers, Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II, came before him in Damascus, he put off a decision. Aristobulus grew suspicious and left to prepare for war, which gave Pompey a reason to march south.

Aristobulus surrendered at first but his followers refused to give up Jerusalem. The city was split. Supporters of Hyrcanus opened the gates to the Romans, while Aristobulus's men retreated to the Temple Mount, cut the bridge to the upper city and prepared to hold out.
Rome takes Jerusalem.happened:
Pompey besieged the Temple Mount for about three months. Josephus explains that the defenders would fight on the Sabbath only if attacked directly, so the Romans used Sabbath days to build earthworks and bring up siege engines without opposition. When the walls were finally breached, Josephus says, the priests continued the daily sacrifices even as they were cut down at the altar. He gives the number of Jewish dead as about 12,000.

Pompey and his officers entered the Holy of Holies. Josephus and the Roman orator Cicero both note that he did not touch the gold vessels or the Temple treasury, and the next day he ordered the Temple to be cleansed and sacrifices to resume. Hyrcanus was restored as High Priest but without the title of king. Aristobulus and his children were taken to Rome and paraded in Pompey's triumph in 61 BCE.
Rome takes Jerusalem.matters:
The fall of Jerusalem ended about eighty years of Jewish independence. Judea was reduced in size, lost its coastal cities and the Greek cities of the Decapolis, and had to pay tribute to Rome. It remained under Roman control, in one form or another, until the empire itself gave way to Byzantium.

The shock is captured in the Psalms of Solomon, Jewish poems written soon afterwards, which lament the foreign conqueror in the sanctuary and later celebrate his death in Egypt in 48 BCE. Captives taken to Rome helped grow the city's Jewish community, one of the oldest in Europe, which still exists today.

Last Hasmonean king.background:
After 63 BCE, Hyrcanus II served as High Priest under Rome, but real power lay with his adviser Antipater and Antipater's sons, Phasael and Herod. Aristobulus II's son, Antigonus, never accepted this and made several attempts to win back his father's throne.

In 40 BCE Rome was distracted by its own civil wars after the murder of Julius Caesar. The Parthians, Rome's great rival from the east, invaded Syria and the Land of Israel. Antigonus offered them money in return for the throne.
Last Hasmonean king.happened:
With Parthian help, Antigonus took Jerusalem. Hyrcanus and Phasael were captured. Phasael died in captivity, by his own hand according to Josephus. Antigonus is said to have mutilated Hyrcanus's ears, since Jewish law did not allow a man with such a blemish to serve as High Priest. Herod escaped, left his family at the fortress of Masada and travelled to Rome. There, on the proposal of Mark Antony and Octavian, the Senate declared him king of Judea.

Antigonus, whose Hebrew name was Mattathias, ruled as king and High Priest for three years. Herod returned with Roman support, fought his way through the country and in 37 BCE besieged Jerusalem with the Roman general Sosius. During the siege he married Mariamne, a Hasmonean princess, to strengthen his claim. After about five months the city fell, and Antigonus was taken to Antioch and executed on Antony's orders.
Last Hasmonean king.matters:
With Antigonus's death, the Hasmonean dynasty, founded by the Maccabees, came to an end after more than a century. Herod later killed the remaining Hasmonean heirs, including Mariamne herself, her young brother and her sons.

Antigonus's small bronze coins are famous. One side shows the seven-branched Temple menorah, the earliest known image of it, and the other probably shows the table of showbread. They carry his Hebrew name, Mattatayah the High Priest. The menorah from his coin appears today on the Israeli 10 agorot coin, linking the last Hasmonean king to the modern state.

Herod the Great.background:
Herod was born around 73 BCE to Antipater, an Idumean whose family had converted to Judaism under John Hyrcanus, and Cypros, a Nabataean noblewoman. His father rose to power as adviser to Hyrcanus II and won the favour of Julius Caesar. In 47 BCE the young Herod was made governor of the Galilee, where he executed a rebel leader named Hezekiah and was summoned before the Sanhedrin, the Jewish court, for acting without its authority.

In 40 BCE the Roman Senate named him king of Judea, and by 37 BCE he had taken Jerusalem from Antigonus, the last Hasmonean ruler.
Herod the Great.happened:
Herod ruled for 33 years as a client king loyal to Rome. When his patron Mark Antony was defeated at Actium in 31 BCE, he quickly won over the victor, Octavian, later the emperor Augustus, who enlarged his kingdom. He kept order with a strong army, a network of fortresses and secret police.

His family life was violent. He married ten wives. He had his Hasmonean wife Mariamne executed in 29 BCE, her brother the young High Priest Aristobulus III drowned in a pool at Jericho, and their two sons, Alexander and Aristobulus, strangled in 7 BCE. Days before his own death he had his eldest son Antipater killed. The Gospel of Matthew adds the story of the killing of the infants of Bethlehem, which is not recorded elsewhere. His building works included Caesarea, the city of Sebaste at Samaria, the Antonia fortress, Herodium, palaces at Masada and Jericho, and the walls around the Tomb of the Patriarchs in Hebron.
Herod the Great.matters:
Herod left a double legacy. Josephus, our main source, paints him as a brilliant but cruel ruler, and Jewish tradition largely remembers him harshly as a foreign usurper who destroyed the Hasmoneans. Yet he gave Judea some of the finest buildings in the Roman world and brought decades of stability and trade.

Many of his works can still be visited. The Western Wall in Jerusalem, the cliff palaces of Masada, the harbour of Caesarea and the cone-shaped hill of Herodium are among Israel's best-known sites, and the massive enclosure at Hebron still stands almost complete. His name remains a byword for both grandeur and tyranny.

Hillel and Shammai.background:
In the centuries before the Temple's destruction, Jewish learning was led by a series of 'pairs', known in Hebrew as the Zugot. Each pair is said to have included a Nasi, or president of the Sanhedrin, and a head of the court. Hillel and Shammai were the last and most famous of these pairs, active from about 30 BCE into the early first century CE, during and just after the reign of Herod.

Hillel came from Babylonia. The Talmud (Yoma 35b) tells that as a poor young man he could not pay the entry fee to the study hall, so he climbed onto the roof to listen through the skylight, and was found half frozen under the snow on a winter Sabbath morning.
Hillel and Shammai.happened:
Hillel rose to become the leading sage of his generation. He is credited with the prozbul, a legal device that allowed loans to be collected after the Sabbatical year so that the poor could still borrow. Shammai, a builder by trade, was known for strictness. Their students formed two schools, Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai, which disagreed on more than 300 questions. One famous example concerns Hanukkah: Beit Shammai said to light eight candles on the first night and count down, while Beit Hillel said to start with one and add one each night.

The Talmud (Shabbat 31a) tells of would-be converts who came with odd demands. Shammai drove them away, while Hillel welcomed them patiently and taught them. Shammai too had gentle teachings, urging people to greet everyone with a cheerful face.
Hillel and Shammai.matters:
The Talmud (Eruvin 13b) says a heavenly voice declared that the views of both schools were the words of the living God, but that the law follows Beit Hillel because its members were kind and humble and even taught their opponents' views before their own. This idea, that disagreement 'for the sake of heaven' can be valuable, is central to Jewish learning.

Hillel's descendants led the Jewish community in the Land of Israel as patriarchs for about four centuries. His sayings in Pirkei Avot, 'Ethics of the Fathers', such as asking who will be for me if I am not for myself, are still widely quoted. And every Hanukkah, Jews follow Hillel by adding one candle each night.

Caesarea built.background:
The Mediterranean coast of the Land of Israel is straight and sandy, with few natural harbours. Herod wanted a great port to link his kingdom to Rome and the wider world, and a showcase city that would display his loyalty to Augustus. He chose the site of a small, decayed Phoenician town called Straton's Tower.

Josephus, in both his Jewish War and his Antiquities, describes the building of the city in detail, saying it took about twelve years.
Caesarea built.happened:
Work began around 22 BCE and the city was dedicated around 10 BCE with lavish games. The harbour, called Sebastos, the Greek form of Augustus, was the boldest part. Builders lowered huge wooden frames into the sea and filled them with concrete made with volcanic ash brought from Italy, which sets under water. Underwater archaeologists have since found these blocks and confirmed Josephus's account.

On land, Herod built a temple to Rome and Augustus on a platform overlooking the harbour, a theatre, a hippodrome for chariot races, a palace jutting into the sea, and an aqueduct bringing water from the Carmel hills. The city was laid out on a Roman grid. Its population was mixed, with Greeks, Syrians and Jews living side by side, which later caused friction.
Caesarea built.matters:
From 6 CE Caesarea became the seat of the Roman governors of Judea. In 1961 archaeologists found a stone in its theatre bearing the name of Pontius Pilate, the only inscription naming him from his lifetime. Tension between Jews and Greeks over rights in the city grew, and in 66 CE a provocation outside a synagogue there helped spark the Great Revolt. Josephus says the city's Jews were then massacred.

Caesarea later became a centre of learning for Jews and Christians, home to the sage Rabbi Abbahu and the Christian scholars Origen and Eusebius. Jewish tradition holds that Rabbi Akiva was executed there. Today its Roman, Byzantine and Crusader ruins form a popular national park, and the restored theatre hosts concerts.

Herod rebuilds the Temple.background:
The Second Temple had been built by Jews returning from Babylon around 516 BCE. It was modest compared with Solomon's Temple and had been damaged in wars over the centuries. Herod, eager to win the favour of his Jewish subjects and to leave a monument to himself, announced a complete rebuilding in about 20 BCE, the eighteenth year of his reign according to Josephus.

Many feared he would tear down the old Temple and never finish the new one. Josephus says Herod reassured them by gathering all the materials before work began.
Herod rebuilds the Temple.happened:
Herod hired 10,000 workers and, out of respect for Jewish law, had 1,000 priests trained as masons and carpenters so that only priests would work in the sacred areas. The sanctuary itself was finished in about eighteen months, but work on the courts and surroundings went on for decades, until shortly before the revolt of 66 CE.

To enlarge the Temple Mount, builders raised enormous retaining walls and filled the space inside, creating a platform of about 15 hectares, one of the largest in the ancient world. One stone in the Western Wall Tunnels is about 13.6 metres long and is estimated to weigh hundreds of tonnes. Around the courts ran columned halls, including the Royal Stoa on the southern side. A stone barrier carried warnings in Greek and Latin forbidding non-Jews to go further, and two of these inscriptions have been found.
Herod rebuilds the Temple.matters:
The Talmud (Sukkah 51b and Bava Batra 4a) praises the beauty of Herod's Temple, describing walls of white and blue-green marble that looked like the waves of the sea. Josephus says it gleamed so brightly in the sun that it dazzled viewers. Pilgrims came from across the Jewish world for the festivals of Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot.

The Temple was destroyed by Rome in 70 CE, less than a decade after it was completed. But Herod's retaining walls survived. The Western Wall, the Southern Steps, Robinson's Arch and the stones of the Temple Mount platform are the most important physical link to the Temple. The Western Wall is today the holiest place where Jews pray.

Death of Herod.background:
By the end of his life, Herod was old, ill and deeply suspicious. He had executed several sons and feared plots everywhere. Josephus describes his final illness in grim detail, including fever, swelling and great pain, and says he went to the hot springs at Callirrhoe by the Dead Sea for treatment, without success.

Shortly before his death, students of two teachers, Judas and Matthias, tore down a golden eagle Herod had placed over a Temple gate, seeing it as a forbidden image. Herod had the teachers and some of the students burned alive.
Death of Herod.happened:
Herod died at Jericho in the spring of 4 BCE, the date accepted by most historians, though some argue for 1 BCE. Josephus says he had ordered leading men to be locked in the hippodrome and killed when he died, so that there would be mourning in the land, but his sister Salome released them. His body was carried in a grand procession to Herodium.

Augustus largely confirmed Herod's will. Archelaus became ethnarch, not king, of Judea, Samaria and Idumea. Herod Antipas became tetrarch of the Galilee and Perea, and Philip tetrarch of the lands north-east of the Sea of Galilee. Unrest followed at once. Archelaus's troops killed about 3,000 people at Passover in the Temple courts, and revolts broke out across the country. Varus, the Roman governor of Syria, crushed them, and Josephus says he crucified 2,000 rebels.
Death of Herod.matters:
Herod's death ended the last united Jewish kingdom under one ruler until his grandson Agrippa I briefly reunited it decades later. The split between his sons shaped the world described in the New Testament: Antipas is the Herod who executed John the Baptist, and Pilate later governed the part once ruled by Archelaus.

For centuries the location of Herod's tomb was unknown. After a long search, archaeologist Ehud Netzer found it on the slope of Herodium in 2007, including fragments of a decorated reddish stone sarcophagus. Netzer died after a fall at the site in 2010. The finds were shown in a major exhibition at the Israel Museum in 2013, and Herodium is now a national park.

Judea under Roman governors.background:
Archelaus ruled Judea for about ten years after Herod's death. He was unpopular with both Jews and Samaritans, who sent delegations to Rome to complain. In 6 CE Augustus removed him and exiled him to Vienne in Gaul.

Judea, together with Samaria and Idumea, was then placed under a Roman official of equestrian rank, a prefect, who answered to the governor of Syria. The first was Coponius. The governors lived in Caesarea and came up to Jerusalem at the festivals with troops.
Judea under Roman governors.happened:
To set taxes for the new province, Quirinius, governor of Syria, held a census of property. According to Josephus, a man called Judas of Galilee, together with a Pharisee named Zadok, urged people to refuse, teaching that it was wrong to accept any master but God. Josephus calls their movement a 'fourth philosophy' beside the Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes, and links it to the later Zealots.

Day-to-day affairs, including the Temple, were left to the High Priest and the Jewish council, but Rome appointed and removed High Priests at will. Pontius Pilate, prefect from about 26 to 36 CE, brought military standards bearing the emperor's image into Jerusalem. Josephus says crowds protested at Caesarea and bared their necks rather than accept it, and Pilate backed down. He later used Temple funds to build an aqueduct, provoking riots that he put down with force.
Judea under Roman governors.matters:
The period of direct Roman rule saw steadily rising tension. After Agrippa I's short reign, governors returned from 44 CE, and several, such as Felix and Florus, were known for cruelty and corruption. Armed groups, including the Sicarii, named after the small daggers they carried, became active. The pressure finally exploded in the revolt of 66 CE.

Archaeology has brought this era vividly to life. Besides Pilate's inscription from Caesarea, an ornate ossuary, or bone box, found in Jerusalem in 1990 carries the name of Caiaphas, the High Priest of the time. This was also the world in which Jesus lived and was crucified, which is why the period is widely studied by both Jews and Christians.

Jesus of Nazareth.background:
In the early first century CE, Judea was under Roman governors and the Galilee was ruled by Herod Antipas. Many Jews hoped for God's intervention and a coming 'messiah', meaning 'anointed one', who would restore Israel. Prophetic figures appeared, among them John the Baptist, who called people to repent and immerse in the Jordan River.

Jesus, in Hebrew Yeshua, was born around 6 to 4 BCE and grew up in the village of Nazareth in the Galilee. He was raised as a Jew, and the Gospels show him attending synagogue and going to Jerusalem for the festivals.
Jesus of Nazareth.happened:
According to the Gospels, Jesus was baptised by John and then taught for a few years in the towns around the Sea of Galilee, such as Capernaum. He spoke in parables, gathered disciples and was known as a healer. Around 30 CE, or possibly 33 CE, he came to Jerusalem at Passover. He was arrested, brought before the High Priest Caiaphas and handed to the Roman prefect Pontius Pilate, who had him crucified, a Roman punishment for rebels and slaves.

Outside Christian writings, Jesus is mentioned by Josephus, in a passage that most scholars think was later added to by Christian copyists, and by the Roman historian Tacitus. His followers believed he had risen from the dead. Led at first by his brother James and the apostle Peter in Jerusalem, they remained a group within Judaism. Paul of Tarsus, a former Pharisee, spread the message to non-Jews across the Roman world.
Jesus of Nazareth.matters:
Over the next few centuries, the movement became a separate religion. Historians describe a gradual 'parting of the ways', shaped by debates over whether non-Jewish followers needed to keep Jewish law, by the destruction of the Temple and by growing hostility on both sides. The timing of the split is still debated.

The relationship between Christianity and Judaism has been one of the most important in Jewish history. For many centuries the charge that Jews were collectively responsible for Jesus's death fuelled persecution. In 1965 the Catholic Church's declaration Nostra Aetate rejected this charge, and many churches have since worked to build better relations. Today scholars widely study Jesus as a figure within the Judaism of his time.

Riots in Alexandria.background:
Alexandria, founded by Alexander the Great, was the great city of the eastern Mediterranean. Its Jewish community was very old and very large. Philo claimed there were about a million Jews in Egypt, though this is likely an exaggeration. Here the Torah had been translated into Greek, the version known as the Septuagint. Jews had their own council and lived mainly in two of the city's five districts, but they were not full citizens, and their rights were bitterly disputed by the Greek population.

In 37 CE the emperor Caligula came to power. The Roman prefect of Egypt, Aulus Avillius Flaccus, who had been close to the previous emperor, felt insecure and sought the support of anti-Jewish Greek leaders.
Riots in Alexandria.happened:
In 38 CE the Jewish king Agrippa I passed through Alexandria on his way to his new kingdom. A Greek crowd mocked him by dressing a local madman named Carabas as a king. The mob then demanded that images of Caligula be placed in synagogues. Flaccus declared the Jews to be foreigners and aliens. Jews were driven into one district, their homes and shops in other areas were looted, synagogues were burned or wrecked, and many were beaten, burned or killed. Philo says 38 members of the Jewish council were flogged in the theatre.

Later that year Flaccus was arrested and exiled, and he was later executed. Both communities sent delegations to Caligula. Philo led the Jewish one. The emperor received them with mockery and gave no decision.
Riots in Alexandria.matters:
Philo's two works on these events, Against Flaccus and On the Embassy to Gaius, are among the most detailed eyewitness accounts of anti-Jewish violence in the ancient world. They show how local rivalries, political ambition and religious hatred could combine against a minority.

After Caligula's death, the new emperor Claudius wrote a letter to the Alexandrians in 41 CE, preserved on a papyrus now in the British Library. It ordered the Greeks not to interfere with Jewish customs and told the Jews not to seek more rights. Peace did not last, and the community suffered again in 66 CE and was nearly destroyed in 115 to 117 CE. The riots of 38 CE are often studied as an early example of what later ages would call a pogrom.

Caligula's statue.background:
The emperor Gaius, nicknamed Caligula, ruled from 37 to 41 CE. Unlike earlier emperors, he demanded to be worshipped as a living god. Most of the empire went along with emperor worship, but Jews refused, since their faith forbade worshipping any being but God.

According to Philo, the trouble began in Yavneh (Jamnia) on the coast, where non-Jewish residents built an altar to the emperor to provoke their Jewish neighbours, who tore it down. When Caligula heard, he ordered a giant statue of himself as Zeus to be set up in the Temple in Jerusalem.
Caligula's statue.happened:
The order went to Publius Petronius, governor of Syria, who was told to use two legions if needed. Philo and Josephus both describe how tens of thousands of Jews, men, women and children, gathered first at Ptolemais (Acre) and then at Tiberias. They said they would not fight but would rather be killed than allow the Temple to be defiled. Josephus says they stayed for some forty days, neglecting their fields at sowing time.

Petronius was moved and feared famine and revolt. He delayed, telling the craftsmen to work slowly, and wrote to the emperor asking him to reconsider. In Rome, Agrippa I is said to have pleaded with Caligula, who briefly relented. Angered by Petronius's delay, Caligula sent orders for him to take his own life. But Caligula was assassinated in January 41 CE, and news of his death reached Petronius before the letter did.
Caligula's statue.matters:
The episode is one of the earliest recorded examples of mass non-violent protest. Ordinary people faced the world's greatest power and, with help from a thoughtful Roman official and some luck, prevented the desecration of their Temple. Both Philo and Josephus, writing for Greek and Roman readers, held it up as proof of Jewish devotion. The Roman historian Tacitus also mentions it briefly.

Many scholars think the cancellation is the event marked in Megillat Taanit, an ancient list of joyful days, on the 22nd of the month of Shevat. The crisis also left deep fear among Jews that Rome might again try to defile the Temple, a fear that fed the tensions leading to the revolt of 66 CE.

King Agrippa I.background:
Agrippa, born in 10 BCE, was a grandson of Herod the Great and of the Hasmonean princess Mariamne. After his father Aristobulus was executed by Herod, he was raised in Rome among the imperial family, growing up alongside the future emperor Claudius. He ran up huge debts and was imprisoned by the emperor Tiberius for an unwise remark.

When his friend Caligula became emperor in 37 CE, Agrippa was freed and given the territories of his late uncle Philip, with the title of king. He later added the Galilee and Perea after his uncle Herod Antipas was exiled.
King Agrippa I.happened:
In January 41 CE, after Caligula was murdered, Agrippa helped persuade the Senate to accept Claudius as emperor. Claudius rewarded him with Judea and Samaria, so that Agrippa now ruled a kingdom as large as his grandfather's. Josephus says he lived in Jerusalem, kept Jewish law carefully and offered sacrifices daily.

The Mishnah tells that Agrippa carried his own basket of first fruits to the Temple like any farmer. It also describes the Hakhel ceremony, when the king read the Torah to the people. When Agrippa reached the verse forbidding a foreign king, he wept, recalling his Idumean ancestry, and the people called out to reassure him that he was their brother. He began a third wall to protect a new district of Jerusalem, but the governor of Syria warned Claudius, who ordered the work stopped. In 44 CE, at games in Caesarea, he fell suddenly ill and died a few days later. Both Josephus and the Book of Acts describe his death.
King Agrippa I.matters:
Agrippa's reign was remembered fondly in Jewish tradition as a short return to a Jewish king who respected the Torah and the Temple. His death at 54 was a turning point. His son, Agrippa II, was only seventeen, and Claudius decided not to give him the kingdom. Judea returned to Roman governors, and the slide towards war resumed.

The Book of Acts presents him less kindly, as the king who executed the apostle James and imprisoned Peter, showing how differently Jewish and Christian sources viewed him. His coins, some showing a canopy, and the remains of the 'Third Wall' north of the Old City of Jerusalem, which was completed during the revolt, still survive.

Great Revolt.background:
By the 60s CE, relations between Jews and Rome in Judea were at breaking point. Roman governors were often corrupt, violence between Jews and Greeks in mixed cities was rising, and armed groups were active. In 66 CE the governor Gessius Florus took 17 talents from the Temple treasury. When people mocked him, he let his soldiers loose in Jerusalem, and many were killed.

At the same time, Greeks and Jews clashed in Caesarea. In the Temple, Eleazar son of Ananias, captain of the Temple, persuaded the priests to stop the daily sacrifice offered on behalf of the emperor, which amounted to a declaration of rebellion.
Great Revolt.happened:
The rebels took Jerusalem and wiped out the Roman garrison. Cestius Gallus, the governor of Syria, marched on the city but withdrew, and his army was ambushed at the pass of Beth Horon in late 66, losing thousands of men. A provisional government in Jerusalem sent commanders to the regions, including Joseph ben Matityahu, the future historian Josephus, to the Galilee. The rebels minted silver shekels inscribed 'Jerusalem the holy' and bronze coins proclaiming 'freedom of Zion'.

Nero sent the general Vespasian, who took the Galilee in 67 and then the countryside. In Jerusalem, rival factions led by John of Gischala, Simon bar Giora and Eleazar son of Simon fought each other. In 69 Vespasian became emperor, and his son Titus besieged Jerusalem in 70, destroying the city and Temple. The last fortresses, Herodium, Machaerus and Masada, fell over the following years.
Great Revolt.matters:
The revolt was a catastrophe. Josephus claims over a million died, a figure most historians consider exaggerated, but the losses were enormous and many thousands were enslaved. Rome issued coins reading 'Judaea Capta', 'Judea captured', and imposed a special tax on all Jews, the fiscus Judaicus, paid to the temple of Jupiter in Rome.

The revolt ended the Temple and the priestly leadership, and with them the Sadducees. Judaism was rebuilt around prayer, the synagogue and the study of Torah, led by the rabbis. Josephus's Jewish War, written in Rome in the 70s, is our main source. The destruction is still mourned each year on the fast of Tisha B'Av.

Galilee falls.background:
When the revolt broke out in 66 CE, the rebel government in Jerusalem sent Joseph ben Matityahu, a young priest about 29 years old, to organise the defence of the Galilee. He fortified towns and trained troops, but also struggled with local rivals, especially John of Gischala, and with the pro-Roman city of Sepphoris.

In spring 67 the general Vespasian gathered his forces at Ptolemais (Acre). With his son Titus he commanded three legions, the Fifth, Tenth and Fifteenth, together with auxiliary troops and soldiers sent by allied kings. Josephus gives the total as about 60,000.
Galilee falls.happened:
Sepphoris opened its gates to Rome. Vespasian then besieged Yodfat (Jotapata), where Josephus himself commanded. The siege lasted 47 days. When the town fell, Josephus hid in a cave with forty men, who decided to die rather than surrender. By his own account, they drew lots to kill one another, and he was one of the last two left alive, at which point he gave himself up. Brought before Vespasian, he predicted that the general would become emperor.

Tiberias surrendered and Magdala (Taricheae) was taken after a battle on the Sea of Galilee. In the Golan, the hilltop town of Gamla held out for about a month. Josephus says about 4,000 were killed and 5,000 threw themselves into the ravine. Gischala fell last, and John fled to Jerusalem with his followers.
Galilee falls.matters:
The fall of the Galilee removed the rebels' northern base and left Jerusalem exposed. It also turned Joseph ben Matityahu into Flavius Josephus. When Vespasian became emperor in 69, Josephus was freed, took the family name Flavius and later lived in Rome, writing The Jewish War, Jewish Antiquities, an autobiography and a defence of Judaism called Against Apion. Without him we would know far less about this period, though many Jews long saw him as a traitor.

Archaeology has confirmed much of his story. Excavations at Gamla, begun in 1976, found Roman arrowheads, sling stones and one of the oldest known synagogues. Yodfat has also been excavated. Gamla, sometimes called 'the Masada of the north', is now a nature reserve.

Qumran destroyed.background:
Khirbet Qumran is a small site on a dry plateau near the north-western shore of the Dead Sea. It was occupied from about the first century BCE by a community that built water channels, ritual baths, a large dining room and a room some scholars identify as a writing room, or scriptorium.

Many scholars think the community were Essenes. The Roman writer Pliny the Elder placed an Essene settlement on the western shore of the Dead Sea, and the scrolls describe a group living by strict rules of purity and shared property. Others suggest different explanations for the site, so the question remains debated.
Qumran destroyed.happened:
In 68 CE, after taking the Galilee and the coastal plain, Vespasian moved his forces through the Jordan Valley towards Jericho. Archaeologists found that Qumran was destroyed at about this time, with a layer of ash, collapsed roofs and Roman-style arrowheads. The latest Jewish coins found there date from the second or third year of the revolt. Afterwards, Roman soldiers seem to have used the site briefly as an outpost.

Before or during this time, hundreds of scrolls were hidden in caves nearby, some carefully stored in clay jars. In 1947 a Bedouin shepherd searching for a lost goat found the first cave. Over the following years eleven caves yielded fragments of around 900 manuscripts. Excavations of the settlement were led by the French scholar Roland de Vaux in the 1950s.
Qumran destroyed.matters:
The Dead Sea Scrolls are among the most important finds of the twentieth century. They include copies of every book of the Hebrew Bible except Esther, about a thousand years older than the oldest complete Hebrew Bible manuscripts known before. The Great Isaiah Scroll is almost complete and closely matches the text used today. They also include the community's own writings, such as the Community Rule and the War Scroll.

The scrolls have transformed our understanding of Judaism in the Second Temple period and the background to early Christianity. Many are kept in the Shrine of the Book at the Israel Museum in Jerusalem, opened in 1965, whose white dome is shaped like the lid of a scroll jar. Many images are now available online.

Second Temple destroyed.background:
After Vespasian became emperor in 69 CE, he left the war to his son Titus. Inside Jerusalem, rival rebel factions led by John of Gischala, Simon bar Giora and Eleazar son of Simon had been fighting each other. During the infighting, stores of grain that could have fed the city for years were burned. Both Josephus and the Talmud tell of this.

In spring 70, around Passover, Titus arrived with four legions and surrounded the city, which was crowded with pilgrims. Jerusalem was protected by three walls on its northern side.
Second Temple destroyed.happened:
The Romans broke through the outer walls one by one and built a siege wall around the city to starve it. Josephus, now with the Romans, describes terrible famine. In July the Antonia fortress beside the Temple fell, and the daily sacrifice ceased. In the Hebrew month of Av, the Romans fought their way into the Temple courts and the sanctuary was set on fire. Josephus says Titus wanted to save it, but a later Roman source suggests he ordered its destruction, and historians debate which is true.

The upper city held out for another month before falling. The city was largely destroyed. Josephus says 97,000 people were taken captive. Simon bar Giora was paraded in Titus's triumph in Rome in 71 and executed, and the Temple treasures, including the menorah, were displayed and later kept in Rome's Temple of Peace.
Second Temple destroyed.matters:
Jewish tradition holds that both Temples were destroyed on the 9th of Av, and Tisha B'Av became the saddest day of the Jewish year, a fast when the Book of Lamentations is read. The Talmud (Gittin 55b to 56a) tells the story of Kamtza and Bar Kamtza, teaching that the Temple fell because of baseless hatred among Jews. Customs such as breaking a glass at weddings recall the loss.

Archaeology shows the destruction vividly: the 'Burnt House' in Jerusalem's Jewish Quarter, and huge stones thrown down onto a first-century street below the Western Wall. The Arch of Titus still stands in Rome. Without the Temple, sacrifice ended, and prayer, study and the synagogue became the heart of Jewish life.

Yohanan ben Zakkai and Yavneh.background:
Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai was one of the leading sages of the late Second Temple period, remembered in tradition as the youngest student of Hillel. He taught in Jerusalem and argued against the Sadducees.

During the Roman siege of 70 CE, the city was controlled by militant groups who would not allow anyone to leave or to discuss surrender. According to the Talmud (Gittin 56a), Yohanan's nephew, called Abba Sikra, was a leader of the rebels, and Yohanan asked him to help him escape.
Yohanan ben Zakkai and Yavneh.happened:
The Talmud tells that Yohanan pretended to be ill and then dead. His students Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua carried him out of the city in a coffin. Brought before Vespasian, he greeted him as king, and just then news arrived that Vespasian had been made emperor. Offered a request, Yohanan asked for Yavneh and its sages, for the family of Rabban Gamaliel, the descendants of Hillel, to be spared, and for doctors to heal the ailing sage Rabbi Tzadok. Another version appears in the work Avot de-Rabbi Natan. Historians debate the details, and some suggest Yavneh was a place where the Romans held surrendering Jews.

At Yavneh, a small town near the coast, Yohanan gathered scholars and set up a court and academy. He made decrees to adapt Jewish life, for example allowing the shofar to be blown there on a Rosh Hashanah that fell on the Sabbath, and ordering the lulav to be waved for all seven days of Sukkot everywhere in memory of the Temple.
Yohanan ben Zakkai and Yavneh.matters:
Yavneh is seen as the place where Judaism learned to survive without a Temple. Under Yohanan and his successor, Rabban Gamaliel II, the sages organised the daily prayers, including the Amidah, began collecting the laws that would form the Mishnah and helped settle the content of the Hebrew Bible. The older idea of a formal 'Council of Jamnia' that fixed the Bible is now doubted by scholars.

A saying attributed to Yohanan in Avot de-Rabbi Natan teaches that if you are planting a sapling and hear the Messiah has come, you should finish planting first. The phrase 'Yavneh and its sages' has become shorthand for choosing to preserve learning and community in a crisis. Yavneh is today a city in central Israel.

Fall of Masada.background:
Masada is a flat-topped rock rising about 400 metres above the shore of the Dead Sea. Herod turned it into a fortress-palace, with storerooms, huge cisterns and a three-tiered palace hanging from the northern cliff.

At the start of the revolt in 66 CE, a group of Sicarii, a radical faction, captured Masada from its Roman garrison. After their leader Menahem was killed in Jerusalem, his relative Eleazar ben Yair led the group at Masada. After Jerusalem fell in 70, other refugees joined them, and they raided the surrounding area, including, according to Josephus, the Jewish village of Ein Gedi.
Fall of Masada.happened:
In 73 CE, or possibly 74 as some scholars argue, the Roman governor Lucius Flavius Silva marched on Masada with the Tenth Legion, auxiliaries and many Jewish captives used as labourers. They surrounded the mountain with a siege wall and eight camps, still visible today, and built a ramp up a natural spur on the western side. A battering ram broke the wall, and the defenders built a second wall of timber and earth, which the Romans set on fire.

Josephus says that on the last night Eleazar gave two speeches urging his followers to die free rather than be enslaved. The men killed their families and then each other, and the last man killed himself. Josephus gives the number of dead as 960. Two women and five children who had hidden in a cistern survived and told the story.
Fall of Masada.matters:
Masada was excavated by Yigael Yadin from 1963 to 1965. Volunteers found the palaces, a synagogue, ritual baths, scroll fragments including books of the Bible and Ben Sira, and small pottery shards with names, one reading 'ben Yair', which some think were the lots described by Josephus. Historians still debate how accurate Josephus's account of the mass suicide is, as relatively few skeletons were found.

In modern Israel, Masada became a powerful symbol of resistance and the will to stay free, though some have questioned using a mass suicide as a national symbol. Some army units have held ceremonies on its summit. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001, and visitors climb the Snake Path at dawn to watch the sun rise over the Dead Sea.

Diaspora revolt.background:
Forty years after the destruction of the Temple, large Jewish communities lived across the eastern Roman Empire and beyond, in Egypt, Cyrenaica (eastern Libya), Cyprus and Mesopotamia. Many had suffered from tension with their Greek neighbours, and all Jews in the empire now paid the humiliating special tax to the temple of Jupiter. Hopes for redemption and the rebuilding of the Temple ran high.

In 114 CE the emperor Trajan launched a great campaign against the Parthian Empire, taking armies far to the east into Mesopotamia. This left the eastern provinces with fewer troops.
Diaspora revolt.happened:
Around 115 CE, Jews in Cyrene rose up under a leader whom Eusebius calls Lukuas and describes as their king, while Cassius Dio calls him Andreas. The fighting spread to Egypt, where Greek and Jewish forces fought across the countryside, as papyrus letters from Roman officials show. In Cyprus the rebels were led by a man called Artemion. In Mesopotamia, Jews joined the local resistance to Trajan's conquest.

The ancient sources describe great brutality on all sides. Cassius Dio gives huge death tolls among non-Jews in Cyrene and Cyprus, figures historians treat with caution. Trajan sent the general Marcius Turbo to Egypt and Cyrene, and the Moorish general Lusius Quietus to Mesopotamia, who crushed the uprisings by 117. Quietus was then made governor of Judea, and rabbinic sources remember this as the 'war of Kitos', a form of his name.
Diaspora revolt.matters:
The revolt nearly ended the Jewish presence in several regions for generations. In Alexandria, the great community of Philo's time was destroyed, along with its famous synagogue, which the Talmud (Sukkah 51b) describes as so large that flags were waved to tell the congregation when to answer 'Amen'. Jews were banned from Cyprus. A papyrus shows that the Greek town of Oxyrhynchus in Egypt was still celebrating its victory over the Jews eighty years later.

Because there was no Jewish historian like Josephus to record it, this revolt is far less known than the wars in Judea. Its outcome shifted the centre of Jewish life further towards the Land of Israel and Babylonia, where the great rabbinic academies would develop.

Bar Kokhba revolt.background:
Sixty years after the Temple's destruction, many Jews still hoped Jerusalem and its Temple would be restored. Around 130 CE the emperor Hadrian visited the region and decided to refound Jerusalem as a Roman colony called Aelia Capitolina, with a temple to Jupiter. According to one late Roman source, he also banned circumcision, though historians debate whether this was a cause of the war or came later as a punishment.

The Jews of Judea prepared in secret. Archaeologists have found networks of underground hiding tunnels in the Judean foothills, many probably dug for this war.
Bar Kokhba revolt.happened:
The revolt broke out in 132 CE under Shimon ben Kosiba. Rabbinic tradition (Jerusalem Talmud, Taanit 4:5) says Rabbi Akiva called him Bar Kokhba, 'son of a star', after the verse in Numbers about a star rising from Jacob, and saw him as the messiah. Other sages disagreed, and later writers called him Bar Koziba, 'son of lies'. His letters, found in the Judean Desert caves in the 1950s and 1960s, show a hands-on commander signing as 'Shimon bar Kosiba, prince of Israel'. He minted coins over Roman ones, marked 'Year one of the redemption of Israel' and showing the Temple front.

Hadrian brought in his best general, Julius Severus, from Britain. The Romans fought a slow war of attrition. The Roman historian Cassius Dio says 50 fortresses and 985 villages were destroyed and 580,000 killed in battle. The last stronghold, Betar, south-west of Jerusalem, fell in 135, on the 9th of Av according to tradition.
Bar Kokhba revolt.matters:
The defeat was a turning point. Judea was emptied of much of its Jewish population, Jerusalem became the pagan city of Aelia Capitolina, and Jews were forbidden to enter it. The province's name was changed from Judaea to Syria Palaestina. Rabbinic memory, though, was mixed: Bar Kokhba was seen as both a hero and a false messiah who brought disaster.

The finds made by Yigael Yadin in the 'Cave of Letters' at Nahal Hever in 1960 and 1961, including letters, documents and personal belongings of refugees, brought the revolt to life. In modern Israel, Bar Kokhba became a symbol of Jewish bravery, and the festival of Lag BaOmer, with its bonfires, has become linked to his memory, especially among children.

Rabbi Akiva martyred.background:
Akiva ben Yosef was born around 50 CE. Tradition says he was an unlearned shepherd working for a rich man of Jerusalem, Kalba Savua, whose daughter, called Rachel in later sources, married him on condition that he study. Avot de-Rabbi Natan tells that at about forty he saw water dripping on a rock and wearing a hole in it, and decided that if water could shape stone, Torah could shape his heart.

He studied for many years and became the leading sage of his generation, organising the oral teachings in ways that paved the way for the Mishnah. After the Bar Kokhba revolt, which he had supported, Hadrian's government outlawed public teaching of Torah and other Jewish practices.
Rabbi Akiva martyred.happened:
The Talmud (Berakhot 61b) tells that Akiva kept teaching in public. When asked if he was not afraid, he answered with a parable: a fox urged fish to escape the fishermen's nets by coming onto dry land, and the fish replied that if they were in danger in the water, their home, how much more would they be on land. For Jews, he explained, Torah is like water for fish.

He was arrested and imprisoned for a long period, and was then executed, according to tradition at Caesarea under the governor Tinneius Rufus, known in rabbinic sources as Turnus Rufus. His flesh was torn with iron combs. As he died he recited the Shema, and his students asked how he could do so. He replied that all his life he had wondered how he could fulfil the command to love God 'with all your soul', even if it costs your life, and now he could.
Rabbi Akiva martyred.matters:
