Rabbi Akiva became the model of the scholar who gives his life for the Torah. His death is recalled in the liturgical poem Eileh Ezkerah, 'These I will remember', recited on Yom Kippur, and in the mourning poems of Tisha B'Av, among the Ten Martyrs.

The Talmud also says 24,000 of his students died in a plague between Passover and Shavuot, which is why many Jews observe mourning customs during part of the Omer period, the seven weeks between the two festivals, ending on Lag BaOmer. His teaching that loving your neighbour as yourself is a great principle of the Torah is often quoted.

Sages regroup at Usha.background:
The Bar Kokhba war and the harsh decrees that followed devastated Judea and its scholars. Rabbi Akiva and other leading sages were executed, and the academy at Yavneh ceased to function. Tradition says Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava secretly ordained five of Akiva's students before he was caught and killed by the Romans.

After Hadrian died in 138 CE, his successor Antoninus Pius eased the persecution. The surviving sages, many of whom had fled or hidden, could gather again. The Galilee, less damaged than Judea, became their new home.
Sages regroup at Usha.happened:
The sages met at Usha, a village in the western Galilee east of today's Haifa. They included Akiva's students Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai, Rabbi Yose ben Halafta, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and Rabbi Nehemiah. Rabban Shimon ben Gamaliel II, a descendant of Hillel, became Nasi, or patriarch, restoring the leadership of Hillel's family.

They re-established the Sanhedrin and passed a series of decrees, known as the takkanot of Usha, recorded in the Talmud (Ketubot 49b to 50a). These said, for example, that a father must support his young children, that a person should not give away more than a fifth of their wealth to charity so as not to become poor themselves, and that parents should be patient in teaching a son until he is about twelve. The rulings aimed to rebuild families and communities after the disaster.
Sages regroup at Usha.matters:
Usha marks the moment when the centre of Jewish life in the Land of Israel moved from Judea to the Galilee, where it would stay for centuries. The Talmud (Rosh Hashanah 31a) lists the ten 'journeys' of the Sanhedrin after it left the Temple, from Jerusalem to Yavneh, to Usha and on to Shefar'am, Beit She'arim, Sepphoris and finally Tiberias.

The generation of Usha did much of the work that Rabbi Judah the Prince later gathered into the Mishnah, and its sages are among the names most often quoted there. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, linked by later tradition to the Zohar, is honoured at his tomb in Meron each Lag BaOmer. A kibbutz named Usha, founded in 1937, stands near the ancient site.

The Mishnah.background:
Jewish tradition holds that alongside the written Torah, Moses received an Oral Torah, explaining how its laws should be carried out. For centuries these teachings were passed from teacher to student by repetition. The word 'mishnah' comes from a Hebrew root meaning 'to repeat' or 'to study'. The sages of this period are called Tannaim, from an Aramaic word for 'repeaters'.

After the destruction of the Temple and the wars against Rome, many teachers had died and the body of teachings had grown huge and varied. Earlier sages such as Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Meir had already begun to arrange the material.
The Mishnah.happened:
Rabbi Judah the Prince, known simply as 'Rabbi', led the Jewish community in the Land of Israel around 200 CE. A descendant of Hillel, he was wealthy, respected by the Romans, and, according to the Talmud, a friend of an emperor called Antoninus. He lived first at Beit She'arim and later at Sepphoris in the Galilee.

With his court, he selected, edited and organised the teachings into the Mishnah, written in clear Hebrew. It has six orders: Zeraim (seeds, farming laws and blessings), Moed (festivals), Nashim (women, marriage and divorce), Nezikin (damages and civil law), Kodashim (holy things and the Temple) and Tohorot (purity). These are divided into 63 tractates. It often records several opinions on a question, including minority views. Scholars debate whether Rabbi Judah actually wrote it down or fixed a precise text that was still memorised.
The Mishnah.matters:
The Mishnah became the foundation of rabbinic Judaism. Over the next three centuries, scholars in the Land of Israel and Babylonia discussed it line by line, and their debates became the Gemara. Mishnah and Gemara together form the Talmud. Nearly all later Jewish law builds on it.

The Mishnah is still studied daily around the world, including through programmes that complete it in a set cycle, and finishing a tractate is marked with a celebration called a siyum. One tractate, Pirkei Avot, 'Ethics of the Fathers', full of moral sayings, is read by many on Sabbath afternoons in summer. Rabbi Judah's burial place at Beit She'arim, with its catacombs, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015.

Academy of Sura.background:
Jews had lived in Babylonia, in what is now Iraq, since the exile of the sixth century BCE. By the early third century CE it had a large, settled community under the Parthian Empire, and from 224 CE under the new Persian Sasanian dynasty. It was led by a hereditary Exilarch, or 'head of the exile', who claimed descent from King David.

Abba Arikha, called Rav, meaning 'the master', was a Babylonian who went to study in the Land of Israel with Rabbi Judah the Prince, editor of the Mishnah. He brought the Mishnah back with him.
Academy of Sura.happened:
According to the letter of Rav Sherira Gaon, written in 987 CE, Rav returned to Babylonia in 219 CE and founded an academy at Sura, on a branch of the Euphrates, where Jewish learning had been weak. Thousands of students are said to have come. His colleague Shmuel led the academy at Nehardea. After the city of Nehardea was destroyed in 259, its scholars moved to Pumbedita, where Rav Yehuda bar Yehezkel led a new academy.

Rav and Shmuel's many debates fill the pages of the Talmud. Rav tended to rule on ritual matters and Shmuel on civil law, and Shmuel's principle that 'the law of the land is the law' guided Jews living under foreign rulers. The academies held study gatherings called kallah months twice a year, in Adar and Elul, when ordinary people came to learn.
Academy of Sura.matters:
For the next eight centuries, Sura and Pumbedita were the heart of Jewish learning. Their scholars produced the Babylonian Talmud, completed around 500 CE under Rav Ashi and Ravina. From the late sixth century their heads, called Geonim, meaning 'excellencies', answered questions of Jewish law from communities as far as Spain and North Africa. Famous Geonim included Saadia Gaon of Sura and Hai Gaon of Pumbedita, who died in 1038.

The Babylonian Talmud became the most authoritative text of Jewish law and study, and is still learned daily worldwide. Tradition also credits Rav with composing the prayer Aleinu for the Rosh Hashanah service. The Jewish community of Iraq lasted until most of its members left in the mid-twentieth century.

Dura-Europos synagogue.background:
Dura-Europos was founded around 300 BCE by the Seleucid Greeks on a cliff above the Euphrates, in what is now eastern Syria. It later came under Parthian rule and from about 165 CE belonged to Rome, serving as a frontier fortress facing Persia. Its population mixed Greeks, Semitic peoples, Romans and Jews, and it had temples to many gods, a Mithraeum and an early Christian house church.

It was long thought that ancient Jews avoided images of people in religious settings, because of the second commandment against making graven images.
Dura-Europos synagogue.happened:
The Jewish community enlarged and redecorated its synagogue, and an Aramaic inscription dates the work to about 244 to 245 CE. The walls of the main hall were covered from floor to ceiling with paintings in several bands. They show scenes from the Bible, including Pharaoh's daughter finding baby Moses, the crossing of the Red Sea, Samuel anointing David, Elijah on Mount Carmel, the story of Esther and Mordecai, and Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones coming back to life. Above the Torah niche are the Temple, a menorah and the binding of Isaac.

Around 256 CE, as the Persian Sasanian army under Shapur I threatened, the defenders built a large earth bank against the inner side of the city wall, burying the buildings along it, including the synagogue. The city fell anyway and was abandoned. In 1932 a Yale and French team uncovered the synagogue, its paintings preserved by the earth.
Dura-Europos synagogue.matters:
The discovery changed scholars' understanding of ancient Jewish art. It showed that in at least some communities, Jews were comfortable with rich pictures of biblical figures in their synagogue. The paintings are also an early visual commentary on the Bible, sometimes reflecting stories known from later rabbinic writings, called midrash.

The paintings were taken down and reassembled in a reconstructed hall at the National Museum in Damascus. The site itself was badly damaged by looting during the Syrian civil war that began in 2011. Copies and reconstructions can be seen elsewhere, including at Yale University and at ANU, the Museum of the Jewish People in Tel Aviv.

Rome becomes Christian.background:
For its first three centuries, Christianity was a minority faith in the Roman Empire, at times persecuted. Constantine, who won power at the Battle of the Milvian Bridge in 312 CE, credited the Christian God with his victory. In 313 the Edict of Milan granted religious tolerance, and Constantine increasingly favoured the Church.

The Jews of the empire were a recognised and legal religion. But Christian leaders saw Judaism as a rival and wanted to draw a clear line between the two faiths, which had shared so much.
Rome becomes Christian.happened:
In 325 CE Constantine called the Council of Nicaea, the first gathering of bishops from across the empire. Among its decisions, it ruled that all churches should celebrate Easter on the same day, and that the date should no longer depend on the Jewish calculation of Passover. Constantine's letter announcing this used hostile language about the Jews.

Laws followed over the next century, later collected in the Theodosian Code of 438. Constantine's laws punished Jews who attacked converts to Christianity and forbade Jews from converting Christians or circumcising Christian slaves. Under his son Constantius II, marriages between Jewish men and Christian women were banned in some cases. In the early fifth century, Theodosius II forbade the building of new synagogues. In Jerusalem, Constantine's mother Helena visited, and the Church of the Holy Sepulchre was dedicated in 335.
Rome becomes Christian.matters:
The Christianisation of Rome changed the position of Jews for the next 1,500 years. Judaism remained legal, but Jews were increasingly treated as second-class subjects. Church teaching held that Jews should survive as witnesses but in a lowly state, an idea later developed by Augustine. These attitudes shaped Jewish life throughout Christian Europe.

Jerusalem became a Christian holy city filled with churches. The Bordeaux Pilgrim, a Christian traveller of 333, describes Jews coming once a year to mourn near a pierced stone on the Temple Mount, and later writers such as Jerome describe the same custom on the 9th of Av. This annual lament is one of the roots of Jewish prayer at the Western Wall.

Hillel II fixes the calendar.background:
The Jewish calendar is lunisolar. Months follow the moon, but the year must keep in step with the sun so that Passover always falls in spring. This is done by adding a thirteenth month, a second Adar, seven times in every nineteen years.

In ancient times the Sanhedrin decided both questions. The Mishnah (Rosh Hashanah, chapter 2) describes witnesses coming to the court to report seeing the new moon. The court then declared the new month, and the news was spread by fire signals on hilltops and later by messengers. Communities too far away to hear in time kept two days of each festival, out of doubt about the date.
Hillel II fixes the calendar.happened:
By the fourth century the Jewish community in the Land of Israel was weakened and Christian Roman rulers restricted the authority of the patriarchs. According to a tradition preserved by the medieval scholar Abraham bar Hiyya, quoting Hai Gaon, in the year 4119 of the Jewish calendar, about 359 CE, the patriarch Hillel II, a descendant of Hillel the Elder, published the rules for calculating the calendar.

The system uses an average lunar month of just over 29 and a half days, a fixed nineteen-year cycle of leap years and rules that adjust the start of the year. These rules make sure, for example, that Yom Kippur never falls on a Friday or Sunday, which would put two days of strict rest back to back. Many historians think the calendar developed gradually and was not fully fixed until the ninth or tenth century, when a famous dispute between Saadia Gaon and Aaron ben Meir was settled.
Hillel II fixes the calendar.matters:
The fixed calendar allowed Jews anywhere in the world to keep the festivals on the same dates without depending on a court in the Land of Israel. It is still the calendar used today, setting the dates of Rosh Hashanah, Passover and every other Jewish holiday, as well as bar and bat mitzvahs and memorial days.

Even so, Jews outside Israel still keep a second day of most festivals. The Talmud (Beitzah 4b) explains this as keeping the custom of their ancestors, even though the dates are now known. The calendar also remains a lasting link to the ancient practice of watching the new moon.

Julian's Temple plan.background:
Julian was a nephew of Constantine. Raised as a Christian, he turned to the traditional Greek and Roman religion, which is why Christians called him 'the Apostate'. He became sole emperor in 361 CE and set out to reverse the rise of Christianity, restoring pagan temples and removing privileges from the Church.

He was also interested in sacrifice and in old religions. Rebuilding the Jewish Temple, destroyed by Rome nearly three centuries earlier, would both honour an ancient form of worship and disprove the Christian belief that the Temple's destruction was permanent.
Julian's Temple plan.happened:
In 362 to 363 Julian announced that the Temple should be rebuilt and put Alypius of Antioch, a former official in Britain, in charge. A letter addressed to the Jewish community and promising help is preserved under his name, though its authenticity is debated. Jews are said to have gathered to help, and materials were collected.

The pagan Roman historian Ammianus Marcellinus, who served in Julian's army, wrote that as work began on the foundations, frightening balls of fire burst out near them, burning some of the workers, and the work was abandoned. A strong earthquake hit the region on 18 to 19 May 363, damaging many cities, and it may explain the fires. Julian marched against Persia and was killed in battle on 26 June 363. His Christian successors had no interest in the project.
Julian's Temple plan.matters:
Christian writers such as Gregory of Nazianzus and John Chrysostom saw the failure as a sign from God. In Jewish sources the episode is barely mentioned, perhaps because the hope ended so quickly. It was the last time before the modern era that a ruler seriously planned to rebuild the Temple.

In 1969, during excavations by the Western Wall, archaeologist Benjamin Mazar found a verse from Isaiah carved on one of the stones, about seeing and rejoicing and bones flourishing like grass. Some scholars link it to the hopes of Julian's time, while others date it differently. The episode remains a striking 'what if' of Jewish history.

Jerusalem Talmud.background:
After the Mishnah was completed around 200 CE, scholars in both the Land of Israel and Babylonia began studying it in depth. These later sages are called Amoraim, meaning 'speakers' or 'interpreters'. In the Land of Israel the main academies were in the Galilee and on the coast, at Tiberias, Sepphoris and Caesarea.

Leading figures included Rabbi Yohanan bar Nappaha, who headed the academy in Tiberias for many decades in the third century, and his brother-in-law and study partner Resh Lakish, a former gladiator according to tradition. Their students and successors carried on the work.
Jerusalem Talmud.happened:
Over about 150 years, the discussions of these sages were gathered and edited into the Talmud Yerushalmi, known in English as the Jerusalem Talmud or the Talmud of the Land of Israel. It is written mostly in a western dialect of Aramaic, with Hebrew passages, and was completed around 350 to 400 CE.

It covers 39 tractates of the Mishnah, mostly from the first four orders. It has no commentary on the orders of Kodashim, about the Temple, or Tohorot, about purity, except part of one tractate. Its text is shorter and often less polished than the Babylonian Talmud. Historians link this to hard times in the Land of Israel: a Jewish revolt against the Roman ruler Gallus in 351 to 352, the earthquake of 363, Christian pressure, and the end of the patriarchate around 425.
Jerusalem Talmud.matters:
The Babylonian Talmud, edited for another century or more in more stable conditions, became the main authority in Jewish law, partly due to the influence of the Babylonian Geonim. The Jerusalem Talmud was studied less, and only one complete medieval manuscript survives, copied in 1289 and now in Leiden in the Netherlands. It was first printed in Venice by Daniel Bomberg in 1523.

It remains essential for understanding the laws tied to the Land of Israel, such as tithes and the Sabbatical year, called shmita, which have become practical questions again in modern Israel. It also preserves valuable details about daily life, history and geography in Roman and Byzantine Palestine, and today it is studied in a daily page cycle of its own.

End of the Patriarchate.background:
After the Romans crushed the Bar Kokhba revolt in 135 CE, the Jews of the Land of Israel rebuilt their community life in the Galilee. At its head stood the Patriarch, called the Nasi in Hebrew, meaning "prince". The office passed from father to son in the family of Hillel the Elder, the great sage of the 1st century BCE. The most famous Patriarch, Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi, edited the Mishnah, the first written collection of Jewish oral law, around 200 CE.

The Patriarchs moved their seat several times, from Usha to Beit She'arim, Sepphoris and finally Tiberias. The Roman state recognised them as the official leaders of the Jews across the empire. They appointed judges, sent messengers to distant communities, collected a tax from Jews abroad and fixed the Hebrew calendar.
End of the Patriarchate.happened:
Once the empire became Christian in the 4th century, the Patriarch's position grew uncomfortable. Imperial laws began to limit Jewish rights. In 415 Emperor Theodosius II stripped Gamaliel VI of his honorary rank, accusing him of building new synagogues and judging cases between Jews and Christians. Gamaliel died around 425 without a son to succeed him.

The government chose not to appoint anyone new. A law of 429 refers to the time "after the passing of the Patriarchs" and orders that the tax once paid to them now go to the imperial treasury. With that, an office that had lasted for over three hundred years quietly came to an end.
End of the Patriarchate.matters:
With no central leader in the Land of Israel, the balance of the Jewish world slowly shifted east to Babylonia. There the Exilarch, or Head of the Exile, and the heads of the great academies became the main authorities for centuries. Their work would produce the Babylonian Talmud, which outweighed its Galilean counterpart, the Jerusalem Talmud.

The Patriarchs' era is still visible on the ground. At Beit She'arim, in the hills of lower Galilee, rock-cut catacombs hold the tombs of Judah ha-Nasi's family and of Jews brought from as far as Syria and Mesopotamia to be buried near him. The inscriptions in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek give a rare picture of Jewish life at the time. The site was listed by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site in 2015.

Babylonian Talmud.background:
Jews had lived in Babylonia, in today's Iraq, since the exile of 586 BCE. By the 3rd century CE it was one of the largest and most settled Jewish communities in the world, living under Persian rule with its own leader, the Exilarch. Around 219 CE the sage Rav returned from studying with Judah ha-Nasi in the Galilee and founded an academy at Sura. His colleague Shmuel led the academy at Nehardea, and after Nehardea was destroyed in 259 its students moved to Pumbedita.

The rabbis of this period are called Amoraim, meaning "speakers" or "explainers". Their task was to study the Mishnah line by line, work out its reasoning, settle contradictions and apply it to new situations.
Babylonian Talmud.happened:
For about three centuries the discussions of these academies were memorised, repeated and gradually shaped into a written text called the Gemara, meaning "study". Together the Mishnah and the Gemara make up the Talmud. Tradition, based on a famous letter of Rav Sherira Gaon written in 987, names Rav Ashi of Sura and later Ravina as its chief editors, with Ravina's death in 499 marking the close of the Talmud. Later scholars called Savoraim added finishing touches over the following generations.

The Talmud is written mostly in Aramaic, the everyday language of Babylonian Jews, with Hebrew quotations. It covers 37 of the Mishnah's 63 tractates and records arguments between rabbis across many generations, often leaving questions open. Legal debate sits side by side with sermons, legends, dreams, medical advice and humour.
Babylonian Talmud.matters:
The Babylonian Talmud became the foundation of Jewish law and learning everywhere. Later codes of law, from Maimonides to the Shulchan Aruch, are built on it. The page layout used today was set by Daniel Bomberg's printed edition in Venice in the 1520s and the Vilna edition of the 1880s, so a reference to a page and side means the same thing in any yeshiva in the world.

In 1923 Rabbi Meir Shapiro proposed Daf Yomi, the study of one page a day by Jews everywhere at the same pace. A full cycle of 2,711 pages takes about seven and a half years. Its completion is marked by a celebration called the Siyum HaShas, and the 2020 siyum filled MetLife Stadium in New Jersey with around 90,000 people.

Jewish kingdom of Himyar.background:
Himyar was a wealthy kingdom in the south-west of the Arabian peninsula, in today's Yemen, grown rich on trade in incense and its position on the Red Sea routes. Jews had probably lived there for centuries. In the late 4th century the Himyarite kings stopped mentioning the old pagan gods in their inscriptions and began to honour one God, called Rahmanan, "the Merciful". Some inscriptions also use Jewish phrases such as "Israel" and "Amen", and most historians conclude that the ruling family had adopted Judaism or a form of monotheism close to it.

Himyar sat between two great powers. To the north was Christian Byzantium, and across the Red Sea lay the Christian kingdom of Aksum in Ethiopia. The town of Najran, in the north of Himyar, had a large Christian community with links to both.
Jewish kingdom of Himyar.happened:
Around 522 a Jewish ruler named Yusuf As'ar Yath'ar, known in Arabic sources as Dhu Nuwas, took power. He fought against the Aksumite garrison and its local allies, and in 523 he besieged Najran. Christian sources such as the Letter of Simeon of Beth Arsham and the Book of the Himyarites describe how, after the town surrendered, many Christians who refused to give up their faith were killed, among them a leader named al-Harith, remembered as Saint Arethas. The numbers in these accounts are large but hard to check.

The news shocked the Christian world. With Byzantine encouragement, King Kaleb of Aksum sent an army across the Red Sea around 525. Dhu Nuwas was defeated and killed.
Jewish kingdom of Himyar.matters:
Himyar is one of the very few places where Judaism became the faith of a ruling dynasty, alongside the later Khazars. Its story shows how far Judaism had spread in the ancient world. Many Muslim commentators link the Najran killings to the "People of the Ditch" mentioned in chapter 85 of the Quran, and the Christians of Najran honour their martyrs to this day.

The fall of the kingdom did not end Jewish life in Yemen. Yemenite Jews kept their own rich traditions of prayer, Torah reading with Aramaic translation, and poetry for about 1,400 more years. Between 1949 and 1950 almost the whole community, around 49,000 people, was airlifted to Israel in Operation On Wings of Eagles, also known as Operation Magic Carpet.

Justinian's decree.background:
The Byzantine, or Eastern Roman, Empire was by now firmly Christian. Earlier emperors had already passed laws limiting Jewish rights, gathered in the Theodosian Code of 438. Emperor Justinian, who ruled from 527 to 565, set out to reorganise all Roman law, producing the great collection later called the Corpus Juris Civilis. He also wanted a single Christian faith across his lands, and he pressed hard on pagans, heretics, Samaritans and Jews.

In many synagogues around the Mediterranean, Jews spoke Greek rather than Hebrew. A dispute broke out within Jewish communities over whether the Torah reading should be in Hebrew only, or translated into Greek so everyone could follow it. The matter reached the emperor.
Justinian's decree.happened:
On 8 February 553 Justinian issued Novella 146, addressed to the Jews. It allowed the Bible to be read in Greek, Latin or any other language the congregation understood, and recommended the Greek Septuagint or the translation of Aquila. But it banned what it called the deuterosis, the "second teaching", meaning the Mishnah and the rabbinic interpretation of the Bible. Jewish leaders who tried to stop the translated reading, or who taught the oral tradition, could be punished.

The law also went beyond questions of language. It warned against Jewish beliefs the emperor considered errors, such as denying the resurrection. Other laws of Justinian kept Jews out of most public posts while still demanding that they pay the heavy costs of serving on town councils.
Justinian's decree.matters:
Novella 146 is one of the earliest cases of a government stepping inside the synagogue to dictate how Jews should read and explain their own scriptures. It treated the oral law, which rabbis saw as given at Sinai alongside the written Torah, as something dangerous to be suppressed.

How strictly it was enforced is unclear, and Jewish learning carried on. Some historians suggest that limits on traditional sermons may have helped the rise of synagogue poetry, the piyyut, which wove rabbinic teaching into hymns. This idea is debated. Justinian's legal code went on to shape European law for centuries, carrying its restrictions on Jews with it.

The first piyyutim.background:
Early Jewish prayer was quite flexible. The basic themes of the main prayers were fixed, but the leader of the service could express them in his own words. In the Land of Israel, especially from the 5th century onwards, prayer leaders began to compose elaborate new poems to decorate the fixed prayers on Sabbaths and festivals. These poems are called piyyutim, from the same Greek root as the word "poetry", and their authors are called paytanim.

The first poet known by name is Yose ben Yose, who probably lived in the 4th or 5th century. His poems for the Day of Atonement are still part of some services today.
The first piyyutim.happened:
Yannai, who lived in the Land of Israel in the 6th century, was the first major paytan to use rhyme throughout his work. He wrote cycles of poems, called kerovot, for the weekly Torah readings, retelling the Bible through rabbinic legends and laws. Much of his work was lost for centuries, until thousands of fragments were found among the manuscripts of the Cairo Genizah, the storeroom of an old Cairo synagogue, and published from the 1930s onwards.

Eleazar Kalir, who lived a little later, probably in the 6th or 7th century, became the most famous of the early poets. His style is dense and difficult, full of rare words, puzzles and acrostics where the lines spell out the alphabet or the poet's name. A later legend claims that Yannai became jealous of his gifted student, but historians treat this as folklore.
The first piyyutim.matters:
Kalir's poems became deeply rooted in the Ashkenazi tradition. Many of the kinot, or laments, recited on Tisha B'Av, the fast mourning the destruction of the Temples, are attributed to him. So are the prayer for rain recited on Shemini Atzeret and the prayer for dew on the first day of Passover.

Not everyone admired the style. Abraham ibn Ezra, the 12th-century Spanish scholar, criticised Kalir's obscure language. Yet piyyut grew into one of the great traditions of Hebrew writing, from Spain to Germany. The High Holy Day prayer book, the machzor, is still full of these poems, and they were key in keeping Hebrew alive as a creative language long before modern times.

Persians take Jerusalem.background:
For centuries Byzantium and Sasanian Persia fought over the Near East. In 602 a new war broke out, and under King Khosrow II the Persians pushed deep into Byzantine lands, taking Antioch and Damascus. For the Jews of the Land of Israel, who suffered under Byzantine laws and had been barred from Jerusalem, the Persian advance raised hopes of freedom and even of redemption.

Jews had lived under Persian rule in Babylonia in relative peace for centuries. According to Christian chroniclers, Jewish men from Tiberias and the Galilee joined the advancing Persian army. A wealthy Jew of Tiberias named Benjamin is said to have helped fund and arm them.
Persians take Jerusalem.happened:
In the spring of 614 the Persian general Shahrbaraz besieged Jerusalem. After about three weeks the walls were breached. Christian accounts, especially that of the monk Strategius, describe a terrible massacre of the city's Christians and the burning of churches, including the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. The relic believed to be the True Cross was carried off to Persia. These accounts blame Jews for some of the killing, and historians debate how far they are accurate.

The Persians handed the city to Jewish rule for a short time. A leader known as Nehemiah ben Hushiel may have begun preparing to restore Temple worship. But within about three years the Persians, needing the support of the Christian majority, turned against the Jews and removed them. In 629 the Byzantine Emperor Heraclius defeated Persia and returned to Jerusalem the following year. Despite promises of safety, Jews were killed and banned once more from the city.
Persians take Jerusalem.matters:
These events left deep scars between Jews and Christians in the region. They also produced Jewish writings full of hope and despair, such as the Book of Zerubbabel, an apocalyptic text that imagines the coming of the Messiah amid the wars of Persia and Rome.

The episode was brief, but it was the last time in over 1,300 years that Jews held any kind of rule in Jerusalem. Only a few years later, in 638, the city fell to the Arab armies of Islam, and the history of the region took a completely new direction.

Jews return to Jerusalem.background:
After the Bar Kokhba revolt in 135 CE, the Roman Emperor Hadrian rebuilt Jerusalem as a pagan city named Aelia Capitolina and banned Jews from entering it. Under the Christian Byzantine emperors the ban largely continued. Jews were usually allowed in only once a year, on the 9th of Av, to mourn the destroyed Temple. The brief period of Jewish control after the Persian conquest of 614 ended in expulsion and bloodshed in 630.

In the 630s Arab armies, newly united under Islam, swept out of Arabia. They defeated the Byzantines at the Battle of Yarmouk in 636 and then besieged Jerusalem.
Jews return to Jerusalem.happened:
In 637 or 638 the Patriarch of Jerusalem, Sophronius, agreed to surrender the city. Tradition says he insisted on handing it over to the Caliph Umar in person, and that Umar came to Jerusalem to accept it. A later Christian text claims the surrender terms banned Jews from the city, but historians doubt this document is genuine in its known form.

A letter found in the Cairo Genizah tells a different story. It describes Jewish leaders asking Umar for permission to settle, and Umar allowing seventy Jewish families from Tiberias to move in. They are said to have settled near the southern side of the Temple Mount, close to the Siloam pool. Over time a Jewish quarter formed, with synagogues and a community that included both mainstream Rabbanite Jews and, later, Karaites.
Jews return to Jerusalem.matters:
This was the first time in about five hundred years that Jews could openly live in Jerusalem. From the 10th century the leading academy of the Land of Israel, the Yeshiva of the Land of Israel, moved from Tiberias to Jerusalem, and the city again became a centre of Jewish learning and pilgrimage.

The community suffered many blows in the centuries that followed, including the Crusader massacre of 1099. Yet Jews returned again and again, and a Jewish presence in the city continued in some form almost without a break up to modern times. Muslim rule also turned Jerusalem into a holy city of Islam, adding a third great faith to its long story.

Dome of the Rock built.background:
The Temple Mount in Jerusalem had been the holiest place in Judaism since King Solomon's Temple. Jewish tradition identifies it with Mount Moriah, where Abraham bound Isaac, as told in Genesis and linked in 2 Chronicles 3:1. The Mishnah, in tractate Yoma, speaks of a stone in the Holy of Holies called the Even ha-Shetiyah, the Foundation Stone, on which the Ark of the Covenant once rested. Later tradition saw it as the point from which the world was created.

After the Romans destroyed the Second Temple in 70 CE, the Mount lay largely in ruins under Byzantine rule. When the Arabs took Jerusalem in 638, they cleared the site and built a simple mosque on it.
Dome of the Rock built.happened:
The Umayyad caliphs, ruling from Damascus, then set out to build monuments to match the great churches of Byzantium. Caliph Abd al-Malik ordered a shrine over the great rock at the top of the Mount. Its dedication inscription gives the Islamic year 72, which corresponds to 691 or 692 CE.

The building is an octagon crowned with a dome, decorated with rich mosaics probably made by craftsmen trained in Byzantine workshops. Inside, Arabic inscriptions taken from the Quran run around the walls, many addressed to Christians and their beliefs about Jesus. In Muslim tradition the site became linked to the Prophet Muhammad's Night Journey to "the farthest mosque" and his ascent to heaven. The nearby al-Aqsa Mosque was built soon after.
Dome of the Rock built.matters:
The Dome of the Rock is one of the oldest Islamic buildings still standing in close to its original form, and it has become an icon of Jerusalem. Its golden dome, re-covered in gold leaf in a restoration completed in 1994, dominates the skyline of the Old City.

For Jews it stands on or near the place of the ancient Temple, although historians and archaeologists debate exactly where the Holy of Holies stood. The Mount, called the Haram al-Sharif in Arabic, is now holy to both Jews and Muslims. Under long-standing arrangements it is administered by an Islamic trust, and non-Muslims may visit but not pray there. Jews pray instead at the Western Wall below, and the site remains one of the most sensitive places in the world.

Visigoths enslave Spain's Jews.background:
Jews had lived in Spain since Roman times. After the Western Roman Empire fell, the Visigoths, a Germanic people, ruled Spain from their capital at Toledo. At first they followed Arian Christianity, a form of the faith that most of the Church considered heresy, and they largely left the Jews alone. That changed when King Reccared converted to Catholic Christianity, confirmed at the Third Council of Toledo in 589.

From then on, Church councils at Toledo and Visigothic kings issued a stream of anti-Jewish laws. King Sisebut ordered Jews to be baptised around 613, and many were. The Fourth Council of Toledo in 633, led by Bishop Isidore of Seville, said forced baptism was wrong, but ruled that those already baptised must remain Christians. Later laws banned Jewish rites, marriage customs and circumcision.
Visigoths enslave Spain's Jews.happened:
By the late 7th century many Jews had been baptised under pressure while still practising Judaism in secret, and many others had fled to North Africa. In 694 King Egica told the Seventeenth Council of Toledo that Jews in Spain were plotting with Jews overseas to overthrow the kingdom. There is no independent evidence for this plot.

The council ordered that all Jews who had not truly converted be reduced to slavery. Their property was confiscated and they were handed to Christian masters, who were forbidden to let them practise their religion. Their children were to be taken away from about the age of seven and raised as Christians, and later married only to Christians.
Visigoths enslave Spain's Jews.matters:
The decree marks the lowest point of Jewish life in Visigothic Spain. It shows a pattern that would return in Spanish history: forced conversion, suspicion of converts, and the claim that Jews were a hidden danger to the state. The Inquisition's treatment of the conversos eight centuries later echoes it.

The Visigothic kingdom itself was weak and divided. When Muslim armies crossed from North Africa in 711, it collapsed within a few years. Arab chroniclers record that Jews, freed from Visigothic laws, helped the newcomers, and under Muslim rule Spanish Jewry recovered and later flourished.

Muslims conquer Spain.background:
By the start of the 8th century the Umayyad Caliphate stretched from Persia to the Atlantic coast of Morocco. Across the narrow strait lay the Visigothic kingdom of Spain, torn by quarrels among its nobles over the throne of King Roderic. Its Jewish population had suffered decades of forced baptism, and since 694 Jews who refused to convert had been declared slaves.

The governor of North Africa, Musa ibn Nusayr, saw an opportunity. In the spring of 711 he sent a force of mostly Berber soldiers under his commander Tariq ibn Ziyad across the strait.
Muslims conquer Spain.happened:
Tariq landed at the great rock that still bears his name, Gibraltar, from the Arabic Jabal Tariq, "Mount of Tariq". In the summer of 711 he defeated Roderic, who was killed, at a battle usually placed near the Guadalete river. Tariq then marched north and took the Visigothic capital, Toledo. Musa followed with a larger army in 712, and within a few years most of the peninsula was under Muslim control.

Arab chronicles describe how, as cities fell, the conquerors gathered the local Jews and left them to hold places such as Córdoba, Granada and Seville alongside a small Muslim force, while the army moved on. The newcomers called their new province al-Andalus.
Muslims conquer Spain.matters:
Under Islamic law, Jews and Christians were treated as dhimmis, protected but second-class subjects who paid a special tax. This was still a great improvement on Visigothic rule. In 756 Abd al-Rahman I, a survivor of the Umayyad family, founded an independent emirate based in Córdoba, which became a caliphate in 929. The city grew into one of the great centres of learning in the world.

Jewish life revived, and from the 10th century al-Andalus saw the Golden Age of Spanish Jewry, in poetry, philosophy, science and law. Historians today debate how peaceful this era of coexistence, sometimes called convivencia, really was. Christian kingdoms in the north slowly pushed south in what they called the Reconquista, which ended with the fall of Granada in 1492.

The Khazars convert.background:
The Khazars were a Turkic people who built a powerful empire on the steppes north of the Caucasus, between the Black Sea and the Caspian, from the 7th century. Their capital, Atil, stood on the lower Volga river. Khazaria controlled key trade routes linking Byzantium, the Islamic world, Scandinavia and the lands of the Rus, and it held back Arab armies from pushing north through the Caucasus.

Surrounded by Christian Byzantium and the Muslim caliphate, Khazar rulers came under pressure to adopt one of the great faiths. Jews from Byzantium and the Islamic lands also came to live in Khazaria.
The Khazars convert.happened:
The main Jewish source is a letter written in the 10th century by King Joseph of Khazaria to Hasdai ibn Shaprut, a Jewish official in Córdoba who had heard of a Jewish kingdom and wrote to ask about it. Joseph tells how an ancestor, King Bulan, invited representatives of Christianity, Islam and Judaism. When the Christian and the Muslim each admitted that Judaism was the better of the other two faiths, Bulan chose Judaism. A later king, Obadiah, is said to have brought in rabbis and built synagogues. Another account, found in the Cairo Genizah and known as the Schechter Letter, tells a somewhat different story.

The date is debated. Some historians place the first step around 740, others in the 9th century. Coins struck around 837 with an inscription naming Moses as the messenger of God support a 9th-century Jewish identity among the ruling class. How far Judaism spread among ordinary Khazars is unclear.
The Khazars convert.matters:
The Khazar empire weakened in the 10th century and was broken by Prince Sviatoslav of Kiev in the 960s. Its fate after that is obscure.

The story captured the Jewish imagination. In the 12th century Judah Halevi used it as the frame for his philosophical work, the Kuzari, in which a rabbi explains Judaism to the Khazar king. In the 20th century some writers claimed that Ashkenazi Jews descend largely from the Khazars. Most historians and geneticists reject this theory, as the evidence points to Ashkenazi roots in the Middle East and southern Europe.

The Karaites.background:
By the 8th century the Babylonian Talmud had become the authority for most Jews. Its laws were applied by the Geonim, the heads of the academies of Sura and Pumbedita, and by the Exilarch, the official leader of Jews in the Islamic caliphate. Not everyone accepted this. Small groups had long questioned the rabbis' claim that an Oral Law, given at Sinai alongside the written Torah, should guide how the Bible is lived.

The Abbasid caliphs had just moved their capital to Baghdad, in the heart of the Jewish heartland of Babylonia, and new ideas were stirring in the Muslim world too, including debates about tradition and the plain meaning of scripture.
The Karaites.happened:
Around 767, when the Exilarch died, his elder relative Anan ben David was passed over and his younger brother Hananiah was chosen instead. According to later Rabbanite accounts, which are hostile to Anan, he set himself up as a rival leader, was imprisoned by the caliph and saved himself by declaring that he led a separate religion. Historians treat these details with caution.

Anan wrote a Book of Commandments in Aramaic, deriving the law directly from the Bible, often more strictly than the rabbis. His followers were first called Ananites. In the 9th century, under thinkers such as Benjamin al-Nahawandi, the wider movement took the name Karaites, from the Hebrew word for scripture, mikra. Karaites set the calendar by sighting the new moon and the ripening barley, and many did not keep lights burning on the Sabbath.
The Karaites.matters:
The challenge pushed Rabbanite Judaism to defend and explain itself. Saadia Gaon wrote fierce works against the Karaites, and the debate encouraged new study of Hebrew grammar and the plain meaning of the Bible on both sides. In the 10th and 11th centuries Karaite scholars in Jerusalem, called the Mourners of Zion, were among the finest Bible scholars of their age.

Karaite communities later lived in Egypt, Byzantium, Crimea and Lithuania, where a small community still survives in Trakai. Most Karaites today live in Israel, numbering in the tens of thousands, with centres in Ramla, Ashdod and Beersheba. In Jerusalem's Old City a Karaite synagogue named after Anan ben David still stands.

Isaac the Jew's embassy.background:
At the end of the 8th century two great rulers dominated the Mediterranean world. In the west, Charlemagne, King of the Franks, ruled most of today's France, Germany and northern Italy. In the east, the Abbasid Caliph Harun al-Rashid ruled from Baghdad over an empire stretching from North Africa to Central Asia. Both were rivals of Byzantium and of the Umayyad emirate in Spain, and each had reasons to seek the other's friendship.

Travel between these worlds was long and dangerous. Jews, who lived in both Christian and Muslim lands, often knew the languages and routes, and Jewish merchants were already carrying goods between Europe and the East.
Isaac the Jew's embassy.happened:
In 797 Charlemagne sent an embassy to Baghdad led by two noblemen, Lantfrid and Sigimund, with a Jewish man named Isaac as interpreter and guide. The Royal Frankish Annals, the official chronicle of Charlemagne's reign, record that both noblemen died on the way. Isaac alone completed the mission.

In 801 Charlemagne learned that Isaac was returning with gifts from the caliph, including an elephant. Isaac landed at Porto Venere on the Italian coast in October 801, waited out the winter, and crossed the Alps. On 20 July 802 he reached Charlemagne's court at Aachen with the elephant, named Abul-Abbas. The animal lived there for several years and died in 810 while travelling with the army in northern Germany.
Isaac the Jew's embassy.matters:
Isaac is one of the first Jews in medieval Western Europe whose name appears in official records, and he shows how useful Jews could be as go-betweens in a divided world. His journey took about five years and spanned the Mediterranean, the Middle East and the Alps.

Charlemagne's reign is remembered in Jewish tradition as a time of protection. Later legends say he invited a Jewish scholar to Narbonne, and that the Kalonymus family came from Lucca in Italy to Mainz at a Carolingian king's request, helping to found Rhineland Jewry. Historians see these as traditions rather than proven facts, but they reflect the real growth of Jewish communities in Frankish lands from this time.

Caliph's dress laws.background:
Under Islamic rule, Jews and Christians were classed as dhimmis, "protected people". They could practise their religion and run their own communities, but they paid a special poll tax called the jizya and lived under limits meant to show the superiority of Islam. These rules were later gathered in a document called the Pact of Umar, which tradition attributes to the Caliph Umar in the 7th century. Most historians think it took shape gradually over the following centuries.

In practice the rules were often ignored. Jews and Christians served as doctors, bankers, scribes and officials at the Abbasid court in Baghdad. Al-Mutawakkil, who became caliph in 847, wanted to change that and to win the support of strict religious scholars.
Caliph's dress laws.happened:
The historian al-Tabari records the caliph's decrees of the year 235 in the Islamic calendar, which began in 849 and ran into 850. Jews and Christians had to wear honey-coloured hoods and a special belt, and to sew two coloured patches onto their outer clothes. They could ride only with wooden stirrups and with special markings on their saddles. Wooden images of devils were to be nailed to their doors.

New churches and synagogues were to be demolished, and graves levelled with the ground. A tenth of their houses could be taken for mosques. They were banned from government posts, and their children from Muslim schools. A further decree in the following years added more rules on clothing.
Caliph's dress laws.matters:
The decrees were not enforced evenly or for long, and Jews and Christians soon returned to high office under later caliphs. Still, they set a model of marking non-Muslims by their clothing that rulers would revive again and again, as with the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim in the 11th century.

Historians also see a link with Christian Europe. In 1215 the Fourth Lateran Council ordered Jews and Muslims in Christian lands to wear distinguishing dress, and some historians think the Islamic rules were one influence. Out of this came the Jewish badge. The idea that a minority should be made visible in public as inferior has a long and painful history, reaching into the 20th century.

First Jewish prayer book.background:
For centuries Jews prayed mostly from memory. The basic structure of daily prayer, including the Shema and the Amidah, the central standing prayer, had been set by the rabbis of the Mishnah and Talmud. But the exact wording varied from place to place, and writing down prayers was at first discouraged. Communities far from the great academies often did not know the correct order or laws.

In the 9th century the heads of the Babylonian academies, called Geonim, answered questions sent from all over the Jewish world. These letters, known as responsa, were carried along trade routes and copied many times.
First Jewish prayer book.happened:
Around 860 a rabbi in Spain, writing on behalf of his community, asked Rav Amram bar Sheshna, Gaon of the academy of Sura, to explain the right order of prayers. Rav Amram replied with a complete guide: the weekday, Sabbath and festival services for the whole year, with the blessings and the laws for each, explained with reference to the Talmud and earlier Geonim. He also mentioned that he was sending a donation for the academy.

This text is known as Seder Rav Amram, "the Order of Rav Amram". The Hebrew word siddur, meaning prayer book, comes from the same root, meaning "order". The surviving manuscripts differ a great deal, because later copyists updated the prayers to match their own local customs, so the original wording is not always certain.
First Jewish prayer book.matters:
Seder Rav Amram is the oldest known complete order of Jewish prayer. It spread to Spain, North Africa, France and Germany and became the foundation for the next generation of prayer books, including that of Saadia Gaon in the 10th century and the Ashkenazi Machzor Vitry around 1100.

Today's prayer books, whether Sephardi, Ashkenazi or the Italian and Yemenite rites, all descend in some way from this framework. When a Jew opens a siddur anywhere in the world and finds the same order of service, it reflects a process that began with one letter from Babylonia to Spain.

Radhanite merchants.background:
In the 8th and 9th centuries the world was split between Christian Europe, the Byzantine Empire and the vast Islamic caliphate, with Tang China at the far end of the trade routes. Christians and Muslims were often at war and distrusted each other's merchants. Jews, who lived in all these lands, shared a common language of prayer and law, and could find fellow Jews to host them in almost any trading city.

Ibn Khordadbeh was a Persian official who served as director of posts and intelligence for the Abbasid caliphs. Around 870 he wrote the Book of Roads and Kingdoms, a guide to the routes, distances and taxes of the known world.
Radhanite merchants.happened:
In his book Ibn Khordadbeh describes Jewish merchants he calls al-Radhaniya. He says they spoke Arabic, Persian, Roman Greek, Frankish, Spanish and Slavic, and travelled from west to east and back by land and sea. From Europe they carried eunuchs, enslaved girls and boys, brocade, beaver and marten furs and swords. From the East they brought musk, aloe wood, camphor, cinnamon and other goods.

He lists four main routes. Some sailed from the land of the Franks to Egypt, crossed to the Red Sea and sailed on to India and China. Others went through Antioch and Baghdad down the Persian Gulf, or overland across North Africa, or north through the lands of the Slavs and the Khazars to Central Asia and China. The origin of their name is debated: it may come from a Persian phrase meaning "those who know the way", a district near Baghdad, or the Rhône valley in France.
Radhanite merchants.matters:
The Radhanites were among the few people who connected Western Europe with India and China at this time. Their trade helped bring spices, silk and other luxuries to Europe, though it also included the trade in enslaved people that was common across all these societies.

Their network seems to have faded by the 10th century, as the Tang dynasty collapsed in China and the Khazar empire fell. But their story is an early example of a lasting pattern: Jewish merchants using family and community ties across borders to link distant economies. Later documents from the Cairo Genizah show similar Jewish trading networks reaching from Spain to India.

Eldad the Danite.background:
According to the Bible, the Assyrians conquered the northern kingdom of Israel in about 722 BCE and carried off its people. Ten of the twelve tribes disappeared from history, becoming the "Lost Tribes". Jewish tradition kept alive the hope that they still lived somewhere far away and would one day return.

Ancient writers also spoke of the Sambatyon, a wondrous river. The Talmud and the midrash describe it as resting on the Sabbath, while Josephus describes a river in Syria that flows only on the seventh day. In rabbinic legend, some of the exiles lived on the far side of it.
Eldad the Danite.happened:
In the 880s a traveller named Eldad arrived in Kairouan, in North Africa. He spoke only Hebrew and said he came from the tribe of Dan. He described an independent Jewish kingdom in the land of Havilah, beyond the rivers of Cush in East Africa, where the tribes of Dan, Naphtali, Gad and Asher lived with their own king and army. He said the Children of Moses, descendants of the Levites, lived beyond the Sambatyon, which threw up stones all week and rested on the Sabbath. He also told of shipwreck and capture by cannibals.

Eldad brought his own laws of ritual slaughter, which differed from the Talmud's. The puzzled Jews of Kairouan wrote to Rav Tzemach Gaon of Sura. The Gaon replied that such differences could be expected among communities long cut off from the rest of the Jewish people.
Eldad the Danite.matters:
Eldad's account was copied and retold for centuries in many versions. It fed legends of hidden Jewish kingdoms, and later medieval stories about Prester John, a mythical Christian king in the East, also mention the Sambatyon. Historians still debate whether Eldad was a genuine traveller, perhaps from Yemen or East Africa, or a gifted storyteller.

His tale had a real modern impact. The 16th-century rabbi David ibn Zimra cited the tradition of Dan in Africa in discussing the Jews of Ethiopia. In 1973 Israel's Sephardi Chief Rabbi, Ovadia Yosef, relied on this line of rulings when he recognised the Beta Israel of Ethiopia as Jews descended from the tribe of Dan, opening the way for their immigration to Israel.

The Masoretes.background:
The Hebrew Bible was originally written with consonants only. Readers knew the right vowels and the melody of the reading from tradition, passed down orally. As Hebrew faded as a spoken language and Jews scattered across many lands, there was a real danger that the exact reading would be lost or that different versions would drift apart.

The scholars who guarded the text are called Masoretes, from masorah, meaning "tradition" or "transmission". They worked between about the 6th and 10th centuries, mainly in Tiberias, on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, but also in Babylonia, where rival systems developed.
The Masoretes.happened:
The Masoretes of Tiberias created a system of small dots and dashes placed above and below the letters to mark vowels. They added accent signs, called te'amim, that show which syllable is stressed, how the verse is divided, and the melody for chanting it in the synagogue. In the margins they wrote notes counting how often unusual words appear, recording spelling variants and marking the middle letters and words of books.

The Ben Asher family led this work for several generations. A codex of the Prophets bears a note saying Moses ben Asher completed it in Tiberias in 895. It was later kept by the Karaite community of Cairo and is known as the Cairo Codex. Some scholars think the surviving manuscript may be a slightly later copy of his work, so its exact date is debated. Moses' son Aaron ben Asher became the most famous Masorete of all.
The Masoretes.matters:
The Tiberian system defeated its rivals and became the standard for all Jewish communities. The text it preserved, called the Masoretic Text, is the Hebrew Bible read in synagogues today and the basis of most modern translations. The Dead Sea Scrolls, found in 1947, showed that the Masoretic consonants go back in close form to the time of the Second Temple.

When a Torah reader chants the weekly portion with its traditional melody, or a student learns the names of the Hebrew vowels, they are using the Masoretes' work. The Leningrad Codex of about 1008, the oldest complete Hebrew Bible, follows the Ben Asher tradition and is the basis of standard scholarly editions.

Kairouan's scholars.background:
Kairouan was founded by Arab armies around 670 in what is now Tunisia, and it became the capital of Muslim North Africa. It sat on the main routes between Egypt and Morocco and between the eastern Islamic world and Spain and Sicily. A Jewish community grew there as merchants and scholars settled in the city.

In 909 the Fatimids, a Shia dynasty, overthrew the earlier Aghlabid rulers and made Ifriqiya, roughly modern Tunisia, their base before later conquering Egypt. The court attracted doctors and scholars of all faiths.
Kairouan's scholars.happened:
Isaac Israeli, born in Egypt in the mid-9th century, served as a court physician in Kairouan, first to the last Aghlabid ruler and then to the first Fatimid caliph, al-Mahdi. He wrote in Arabic on fevers, diets and urine, as well as works of philosophy. Tradition says he lived to over a hundred. In the 11th century the scholar Constantine the African translated his medical books into Latin, and they were studied at the medical schools of Salerno and Montpellier and printed in Lyon in 1515.

Kairouan's Jewish scholars kept close ties with the Babylonian academies. In 987 Jacob ben Nissim of Kairouan asked Rav Sherira Gaon how the Mishnah and Talmud were written, and Sherira's reply became a key source for the history of the Talmud. A famous tale in Abraham ibn Daud's 12th-century chronicle says Rabbi Hushiel came to Kairouan after being captured at sea and ransomed. Historians treat that story as partly legend.
Kairouan's scholars.matters:
Hushiel's son, Rabbenu Chananel, who died around 1055, wrote one of the first commentaries on the Talmud, drawing on both the Babylonian and the Jerusalem Talmuds. It is printed in the margins of the standard Vilna Talmud. His colleague Rabbenu Nissim ben Jacob wrote works of law and a collection of moral stories.

Kairouan's golden era ended when the Banu Hilal tribes sacked the city in 1057, and its Jews scattered to other North African towns. But its scholars formed a vital bridge, carrying the learning of Babylonia westward to Spain and Europe, and Isaac Israeli's books shaped European medicine for centuries.

Saadia Gaon.background:
By the early 10th century the Babylonian academies of Sura and Pumbedita were losing strength, and Jewish life faced challenges from several sides. The Karaites rejected the rabbinic tradition. Arabic had become the everyday language of most Jews, who were exposed to Greek philosophy and Muslim theology, raising new questions about faith and reason.

Saadia ben Joseph was born in 882 in the Fayyum region of Egypt. He studied in Egypt and Tiberias before moving to Babylonia, already known as a brilliant young scholar.
Saadia Gaon.happened:
In 921 and 922 Saadia led the Babylonian side in a bitter quarrel with Aaron ben Meir, a leader in the Land of Israel, over the Hebrew calendar. The dispute meant that for a time communities might celebrate Passover on different days. Saadia's side won. In 928 the Exilarch David ben Zakkai appointed him Gaon of Sura, an unusual honour for someone born outside Babylonia. Within two years they fell out over a legal case, and Saadia was deposed. He used his years out of office to write, and was restored in 937. He died in 942.

Saadia translated the Torah and other books of the Bible into Arabic, written in Hebrew letters, with commentary. He compiled a prayer book with explanations in Arabic, wrote a Hebrew dictionary and works on grammar, and in 933 completed The Book of Beliefs and Opinions, the first systematic Jewish philosophy, arguing that reason and revelation lead to the same truths.
Saadia Gaon.matters:
Saadia set the pattern for medieval Jewish scholarship: careful study of Hebrew, rational defence of faith, and engagement with the culture around him. Maimonides, writing two centuries later, praised him as one who had strengthened the Torah when it was in danger of being forgotten.

His Arabic translation of the Torah, the Tafsir, is still printed and read by Yemenite Jews alongside the Hebrew text and its Aramaic translation. His writings against the Karaites shaped the way Rabbanite Judaism defined itself, and his name remains a byword for the Geonic age.

Aleppo Codex.background:
Before the 10th century the Bible was usually copied as separate scrolls. A codex, a bound book with pages, made it possible to gather all the books of the Hebrew Bible into one volume. In Tiberias, the Masoretes had perfected a system of vowel signs, accents and marginal notes to preserve the exact reading of the text, and the Ben Asher family led this work for generations.

Aaron ben Asher, son of Moses ben Asher, was regarded as the greatest master of this tradition. A carefully corrected manuscript from his hand would serve as a model for others.
Aleppo Codex.happened:
Around 930 the scribe Shlomo ben Buya'a copied the consonants of the whole Hebrew Bible in Tiberias, and Aaron ben Asher added the vowels, accents and Masoretic notes. The book was later bought by a Karaite from Basra and given to the Karaite community in Jerusalem. When the Crusaders took Jerusalem in 1099 it was seized, then ransomed and brought to Fustat, old Cairo. There Maimonides examined it and declared it the most reliable text, using it for the laws of writing a Torah scroll.

Tradition holds that a descendant of Maimonides brought it to Aleppo in Syria in the late 14th century. It was kept in a locked chest in the Great Synagogue and called the Keter, the Crown. In December 1947, after the United Nations vote to partition Palestine, rioters burned the synagogue. The codex survived but many pages were lost.
Aleppo Codex.matters:
In 1957 or 1958 the remaining pages were smuggled out of Syria and given to Israel's President, Yitzhak Ben-Zvi. Of an estimated 487 leaves, about 295 survive, and most of the Torah is missing. A couple of stray fragments have turned up since, and the fate of the rest is still a mystery.

The codex is now kept at the Shrine of the Book in the Israel Museum, Jerusalem. It is the basis of the Hebrew University Bible Project and of several modern editions of the Hebrew Bible. For the Jews of Aleppo it was a sacred treasure, and its story of survival through crusade, riot and smuggling has made it a symbol of the fragility and endurance of Jewish heritage.

Golden Age in Spain.background:
After the Muslim conquest of 711, Spain, called al-Andalus, became home to a large Jewish community living alongside Muslims and Christians. In 929 Abd al-Rahman III declared himself caliph in Córdoba, which grew into one of the richest and most cultured cities in Europe, with libraries, scholars and a thriving economy. Arabic was the language of science, poetry and government, and Jews spoke and wrote it fluently.

The term Golden Age is usually given to roughly the mid-10th to mid-12th centuries, when Jewish culture in Spain flourished as never before.
Golden Age in Spain.happened:
A central figure was Hasdai ibn Shaprut, physician and diplomat to Abd al-Rahman III. He helped translate a Greek medical work into Arabic, corresponded with the King of the Khazars and supported Jewish scholars and poets. Under his patronage the poet Dunash ben Labrat brought Arabic metre into Hebrew verse. In the 11th century Samuel ibn Naghrela rose to be vizier and army commander of Granada while writing Hebrew poetry and Talmudic works.

Solomon ibn Gabirol wrote both religious poems and a philosophical work, The Fountain of Life, which Christian scholars read in Latin for centuries without knowing its author was Jewish. Moses ibn Ezra, Abraham ibn Ezra, Bahya ibn Paquda and Judah Halevi wrote poetry, Bible commentary, ethics and philosophy. Halevi, who longed for Zion, travelled to the Land of Israel near the end of his life around 1141.
Golden Age in Spain.matters:
The Golden Age reshaped Jewish culture. It produced Hebrew grammar and Bible commentary, philosophy that tried to unite faith and reason, and a new tradition of Hebrew poetry about wine, love, nature and longing for God. Ibn Gabirol's long poem Keter Malkhut is read by many on the Day of Atonement, and Halevi's Songs of Zion are recited among the laments of Tisha B'Av.

It began to fade when the Almoravids and then the stricter Almohads invaded from North Africa from the 1090s, and many Jews fled to the Christian north or to Egypt, among them the young Maimonides. Historians debate how harmonious this era really was, but its writings remain among the treasures of Jewish literature.

Rabbenu Gershom's decrees.background:
By around the year 1000, Jewish communities had taken root along the Rhine in towns such as Mainz, Worms and Speyer. They were small, close-knit and mostly made up of merchants. They were far from Babylonia and its Geonim, so they needed their own leaders to settle disputes and set rules for community life.

Gershom ben Judah, born around 960, headed a yeshiva, a school of Talmud study, in Mainz. He trained a generation of scholars, among them the teachers of Rashi, and he carefully copied and corrected manuscripts of the Talmud and the Bible. His learning earned him the title Me'or ha-Golah, "Light of the Exile".
Rabbenu Gershom's decrees.happened:
Rabbenu Gershom, "our rabbi Gershom", is credited with a series of takkanot, or communal decrees, probably agreed at gatherings of community leaders. The best known bans a man from marrying more than one wife. The Bible and Talmud allowed polygamy, although it was already rare among European Jews. A second decree forbids a husband to divorce his wife against her will, a major change, since the Talmud gave the husband the sole power to divorce.

Other decrees banned opening or reading a letter addressed to someone else, and forbade taunting Jews who had been forced to convert and later returned to Judaism. Tradition holds that Gershom's own son had been forcibly converted. The decrees were backed by the threat of cherem, exclusion from the community. Some later rabbis said the polygamy ban was meant to last until the year 1240, but it remained in force.
Rabbenu Gershom's decrees.matters:
These decrees became binding law for Ashkenazi Jews, the Jews of Germany, France and later Eastern Europe, and they still are. Divorce under Jewish law today still requires the wife's consent because of Rabbenu Gershom. Sephardi and Yemenite communities did not formally adopt the polygamy ban, but in 1950 Israel's Chief Rabbinate extended it to all Jews in the country.

The ruling on letters is often cited today as an early defence of privacy. Rabbenu Gershom's broader legacy is the shaping of an independent Ashkenazi tradition of law and learning, which his students passed to Rashi and through him to the whole Jewish world.

Al-Hakim's persecution.background:
The Fatimids, a Shia Muslim dynasty, conquered Egypt in 969 and founded Cairo as their capital. They also ruled the Land of Israel and parts of Syria. Under the early Fatimid caliphs, Jews and Christians generally fared well, and some rose to high office. Jewish communities in Fustat, Jerusalem, Ramla and Tiberias prospered.

Al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah became caliph in 996 at the age of eleven. His reign was marked by sudden and strange decrees affecting all his subjects, including Muslims. He banned certain foods, ordered dogs killed and at times forbade women to leave their homes.
Al-Hakim's persecution.happened:
From about 1004 al-Hakim turned increasingly against non-Muslims. Jews and Christians were ordered to wear black and to carry heavy badges. Christians had to wear wooden crosses around their necks, and Jews blocks of wood, described in some accounts as shaped like a calf, a mocking reminder of the golden calf of the Bible. Churches and synagogues across his lands were destroyed or turned into mosques. In 1009 he ordered the destruction of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem.

Many Jews and Christians converted to Islam under pressure. Then, from around 1013, his policy began to change, and in his final years he allowed those who had been forced to convert to return to their faith and to rebuild their houses of worship. In 1021 al-Hakim vanished on one of his night rides outside Cairo, and his fate remains unknown.
Al-Hakim's persecution.matters:
The destruction of the Holy Sepulchre shocked Christian Europe. Some French chroniclers spread a false rumour that Jews had encouraged al-Hakim, and attacks on Jews followed in several French towns around 1010. Historians see these events as an early sign of the anti-Jewish violence that erupted during the Crusades.

Al-Hakim's reign shows how insecure the position of minorities could be, even in a society that was usually tolerant, when everything depended on one ruler's will. He is also remembered for another reason: the Druze faith, which began during his reign, regards him as a divine figure.

Rashi is born.background:
In the 11th century the Jews of northern France and the Rhineland lived in small communities, often of a few dozen families. They spoke the local language, which for Jews in Champagne was Old French. Studying the Bible and the Talmud was the heart of their culture, but these texts were difficult, written in Hebrew and Aramaic with few explanations. Young men travelled to the yeshivas of Mainz and Worms, founded by Rabbenu Gershom's circle, to learn.

Troyes, the main town of Champagne, was famous for its great trade fairs, and the surrounding region for its vineyards.
Rashi is born.happened:
Shlomo Yitzchaki was born in Troyes in 1040. His name is shortened to Rashi, from the initials of Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki. As a young man he studied in Mainz and Worms with leading scholars, students of Rabbenu Gershom. Around 1070 he returned to Troyes and founded his own school. Tradition holds that he supported himself through winemaking.

Rashi wrote a commentary on nearly the whole Bible and almost all of the Babylonian Talmud. He explained difficult words and ideas briefly and clearly, often translating terms into Old French written in Hebrew letters. These glosses, numbering in the thousands, are now a valuable source for the history of the French language. He lived to see the Crusader massacres of 1096 and died in 1105. He had three daughters, and his grandsons, among them Rabbi Samuel ben Meir and Rabbenu Tam, led the next generation of scholars, the Tosafists.
Rashi is born.matters:
Rashi's commentaries became essential. The first dated printed Hebrew book, produced in Reggio di Calabria in 1475, was his commentary on the Torah. In the printed Talmud, his notes run along the inner margin of every page, and the commentaries of his grandsons and their students, the Tosafot, run along the outer margin.

The semi-cursive Hebrew typeface used to print his commentary is still called Rashi script, although he never wrote in it himself. For centuries, children beginning Torah study have learned the weekly portion with Rashi's commentary, known as "Chumash with Rashi". In Worms, a small chapel next to the rebuilt synagogue is named after him.

Granada massacre.background:
In the early 11th century the Caliphate of Córdoba broke apart into small rival kingdoms called taifas. Granada was ruled by the Zirids, a Berber dynasty who were themselves a minority among the Arab and local Muslim population. They needed capable officials they could trust, and they found one in Samuel ibn Naghrela, a Jewish scholar who had fled Córdoba.

Samuel, known in Hebrew as Shmuel HaNagid, "the Prince", rose to become vizier, the chief minister, of King Habbus and then King Badis, and led Granada's armies into battle for many years. He was also a major Hebrew poet, writing about war, wine and mortality, a Talmud scholar, and the leader of Spanish Jewry. He died in 1056.
Granada massacre.happened:
His son Joseph took over as vizier. Joseph was educated and powerful, but he faced rising hostility. A poet named Abu Ishaq of Elvira wrote verses attacking the Jewish vizier and calling on Muslims to rise against the Jews of Granada. Rumours spread that Joseph was plotting to hand the kingdom to a rival ruler.

On 30 December 1066, which fell on a Sabbath, a mob stormed the royal palace where Joseph had taken refuge. He was killed and, according to the sources, his body was crucified on one of the city gates. The crowd then turned on the Jewish quarter. Accounts speak of about 1,500 Jewish families being killed, a figure often given as some 4,000 people, though exact numbers are uncertain. Joseph's widow and young son escaped to the town of Lucena.
Granada massacre.matters:
The massacre was one of the worst outbreaks of violence against Jews in Muslim Spain. It shows the danger faced by Jews who rose high in a court where their power depended on a ruler's favour and could provoke deep resentment.

Historians often point to Granada when debating the idea of a peaceful coexistence, or convivencia, in Islamic Spain. The Naghrela family's story holds both sides: a Jew could rise to the very top of a Muslim state, yet a single riot could destroy his community. Shmuel HaNagid's poetry, rediscovered in a manuscript in the 20th century, is still studied as one of the summits of medieval Hebrew verse.

First Crusade.background:
In November 1095, at the Council of Clermont in France, Pope Urban II called on Christians to march east to help Byzantium and free Jerusalem from Muslim rule. The response was huge. Alongside the organised armies of knights, popular preachers such as Peter the Hermit gathered large crowds of poorer pilgrims and soldiers who set off early in 1096.

The Rhineland towns had prosperous Jewish communities with famous yeshivas. Many Jews had close ties with local bishops, who were often their protectors. But some crusaders asked why they should travel far to fight the enemies of Christ while Jews lived among them.
First Crusade.happened:
A force led by Count Emicho of Flonheim, often called Emicho of Leiningen, and other bands attacked the Jews of the Rhineland in the spring of 1096. In Speyer on 3 May the bishop protected most of the community, though about a dozen people were killed. In Worms, around 18 and 25 May, some 800 Jews died. In Mainz on 27 May, the archbishop's protection failed and around 1,100 were killed. Further attacks hit Cologne and its surrounding villages, Trier, Metz, Regensburg and Prague.

The crusaders offered baptism or death. Many Jews chose to die, and some killed their own families and themselves rather than be forcibly converted, an act they saw as kiddush Hashem, sanctifying God's name. Three Hebrew chronicles, including the accounts of Solomon bar Samson and Eliezer bar Nathan, record these events in detail. In 1097 Emperor Henry IV allowed those forcibly baptised to return to Judaism.
First Crusade.matters:
The massacres were a turning point for Ashkenazi Jewry. Martyrdom became a central theme of its memory, and communities began keeping memorial books, called Memorbücher, listing the dead. The prayer Av HaRachamim, "Father of Mercy", composed in memory of the martyrs, is recited in many synagogues on Sabbath mornings. Laments, called kinot, about the Rhineland victims are read on Tisha B'Av.

Some Ashkenazi mourning customs during the weeks between Passover and Shavuot, the Omer period, are linked in part to these spring massacres. The old Jewish communities of Speyer, Worms and Mainz, known by their Hebrew initials as ShUM, were recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021.

Crusaders take Jerusalem.background:
Jerusalem had been under Muslim rule since 638. By the late 11th century it was contested between the Seljuk Turks and the Fatimids of Egypt, who recaptured the city in 1098. A Jewish community lived there, including both Rabbanite and Karaite Jews, though it had already suffered from the wars.

The armies of the First Crusade, having passed through the Rhineland massacres of 1096, crossed Byzantium and fought their way through Anatolia and Syria, taking Antioch in 1098. In June 1099 they reached Jerusalem and laid siege to it.
Crusaders take Jerusalem.happened:
On 15 July 1099 the crusaders, led by Godfrey of Bouillon and others, broke through the walls. Christian and Muslim chroniclers describe a terrible massacre of the city's Muslim inhabitants. Jews had taken part in the defence. According to the Damascus chronicler Ibn al-Qalanisi, the Jews gathered in their synagogue and the crusaders burned it with them inside.

Letters found in the Cairo Genizah, written by Jewish leaders in Ashkelon and Egypt soon after, show that not all Jews were killed. Some were taken captive and held for ransom, along with Torah scrolls and books. Jewish communities in Egypt and elsewhere raised large sums to free them, and the letters describe the hardship of the freed captives. Among the books ransomed was the precious Aleppo Codex.
Crusaders take Jerusalem.matters:
The crusaders founded the Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem and banned Jews and Muslims from living in the city. When the traveller Benjamin of Tudela visited around 1170, he found only a small number of Jewish dyers living near the Tower of David. Jewish life in the Land of Israel moved to other towns.

In 1187 Saladin retook Jerusalem and allowed Jews to return, and communities from North Africa and later France and England began to settle there. The Genizah ransom letters are an early example of the Jewish duty of pidyon shevuyim, redeeming captives, which the Talmud and later codes treat as one of the most important forms of charity.

Maimonides is born.background:
In the early 12th century Córdoba was still a great centre of Jewish learning, the heart of the Golden Age of Spanish Jewry. Moses ben Maimon was born there into a family of scholars. His father, Maimon, was a judge in the rabbinic court and his first teacher. The year of his birth is traditionally given as 1135, but many modern historians prefer 1138.

His childhood coincided with the rise of the Almohads, a strict Muslim movement from Morocco. In 1148 they took Córdoba and demanded that Jews and Christians convert to Islam or leave.
Maimonides is born.happened:
