The family fled, living for some years in southern Spain and then in Fez, in Morocco. In 1165 they sailed to the Land of Israel, landing at Acre, but soon moved on to Egypt, where Maimonides settled in Fustat, old Cairo. There he became a court physician and leader of the Jewish community.

His major works include the Commentary on the Mishnah, completed in 1168, in which he set out his Thirteen Principles of Jewish faith. His Mishneh Torah, finished around 1180, is a code of all Jewish law in 14 books, written in clear Hebrew and arranged by topic. His Guide for the Perplexed, written in Arabic around 1190, uses the philosophy of Aristotle to explain difficult ideas in the Bible. He also wrote medical works on subjects such as diet, asthma and poisons. He died in 1204.
Maimonides is born.matters:
Maimonides is often considered the greatest Jewish thinker of the Middle Ages. His ideas caused fierce controversy: in France, opponents of his philosophy denounced his books, and copies were burned in Montpellier in 1232. In time, though, he came to be revered across the Jewish world.

His Thirteen Principles became the poem Yigdal, sung in many synagogues, and the declarations of faith beginning Ani Ma'amin, "I believe". The Mishneh Torah is studied daily by many Jews today. Tradition holds that he is buried in Tiberias, where his tomb is a place of pilgrimage. A statue of him stands in Córdoba's old Jewish quarter.

First blood libel.background:
Jews had come to England after the Norman Conquest of 1066, settling in towns under the protection of the king, who taxed them heavily. They were few in number and often worked as moneylenders, one of the few trades open to them. Norwich, in East Anglia, had one of the largest Jewish communities in England.

In 12th-century Europe, devotion to the suffering of Christ and to the cults of saints and their relics was growing. Towns and churches benefited from pilgrims who came to pray at the tombs of saints.
First blood libel.happened:
In the spring of 1144, around Easter, the body of a twelve-year-old apprentice named William was found in Thorpe Wood outside Norwich. His family accused local Jews of killing him. The town sheriff protected the Jews, and no one was convicted at the time.

Several years later a monk named Thomas of Monmouth arrived at Norwich Cathedral and wrote The Life and Passion of William of Norwich. He claimed that the Jews had tortured William in mockery of the crucifixion of Jesus, and that Jews met each year to choose a town where a Christian child would be killed. He also recorded miracles at William's tomb. The book promoted William as a martyr, and a local cult grew around him.
First blood libel.matters:
This is the first known accusation of ritual murder against Jews in medieval Europe. The charge spread quickly: Gloucester in 1168, Blois in France in 1171, Bury St Edmunds in 1181, and Lincoln in 1255, where 19 Jews were executed. From the 13th century, beginning in Fulda in Germany in 1235, it took the form known as the blood libel, the claim that Jews used Christian blood in their rituals, often for Passover matzah.

Popes, including Innocent IV in 1247, condemned the accusation, but it led to trials, massacres and expulsions across Europe for centuries, and versions of it still appear in antisemitic propaganda today. The cult of Simon of Trent, a child from a similar case in 1475, was only abolished by the Catholic Church in 1965.

Maimonides reaches Egypt.background:
The Almohads, a strict Muslim movement from Morocco, conquered southern Spain and North Africa in the mid-12th century and pressured Jews to convert. Maimonides' family left Córdoba, lived for a time in Fez, and in 1165 sailed to Acre in the Land of Israel, then under Crusader rule. They visited Jerusalem and Hebron but found little opportunity to settle.

Egypt, under the Fatimids and from 1171 under Saladin and his Ayyubid dynasty, was more welcoming. Fustat, the old city next to Cairo, had a large and varied Jewish community, with Rabbanites, Karaites and Jews from the Land of Israel and Babylonia.
Maimonides reaches Egypt.happened:
Maimonides arrived in Egypt around 1166 and soon settled in Fustat. In 1168 he completed his Commentary on the Mishnah, written in Arabic. At first he was supported by his younger brother David, who traded in precious stones. Around 1177 David drowned in the Indian Ocean on a voyage to India, taking much of the family's wealth with him. In a letter, Maimonides wrote that he was ill with grief for about a year.

To support his family he turned to medicine, and became physician to al-Qadi al-Fadil, Saladin's chief minister, and later to Saladin's son al-Afdal. In a famous letter to his translator Samuel ibn Tibbon, he describes riding to Cairo every morning to treat the court, then returning home to find patients filling his house until night. He also served as head of the Jews of Egypt.
Maimonides reaches Egypt.matters:
In Egypt Maimonides wrote almost all his major works, including the Mishneh Torah and the Guide for the Perplexed. He answered letters from across the Jewish world. His Epistle to Yemen, written around 1172, encouraged Yemenite Jews facing forced conversion and warned them against a false messiah.

The Cairo Genizah, the old storeroom of Fustat's Ben Ezra Synagogue, has preserved drafts and letters in his own handwriting. His son Abraham and descendants led Egyptian Jewry for generations. In Cairo's old Jewish quarter, the Rav Moshe Synagogue, linked by tradition to Maimonides, was restored by the Egyptian government in 2010.

Blois blood libel.background:
The false accusation that Jews murdered Christian children first appeared in Norwich, England, in 1144. It spread slowly at first, carried by stories, sermons and the cults built around supposed child martyrs.

Blois, on the Loire river in France, had a small Jewish community of perhaps 40 people. It was ruled by Count Theobald V. According to Jewish sources, a Jewish woman named Pulcelina had close dealings with the count, which caused resentment at his court.
Blois blood libel.happened:
In the spring of 1171 a servant said he had seen a Jew throw a child's body into the Loire while watering horses. The Jew had in fact been carrying untanned hides. No missing child was ever reported and no body was ever found. Even so, the count had the Jewish community arrested. A priest proposed a trial by water, in which the servant was tested and declared truthful.

The Jews were offered baptism to save their lives, and most refused. On 20 Sivan, in the Hebrew year 4931, which fell on 26 May 1171, more than 30 Jews were burned. Jewish accounts, preserved by Ephraim of Bonn and in letters sent to other communities, say that they sang the prayer Aleinu as they died. Some children were forcibly baptised.
Blois blood libel.matters:
Blois was the first time a ritual murder accusation in continental Europe led to executions. Rabbenu Tam, Rashi's grandson and the leading scholar of the generation, declared 20 Sivan a fast day for the communities of France, England and the Rhineland. Jewish leaders also appealed to the French king, Louis VII, who promised to protect his Jews from such charges.

The fast of 20 Sivan was later renewed in Poland by the Council of Four Lands, after the Cossack massacres of 1648 and 1649, which began around the same date. Some communities still mark it today. The singing of Aleinu at Blois helped turn that prayer into a symbol of Jewish faith in the face of death.

Benjamin of Tudela's travels.background:
Tudela was a town on the Ebro river in the kingdom of Navarre, in northern Spain, with a prosperous Jewish community. In the 12th century Jews lived across a vast area, from Spain to Persia and beyond, and were linked by trade, letters, pilgrimage and a shared tradition of learning. Travel was slow and dangerous, but merchants and pilgrims made long journeys.

Little is known about Benjamin himself, beyond the fact that he was the son of Jonah. He may have been a merchant, perhaps in gems, and he may also have hoped to visit the Holy Land.
Benjamin of Tudela's travels.happened:
Benjamin set out around 1165, although some date the start earlier, and returned around 1173. He travelled through Barcelona, southern France and Italy, including Rome, then to Greece and Constantinople, Cyprus, Antioch and the Crusader states of the Land of Israel. He continued to Damascus, Baghdad and Persia, and came home by way of Egypt and Sicily. He also passed on reports he had heard about Arabia, India and China.

His Hebrew book, known as The Travels of Benjamin, or Sefer ha-Massa'ot, lists about 300 places. For many he gives the number of Jews and the names of their leaders, and describes their work and customs. In Rome he notes that Jews served the pope. In Constantinople he describes Jewish silk weavers and Karaites. In Jerusalem he found only a few Jewish dyers near the Tower of David. In Baghdad he describes the honour paid to the Exilarch, the head of the Jews, by the caliph's court.
Benjamin of Tudela's travels.matters:
Benjamin's book is one of the most important sources on Jewish life in the 12th century and a rich record of the medieval Mediterranean and Middle East as a whole. Historians debate how to read his figures, which may count families rather than individuals, and some of his distant reports are hearsay. Yet much of what he described first-hand has been confirmed by other sources.

The book was first printed in Constantinople in 1543 and later translated into Latin and many other languages. Benjamin travelled about a century before Marco Polo and is sometimes compared to him. His name lives on in his hometown of Tudela, where a monument honours him.

York massacre.background:
Jews came to England after the Norman Conquest of 1066 and lived in towns such as London, Norwich, Lincoln and York under the king's protection. They were taxed heavily by the crown and many worked as moneylenders, so many nobles and townspeople owed them money. Religious feeling was rising as preparations began for the Third Crusade to recapture Jerusalem from Saladin.

At Richard I's coronation in Westminster on 3 September 1189, a Jewish delegation bringing gifts was attacked, and a riot spread through London's Jewish quarter. Early in 1190 violence broke out in King's Lynn, Norwich, Stamford and Bury St Edmunds, where 57 Jews were killed.
York massacre.happened:
In York, a group of local men led by debtors such as Richard Malebisse stirred up a mob in March 1190. The house of the late Benedict of York was attacked and his family killed. The rest of the community, around 150 people, fled into the royal castle and took refuge in its wooden keep. When they no longer trusted the castle warden, they refused to let him back in, and the sheriff and the mob besieged them.

On the night of 16 March 1190, which fell on Shabbat HaGadol, the Sabbath before Passover, the trapped Jews faced certain death. According to the chronicler William of Newburgh, Rabbi Yom Tov of Joigny urged them to take their own lives rather than be killed or baptised. Most did, and the tower was set on fire. The few who came out next morning, promised safety if they converted, were murdered. The rioters then went to York Minster and burned the records of debts owed to Jews.
York massacre.matters:
The York massacre is one of the darkest events in English Jewish history.

The stone tower that now stands on the mound, known as Clifford's Tower, was built later in the 13th century. In 1978 a plaque was placed at the foot of the mound, and daffodils, whose six-pointed flowers recall the Star of David, bloom on the slopes each spring around the anniversary. A popular belief grew that Jews should not spend the night in York, but this was never a formal religious ruling, and a Jewish community lives in the city today.

Jewish badge.background:
In 1215 Pope Innocent III called the Fourth Lateran Council in Rome, one of the largest gatherings of the medieval Church, with over 400 bishops. It aimed to reform the Church, fight heresy and prepare a new crusade. It also passed decisions about Jews and Muslims living in Christian lands.

The idea of marking non-believers by dress was not new. In the Islamic world, rules attributed to the Pact of Umar had required Jews and Christians to wear distinctive clothing, as with the decrees of the caliph al-Mutawakkil in the 9th century.
Jewish badge.happened:
Canon 68 of the council stated that in some provinces Jews and Muslims could not be told apart from Christians by their dress, which could lead to mixed relationships. It ordered that Jews and Muslims of both sexes should wear clothing that set them apart in public. Canon 69 barred Jews from holding public office over Christians.

Each country carried this out in its own way. In England a law of 1218 ordered a badge in the shape of the two tablets of the Ten Commandments, later made of yellow felt under Edward I's Statute of the Jewry of 1275. In France King Louis IX in 1269 ordered a round yellow badge called the rouelle. In German lands the pointed Jewish hat, already worn by many Jews, became a required sign. Some rulers sold exemptions to raise money, and enforcement varied over time.
Jewish badge.matters:
The badge made Jews visible and vulnerable, singling them out for insult and violence and marking them as outsiders in the towns where they lived. In some places it remained in force into the 18th century, until it faded with the Enlightenment and emancipation.

The Nazis revived the idea in the 20th century. From late 1939 Jews in occupied Poland were forced to wear a badge or armband, and from September 1941 Jews in Germany had to wear a yellow Star of David with the word "Jude". Because of this history, the badge remains one of the most powerful symbols of persecution, and some Holocaust memorials use the yellow star to honour those who were forced to wear it.

Talmud burned in Paris.background:
Until the 13th century the Church mostly attacked the Jews' rejection of Christianity rather than their books. That changed when Nicholas Donin, a Jew from La Rochelle who had converted to Christianity, presented Pope Gregory IX in 1239 with a list of 35 charges against the Talmud. He claimed it insulted Jesus and Mary, contained blasphemies and taught hostility to Christians.

The pope wrote to the kings of Europe, ordering that all Jewish books be seized on the first Saturday of Lent in 1240, while Jews were in synagogue, and examined. Only France, under the devout King Louis IX, carried out the order fully.
Talmud burned in Paris.happened:
In June 1240 a public hearing was held in Paris before Queen Blanche of Castile, the king's mother, and leading churchmen. Rabbi Yechiel of Paris led the Jewish defence, with other rabbis including Moses of Coucy. Yechiel argued that passages about a certain Jesus referred to a different person, and that the Talmud was essential to Jewish life. Each rabbi was questioned separately. The verdict, given by a commission of theologians, condemned the Talmud.

In 1242, though some sources suggest a slightly different date, 24 cartloads of manuscripts were burned in a public square in Paris, probably the Place de Grève. Because every book was copied by hand, this meant thousands of volumes, the result of years of work, and in many cases a community's entire library.
Talmud burned in Paris.matters:
The burning was a disaster for the great schools of the Tosafists, the French and German scholars who added commentary to Rashi's work. Copies became so scarce that the only complete manuscript of the Babylonian Talmud surviving today, now in Munich, dates from 1342. The trial set a precedent for later attacks on Jewish books, such as the burning of the Talmud in Rome in 1553.

Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg, who witnessed the burning as a young student, wrote a lament beginning Sha'ali Serufah ba-Esh, "Ask, O you who were burned in fire", which is recited on Tisha B'Av. Some communities kept a fast on the Friday before the Torah portion Chukkat to remember the loss. Rabbi Yechiel later moved to Acre in the Land of Israel.

Barcelona Disputation.background:
In the 13th century the Dominican friars led new efforts to convert Jews, studying Hebrew and the Talmud to find passages they believed proved Christian claims. One of them was Pablo Christiani, a Jew from southern France who had converted. In the Crown of Aragon, King James I, known as James the Conqueror, supported the friars while also valuing his Jewish subjects.

Moses ben Nachman, known as Nachmanides or by his initials Ramban, was born in Girona in 1194. He was a doctor and the most respected rabbi in Catalonia, author of Talmud commentaries and later a famous commentary on the Torah.
Barcelona Disputation.happened:
In July 1263 the king ordered Nachmanides to debate Pablo Christiani in his palace in Barcelona, with leading churchmen present, including the Dominican Raymond of Penyafort. Nachmanides asked for and received a promise that he could speak freely. Over four sessions they debated whether the Messiah had already come, whether he was meant to be divine or human, and whether Jews or Christians held the true faith.

Pablo cited passages from the Talmud and midrash to argue that the rabbis themselves had admitted the Messiah had come. Nachmanides replied that such legends, called aggadah, were not binding on Jews, and he argued that the world had not seen the peace promised by the prophets. According to his own account, the king gave him 300 coins when he left.
Barcelona Disputation.matters:
At the Bishop of Girona's request, Nachmanides wrote his account of the debate, known as the Vikuach. The Dominicans accused him of blasphemy for the book. The king tried to soften the punishment, but pressure grew, and Pope Clement IV urged action against him. In about 1267, in his early seventies, Nachmanides left Spain for the Land of Israel.

The Barcelona Disputation is remembered as one of the great public debates between Judaism and Christianity, and Nachmanides' bold defence is a source of pride. It was followed by more forced disputations, such as the Tortosa disputation of 1413 and 1414. Girona's old Jewish quarter, the Call, now holds a museum of Jewish history named after Nachmanides' Catalan name, Bonastruc ça Porta.

Ramban in Jerusalem.background:
After Saladin retook Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187, small groups of Jews settled in the city again. But the 13th century brought more wars. The city changed hands several times between Muslims and Christians, and in 1244 it was sacked by Khwarazmian troops. In 1260 Mongol raiders swept through the region before being defeated by the Mamluks of Egypt at Ain Jalut. The Mamluks then ruled the land.

Nachmanides, forced out of Spain after the Barcelona Disputation, sailed to the Land of Israel, landing at Acre in 1267.
Ramban in Jerusalem.happened:
Nachmanides reached Jerusalem in the late summer of 1267, around the Hebrew month of Elul. In a letter to his son he describes a city in ruins. He says it had about 2,000 inhabitants, among them about 300 Christians, and only two Jewish brothers, dyers, who held services in their home with a few others on the Sabbath.

He and the small group around him found a ruined house with marble pillars and a fine dome and made it into a synagogue. They sent to Shechem, also called Nablus, for Torah scrolls that had been taken there for safety from the Mongols. He wrote that people came from Damascus and other places to see Jerusalem, and that they began to pray there soon after, in time for the High Holy Days.
Ramban in Jerusalem.matters:
Nachmanides' arrival is seen as the start of a lasting renewal of Jewish community life in Jerusalem. He later moved to Acre, where he taught, and died around 1270. His burial place is disputed, with traditions placing it in Acre, Haifa or Hebron. He finished his famous Torah commentary in the Land of Israel and added comments drawn from seeing its places for himself.

The Ramban Synagogue in the Jewish Quarter of the Old City bears his name, though historians debate whether it is the same building he founded. It was closed by Ottoman authorities in the late 16th century and used for other purposes, then restored as a synagogue after 1967. It stands beside the rebuilt Hurva Synagogue and is still in use today.

The Zohar appears.background:
Kabbalah, meaning "received tradition", is the Jewish mystical tradition. It seeks to understand the hidden nature of God, creation and the soul. Earlier mystical texts, such as the Sefer Yetzirah and the Sefer ha-Bahir, had circulated for centuries. In the 13th century, circles of Kabbalists flourished in Provence and in Spain, in Girona and Castile.

They taught about the ten Sefirot, the divine qualities through which God acts in the world, and about the Shekhinah, the divine presence. Moses de León, born around 1240, was a Kabbalist who lived in Guadalajara and later Ávila in Castile.
The Zohar appears.happened:
From around the 1280s Moses de León began to share sections of a book he called the Zohar, "Radiance" or "Splendour". Written mostly in Aramaic, it presents itself as the teachings of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, a sage of the 2nd century, and his circle as they wander in the Land of Israel and explain the hidden meanings of the Torah.

Questions about its origins arose early. The Kabbalist Isaac of Acre reported investigating, and an account preserved by the chronicler Abraham Zacuto says that de León's widow claimed her husband wrote it himself. In the 20th century the scholar Gershom Scholem argued that Moses de León was its main author. Others, such as Yehuda Liebes, have suggested it came from a wider circle of Kabbalists. Many traditional Jews hold that it records ancient teachings.
The Zohar appears.matters:
The Zohar became the central text of Kabbalah and, for many, a sacred book alongside the Bible and Talmud. It was first printed in Italy, in Mantua and Cremona, between 1558 and 1560. In the 16th century the mystics of Safed, especially Rabbi Isaac Luria, built new teachings on it, which later shaped Hasidism.

Passages from the Zohar entered the prayer book, such as Brikh Shmeh, recited when the Torah is taken from the ark. Each year on Lag BaOmer, which tradition links to Shimon bar Yochai's death, large crowds gather at his tomb in Meron in northern Israel to celebrate with bonfires, music and dancing.

Expelled from England.background:
Jews had lived in England since soon after the Norman Conquest of 1066, under the direct control of the king, who treated them almost as his property. The crown taxed them heavily, and they suffered the York massacre of 1190, ritual murder accusations, and the badge law of 1218. By the reign of Edward I, repeated heavy taxes had left the community impoverished.

In 1275 Edward's Statute of the Jewry banned Jews from lending money at interest, the main trade they had been allowed, while offering few real alternatives. In 1278 and 1279 hundreds of Jews were arrested on charges of clipping coins, and around 269 were hanged in London.
Expelled from England.happened:
On 18 July 1290 Edward I issued an edict ordering all Jews to leave England by All Saints' Day, 1 November. By Jewish reckoning the date of the edict fell on Tisha B'Av, the fast that mourns the destruction of the Temples. Shortly afterwards Parliament granted the king a large tax, and historians see the expulsion as linked to that grant.

Between about 2,000 and 3,000 Jews left. They could take some movable goods, but their houses passed to the crown, and the debts owed to them were collected by the king. Some travelled to France, Flanders and Germany. Chroniclers record that one ship's captain left a group of Jews to drown on a sandbank in the Thames estuary, and that he was later punished.
Expelled from England.matters:
England was the first country in medieval Europe to expel all its Jews, and France and Spain later followed. For over 350 years there was officially no Jewish community in England, though a few individuals lived there, often in secret. London's street name Old Jewry is a reminder of the medieval community.

In 1655 Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel of Amsterdam asked Oliver Cromwell to readmit the Jews. No law was passed, but from 1656 Jews were quietly allowed to live and worship openly. The Sephardi synagogue in Creechurch Lane opened soon after, followed by Bevis Marks Synagogue in 1701, which is still in use as the oldest synagogue in Britain.

Expelled from France.background:
Jews had lived in France since Roman times. In the north, communities such as those of Troyes and Paris produced Rashi and the Tosafists. But from the 12th century their position grew worse, with the Blois blood libel of 1171, a first expulsion from the royal lands by Philip II Augustus in 1182 followed by readmission in 1198, and the burning of the Talmud in 1242.

King Philip IV, known as Philip the Fair, ruled from 1285. His wars with England and Flanders were expensive, and he searched for new sources of money. He debased the coinage and seized the wealth of Italian bankers, and in 1307 he would turn on the Knights Templar.
Expelled from France.happened:
On a single day in July 1306, the day after Tisha B'Av, royal officials arrested the Jews throughout Philip's lands. They were told to leave the kingdom within about a month and to leave behind their property. The king sold their houses, synagogues and goods, and his officials collected the debts owed to them for the crown.

The number expelled is often given as about 100,000, though some historians think the true figure was lower. Many went to regions not under the king's rule, such as Provence, Lorraine, Savoy and the Comtat Venaissin around Avignon, which belonged to the pope. Others went to Spain or Germany. Among the exiles was Estori Haparchi, who travelled to the Land of Israel and wrote the first Hebrew book on its geography.
Expelled from France.matters:
The expulsion ended the great age of northern French Jewish scholarship. In 1315 Louis X allowed Jews to return for a limited period, but they faced violence during the Shepherds' Crusade of 1320 and the Black Death of 1348. In 1394 Charles VI expelled the Jews again.

Jewish life in France survived only in places outside royal control. In the papal lands around Avignon, communities known as the Pope's Jews lived on in towns such as Carpentras and Cavaillon, whose historic synagogues still stand. Full Jewish life returned to France only with emancipation after the French Revolution, granted to Sephardi Jews in 1790 and to all Jews in 1791.

Shepherds' Crusade.background:
In the early fourteenth century France was suffering. Bad harvests, high prices and hunger hit the countryside hard, and the dream of a new crusade to win back the Holy Land was still alive in sermons and royal promises. King Philip V had talked of leading one, but nothing came of it.

The Jews of France were already in a fragile position. Philip IV had expelled them in 1306, and only some had been allowed back in 1315, on strict terms and mainly to collect old debts for the crown. This made them easy targets for anger about money, taxes and royal officials.
Shepherds' Crusade.happened:
In spring 1320 a movement known as the Pastoureaux, French for shepherds, began in northern France, reportedly after a young shepherd claimed a heavenly vision. Thousands of youths, peasants and drifters marched to Paris, then headed south towards Aquitaine and Languedoc. Along the way they attacked royal officials, clergy and, above all, Jews. In Toulouse Jews were offered baptism or death. Records kept by the inquisitor Jacques Fournier, later Pope Benedict XII, include the testimony of a Jew named Baruch who was forcibly baptised there.

At Verdun-sur-Garonne Jews took refuge in a royal tower. When the attackers set fire to the gate, later Jewish accounts say the defenders chose to die by their own hands rather than be taken. The bands then crossed into the Kingdom of Aragon, striking communities such as Jaca and Montclus. Pope John XXII in Avignon condemned the movement, and royal forces in France and King James II of Aragon finally broke it up by the end of the summer.
Shepherds' Crusade.matters:
The Shepherds' Crusade showed how quickly religious excitement and social anger could turn against Jews, who had little protection when royal power broke down. It also deepened distrust between Jews and the French crown, which had failed to defend them. Within a few years, French Jews faced new accusations, and in 1394 they were expelled from France for good.

The massacres are remembered mainly through later Jewish chronicles such as Solomon ibn Verga's Shevet Yehudah, written after the expulsion from Spain, which collected stories of persecution. Together with the Christian inquisition records, they give historians a rare double view of the violence.

Black Death massacres.background:
The Black Death reached Europe in 1347, carried along trade routes from the Black Sea. Nobody understood how it spread. Within a few years it killed perhaps a third of the population, emptying towns and villages. People searched desperately for a cause, and many blamed God's anger, bad air or hidden enemies.

Jews, who lived as a small and often resented minority, had long been the subject of false charges such as ritual murder. The idea that they were secretly poisoning wells fitted easily into these older fears, especially in towns where people owed money to Jewish lenders.
Black Death massacres.happened:
In September 1348, at Chillon castle on Lake Geneva, Jews were tortured until they gave false confessions of a plot to poison the water. Copies of these confessions were sent from town to town. Pope Clement VI issued bulls that year pointing out that Jews were dying of the plague too, and he forbade attacks on them, but few listened.

The killing spread through Switzerland, Alsace, the Rhineland and central Germany in 1348 and 1349. In Basel Jews were burned in a wooden building on an island in the Rhine. In Strasbourg, on 14 February 1349, the Jews were burned in their cemetery after the town council that had tried to protect them was overthrown. Erfurt, Mainz, Cologne and many other communities were destroyed. Often the violence came before the plague had even arrived, and debts owed to Jews were cancelled.
Black Death massacres.matters:
These massacres were among the worst in medieval Europe, and they changed the map of Jewish life. Many German Jews moved east, where King Casimir III of Poland offered protection. Over the next centuries Poland and Lithuania became the heart of Ashkenazi Jewry, and Yiddish, rooted in German, went with them.

Traces remain today. In Erfurt, a hoard of coins and jewellery buried by a Jewish family in 1349 was found in 1998 and is now shown in the town's Old Synagogue, one of the oldest in Europe. Memorial books from German communities list the names of the dead, and the period is often studied as a warning of how fear can turn into scapegoating.

Riots in Spain.background:
For centuries the Jews of Castile and Aragon had held important roles as doctors, tax farmers, courtiers and scholars. But during the later fourteenth century their position grew weaker. Civil war in Castile in the 1360s had brought anti-Jewish propaganda into politics, and preachers increasingly attacked Jews in sermons.

Ferrand Martínez, archdeacon of Écija, had preached against the Jews of Seville for years and ignored royal orders to stop. In 1390 both the archbishop of Seville and King John I of Castile died. The new king, Henry III, was a boy, and with weak authority at the top, nothing held Martínez back.
Riots in Spain.happened:
On 4 June 1391 crowds broke into the Jewish quarter of Seville. Homes were looted, synagogues were turned into churches and many people were killed or baptised under threat. Over the summer the riots spread through Andalusia to Córdoba, then north to Toledo and east into the Kingdom of Aragon, reaching Valencia, Majorca, Barcelona and Girona by August.

The philosopher Hasdai Crescas, a leader of Aragonese Jewry, lost his only son in Barcelona. In a letter to the community of Avignon he described the destruction city by city, and this letter remains one of the main sources for the events. Exact numbers are not known, but whole communities, including Barcelona's, ceased to exist, and conversion took place on a huge scale.
Riots in Spain.matters:
The riots of 1391 marked the beginning of the end for Spanish Jewry. For the first time a very large group of people were Christians in name but Jewish by family, memory and sometimes secret practice. These conversos, also called New Christians, faced suspicion from Old Christians, and the question of their loyalty led to the purity of blood laws and the Inquisition.

The communities that survived were smaller and poorer, and their leaders spent the next century trying to rebuild. Today the former Jewish quarters of Seville, Toledo, Girona and other cities draw visitors, and some old synagogues, like Santa María la Blanca in Toledo, still stand as churches or museums.

Disputation of Tortosa.background:
Public debates between Christians and Jews had been staged before, in Paris in 1240 and in Barcelona in 1263, where Nahmanides defended Judaism before King James I. After the riots of 1391 the Church in Spain pressed harder for conversion, and the Jews who remained were frightened and divided.

Pedro de Luna, known as Benedict XIII, was one of the rival popes during the Great Schism and was backed by the Crown of Aragon. His personal doctor was Joshua ha-Lorki, a learned Jew who had converted and taken the name Gerónimo de Santa Fe. Gerónimo claimed he could prove from the Talmud itself that the Messiah had already come.
Disputation of Tortosa.happened:
In early 1413 leading rabbis and scholars from across Aragon were summoned to Tortosa, on the Ebro river. Among them were Joseph Albo, Vidal Benveniste and Astruc ha-Levi. The sessions dragged on until November 1414. The Jewish speakers were not free to argue as equals: they had to answer Gerónimo's points before the pope and his court, knowing that a bold reply could bring danger.

While the debate went on, the preacher Vicente Ferrer and others travelled through Aragon urging Jews to convert, and many communities lost large numbers of members to baptism. At the end the Talmud was declared harmful, and in 1415 Benedict issued a bull restricting Jewish books, preaching and economic life.
Disputation of Tortosa.matters:
Tortosa was the longest and most damaging of the medieval disputations. It weakened Aragonese Jewry further, even though Benedict XIII himself soon lost power when the Council of Constance ended the schism. The record of the sessions survives in Latin and Hebrew accounts, which differ in tone.

The debate also shaped Jewish thought. Joseph Albo went on to write Sefer ha-Ikkarim, the Book of Principles, which tried to set out the core beliefs of Judaism clearly. Historians see Tortosa as a key step between the riots of 1391 and the expulsion of 1492.

Vienna Gesera.background:
Vienna had one of the most important Jewish communities in the German-speaking world, with famous scholars and a large synagogue on what is now Judenplatz. Jews lived there under the protection of the dukes of Austria, who taxed them heavily.

In the early fifteenth century the Hussites, followers of the reformer Jan Hus in Bohemia, rose against the Church and the empire. Duke Albert V was fighting them and needed money. Rumours spread that Jews were helping the Hussites, and a charge that Jews in the town of Enns had desecrated a consecrated wafer added to the hostility. The Hebrew word gesera means a harsh decree.
Vienna Gesera.happened:
In May 1420 Albert ordered the arrest of the Jews of Vienna and Lower Austria. Their property was seized. Poorer Jews were put on boats on the Danube and sent away. Wealthier Jews were held and pressed to accept baptism, and children were taken from their parents to be raised as Christians. According to Jewish accounts, a group who had gathered in the synagogue chose to die by their own hands rather than convert.

On 12 March 1421 the remaining prisoners, about two hundred people, were burned at a place called the Gänseweide in the Erdberg area, outside the city walls. Albert then banned Jews from Austria for ever, and the synagogue was pulled down and its stones reused.
Vienna Gesera.matters:
The Gesera ended medieval Jewish life in Vienna. A Latin inscription on a house on Judenplatz, put up later in the fifteenth century, praises the burning, and it can still be seen today, now with a modern plaque beside it explaining what happened.

In the 1990s archaeologists uncovered the foundations of the medieval synagogue under the square. They are now shown in the Museum Judenplatz, and above them stands Rachel Whiteread's Holocaust memorial, opened in 2000. The site links the medieval tragedy with the twentieth century, and makes Judenplatz one of Vienna's main places of Jewish memory.

\"Purity of blood\" laws.background:
After the riots of 1391 and the mass baptisms that followed, Spain had a large group of New Christians, or conversos. Many rose quickly in society. Freed from the limits placed on Jews, they became officials, merchants, churchmen and even bishops. Their success caused resentment among some Old Christians, who suspected them of being secret Jews.

In 1449 Toledo was in turmoil. Álvaro de Luna, the powerful minister of King John II of Castile, demanded a large loan from the city for war. Converso officials were blamed for collecting it, and anger turned into a revolt led by Pero Sarmiento, the city's governor.
\"Purity of blood\" laws.happened:
Rioters attacked the homes of wealthy conversos in the Magdalena district. Sarmiento and the city council then issued what became known as the Sentencia-Estatuto. It declared that people of Jewish descent could not hold public office or act as witnesses or notaries in Toledo, no matter how sincere their Christian faith.

The statute was controversial even at the time. Pope Nicholas V condemned it in 1449, and the converso bishop Alonso de Cartagena wrote a defence of the unity of all Christians. Yet over the next century similar rules were adopted by colleges, military orders, cathedral chapters, religious orders and town councils across Spain and Portugal, and people had to prove their family line was free of Jewish or Muslim ancestry.
\"Purity of blood\" laws.matters:
The purity of blood rules shifted hostility from what a person believed to who their ancestors were. Families hid their histories, paid for false family trees, and lived in fear of being exposed. The system also spread to Spanish and Portuguese colonies in the Americas, where it shaped ideas about race and descent.

The rules lasted into the nineteenth century before they were finally abolished. Historians often discuss them as an early example of discrimination based on descent rather than religion, and they remain an important part of the story of Spain's conversos and their descendants.

Ottomans take Constantinople.background:
Constantinople had been the capital of the Byzantine Empire for over a thousand years. Its Jewish community was small and lived under many restrictions. The Jews of the Byzantine lands, known as Romaniotes, spoke Greek and had their own customs, older than both the Sephardic and Ashkenazi traditions.

The Ottoman Turks had been expanding through Anatolia and the Balkans for a century. Under Ottoman rule Jews and Christians were treated as protected non-Muslims. They paid a special tax and faced some limits, but they could practise their religion and run many of their own affairs.
Ottomans take Constantinople.happened:
On 29 May 1453, after a siege of nearly two months, the army of Sultan Mehmed II broke through the city walls. Much of the population had fled or been killed, and Mehmed wanted to rebuild Istanbul quickly as a great capital. He used a policy called sürgün, moving whole communities from other parts of the empire into the city. Jews from the Balkans and Anatolia were among them, settling in districts such as Balat along the Golden Horn.

A letter by Rabbi Isaac Sarfati, sent to the Jews of German lands, praised life under the Ottomans compared with the hardship in Christian Europe and encouraged them to come. Its exact date is debated by historians. Moses Capsali, a Romaniote rabbi, came to be seen as the leading rabbi of the city.
Ottomans take Constantinople.matters:
The fall of Constantinople opened a new chapter for Jews in the eastern Mediterranean. When Jews were driven from Spain in 1492 and Portugal soon after, Sultan Bayezid II allowed tens of thousands to settle in Istanbul, Salonika, Izmir and other cities. They brought printing, medicine, trade links and the Judeo-Spanish language, Ladino.

For centuries the Ottoman Empire was home to some of the largest Jewish communities in the world. Istanbul still has a Jewish community today, and the story of the Ottoman welcome is often recalled in Turkey and among Sephardic Jews.

First Hebrew printed book.background:
Before printing, every Jewish book had to be copied by hand. Scribes worked slowly, books were costly, and mistakes crept in with each copy. Students often shared one book or learned texts by heart.

Johannes Gutenberg's printing press appeared in Mainz around 1450 and spread quickly. Italy, with its wealthy towns and educated Jewish communities, became the early centre of Hebrew printing. Some undated Hebrew books from Rome may even be slightly older than the first dated one, and scholars still debate their exact age.
First Hebrew printed book.happened:
On 17 or 18 February 1475, in Reggio di Calabria in southern Italy, Abraham ben Garton finished printing Rashi's commentary on the Torah. Rashi, an eleventh century French rabbi, wrote the most widely studied explanation of the Bible, so he was a natural choice. The only known surviving copy is kept in the Palatine Library in Parma.

That same year Meshullam Cusi printed the law code Arba'ah Turim in Piove di Sacco near Padua. The Soncino family, named after their small town in Lombardy, became the most famous early Hebrew printers, issuing the complete Hebrew Bible in 1488. Gershom Soncino later carried his craft to Turkey. In Venice in the 1520s the Christian printer Daniel Bomberg produced the first complete printed Talmud.
First Hebrew printed book.matters:
Printing changed Jewish life deeply. Books became cheaper and identical, so a student in Poland and a student in Morocco could study the same page. Bomberg's Talmud set the page numbers and layout that are still used today, which is why scholars everywhere can cite the same page reference.

Printing also spread new works quickly, such as the Shulchan Aruch, and later helped Hebrew literature and newspapers grow. Early Hebrew printed books, called incunabula when made before 1501, are now treasured in libraries and are a lasting sign of how eagerly Jews embraced the new technology.

Spanish Inquisition.background:
By the 1470s Spain had a large population of conversos, descended from Jews baptised in 1391 and after. Some kept Jewish customs in secret, while many were sincere Christians. Suspicion grew, encouraged by preachers who claimed that conversos were mocking the Church and being drawn back to Judaism by their Jewish neighbours.

Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile had united their kingdoms through marriage and wanted religious unity too. Unlike the older papal inquisitions, they asked for a tribunal under royal control.
Spanish Inquisition.happened:
On 1 November 1478 Pope Sixtus IV issued a bull allowing the monarchs to appoint inquisitors. The first tribunal began work in Seville in 1480, and the first auto-da-fé, meaning act of faith, was held there in February 1481, when six people were burned. Tomás de Torquemada, a Dominican friar, became Inquisitor General in 1483 and set up tribunals across Spain.

Inquisitors read out lists of signs of secret Judaism, such as lighting candles on Friday night, refusing pork or changing clothes for the Sabbath, and invited neighbours to report each other. Suspects were held in secret, their property seized, and torture was used to gain confessions. Most of those convicted were given penances, but many were burned. Historians estimate several thousand executions over the Inquisition's whole history, with the harshest years in its first decades.
Spanish Inquisition.matters:
The Inquisition cast a long shadow over Spain and Portugal, which set up its own tribunal in 1536, and over their colonies in the Americas. It operated, with breaks, until it was finally abolished in 1834. Its detailed trial records, many kept in Spain's national archives, are now an important source for historians, preserving the voices of ordinary conversos and the customs they tried to keep.

For Jews, the Inquisition became a symbol of religious persecution. Families descended from conversos, in places as far apart as Mexico, Portugal and the American Southwest, sometimes kept faint traces of Jewish practice for generations, a heritage that some are rediscovering today.

Expelled from Spain.background:
Jews had lived in Spain since Roman times. Under Muslim and later Christian rule they produced poets, philosophers and statesmen, such as Judah Halevi and Maimonides. But after the riots of 1391, the disputation of Tortosa and the founding of the Inquisition, the remaining communities were smaller and under heavy pressure.

In January 1492 Ferdinand and Isabella conquered Granada, the last Muslim kingdom in Spain. Torquemada and others argued that as long as Jews remained, conversos would be tempted back to Judaism.
Expelled from Spain.happened:
On 31 March 1492 the monarchs signed the Alhambra Decree, ordering all Jews to leave their kingdoms by the end of July unless they were baptised. They could sell their property, but were forbidden to take gold, silver or horses out of the country, so many sold homes for almost nothing. Don Isaac Abravanel, a leading Jewish financier and scholar, pleaded with the king and queen to change their minds, without success. Another courtier, Abraham Senior, chose baptism.

The final departures took place around the start of August, close to Tisha b'Av, the fast that mourns the destruction of the Temples. Numbers are debated, with estimates ranging from about 40,000 to 200,000 people leaving, while many others converted to stay. Many crossed into Portugal, others sailed to North Africa, Italy and the Ottoman Empire.
Expelled from Spain.matters:
The expulsion ended Jewish life in Spain for nearly four centuries and scattered Sephardic culture around the Mediterranean and beyond. Exiles carried their Judeo-Spanish language, Ladino, their songs, recipes and prayers, and some families kept the keys of their old Spanish houses for generations.

The year 1492 is remembered alongside Columbus's first voyage, which set sail just after the deadline. In 1992, on the 500th anniversary, King Juan Carlos visited a Madrid synagogue in a gesture of reconciliation, and in 2015 Spain passed a law offering citizenship to descendants of the expelled Jews for a limited period.

Forced conversion in Portugal.background:
When the Jews were expelled from Spain in 1492, tens of thousands crossed into Portugal. King João II let them in for a fee, but most were allowed to stay only for a short time, and those who could not leave were treated harshly. Some children were taken and sent to the island of São Tomé off Africa.

His successor, Manuel I, at first treated the Jews more kindly. But he wanted to marry Isabella, daughter of Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain, and the Spanish monarchs insisted that Portugal first rid itself of Jews. At the same time, Manuel valued Jewish skills in trade, medicine and science and did not want to lose them.
Forced conversion in Portugal.happened:
In December 1496 Manuel ordered all Jews to leave Portugal by October 1497. Then he changed course. Around Passover 1497 he ordered Jewish children to be taken from their families and baptised. Later in the year, Jews who gathered in Lisbon expecting ships to take them away were instead held and baptised by force. Only a very small number managed to leave.

Manuel promised the New Christians that for twenty years no one would investigate their religious life, and many continued Jewish customs in private. Tensions grew. In April 1506, during a drought and plague, a crowd in Lisbon, urged on by preaching friars, attacked New Christians over three days. Contemporary estimates of the dead run from about a thousand to several thousand.
Forced conversion in Portugal.matters:
The forced conversion created the large community of Portuguese New Christians who would play a key role in later Jewish history. After Portugal set up its own Inquisition in 1536, many fled to Amsterdam, Hamburg, London, the Ottoman Empire and the Americas, where they returned openly to Judaism. This network became known as the Portuguese Nation.

Some stayed and kept hidden traditions for centuries. In the 1910s a community of secret Jews was found in the mountain town of Belmonte. In 2008 a memorial to the victims of the 1506 massacre was unveiled in Lisbon's Largo de São Domingos, and in 2015 Portugal also offered citizenship to descendants of Sephardic Jews.

First ghetto, Venice.background:
Venice was a rich trading republic, and for a long time it allowed Jews only short stays, mainly as moneylenders in nearby Mestre. During the War of the League of Cambrai, from 1509, many Jews fled into the city itself. Some Venetians wanted them expelled, while the government valued the loans and taxes they brought.

The compromise was to let Jews live in Venice but keep them apart. The chosen site was an island in the Cannaregio district where a foundry, or getto in Venetian, had once cast metal. Historians think the word ghetto comes from this foundry.
First ghetto, Venice.happened:
On 29 March 1516 the Venetian Senate ordered the Jews to move into the Ghetto Nuovo, the New Ghetto. Its gates were locked at sunset and opened at dawn, and boats patrolled the canals around it. Jews had to wear a yellow and later a red hat or badge when outside. Their right to live in the city depended on charters, called condotte, renewed every few years.

The area was enlarged in 1541 with the Ghetto Vecchio, for Levantine Jewish merchants from the Ottoman lands, and again in 1633. Different groups, Ashkenazi, Italian, Levantine and Spanish, built their own small synagogues, or scuole, hidden inside ordinary buildings. With space so limited, houses rose to seven storeys or more.
First ghetto, Venice.matters:
Despite its limits, the Venice ghetto became a lively centre of Jewish culture and Hebrew printing, home to scholars such as Rabbi Leon Modena. Christians visited its synagogues, and ideas flowed in both directions.

The gates were torn down in 1797 after Napoleon's troops took Venice. The word ghetto spread across Europe for enforced Jewish quarters and later took on wider meanings. Today the area still has working synagogues, a Jewish museum and Holocaust memorials, and in 2016 Venice marked the ghetto's 500th anniversary with exhibitions and a performance of Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice in its main square.

David Reubeni.background:
In the early sixteenth century many Jews, shaken by the expulsions from Spain and Portugal, longed for signs of redemption. Stories of the Ten Lost Tribes of Israel, said to live in distant lands, were popular among both Jews and Christians. At the same time, the Ottoman Empire was pushing into Europe, and Christian rulers were looking for allies.

In Portugal, conversos lived under growing pressure, still remembering the forced baptisms of 1497. A messenger from a powerful Jewish kingdom would stir great hope among them.
David Reubeni.happened:
In 1523 or 1524 a small, dark man calling himself David, son of King Solomon and brother of King Joseph, ruler of the tribe of Reuben in Arabia, arrived in Venice. He travelled to Rome, where Pope Clement VII received him, and then to Portugal, where King João III welcomed him in 1525. He proposed an alliance and asked for weapons and ships to fight the Ottomans. Conversos flocked to see him.

One of them, a young royal official named Diogo Pires, was so moved that he returned to Judaism, took the name Solomon Molcho and became a mystic preacher in Italy and the Ottoman lands. In 1532 the two went to meet Emperor Charles V in Regensburg. Charles had them arrested. Molcho was burned in Mantua, and Reubeni was taken to Spain, where he is thought to have died in an Inquisition prison some years later.
David Reubeni.matters:
Historians still debate who David Reubeni really was, and whether he believed his own claims. A diary attributed to him, written in Hebrew, survives in the Bodleian Library in Oxford and gives a vivid picture of his travels.

His story shows how strong messianic hopes were in this period, a mood that would rise again with the Kabbalists of Safed and, more dramatically, with Shabbetai Tzvi. Solomon Molcho became a martyr in Jewish memory, and tradition holds that some of his garments were kept in Prague for centuries.

Luther turns on the Jews.background:
Martin Luther began the Protestant Reformation in 1517 by challenging the Catholic Church. In 1523 he wrote a pamphlet called That Jesus Christ Was Born a Jew, which criticised the harsh treatment of Jews and suggested that, shown kindness and the true Gospel, they would convert.

They did not. Over the next two decades Luther grew bitter. He was also angered by reports that Jews were persuading some Christians to keep Jewish practices, and by Jewish readings of the Bible that differed from his own.
Luther turns on the Jews.happened:
In 1543 Luther published On the Jews and Their Lies, a long treatise attacking Judaism. He urged rulers to burn synagogues and schools, destroy Jewish homes, take away prayer books and the Talmud, forbid rabbis to teach, ban Jews from travelling, seize their money and make them do hard labour. The same year he published another pamphlet with crude attacks on Jewish beliefs.

Josel of Rosheim, the leading spokesman for German Jews, worked hard to persuade princes and cities not to follow Luther's advice. Some rulers did tighten restrictions or expel Jews, but many others ignored the call, and the writings had limited direct impact at the time.
Luther turns on the Jews.matters:
In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, Luther's later writings were taken up again by German nationalists and then by the Nazis, who presented him as a forerunner. At the Nuremberg trials Julius Streicher cited Luther in his defence. In 1938 a Lutheran bishop celebrated Kristallnacht, which fell on the eve of Luther's birthday, with a pamphlet quoting him.

After the Holocaust many Lutheran churches faced this legacy. In 1994 the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America formally rejected Luther's anti-Jewish writings, and other Lutheran bodies, including the main Protestant church in Germany, have made similar statements. These texts are now studied as a painful part of the history of Christian antisemitism.

Rome's ghetto.background:
The Jews of Rome are among the oldest Jewish communities in Europe, present since before the destruction of the Second Temple. For centuries they lived under the popes, sometimes protected and sometimes restricted, but not confined to one area.

In the 1550s the Catholic Church was responding to the Protestant Reformation with a hard line on religious matters. In 1553 the Talmud was condemned, and copies were burned in Rome's Campo de' Fiori on the Jewish New Year. Cardinal Gian Pietro Carafa, who had pushed for this, became Pope Paul IV in May 1555.
Rome's ghetto.happened:
On 14 July 1555 Paul IV issued a bull known by its opening words, Cum nimis absurdum, meaning since it is absurd. It ordered Jews in the Papal States to live in a separate quarter with one entrance and one exit. In Rome walls were built around a crowded area near the Tiber, opposite Tiber Island, which often flooded. Jews had to wear a yellow hat or veil, could not own property, could have only one synagogue and were limited mostly to dealing in second-hand goods.

Because only one synagogue building was allowed, the community placed five congregations in a single building, known as the Cinque Scole. Over time Jews were also forced to attend sermons aimed at converting them.
Rome's ghetto.matters:
The Rome ghetto lasted, with brief breaks under French rule, until 1870, when the city became part of united Italy. Its walls were torn down soon after, and the Great Synagogue of Rome, with its square dome, was opened on the riverbank in 1904.

The old ghetto area is still the centre of Roman Jewish life, with kosher restaurants serving local dishes such as fried artichokes. In 1986 Pope John Paul II visited the Great Synagogue, the first modern pope to do so, a moment many saw as a turning point in Catholic and Jewish relations.

Shulchan Aruch printed.background:
By the sixteenth century Jewish law, or halakhah, was spread across the Talmud and centuries of commentaries and rulings. Different communities followed different customs, and finding a clear answer could be hard even for scholars. The Spanish expulsion had also mixed communities together, adding to the confusion.

Joseph Karo was born in 1488, probably in Toledo, and his family left Spain as refugees. After years in the Ottoman Balkans he settled in Safed in the Galilee. There he spent decades writing Beit Yosef, a vast commentary on the earlier law code Arba'ah Turim, tracing each law back to its sources.
Shulchan Aruch printed.happened:
Karo then condensed his findings into a short, practical guide, the Shulchan Aruch, first printed in Venice in 1565. Like the Arba'ah Turim, it is divided into four parts covering daily life and prayer, forbidden things such as dietary laws, marriage and divorce, and civil and business law. In deciding between opinions, Karo usually followed the majority of three great earlier authorities: Isaac Alfasi, Maimonides and Asher ben Jehiel.

In Kraków, Rabbi Moses Isserles, known as the Rema, saw that Karo's rulings often reflected Sephardic practice. He wrote glosses called the Mappah, the tablecloth, adding Ashkenazi customs and rulings. From around 1570 the two were printed together.
Shulchan Aruch printed.matters:
The combined work became the most authoritative code of Jewish law. Sephardic Jews generally follow Karo, and Ashkenazi Jews follow Isserles where they differ. Later commentaries, such as the Mishnah Berurah of the Chafetz Chaim in the early twentieth century, are studied alongside it.

Today rabbis still use the Shulchan Aruch as the starting point for questions of practice, and many observant Jews study a section daily. Karo's synagogue still stands in Safed's old city, and the printing press made it possible for his code to reach nearly every Jewish community within a generation.

Luria in Safed.background:
After the Spanish expulsion, many scholars came to the small hill town of Safed in Ottoman Galilee, close to the tomb of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, traditionally linked to the Zohar, the central book of Kabbalah. The town's wool industry brought prosperity, and by the mid sixteenth century it was full of rabbis, mystics and students, including Joseph Karo and Moses Cordovero.

Isaac Luria was born in Jerusalem in 1534 and grew up in Egypt, where he worked in trade and studied Kabbalah in seclusion. Around 1570 he moved to Safed, where he studied briefly with Cordovero before gathering his own circle.
Luria in Safed.happened:
Luria taught only for about two years before he died in an epidemic in 1572, aged around 38. He wrote little himself. His teachings were recorded mainly by his student Hayyim Vital, whose writings, later collected as Etz Hayyim, the Tree of Life, set out the Lurianic system.

Luria described creation in three stages: tzimtzum, God's withdrawal to make space for the world; the breaking of the vessels, when divine light shattered and scattered sparks; and tikkun, repair, in which people help gather those sparks through prayer and good deeds. He also shaped customs, such as greeting the Sabbath in the fields at sunset, a practice linked to the hymn Lekha Dodi, written in Safed by Shlomo Alkabetz.
Luria in Safed.matters:
Lurianic Kabbalah spread quickly across the Jewish world and influenced prayer books, customs and later movements, including Hasidism. The Kabbalat Shabbat service, now said in synagogues everywhere on Friday evening, owes much to the Safed mystics.

The phrase tikkun olam, repairing the world, is older than Luria, but his ideas gave it new depth, and today it is often used for social action. In Safed, the Ari Ashkenazi and Ari Sephardi synagogues and Luria's grave in the old cemetery draw visitors and pilgrims, especially on the anniversary of his death.

Council of Four Lands.background:
By the sixteenth century the Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania were home to a fast-growing Jewish population, welcomed by kings and nobles for their role in trade, crafts and estate management. Each Jewish community, or kahal, managed its own affairs, including schools, charity and courts.

The Polish crown wanted an efficient way to collect a single poll tax from all Jews. Rabbis and leaders also saw the need for wider rules, for example on credit, competition and the printing of books.
Council of Four Lands.happened:
From around 1580, though historians debate the exact start, delegates from regional councils began meeting regularly, usually twice a year at the great trade fairs of Lublin and Jarosław. The four lands were Greater Poland, Lesser Poland, Red Ruthenia and Volhynia. Lithuania formed its own council in 1623.

The Council, known in Hebrew as the Va'ad Arba Aratzot, divided the tax burden among communities and handed the money to the treasury. It also issued rulings on religious and economic matters, approved new books, helped ransom captives and set fast days, such as the one marking the massacres of 1648. Its original minute book was lost, but historians have pieced together many of its decisions from other records.
Council of Four Lands.matters:
For nearly two centuries the Council gave Polish Jewry a rare degree of self-government, at a time when it was the largest Jewish community in the world. It helped make Poland a great centre of Torah learning and community life.

The Polish parliament abolished it in 1764, partly because of debts and partly as part of tax reforms. Historians often point to the Council as a model of organised Jewish autonomy in the diaspora, and its records are an important source for understanding everyday Jewish life in early modern Poland.

Jews settle in Amsterdam.background:
After the forced conversions in Portugal and the founding of the Portuguese Inquisition in 1536, many New Christians looked for places where they could live safely and, if they wished, return to Judaism. The Dutch provinces had rebelled against Spanish rule, and the Union of Utrecht in 1579 promised freedom of conscience.

Amsterdam was becoming a booming trading city, and Portuguese merchants with links to Brazil, Africa and Asia were welcome there. At first many arrived quietly as Christians.
Jews settle in Amsterdam.happened:
In the 1590s and early 1600s a small group of Portuguese conversos began meeting for Jewish worship in Amsterdam. A popular tradition, recorded later, tells of a rabbi from Emden, Moses Uri Halevi, who helped them reconnect with Jewish practice, but historians treat some details with caution. Congregations named Beth Jacob, Neve Shalom and Beth Israel were founded, and in 1639 they joined to form one community, Talmud Torah.

In 1626 Menasseh ben Israel opened the city's first Hebrew printing press. Amsterdam printers produced prayer books, Bibles and law codes for Jews across Europe and the Ottoman Empire. Ashkenazi Jews from Germany and Poland arrived later in the century and formed their own community.
Jews settle in Amsterdam.matters:
Amsterdam became a model of a free Jewish community in Western Europe, nicknamed the Jerusalem of the West. Its merchants helped found Jewish communities in London, the Caribbean and North America, and its printers made it a leading centre of Hebrew books.

Rembrandt lived on the Breestraat in the Jewish quarter, and he drew and painted Jewish neighbours, though historians debate how many of his biblical figures were modelled on them. During the Second World War most Dutch Jews were murdered, but the Jewish Cultural Quarter, including the Portuguese Synagogue and the Jewish Museum, still tells the story of this community.

Fettmilch uprising.background:
Frankfurt am Main was a free imperial city with one of the largest Jewish communities in Germany. Since 1462 Jews had been forced to live in the Judengasse, a single narrow street enclosed by walls and gates, which grew extremely crowded. They were under the protection of the emperor, but the city council controlled their daily lives.

In the early 1600s Frankfurt's guilds were angry with the council, accusing it of corruption and secret debts. Jews, who lent money and were linked to the council's protection, became a target of this anger.
Fettmilch uprising.happened:
From 1612 a gingerbread baker named Vincenz Fettmilch led the guilds in a revolt that eventually pushed the old council aside. On 22 August 1614 a crowd stormed the Judengasse. The Jews defended the gates for a time, then fled to the cemetery. Their homes were plundered, and the next day all of them, around 1,400 people, were forced to leave the city. Similar unrest led to the expulsion of the Jews of Worms in 1615.

The emperor declared Fettmilch an outlaw. He was arrested, tried and executed in 1616. On the same day, 20 Adar in the Jewish calendar, the Jews were led back into the Judengasse with honour, and the imperial eagle was placed on the gates as a sign of the emperor's protection.
Fettmilch uprising.matters:
Frankfurt's Jews marked 20 Adar as a local festival, Purim Vinz, named after Vincenz Fettmilch. A song telling the story, known as the Megillat Vinz, was written in Yiddish and Hebrew and read in the style of the Purim scroll. The custom of local Purims, celebrating rescue from a specific danger, was found in several communities.

The Judengasse remained until the nineteenth century. Its foundations were uncovered in the 1980s and are now part of the Museum Judengasse, one of the sites of Frankfurt's Jewish Museum.

First synagogue in the Americas.background:
In 1630 the Dutch West India Company seized the sugar-rich region of Pernambuco in northeast Brazil from Portugal. Under Dutch rule, Jews could practise openly, unlike in Portuguese and Spanish colonies, where the Inquisition was active.

Portuguese Jews from Amsterdam, along with local New Christians who returned to Judaism, settled in the town of Recife. Many worked in the sugar trade, as merchants, brokers and tax farmers, and their language and connections were useful to the Dutch.
First synagogue in the Americas.happened:
The community, called Kahal Zur Israel, Rock of Israel, was organised around 1636 and built its synagogue on a street that became known as the Street of the Jews. A second congregation existed in nearby Maurícia. By the 1640s Dutch Brazil may have had over a thousand Jews. Isaac Aboab da Fonseca came from Amsterdam as rabbi, the first rabbi in the Americas, and wrote a Hebrew poem about the Portuguese siege, often called the first Hebrew literary work written in the New World.

Portuguese settlers rebelled in 1645, and after years of fighting the Dutch surrendered Recife in January 1654. The Jews were given a few months to leave. Most returned to Amsterdam, while others went to the Caribbean and, in one famous case, New Amsterdam.
First synagogue in the Americas.matters:
The Recife community lasted less than twenty years, but its members helped found Jewish communities in Curaçao, Suriname, Barbados, Jamaica and New York. Its records, kept in Amsterdam, survive.

In the late 1990s and early 2000s archaeologists excavated the site in Recife's old centre and found the remains of the synagogue, including a ritual bath, or mikveh. The building was restored and opened as a museum and cultural centre in the early 2000s, and it is now a place of pilgrimage for Jews from across the Americas.

Khmelnytsky massacres.background:
In the early seventeenth century, Polish nobles controlled vast estates in what is now Ukraine. Many leased the running of these estates, mills, inns and toll collection to Jewish agents, who became the visible face of a system that weighed heavily on Orthodox Ukrainian peasants. The Cossacks, free warrior communities on the Dnieper, also resented Polish attempts to limit their rights.

Bohdan Khmelnytsky was a Cossack officer who had suffered personal wrongs from a Polish noble. In 1648 he allied with the Crimean Tatars and led a revolt.
Khmelnytsky massacres.happened:
After defeating Polish armies in spring 1648, Cossack and peasant forces swept through towns across Ukraine. Jews, Poles and Catholic clergy were killed. At Nemyriv in June 1648 the Jewish community was massacred, and at Tulchyn and Polonne similar horrors followed. Many Jews were sold as captives to the Tatars, and communities in the Ottoman Empire and Italy raised money to ransom them.

The wars continued for years, joined by Russian and Swedish invasions of Poland in the 1650s. Nathan Hannover's chronicle Yeven Metzulah, The Deep Mire, published in 1653, described the events. Older Jewish chronicles gave very high death tolls, but modern historians estimate that tens of thousands of Jews died, and debate the exact numbers.
Khmelnytsky massacres.matters:
In Jewish memory the period is known as Gezerot Tah ve-Tat, the decrees of 1648 and 1649, after their Hebrew years. The Council of Four Lands set 20 Sivan as a fast day, and special prayers were written for it. The trauma helped prepare the ground for the messianic hopes around Shabbetai Tzvi and, later, the rise of Hasidism.

In Ukraine, Khmelnytsky is remembered very differently, as a national hero who led a fight for independence from Poland. The two memories sit side by side, and historians continue to study the uprising from both perspectives.

First Jews in America.background:
When Portugal retook Recife in Dutch Brazil in January 1654, the Jewish community there had to leave. Most sailed back to Amsterdam, but some ships headed for the Caribbean.

New Amsterdam, on the tip of Manhattan, was a small Dutch trading post run by the Dutch West India Company. Its director general, Peter Stuyvesant, was a strict member of the Dutch Reformed Church and wanted to keep the colony free of other faiths, including Lutherans and Quakers as well as Jews.
First Jews in America.happened:
In early September 1654, 23 Jewish refugees, men, women and children, arrived on a ship known as the Sainte Catherine. They were poor, and the captain took some of their goods to cover the cost of the voyage. Stuyvesant wrote to the Company in Amsterdam asking permission to send them away.

In 1655 the Company replied that the Jews could stay, as long as they looked after their own poor. It pointed to the losses Jews had suffered in Brazil and the investment of Jewish shareholders. The newcomers still had to fight for basic rights. Asser Levy, one of the group, demanded the right to stand guard like other citizens and to become a burgher, a full citizen of the town, and he won both. In 1656 the community was granted land for a burial ground.
First Jews in America.matters:
These 23 people are seen as the founders of Jewish life in what became the United States. Their congregation, Shearith Israel, meaning Remnant of Israel, followed Spanish and Portuguese customs and was the only Jewish congregation in New York until the 1820s. Its first purpose built synagogue opened in 1730 on Mill Street.

Today Shearith Israel worships on Central Park West, and a small cemetery it used from the 1680s survives near Chatham Square in Lower Manhattan. American Jews marked the 350th anniversary of the arrival in 2004, and the story is often told as an early test of religious tolerance in America.

Jews readmitted to England.background:
Edward I had expelled all Jews from England in 1290. For over three centuries no open Jewish community existed there, although a few conversos lived quietly in London as Spanish or Portuguese merchants.

In the 1640s and 1650s, during the English Civil War and Commonwealth, many Puritans took a strong interest in the Hebrew Bible and in prophecies about the end of days. Menasseh ben Israel, a rabbi and printer in Amsterdam, argued that the Messiah would come only when Jews were scattered to every corner of the earth, including England. His book The Hope of Israel, published in 1650, also claimed that lost tribes lived in the Americas.
Jews readmitted to England.happened:
In 1655 Menasseh came to London and presented a petition to Oliver Cromwell, the Lord Protector. Cromwell called a conference at Whitehall in December 1655 of lawyers, merchants and clergy. The lawyers said there was no law that actually forbade Jews from living in England, but merchants and some clergy opposed any formal readmission, and the conference ended without a decision.

In 1656 a case arose when the property of Antonio Robles, a converso merchant, was seized as that of a Spaniard during war with Spain. Robles declared himself a Jew and his goods were returned. Later that year Cromwell let it be known that Jews could live and worship privately. The community rented a house in Creechurch Lane in the City of London as a synagogue. Menasseh himself died in 1657, disappointed that he had not won more.
Jews readmitted to England.matters:
This quiet resettlement, without any formal law, is the starting point of modern Anglo-Jewry. The Spanish and Portuguese community later built Bevis Marks Synagogue, opened in 1701, which is still in use and is the oldest synagogue in Britain.

In 2006 British Jews marked 350 years since the resettlement. The same summer of 1656, in Amsterdam, the young Baruch Spinoza was placed under a herem, a ban of exclusion, by the Portuguese community. He went on to become one of the most influential philosophers of the modern age.

Shabbetai Tzvi.background:
By the mid seventeenth century many Jews were living through hard times. The Khmelnytsky massacres of 1648 had devastated Polish Jewry, and the memory of the Spanish expulsion and the Inquisition was still fresh. Lurianic Kabbalah taught that the world was close to being repaired, and some calculations pointed to 1648 or 1666 as years of redemption.

Shabbetai Tzvi was born in Smyrna, now Izmir, in 1626. He was learned and charismatic, but suffered from extreme swings of mood. He sometimes broke Jewish law in strange public acts, and rabbis in several cities had sent him away.
Shabbetai Tzvi.happened:
In 1665 Shabbetai met Nathan, a young Kabbalist in Gaza, who declared that Shabbetai was the Messiah and that he himself was his prophet. News spread by letters and travellers across the Ottoman Empire, Italy, Amsterdam, Hamburg, Poland and Yemen. People fasted, did penance and prepared to travel to the Land of Israel. The memoirist Glückel of Hameln recalled that her father-in-law packed barrels of food in readiness for the journey. Some followers stopped fasting on traditional fast days.

Early in 1666 Shabbetai sailed to Constantinople, where he was arrested and held in the fortress of Gallipoli, which became a place of pilgrimage. In September 1666 he was brought before Sultan Mehmed IV at Edirne and, given the choice between death and Islam, he converted, taking the name Aziz Mehmed Effendi. He died in exile in Ulcinj, in today's Montenegro, in 1676.
Shabbetai Tzvi.matters:
The conversion shocked the Jewish world. Most followers returned to normal life, but some believed the conversion was part of a hidden plan. A group of them in Salonika converted to Islam while keeping secret traditions, becoming known as the Dönme.

The movement left rabbis wary of messianic claims and of popular Kabbalah for generations, as the later disputes over the Ramchal and the Frankists show. The scholar Gershom Scholem's major study, published in the twentieth century, made Shabbetai Tzvi one of the most discussed figures in Jewish history.

Portuguese Synagogue, Amsterdam.background:
By the 1670s the Portuguese Jewish community of Amsterdam had grown wealthy and confident. Its members were merchants, doctors and printers, many of them former conversos or their children. Their earlier synagogues were too small.

Across the street, the Ashkenazi community had opened its own Great Synagogue in 1671. The Portuguese community decided to build a grand new building that would express its pride and its gratitude for freedom in the Dutch Republic.
Portuguese Synagogue, Amsterdam.happened:
Designed by the architect Elias Bouman, the synagogue was built between 1671 and 1675 on what was then the edge of the city. It was dedicated on 2 August 1675 with celebrations lasting several days. Its design was said to be inspired by descriptions of Solomon's Temple. The building is a huge brick hall with tall windows, wooden pews and a floor covered in fine sand, a custom some link to muffling noise and others to the desert wanderings.

The synagogue complex also houses the Ets Haim library, one of the oldest working Jewish libraries in the world, with manuscripts and early printed books. The building has no electric lighting in the main hall. Its brass chandeliers hold hundreds of candles, around a thousand in total, which are lit for special services.
Portuguese Synagogue, Amsterdam.matters:
The Esnoga, from the Portuguese word for synagogue, became a symbol of Amsterdam as a haven for Jews. Visitors, Jewish and Christian, came to admire it, and it was copied by Sephardic communities in London, the Caribbean and elsewhere.

During the Second World War the building survived the Nazi occupation, though most of its congregation was murdered. Today it is still used for services, especially in summer and on festivals, and is part of Amsterdam's Jewish Cultural Quarter. The Ets Haim library was added to UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 2003.

Judah HeHasid's aliyah.background:
After the collapse of the Shabbetai Tzvi movement, some Jews still hoped that redemption was near. Rabbi Judah HeHasid, meaning Judah the Pious, was a preacher in Poland who urged repentance and taught that moving to the Land of Israel could help bring the Messiah. Some historians think his circle included people with lingering Sabbatean sympathies, but this is debated.

The word aliyah, going up, is used for Jewish immigration to the Land of Israel. Jerusalem at this time was a small Ottoman town with a poor Jewish population, mostly Sephardic.
Judah HeHasid's aliyah.happened:
In 1699 and 1700 Judah HeHasid and his companion Hayyim Malach led several hundred followers on a long journey through Germany, Italy and the Ottoman lands. Many died on the way. The group reached Jerusalem in the autumn of 1700, and Judah died only a few days after arriving.
