Without their leader, the group split and struggled. They borrowed money, much of it from local Arab lenders, to build a synagogue and homes in the Jewish quarter. Unable to repay, they fell deeper into debt. In 1720 the creditors broke in and set fire to the synagogue, and Ashkenazi Jews were barred from Jerusalem by the authorities for many years.
Judah HeHasid's aliyah.matters:
For more than a century the burned site stood in ruins and was known as the Hurva, meaning the ruin. In the nineteenth century disciples of the Vilna Gaon, known as the Perushim, cleared the debts and built a great domed synagogue there, opened in 1864. It became the main Ashkenazi synagogue in Jerusalem.

The building was blown up during the fighting in the Old City in 1948. A single stone arch was put up in 1977 as a memorial, and the synagogue was rebuilt in its nineteenth century form and rededicated in 2010. It still carries the name Hurva and is a landmark of the Jewish Quarter.

Ramchal.background:
Moshe Chaim Luzzatto was born in Padua in 1707 into a wealthy and learned Italian Jewish family. He studied Bible, Talmud, Kabbalah, Latin and classical literature, and wrote Hebrew poetry and plays while still very young. His name is often shortened to the Ramchal, from the Hebrew initials of Rabbi Moshe Chaim Luzzatto.

After the disaster of Shabbetai Tzvi, rabbis across Europe were deeply suspicious of anyone claiming new mystical revelations, especially young men gathering followers.
Ramchal.happened:
In his twenties Luzzatto said he received teachings from a heavenly voice, a maggid, and he wrote many Kabbalistic works. Rumours spread that his circle saw him in messianic terms. Rabbi Moses Hagiz and other rabbis led a campaign against him. In 1730 he agreed to stop writing such works without permission, and later he swore in Frankfurt to stop teaching Kabbalah. Some of his manuscripts were burned.

He moved to Amsterdam around 1735, where he earned his living grinding lenses and continued to write. His ethical book Mesillat Yesharim, The Path of the Just, was printed there in 1740. It leads the reader step by step through qualities such as watchfulness, zeal and humility. He also wrote Derech Hashem, The Way of God, on the basics of Jewish belief, and the play La-Yesharim Tehillah. In 1743 he moved to the Land of Israel and died in Acre, probably of plague, in 1746.
Ramchal.matters:
Mesillat Yesharim became one of the most widely read Jewish books on character and spiritual growth. It was central to the Mussar movement, founded in nineteenth century Lithuania by Rabbi Israel Salanter, and is still studied in yeshivas and by individuals today.

Luzzatto is also remembered as a pioneer of modern Hebrew literature, admired by later writers of the Jewish Enlightenment for the beauty of his language. Tradition holds that he is buried in Tiberias, near the grave attributed to Rabbi Akiva.

Hasidism begins.background:
In the eighteenth century, Jews in the Polish lands, especially in Podolia and Volhynia in today's Ukraine, were still recovering from the massacres of 1648 and the shock of Shabbetai Tzvi. Jewish life was led by a learned elite, and ordinary people with little schooling could feel shut out of the most valued religious life, which was Torah study.

At the same time, there were wandering healers and popular mystics, called baalei shem, masters of the divine name, who wrote amulets and offered blessings.
Hasidism begins.happened:
Israel ben Eliezer was born around 1700 and became known as the Baal Shem Tov, Master of the Good Name, often shortened to the Besht. Around 1740 he settled in the town of Medzhybizh, where he attracted a circle of followers, including respected scholars. He taught that God is present everywhere, that sincere prayer and joy matter as much as learning, and that every person can draw close to God, even in daily work.

He left almost no writings. His teachings were passed on by students, and stories about him were collected in Shivhei ha-Besht, In Praise of the Baal Shem Tov, printed in 1814. After his death in 1760, Rabbi Dov Ber, the Maggid of Mezeritch, organised the movement, and his students spread it across Ukraine, Poland, Belarus and Hungary.
Hasidism begins.matters:
Hasidism introduced the figure of the rebbe, or tzaddik, a spiritual leader around whom a community gathers, often in a dynasty passing from father to son. Groups took the names of their home towns, such as Chabad, Ger, Belz and Satmar. Customs such as wordless melodies, called nigunim, and the rebbe's table gatherings became central features.

The Holocaust destroyed much of Hasidic Europe, but survivors rebuilt in Israel, the United States and elsewhere. Today Hasidic communities are among the fastest growing in the Jewish world, and the Baal Shem Tov's grave in Medzhybizh draws pilgrims.

Expulsion from Prague.background:
Prague had one of the oldest and largest Jewish communities in Europe, with famous synagogues such as the Old New Synagogue and a long tradition of scholarship. In 1740 Maria Theresa inherited the Habsburg lands, and rival powers soon attacked, starting the War of the Austrian Succession.

In 1744 Prussian forces under Frederick the Great occupied Prague for a time. After they withdrew, the Jews were accused of having helped the enemy, though there was no real evidence. Maria Theresa was also known for her personal dislike of Jews.
Expulsion from Prague.happened:
In December 1744 the empress ordered the Jews to leave Prague, and soon after extended the order to all of Bohemia and Moravia. The Jews of Prague had to leave the city in the depths of winter, and by the spring of 1745 the Jewish quarter was largely empty. Many took shelter in nearby villages, hoping for a reversal.

Jewish leaders appealed to communities and governments across Europe. Britain, the Dutch Republic and other states sent diplomatic protests. Bohemian officials also warned that trade was suffering and that the crown was losing tax income. In 1748 Maria Theresa allowed the Jews to return to Prague in exchange for a heavy tax, renewed every few years. The expulsion from the rest of Bohemia and Moravia was cancelled too.
Expulsion from Prague.matters:
The expulsion showed how vulnerable Jews remained to the will of a ruler, even in a great city with a long history. It was also an early example of international Jewish networks lobbying foreign governments to help a threatened community, a pattern that would recur in later centuries.

The community recovered and Prague remained a major Jewish centre. Maria Theresa's son, Joseph II, took a very different approach with his Edict of Tolerance in 1782. Today the Jewish Museum in Prague, with its synagogues and old cemetery, tells the story of this community.

Jew Bill in Britain.background:
By the 1750s about eight thousand Jews lived in Britain, mostly in London. Jews born in Britain were subjects, but foreign-born Jews could not become naturalised, because the process required taking the sacrament in a Christian church. This limited their rights, for example to own land or ships.

Wealthy Jewish merchants, such as Joseph Salvador, had helped the government with loans, and the Whig ministry of Henry Pelham was willing to grant a modest reform.
Jew Bill in Britain.happened:
The Jewish Naturalisation Act passed through Parliament in spring 1753 and received royal assent in the summer. It allowed foreign-born Jews to apply to Parliament for naturalisation without taking the sacrament. In practice few would have used it, because private acts were expensive.

The opposition Tories, many clergy and London merchants seized on the act. Pamphlets, sermons and satirical prints warned that Jews would buy up England, and some claimed it went against Christian prophecy. With a general election due in 1754, the government gave way, and the act was repealed in December 1753, only months after it passed. William Hogarth referred to the uproar in his series of paintings and prints about an election.
Jew Bill in Britain.matters:
The episode showed how easily public fear could be stirred against Jews even in a country where they lived relatively safely. It slowed the push for Jewish rights in Britain for decades.

Emancipation came gradually in the nineteenth century. In 1858, after years of campaigning, Parliament changed the oath for members, and Lionel de Rothschild took his seat as the first Jewish member of the House of Commons. Historians often look back at the 1753 controversy as an early example of modern political antisemitism using the press and print culture.

The Frankists.background:
Even after Shabbetai Tzvi's conversion, small groups of believers survived in secret, especially in Podolia, then part of Poland. Rabbis had tried to stamp them out with bans.

Jacob Frank was born in Podolia in 1726 and spent years in the Ottoman Empire, where he came into contact with the Dönme, the followers of Shabbetai Tzvi who had converted to Islam. Around 1755 he returned to Poland and presented himself as a successor to Shabbetai Tzvi.
The Frankists.happened:
In 1756 Frank and his followers were caught holding a secret ritual in the village of Lanckorona, and the rabbis excommunicated them. The Frankists turned to the Catholic bishop of Kamieniec, declaring that they rejected the Talmud. A disputation was held in Kamieniec in 1757, after which copies of the Talmud were burned.

In 1759 a second disputation was held in Lwów, now Lviv, over several weeks. The Frankists repeated a number of claims against the Talmud, including the false blood libel, the old charge that Jews use Christian blood. Afterwards around 500 Frankists were baptised, with Polish nobles standing as godparents, and Frank himself was baptised in Warsaw with King Augustus III as his godfather. Church authorities soon doubted his sincerity, and he was imprisoned in the monastery fortress of Częstochowa from 1760 to 1773.
The Frankists.matters:
After his release Frank lived in Moravia and then Offenbach in Germany, where he died in 1791. His daughter Eva led the group after him. Many Frankist families blended into Polish Catholic society, some becoming part of the gentry.

The affair deepened Jewish fear of messianic movements and added to tensions in Polish Jewry during the same years that Hasidism was spreading. In 2014 the Polish writer Olga Tokarczuk published The Books of Jacob, a large novel about Frank and his followers, which brought new attention to this unusual chapter of history.

Touro Synagogue.background:
Rhode Island was founded in the 1630s by Roger Williams, who believed in freedom of conscience, and it became a refuge for many religious minorities. Jews, mainly of Spanish and Portuguese descent, settled in Newport from the second half of the seventeenth century and bought land for a cemetery in 1677.

By the 1750s Newport was a busy port, and its Jewish community, Jeshuat Israel, had grown with merchants such as Aaron Lopez. Isaac Touro, who came from Amsterdam, served as its religious leader, and the community decided to build a synagogue.
Touro Synagogue.happened:
The architect Peter Harrison, who also designed other notable buildings in colonial America, created an elegant Georgian building, set at an angle on its plot so that worshippers face east towards Jerusalem. Inside, twelve columns on the lower level support a women's gallery above. The synagogue was dedicated in December 1763, during Hanukkah.

In August 1790 President George Washington visited Newport. The warden Moses Seixas welcomed him with a letter, and Washington wrote back to the congregation. In his reply he echoed Seixas's words, stating that the government of the United States gives no approval to bigotry and no help to persecution, and asked only that those living under its protection behave as good citizens.
Touro Synagogue.matters:
Touro Synagogue is the oldest surviving synagogue building in the United States. The community declined after the American Revolution, but bequests from Isaac Touro's sons, Abraham and Judah, kept the building and cemetery cared for, and the synagogue later took their family name. It was reopened for regular worship in the 1880s.

It was named a National Historic Site in 1946. Washington's letter is read aloud at a public event in Newport every August and is often quoted as one of the clearest early statements of religious liberty in America.

Ban on the Hasidim.background:
By the 1770s Hasidism had spread from Ukraine into Belarus and Lithuania. Its followers formed their own prayer groups, adopted a prayer book based on the customs of the Safed Kabbalists, and gathered around rebbes. To many traditional leaders this looked like a split in the community, and memories of Shabbetai Tzvi and the Frankists made them fear another dangerous sect.

Vilna, in Lithuania, was the leading centre of rabbinic learning in Eastern Europe, and its most respected figure was Rabbi Elijah, the Vilna Gaon, a scholar of enormous authority.
Ban on the Hasidim.happened:
In 1772, with the Gaon's backing, the community leaders of Vilna issued a herem, a formal ban of excommunication, against the Hasidim. Similar bans followed in Brody and other towns. A pamphlet titled Zemir Aritzim, collecting letters against the movement, was printed the same year. The opponents accused the Hasidim of neglecting Torah study, praying late and with wild movements, changing the prayer rite, using different knives for kosher slaughter and treating their rebbes with excessive devotion.

That year two Hasidic leaders, Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk and Shneur Zalman of Liadi, travelled to Vilna to try to make peace, but the Gaon refused to meet them. Further bans were issued in 1781 and 1796. In 1798 opponents denounced Shneur Zalman to the Russian authorities, and he was arrested in St Petersburg, then released.
Ban on the Hasidim.matters:
The opponents of Hasidism became known as Mitnagdim, meaning those who oppose. The rivalry shaped Eastern European Jewish life for generations, and the Lithuanian yeshiva world grew partly as a response. Chabad Hasidim still celebrate 19 Kislev, the date of Shneur Zalman's release, as a festival.

During the nineteenth century both sides came to see the Haskalah and secular modernity as a greater threat, and the conflict softened. Today Hasidic and Lithuanian, or Litvish, communities live side by side within the wider Haredi world, though differences of custom and style remain.

Hasidic aliyah.background:
Hasidism grew quickly after the death of the Baal Shem Tov, but its leaders faced fierce opposition from the Mitnagdim, including the bans of 1772. For some, settling in the Land of Israel was both a deep spiritual goal and a way to step away from conflict.

In the 1770s the Galilee was part of the Ottoman Empire. The local Jewish population was small and poor, mostly Sephardic, living in towns such as Safed and Tiberias, which had been partly rebuilt by the local ruler Zahir al-Umar.
Hasidic aliyah.happened:
In 1777 Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk, a leading student of the Maggid of Mezeritch, set out with Rabbi Abraham of Kalisk and Rabbi Israel of Polotsk at the head of a group of around 300 people, including families and followers who were not Hasidim. They travelled overland and then by sea, arriving in the autumn of that year.

They settled first in Safed, but faced hardship and tension, partly because the Mitnagdim had sent letters warning local Jews about them. After a few years most moved to Tiberias. They depended on money collected in Eastern Europe, a system called halukah, meaning distribution. Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi took on much of the work of raising these funds. Menachem Mendel led the community from afar through letters to his followers back home until his death in 1788.
Hasidic aliyah.matters:
This group is often seen as the first organised Hasidic settlement in the Land of Israel, and it strengthened the Jewish presence in Tiberias and Safed. Its letters home are an important source for life in the Galilee at the time.

The halukah system, with funds organised by region of origin in groups called kollelim, supported much of the Jewish population of the Holy Land until the late nineteenth century. Menachem Mendel's grave in the old cemetery of Tiberias is still visited, and Hasidic communities in the city trace their roots to this journey.

Edict of Tolerance.background:
Joseph II became sole ruler of the Habsburg lands in 1780 after the death of his mother, Maria Theresa, who had expelled the Jews of Prague. Joseph was influenced by Enlightenment ideas and wanted a more efficient, united state in which all subjects were useful to the economy.

At the time, Jews in Vienna lived only by special permission, paid heavy special taxes, could not own land, were barred from many trades and had to wear distinctive signs.
Edict of Tolerance.happened:
Joseph issued a series of tolerance patents for different parts of his empire, starting with Bohemia in October 1781. The Edict of Tolerance for the Jews of Vienna and Lower Austria followed on 2 January 1782. It removed the badge, abolished the body tax Jews paid when travelling and allowed them to learn trades, set up factories, attend universities and send their children to Christian schools or set up their own state approved schools.

There were limits and conditions. Jews still could not freely settle in Vienna and needed permits. Hebrew and Yiddish were banned in public records and business documents, and German was required. In later years Jews were made to take German surnames and to serve in the army. The Jewish writer Naphtali Herz Wessely welcomed the reforms in a Hebrew pamphlet, while many rabbis feared they would weaken Jewish life.
Edict of Tolerance.matters:
The edict was one of the first attempts by a European ruler to bring Jews into wider society by law, and it opened schools, universities and professions to many Jews. It also showed the price attached: rulers expected Jews to change their language, education and culture.

This tension between emancipation and assimilation shaped Jewish life in Central Europe for the next century. Vienna's Jewish community grew into one of the most important in Europe, producing figures in medicine, music, science and literature, until the Holocaust destroyed it.

The Haskalah.background:
Moses Mendelssohn was born in 1729 in Dessau, the son of a poor Torah scribe. As a teenager he followed his teacher to Berlin, where he taught himself German, Latin, mathematics and philosophy. He became famous as a philosopher, and his friend Gotthold Ephraim Lessing is thought to have based the wise Jewish hero of his play Nathan the Wise on him.

In 1769 the Swiss pastor Johann Kaspar Lavater publicly challenged Mendelssohn either to refute Christianity or convert. Mendelssohn replied politely but firmly that he remained a faithful Jew, and the episode made him think deeply about how Jews could live in modern society.
The Haskalah.happened:
Mendelssohn produced a German translation of the Torah, printed in Hebrew letters, with a Hebrew commentary, published between 1780 and 1783. It helped Jews who spoke Yiddish learn standard German while studying the Bible. In 1783 he published Jerusalem, or on Religious Power and Judaism, which argued that the state should not force belief and that Judaism was a religion of laws and practice rather than of required dogmas.

Around him gathered a circle of writers and teachers called maskilim, from the word Haskalah, meaning enlightenment or wisdom. They opened a modern Jewish school in Berlin in 1778, and in 1784 began publishing Ha-Me'assef, a Hebrew journal on science, literature and education.
The Haskalah.matters:
The Haskalah spread from Germany to Galicia, Russia and beyond during the nineteenth century. It encouraged modern schooling, new Hebrew literature, the study of Jewish history and engagement with European culture. It helped give rise to Reform Judaism, modern Orthodoxy, Hebrew and Yiddish literature and, later, Zionism.

Mendelssohn's legacy is debated. Some of his grandchildren, including the composer Felix Mendelssohn, were raised as Christians, which critics saw as a warning. Others see him as proof that a person can be fully modern and fully Jewish, a question Jews still discuss today.

Citizenship in France.background:
Before the Revolution, about forty thousand Jews lived in France, in very different groups. Sephardic Jews in Bordeaux and Bayonne were largely accepted merchants. Ashkenazi Jews in Alsace and Lorraine, the majority, spoke Yiddish, lived under heavy restrictions and were often resented as moneylenders. A small community also lived in the papal territory around Avignon.

In August 1789 the National Assembly adopted the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, which said that all men are born free and equal in rights. The question was whether this included Jews.
Citizenship in France.happened:
The debate was long and heated. In December 1789 Count Stanislas de Clermont-Tonnerre argued for Jewish equality, saying that Jews should be granted everything as individuals but nothing as a separate nation. The Abbé Henri Grégoire, a Catholic priest, also campaigned for their rights. Others, especially deputies from Alsace, strongly opposed it.

On 28 January 1790 the Sephardic Jews of the south were granted citizenship. The Ashkenazi Jews had to wait longer. Finally, on 27 September 1791, the Assembly voted to give full citizenship to all Jews who took the civic oath, and the law was confirmed the next day.
Citizenship in France.matters:
France became the first country in modern Europe to grant Jews full and equal citizenship. The decision rested on a bargain: Jews would be equal citizens, but their communities would lose the separate legal powers they had held.

As French armies spread across Europe, Jewish emancipation followed in places such as the Netherlands in 1796 and parts of Italy and Germany, though some of these gains were reversed after Napoleon's fall. The French model, and the question of how far Jews should keep a distinct identity, shaped debates about Jewish life across Europe for the next century.

Pale of Settlement.background:
Before the late eighteenth century, very few Jews lived in the Russian Empire, as Russian rulers had long barred them. That changed with the partitions of Poland in 1772, 1793 and 1795, when Russia, Prussia and Austria divided the Polish state. Russia gained huge territories in the west with hundreds of thousands of Jewish inhabitants.

Russian merchants in Moscow and other cities did not want Jewish competition, and the government was wary of a large population with its own language and religion.
Pale of Settlement.happened:
In 1791 Catherine the Great issued a decree that stopped Jewish merchants from registering in central Russian cities and confined them to the newly gained western regions and some areas around the Black Sea. Over the following decades, laws in 1804 and 1835 set the borders of what became known as the Pale of Settlement, from the word pale, meaning a boundary. It stretched from the Baltic to the Black Sea, covering much of today's Lithuania, Belarus, Ukraine, Moldova and eastern Poland.

Within the Pale, Jews were often also barred from villages and certain cities, such as Kyiv for long periods. Only some groups, such as wealthy merchants, university graduates and certain craftsmen, were later allowed to live outside it. The 1897 census counted about five million Jews in the Russian Empire, the great majority within the Pale.
Pale of Settlement.matters:
The Pale was home to the world's largest Jewish population for over a century. In its towns and shtetls, the small market towns, Yiddish culture, Hasidism, the Lithuanian yeshivas, the Jewish labour movement and early Zionism all flourished, despite poverty, overcrowding and waves of pogroms.

The Pale was abolished in 1917 after the February Revolution. Hardship there drove millions to emigrate to America, Britain, South Africa and Palestine between the 1880s and 1914. The world of the shtetl lives on in the stories of Sholem Aleichem, the musical Fiddler on the Roof and the family histories of millions of their descendants.

The Vilna Gaon.background:
Elijah ben Solomon Zalman was born in 1720 near Vilna, today Vilnius, which was then in the Polish Lithuanian Commonwealth. He was a child prodigy, said to have given a talk in the great synagogue at the age of six. As an adult he refused any official rabbinic post and lived mostly in seclusion, supported by a community allowance, devoting himself to study day and night.

His title, the Gaon, meaning genius, was a mark of deep respect. Vilna was known as the Jerusalem of Lithuania, and the Gaon became its most famous figure.
The Vilna Gaon.happened:
The Gaon studied the whole range of Jewish texts, from the Bible and Talmud to Kabbalah, and also valued mathematics, astronomy and grammar as tools for understanding the Torah. He insisted on careful, accurate texts and corrected errors that had crept into books over the centuries. His notes and commentaries, mostly published after his death by his students, cover a huge number of works, and his comments on the Shulchan Aruch are especially well known.

He was a leading opponent of Hasidism and supported the bans against it. He died on 9 October 1797, during the festival of Sukkot. His grave was later moved when the Soviet authorities destroyed the old Jewish cemetery, and it now lies in a newer Vilnius cemetery.
The Vilna Gaon.matters:
The Gaon's students shaped Lithuanian Jewish life. Rabbi Hayyim of Volozhin founded the Volozhin yeshiva in 1803, the model for the great Lithuanian yeshivas, with their focus on deep Talmud study. That model continues in yeshivas across Israel, the United States and elsewhere.

Other students, known as the Perushim, moved to the Land of Israel from 1808, settling in Safed and Jerusalem and later rebuilding the Hurva synagogue. In Lithuania the Gaon is remembered as a national figure, and the country's Jewish museum bears his name.

Napoleon's Sanhedrin.background:
French Jews had been citizens since 1791, but tensions remained, especially in Alsace, where peasants complained about Jewish moneylenders. Napoleon, now emperor, wanted to settle what he saw as the Jewish question and to make sure Jews were loyal French citizens first.

In 1806 he called an Assembly of Jewish Notables, about a hundred leading Jews from France and French-ruled Italy, and gave them twelve questions on topics such as marriage, divorce, intermarriage, loyalty to France and moneylending.
Napoleon's Sanhedrin.happened:
The Assembly answered carefully, trying to show that Jewish law and French law could live together. Napoleon then decided to give their answers religious authority by calling a Grand Sanhedrin, named after the ancient court of 71 sages in Jerusalem. It met in Paris in February and March 1807, with about two-thirds rabbis and one third laymen, led by Rabbi David Sintzheim of Strasbourg.

The Sanhedrin confirmed that Jews regard France as their homeland and its citizens as their brothers, that civil marriage and divorce must come first, that Jews must obey the laws of the state and serve in its army, and that charging excessive interest was forbidden. In 1808 Napoleon issued decrees creating a system of consistories, official regional bodies to run Jewish religious life under state supervision. He also issued what Jews called the Infamous Decree, which for ten years restricted Jewish moneylending and the right to settle in some areas.
Napoleon's Sanhedrin.matters:
The Sanhedrin raised fears among some traditional Jews and rulers elsewhere, and Russian and Austrian authorities saw it as a political move to win Jewish support. Yet it set out a model of Jews as citizens whose religion was a private faith, an idea that shaped Jewish communities in France and beyond.

The consistory system Napoleon created still exists today. The Consistoire central israélite de France remains the main body for Jewish religious affairs in France, and the Chief Rabbi of France is chosen through it.

Reform Judaism begins.background:
For most of the Middle Ages, Jews in German lands lived apart, with their own courts, taxes and rules. In the late 1700s the ideas of the Enlightenment began to change this. The philosopher Moses Mendelssohn urged Jews to learn German and join wider culture, and the Haskalah, or Jewish Enlightenment, spread these ideas. When Napoleon's armies swept across Europe, some territories granted Jews equal rights for the first time.

Many younger Jews felt that long, traditional Hebrew services did not fit the modern world, and some were converting to Christianity to advance their careers.
Reform Judaism begins.happened:
Israel Jacobson was a wealthy banker and head of the Jewish Consistory, an official council for Jewish affairs, in the Kingdom of Westphalia, ruled by Napoleon's brother Jérôme. In 1801 he had founded a school in the small town of Seesen. In July 1810 he dedicated a temple at the school with a bell tower, an organ, sermons in German and some prayers sung in German by a choir. He deliberately called it a temple rather than a synagogue.

In 1818 a group of laymen opened the New Israelite Temple in Hamburg, with its own prayer book that removed or softened prayers for a return to Zion and the rebuilding of the ancient Temple. Leading rabbis issued a public condemnation. In the following decades scholars such as Abraham Geiger and Samuel Holdheim gave Reform a fuller set of ideas, arguing that Judaism had always changed over time.
Reform Judaism begins.matters:
The split shaped Jewish life ever since. Traditionalists such as Rabbi Moses Sofer of Pressburg rejected any change to Jewish law. In Frankfurt, Rabbi Samson Raphael Hirsch developed a modern Orthodoxy that combined strict observance with secular education. Zacharias Frankel, who felt Reform went too far, led a middle path at the Breslau seminary from 1854, which later grew into Conservative Judaism, known in Israel as Masorti.

Reform flourished most in the United States, where Isaac Mayer Wise founded Hebrew Union College in 1875. Today Reform is the largest Jewish denomination in America, and Reform, Liberal and Progressive congregations exist around the world. Organs, mixed seating and prayers in local languages all trace back to this movement.

Cantonist decree.background:
Russia gained most of its Jewish subjects when Poland was divided at the end of the 1700s. The tsars confined Jews to a western region called the Pale of Settlement and viewed them with suspicion. Nicholas I, who came to the throne in 1825, wanted to make Jews more "useful" and to draw them towards the Russian Orthodox Church.

Russia already had cantonist schools, military schools for the sons of soldiers. Jews had previously paid a tax instead of serving in the army. Nicholas decided to end this exemption and use the army as a tool for changing Jewish society.
Cantonist decree.happened:
The statute of August 1827 made Jews liable for conscription. Each Jewish community council, the kahal, had to deliver a fixed quota of recruits. Officially recruits were 12 to 25 years old, but boys under 18 were sent to cantonist schools, and their 25 years of service only began counting at 18. In practice community leaders often filled the quota with the children of the poor, orphans and families without influence, while wealthier families bought exemptions.

When quotas could not be met, communities hired khappers, Yiddish for "grabbers", who seized children from homes and streets, sometimes younger than the law allowed. The boys were marched hundreds of miles to distant provinces. There they faced beatings, hunger and heavy pressure to be baptised. Many died on the way or in the schools. The writer Alexander Herzen later described meeting a convoy of exhausted Jewish boys being marched through the Russian countryside. In 1853 rules even allowed communities to seize Jews without proper papers as recruits.
Cantonist decree.matters:
The decree left deep scars. It turned the community's own leaders into enforcers and broke trust between rich and poor Jews. Tsar Alexander II abolished the cantonist system in 1856, and later laws reduced military service to a few years. Some former cantonists, known as Nicholas soldiers, who had kept their faith, were allowed to live outside the Pale and helped found communities in places such as Siberia and St Petersburg.

The khappers and the stolen children live on in Yiddish folk songs, stories and memoirs. The fear of conscription was one of the reasons many Jewish families later chose to leave the Russian Empire.

Galilee earthquake.background:
Safed, high in the hills of the Galilee, is one of Judaism's four holy cities, along with Jerusalem, Hebron and Tiberias. In the 1500s it was a world centre of Jewish learning. There Rabbi Isaac Luria taught Kabbalah, Jewish mysticism, and Rabbi Joseph Karo wrote the Shulchan Aruch, the great code of Jewish law.

By the 1830s Safed had a mixed community of Sephardi Jews and Ashkenazi Hasidim and students of the Vilna Gaon who had come from Eastern Europe. The region was then ruled by Muhammad Ali of Egypt. Life was already hard: in 1834, during a local revolt, Safed's Jews had been attacked and their homes plundered for weeks.
Galilee earthquake.happened:
On the afternoon of 1 January 1837 a powerful earthquake struck the Galilee and southern Lebanon. In Safed, houses were built in terraces down the steep slope, with the roof of one serving as the courtyard of the next. When the ground shook, the upper houses collapsed onto those below, burying whole families. The Jewish quarter, on the steepest part of the hill, was almost totally destroyed. Rescue was slow and survivors dug through the rubble with their hands for days.

Around 2,000 of Safed's Jews died, along with many Muslim residents. In Tiberias, on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, the city walls and many buildings fell, and hundreds were killed. Relief money was sent from Jewish communities in Europe, and when Sir Moses Montefiore visited in 1839 he found the communities still struggling to recover.
Galilee earthquake.matters:
The earthquake shifted the centre of Jewish life in the Land of Israel. Many survivors moved to Jerusalem, which from then on held the largest Jewish population in the country. Safed was hit again in 1838 by an attack during a Druze revolt, and it took decades to rebuild.

Today visitors to Safed's old quarter can see rebuilt synagogues named after the famous rabbis of the 1500s, such as the Ari and Abuhav synagogues. According to local tradition, the southern wall of the Abuhav synagogue, which holds the Torah ark, was the only part left standing. The old cemetery on the hillside contains graves of victims of the disaster, alongside those of the great mystics.

Damascus affair.background: In 1840 Damascus was under the rule of Muhammad Ali of Egypt, whose forces had taken Syria from the Ottoman Empire. European powers competed for influence in the region, and France saw itself as the protector of Catholics there. The blood libel, the false claim that Jews use Christian blood for rituals, had long existed in Europe but was less common in the Muslim world.
Damascus affair.happened:
In February 1840 a Capuchin friar known as Father Thomas and his servant disappeared in Damascus. The French consul, Ulysse de Ratti-Menton, backed claims that Jews had killed them for their blood ahead of Passover. The governor, Sherif Pasha, had a Jewish barber arrested and tortured until he named leading members of the community. Several prominent men were then tortured. Two died, and one converted to Islam to save himself. Sixty-three Jewish children were held to force their parents to reveal hidden blood.

News reached Europe and caused alarm. In Britain, France and the United States, Jews held protest meetings, and President Martin Van Buren instructed American diplomats to intervene, the first such action by the United States on behalf of Jews abroad. In the summer of 1840 Sir Moses Montefiore and Adolphe Crémieux, joined by the scholar Solomon Munk, travelled to Alexandria and persuaded Muhammad Ali to release the surviving prisoners in August. Montefiore then went to Constantinople, where in November Sultan Abdulmejid issued a decree declaring the blood libel false and promising protection to Jews.
Damascus affair.matters:
The affair showed Jews in Western Europe that their new rights at home did not protect Jews elsewhere, and that they could use their influence to help. It encouraged the growth of a Jewish press, including the Jewish Chronicle in London, founded in 1841, which kept readers informed about Jews across the world. It also inspired the founding of international bodies such as the Alliance Israélite Universelle twenty years later.

Montefiore became a hero to Jews everywhere, and his name is still remembered in Jerusalem and beyond. The case is also studied as an early example of how the European blood libel spread to the Middle East.

Revolutions of 1848.background: After Napoleon's defeat, the rulers of Europe tried to restore the old order. In the German states and the Austrian Empire, many of the rights Jews had gained were taken back. Jews faced limits on where they could live, which jobs they could hold, and in Bavaria even on how many Jewish families could marry. Meanwhile liberals and nationalists demanded constitutions, free speech and elected parliaments.
Revolutions of 1848.happened:
In February 1848 revolution broke out in Paris and spread within weeks to Vienna, Berlin, Budapest and many other cities. Jews were active among the students, journalists and fighters. In Vienna, the young Jewish doctor Adolf Fischhof gave one of the speeches that sparked the uprising in March, and two Jewish students were among those killed. Rabbi Isaac Noah Mannheimer spoke at their joint funeral with Christian victims. Jews also died in the Berlin street fighting.

Several Jews were elected to the new assemblies. In the Frankfurt Parliament, which tried to create a united Germany, the lawyer Gabriel Riesser, a leading campaigner for Jewish rights, served as a vice-president. In December 1848 it adopted fundamental rights stating that civil rights did not depend on religion. Fischhof and Mannheimer sat in the Austrian parliament, and in July 1849 the Hungarian revolutionary parliament passed a law emancipating Jews. At the same time, in some areas peasants and townspeople attacked Jews, blaming them for economic hardship. By 1849 armies loyal to the kings had crushed the revolutions, and most of the new laws were cancelled.
Revolutions of 1848.matters:
Although the revolutions failed, the principle of equal rights regardless of religion had been publicly declared, and most German states granted Jews full equality within the next twenty years. Many of the ideas of 1848 returned in later constitutions.

The disappointment, together with poverty and restrictive laws, pushed thousands of young Jews from Bavaria, Bohemia and other regions to emigrate. The Jewish population of the United States grew from roughly 15,000 in 1840 to around 150,000 by 1860. These German-speaking immigrants spread across America as merchants and peddlers, built many of the country's early Reform synagogues, and founded businesses and institutions that still exist.

First Hebrew novel.background:
For centuries Hebrew was the language of prayer, law and scholarship, while Jews in Eastern Europe spoke Yiddish in daily life. In the 1800s the Haskalah, the Jewish Enlightenment movement, encouraged Jews to read modern literature and science. Its writers turned to the Hebrew of the Bible as a pure and beautiful language, but they had produced mostly poems, essays and satire rather than novels.

Abraham Mapu was born in 1808 near Kovno, today Kaunas in Lithuania. He grew up studying the Talmud, taught himself languages, and worked for years as a poorly paid teacher in small towns before settling in Kovno.
First Hebrew novel.happened:
Mapu worked on Ahavat Zion for about two decades before it was published in Vilna in 1853. The story is set in the Kingdom of Judah in the 700s BCE, during the reign of King Hezekiah and the time of the prophet Isaiah. It follows the love of Amnon, a shepherd who is secretly of noble birth, and Tamar, daughter of a wealthy family, through mistaken identities, plots and rivals, before a happy ending.

Mapu wrote in a style built from phrases of the Bible, because modern Hebrew did not yet exist. Yet the result felt fresh. His descriptions of the hills, vineyards and city of Jerusalem gave readers in grey, crowded towns a vivid picture of a free Jewish life in their own land. Many yeshiva students were forbidden to read such books and hid them inside their Talmud volumes. Mapu later wrote a second biblical novel, Ashmat Shomron, "The Guilt of Samaria", and a novel attacking hypocrisy in the Jewish society of his day.
First Hebrew novel.matters:
Ahavat Zion went through many editions and was translated into Yiddish, English and other languages. It showed that Hebrew could be used for modern storytelling, not only for holy texts, which paved the way for the revival of Hebrew as a living language a generation later.

Many early Zionists said the novel first stirred their love for the Land of Israel. Mapu died in Königsberg in 1867. Streets named after him can be found in Tel Aviv, Jerusalem and other Israeli cities, and he is remembered as the father of the Hebrew novel.

Mortara affair.background: In the 1850s the Pope was not only head of the Catholic Church but also ruler of the Papal States, a territory across central Italy that included Bologna. Jews there faced many restrictions. Church law held that a baptism, even one performed secretly, made a person a Christian forever. A baptised child could not be raised by Jewish parents. Families were forbidden to employ Christian servants, though in practice many did.
Mortara affair.happened:
On the evening of 23 June 1858, papal police came to the home of Momolo and Marianna Mortara in Bologna and took their six-year-old son Edgardo. The Inquisition had learned that Anna Morisi, a Catholic servant girl, said she had baptised him years earlier when he was a sick baby and she feared he would die. Edgardo was taken to Rome to the House of the Catechumens, an institution for converting Jews.

His parents and the Jewish communities of Rome and elsewhere pleaded for his return. Newspapers across Europe and America condemned the seizure, and Emperor Napoleon III of France was among those who urged the Pope to give him back. Sir Moses Montefiore travelled to Rome in 1859 but was not received by the Pope. Pope Pius IX refused, taking a personal interest in the boy. When Bologna came under the new Italian kingdom in 1859, the local inquisitor was put on trial but acquitted. When Italian troops captured Rome in 1870, Edgardo, by then 19, chose to stay in the Church. He became a priest, Father Pius Edgardo Mortara, preached widely and died in Belgium in 1940.
Mortara affair.matters:
The case became a symbol of the clash between religious authority and modern ideas of individual and family rights. It strengthened support for Italian unification and weakened the Pope's political power. It also pushed Jews to organise internationally: it helped lead to the founding of the Board of Delegates of American Israelites in 1859 and the Alliance Israélite Universelle in 1860.

The story continues to draw attention. Historian David Kertzer's book The Kidnapping of Edgardo Mortara (1997) brought it to a wide audience, and the Italian director Marco Bellocchio made it into the film Kidnapped in 2023.

Outside the Old City walls.background:
In the mid-1800s all of Jerusalem's residents lived inside the stone walls built by the Ottoman Sultan Suleiman in the 1500s. The Jewish Quarter was packed with poor families living in dark, damp rooms. Water was scarce, sanitation was poor and diseases such as cholera spread quickly. Most Jews there relied on charity from abroad, known as the halukka, and the gates were locked at night against bandits.

Judah Touro, a wealthy merchant from New Orleans, died in 1854 and left $50,000 in his will for the Jews of the Holy Land. Sir Moses Montefiore, the British philanthropist, was chosen to carry out the gift.
Outside the Old City walls.happened:
Montefiore bought land on a hill facing Mount Zion, across the valley from the Old City walls. In 1857 he first built a windmill so residents could grind cheap flour and earn a living. Between 1859 and 1860 he completed Mishkenot Sha'ananim, a long, low building with a row of homes, a crenellated roofline and two small synagogues, one for Ashkenazi and one for Sephardi Jews. The name means "peaceful dwellings" and comes from the Book of Isaiah. An iron gate and wall surrounded the complex.

At first the homes stood empty. People feared robbers and wild animals outside the walls, and some families returned to the Old City at night. To attract residents, the homes were offered free of rent, and gradually the fear faded as more people moved in.
Outside the Old City walls.matters:
Mishkenot Sha'ananim began a building boom outside the walls. Groups of families formed cooperatives to build new Jewish neighbourhoods, including Nahalat Shiva in 1869, Me'a She'arim in 1874 and Yemin Moshe, named after Montefiore, in 1892. Christian and Muslim neighbourhoods also grew outside the walls, and the city's centre gradually moved west.

Between 1948 and 1967 the area sat on the armistice line facing Jordanian positions, and it fell into neglect. After 1967 it was restored. Today Mishkenot Sha'ananim is a guest house for visiting writers and artists and a cultural centre, and the restored Montefiore Windmill remains one of Jerusalem's best-known landmarks.

Alliance Israélite Universelle.background: French Jews had been granted full citizenship in 1791, the first in Europe, and by the mid-1800s many had risen to prominence. Events such as the Damascus blood libel of 1840 and the Mortara affair of 1858 showed them that Jews in other lands still faced persecution, poverty and lack of rights. Many French Jews also believed that education in the ideas of the French Revolution would help Jews elsewhere become free and equal.
Alliance Israélite Universelle.happened:
The Alliance was founded in Paris in May 1860 by a group of young Jewish intellectuals and professionals, including Charles Netter, Narcisse Leven and Isidore Cahen. The lawyer and politician Adolphe Crémieux became its president in 1863. Its Hebrew motto, Kol Yisrael Haverim, means "All Israel are companions". It lobbied governments, raised money for victims of persecution and sent representatives to international conferences.

Its first school opened in Tetouan, Morocco, in 1862. Over the following decades the Alliance built a network of more than a hundred schools for boys and girls in Morocco, Tunisia, Egypt, Iraq, Syria, Iran, Turkey, the Balkans and the Land of Israel. Pupils learned French, Hebrew, Jewish studies, mathematics and trades. In 1870 Charles Netter received land from the Ottoman authorities near Jaffa and founded Mikveh Israel, the first Jewish agricultural school in the country.
Alliance Israélite Universelle.matters:
The Alliance transformed Jewish life across the Mediterranean and Middle East. It created a generation of educated, French-speaking Jews who became teachers, doctors and merchants, and it opened opportunities for girls that had rarely existed. Critics later noted that it also pulled pupils away from local languages and traditions.

Mikveh Israel trained many early farmers of the Jewish settlements, and in 1898 Theodor Herzl met Kaiser Wilhelm II at its gates. It still operates as a school today, and Charles Netter is buried there. The Alliance itself still exists, running schools in France, Morocco, Israel and elsewhere, and its library in Paris is one of the largest Jewish libraries in Europe.

Equality in Germany.background: Before 1871 Germany was a patchwork of separate states, each with its own laws for Jews. Some had granted rights early, others kept strict limits on where Jews could live, marry or work. After the failed revolutions of 1848, rights expanded step by step. In 1869 the North German Confederation, led by Prussia, passed a law ending all restrictions on civil and political rights based on religion.
Equality in Germany.happened:
In 1871, after victory over France, the German Empire was declared, and the 1869 law was extended to all its states, including Bavaria. About half a million Jews, roughly one percent of the population, became equal citizens across the whole country. Most lived in cities, and many moved from small towns to Berlin, Frankfurt, Breslau and Hamburg.

German Jews made striking contributions in the following decades. The banker Gerson von Bleichröder financed Bismarck's government, Emil Rathenau founded the electrical company AEG, Paul Ehrlich pioneered modern medicine and the painter Max Liebermann led German Impressionism. The New Synagogue on Oranienburger Strasse in Berlin, designed by Eduard Knoblauch and seating around 3,000, had opened in 1866 in the presence of Bismarck. Yet informal barriers remained: Jews were rarely appointed as army officers, senior civil servants or full professors unless they converted.
Equality in Germany.matters:
Equality soon met a backlash. After a stock market crash in 1873, many blamed Jews for the economic hardship. The court preacher Adolf Stoecker founded an antisemitic political party in 1878, and the historian Heinrich von Treitschke gave hostility towards Jews academic respectability. The word "antisemitism" spread at this time.

The story of German Jewry, deeply patriotic and successful, yet never fully accepted, became central to how later generations understood the failure of emancipation. The New Synagogue survived Kristallnacht thanks to a local police officer, Wilhelm Krützfeld, but was badly damaged by bombing in 1943. Its golden dome was rebuilt and it reopened in 1995 as the Centrum Judaicum, a museum and centre for Jewish life in Berlin.

Petah Tikva founded.background: By the 1870s most Jews in the Land of Israel lived in the four holy cities and depended on charity from abroad. Some members of Jerusalem's Old Yishuv, the traditional religious community, began to feel that Jews should support themselves by working the land, as their ancestors had. A few had already built homes outside Jerusalem's walls and were looking for land further afield.
Petah Tikva founded.happened:
The founders included Yoel Moshe Salomon, Yehoshua Stampfer, David Gutmann and Zerach Barnett. After the Ottoman governor blocked a plan to buy land near Jericho, they bought land at the Arab village of Mulabbis, near the source of the Yarkon River, in 1878. They named their settlement Petah Tikva, "Door of Hope", from a verse in the Book of Hosea that speaks of the Valley of Achor becoming a door of hope.

The land was cheap because it was surrounded by swamps. The settlers had little farming experience, floods damaged their crops and malaria struck many families. Within a few years most of them left, moving to the nearby village of Yehud. In 1883 they returned, joined by new immigrants from Eastern Europe, including members of the Bilu movement, and supported by the Hovevei Zion organisation. From 1887 Baron Edmond de Rothschild also helped. Settlers drained swamps and planted eucalyptus trees, which absorb water, to fight the mosquitoes.
Petah Tikva founded.matters:
Petah Tikva became known as Em HaMoshavot, the "Mother of the Settlements", because it was the first modern Jewish farming village to last. It became a centre of citrus growing and an early meeting point for young pioneers of the Second Aliyah, including David Ben-Gurion, who worked in its orchards in 1906.

Today Petah Tikva is a city of around 250,000 people and part of the Tel Aviv metropolitan area. The founders' story is remembered in local museums and in the names of many of its streets.

Word \"antisemitism\" coined.background: For many centuries hatred of Jews in Europe was mainly religious. Jews were blamed for the death of Jesus and pressured to convert, and a Jew who was baptised was, in theory, accepted. In the 1800s new ideas about race, nationalism and science spread through Europe. Some thinkers divided humanity into races and spoke of "Semites" and "Aryans", terms borrowed from the study of languages. After Jews gained legal equality in Germany, opponents searched for new arguments against them.
Word \"antisemitism\" coined.happened:
Wilhelm Marr was a Hamburg journalist who had once been a radical democrat. In 1879 he published a pamphlet, The Victory of Judaism over Germandom, claiming that Jews had taken control of German society and that a struggle between Germans and Jews was under way. That autumn he founded the League of Antisemites, the first political organisation built around hostility to Jews. The word "antisemitic" had been used before, but Marr and his circle made it popular as a respectable-sounding label for their cause.

The idea spread quickly. In 1880 and 1881 an Antisemites' Petition collected many thousands of signatures calling on Chancellor Bismarck to limit Jewish rights. In 1887 Otto Böckel became the first candidate elected to the Reichstag purely as an antisemite, and by 1893 antisemitic parties held 16 seats. In Austria Georg von Schönerer led a racial antisemitic movement, and Karl Lueger won election as mayor of Vienna in 1897 partly through anti-Jewish campaigning.
Word \"antisemitism\" coined.matters:
Racial antisemitism was more dangerous than older religious prejudice because it claimed Jewishness was in the blood. Converting or assimilating offered no escape. This idea later became central to Nazi ideology.

The word itself is misleading, since there is no such thing as "Semitism" and the term was only ever aimed at Jews. For this reason many scholars and organisations, including the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance, now prefer to write "antisemitism" without a hyphen. In 2016 the IHRA adopted a working definition of antisemitism, which many governments and institutions use today, although its use is also debated.

Pogroms in Russia.background: By 1881 about five million Jews lived in the Russian Empire, most of them restricted to the Pale of Settlement, a region stretching from the Baltic to the Black Sea. Many were poor craftsmen and small traders. Tsar Alexander II had eased some restrictions, and a small number of Jews had entered universities and the professions. On 13 March 1881 Alexander was killed by a bomb thrown by members of the revolutionary group People's Will. One of the group, Gesya Gelfman, was Jewish, and rumours spread that the Jews were to blame.
Pogroms in Russia.happened:
The first major attack began in Elisavetgrad, in today's Ukraine, in late April 1881. Over the following months mobs attacked Jewish homes, shops and synagogues in Kyiv, Odessa and more than 200 other towns and villages, and in Warsaw in December. Many attacks began around Christian holidays or market days and were often carried out by railway workers and peasants. Police and troops frequently did little to stop them. The word pogrom, Russian for "devastation", entered other languages at this time. Further waves followed in 1882 and 1884.

The government's response blamed the victims. In May 1882 the so-called Temporary Laws, known as the May Laws, banned Jews from settling in new villages and countryside areas. Quotas limited Jewish students in schools and universities from 1887, and in 1891 thousands of Jews were expelled from Moscow.
Pogroms in Russia.matters:
The pogroms and laws set off one of the largest migrations in Jewish history. Between 1881 and 1914 around two million Jews left Eastern Europe. Most went to the United States, where they arrived at Castle Garden and later Ellis Island and filled neighbourhoods such as New York's Lower East Side. Others went to Britain, Argentina, South Africa and Canada. The poet Emma Lazarus, who helped the refugees in New York, wrote her sonnet The New Colossus in 1883, now on the base of the Statue of Liberty.

A smaller number turned to new answers. Leon Pinsker's pamphlet Auto-Emancipation (1882) argued Jews needed their own homeland, and groups such as Hovevei Zion and Bilu began the First Aliyah. Others joined socialist movements. Most American Jews today are descended from this wave of migration.

Ben-Yehuda revives Hebrew.background:
For about two thousand years Hebrew was rarely spoken in daily life. Jews used it for prayer, Torah study and letters, while speaking Yiddish, Ladino, Arabic and other languages at home. Writers of the Haskalah had begun writing modern Hebrew literature, but no one raised children in it.

Eliezer Ben-Yehuda was born Eliezer Perlman in 1858 in Luzhki, in today's Belarus. He studied at a yeshiva, discovered secular Hebrew books, and later studied medicine in Paris. Inspired by national movements around Europe, he became convinced that a nation needs both its land and its own spoken language.
Ben-Yehuda revives Hebrew.happened:
Ben-Yehuda and his wife Devora arrived in Jaffa in October 1881 and settled in Jerusalem. They agreed to speak only Hebrew at home. Their son Ben-Zion, born in 1882, later known as Itamar Ben-Avi, grew up hearing nothing else, and is often called the first native Hebrew speaker of modern times. Ben-Yehuda published Hebrew newspapers, taught in a school where lessons were given in Hebrew, and in 1890 helped found the Hebrew Language Committee.

Because ancient Hebrew lacked words for modern life, he created many, using old roots from the Bible and rabbinic literature, and sometimes from Arabic. Words such as iton (newspaper), milon (dictionary) and glida (ice cream) are linked to him. His great work was a Complete Dictionary of Ancient and Modern Hebrew. He worked on it for decades, and it was finally completed, in 17 volumes, by others in 1959. He faced fierce opposition from some religious Jews, who felt the holy tongue should not be used for everyday talk.
Ben-Yehuda revives Hebrew.matters:
Ben-Yehuda did not revive Hebrew alone. Teachers in the new farming villages, schools such as the Herzliya Gymnasium, and the young pioneers of the Second Aliyah made it the language of the next generation. In 1913 teachers and students won the "war of the languages", when the planned Technion in Haifa agreed to teach in Hebrew rather than German. In 1922 the British made Hebrew an official language of Palestine, shortly before Ben-Yehuda's death that December.

The Hebrew Language Committee became the Academy of the Hebrew Language in 1953, which still coins new words today. Hebrew Language Day is marked in Israel on his birthday, and streets in almost every Israeli city bear his name, including Ben-Yehuda Street in Jerusalem.

First Aliyah.background: Aliyah, Hebrew for "going up", is the word Jews use for moving to the Land of Israel. In the early 1880s around 25,000 Jews lived there, most of them in Jerusalem, Hebron, Safed and Tiberias, supported by charity. The pogroms of 1881 and 1882 in the Russian Empire, and growing hardship in Romania, convinced some young Jews that they needed a homeland of their own. Groups called Hovevei Zion, "Lovers of Zion", sprang up across Eastern Europe. The student group Bilu took its name from the Hebrew initials of a verse in Isaiah, meaning "House of Jacob, come and let us go".
First Aliyah.happened:
The first Bilu members, a small group of students, landed in Jaffa in July 1882. That same year immigrants from Russia founded Rishon LeZion, "First to Zion", and Jews from Romania founded Zikhron Ya'akov on Mount Carmel and Rosh Pinna in the Upper Galilee. Gedera followed in 1884, Rehovot in 1890 and Hadera in 1891. Jews from Yemen also arrived in this period, many settling in Jerusalem.

Most settlers were city people with no farming experience. They faced drought, unfamiliar crops, Ottoman restrictions on land purchase and building, conflict with neighbours and above all malaria, which killed many in the swamps of Hadera. Several villages were close to collapse within a year or two. Baron Edmond de Rothschild of Paris, later known as HaNadiv HaYadua, "the famous benefactor", stepped in. He bought land, paid for houses and wells, and set up vineyards and wineries at Rishon LeZion and Zikhron Ya'akov. His officials ran the villages closely, which many settlers resented.
First Aliyah.matters:
The First Aliyah laid the foundations of the modern Jewish community in the Land of Israel. Its villages, the moshavot, grew into towns and cities, and many are still important today. It was also in Rishon LeZion that Naftali Herz Imber's poem Hatikvah, "The Hope", was first set to the melody that later became Israel's national anthem.

Rothschild supported settlement for decades, and in 1954 he and his wife were reburied at Ramat HaNadiv, a memorial garden near Zikhron Ya'akov. The winery cellars and early founders' houses in Rishon LeZion and Zikhron Ya'akov are now museums.

Dreyfus affair.background:
France was the first European country to give Jews equal rights, in 1791. By the 1890s Jews served as officers, judges and politicians. But France was still bitter over its defeat by Germany in 1870, and spy fears were high. Antisemitism was growing too. Édouard Drumont's book Jewish France (1886) was a bestseller, and his newspaper La Libre Parole attacked Jewish officers in the army.

Alfred Dreyfus, born in 1859 into a Jewish family from Alsace, was a captain on the army's General Staff, one of the few Jews to reach it.
Dreyfus affair.happened:
In 1894 French intelligence found a torn note, the bordereau, offering military secrets to the German embassy. Officers decided Dreyfus's handwriting matched. He was arrested in October and convicted of treason by a secret court-martial in December, partly on a secret file of evidence that his lawyers never saw. On 5 January 1895 he was publicly stripped of his rank in the courtyard of the École Militaire in Paris, while he insisted he was innocent. He was sent to Devil's Island off French Guiana and held in harsh isolation.

In 1896 Colonel Georges Picquart discovered that the real spy was another officer, Major Ferdinand Esterhazy. The army moved Picquart away and acquitted Esterhazy in January 1898. Two days later Émile Zola's open letter, J'accuse, appeared in the newspaper L'Aurore, accusing senior officers of a cover-up. Zola was convicted of libel and fled to England, and France split into Dreyfusards and anti-Dreyfusards. A second court-martial at Rennes in 1899 found Dreyfus guilty again, and he was then pardoned. In 1906 France's highest court cleared him fully, and he was restored to the army.
Dreyfus affair.matters:
The affair changed France. It helped bring about the 1905 law separating church and state, and it led to the founding of the Human Rights League in 1898. It became a lasting example of how prejudice can corrupt justice.

Theodor Herzl covered the case as a reporter in Paris, and later wrote that it made him a Zionist, although historians note that his ideas were shaped by many experiences. Dreyfus later served in the First World War and died in 1935. A statue of him holding a broken sword stands in Paris, and in 2021 a museum dedicated to the affair opened in Médan, in Zola's former house.

Herzl's \"The Jewish State\".background: Theodor Herzl was born in Budapest in 1860 and grew up in a German-speaking, assimilated Jewish family. He trained as a lawyer, then became a successful playwright and journalist. From 1891 to 1895 he was the Paris correspondent of the leading Viennese newspaper, the Neue Freie Presse. He had once imagined solutions to antisemitism such as mass conversion, but the hostility he saw in France and in Vienna, where an antisemitic party was winning elections, changed his thinking.
Herzl's \"The Jewish State\".happened:
In 1895 Herzl wrote his ideas in a burst of activity, at first as a long address to the Rothschild family, which was never delivered. In February 1896 he published them in Vienna as a short book, Der Judenstaat, subtitled "An Attempt at a Modern Solution of the Jewish Question". He argued that the Jewish problem was a national, not a religious or social, question and should be settled through international politics.

He proposed two bodies: a Society of Jews, which would represent the Jewish people politically and negotiate with world powers, and a Jewish Company, which would handle the practical side of moving people and property. He considered both Palestine and Argentina as possible territories. He imagined a modern state with a seven-hour working day and a flag of seven gold stars on white. Many wealthy and assimilated Jews mocked the idea, and some rabbis condemned it. But students and the masses of Eastern Europe greeted him with excitement, and the Christian clergyman William Hechler helped him meet the Grand Duke of Baden and, later, Kaiser Wilhelm II.
Herzl's \"The Jewish State\".matters:
Der Judenstaat turned scattered Zionist groups into a political movement with a clear goal: a recognised homeland gained through diplomacy. It was quickly translated into Hebrew, Yiddish, English, French and other languages. In 1902 Herzl followed it with a utopian novel, Altneuland, "Old New Land", which gave its name in Hebrew translation to Tel Aviv.

Herzl died in 1904 aged 44. In 1949 his remains were brought to Jerusalem and buried on the hill now called Mount Herzl, which became Israel's national cemetery. His portrait hangs in the Knesset and he is often called the visionary of the state.

First Zionist Congress.background: After publishing The Jewish State in 1896, Theodor Herzl tried and failed to win support from wealthy Jewish philanthropists. He decided instead to build a mass movement by calling together representatives of Jewish communities and Zionist groups from around the world. He planned the meeting for Munich, but the city's Jewish leaders objected, fearing it would harm their position, so it moved to Basel in neutral Switzerland.
First Zionist Congress.happened:
The Congress met from 29 to 31 August 1897 in the concert hall of Basel's Stadtcasino. Herzl asked delegates to wear formal dress to show the seriousness of the occasion. About 200 people attended from 17 countries, from Russia and Romania to Western Europe, the United States and Algeria. Women attended as guests, and gained full voting rights at the Second Congress.

Herzl was elected president. Max Nordau, a famous writer and doctor, gave a powerful speech on the condition of Jews around the world. The delegates adopted the Basel Programme, which stated that Zionism sought to create a home for the Jewish people in the Land of Israel secured under public law. It set out practical steps: promoting settlement, organising Jews, strengthening Jewish national awareness and seeking the consent of governments. The Congress created the Zionist Organisation, with members paying a small fee called the shekel to gain the right to vote.
First Zionist Congress.matters:
The Congress gave the Jewish people a representative body for the first time in modern history, and it met regularly from then on. Later Congresses created key institutions, including the Jewish Colonial Trust bank in 1899 and the Jewish National Fund, for buying land, in 1901.

Herzl's famous diary entry looked ahead fifty years, and the State of Israel was declared in 1948. The World Zionist Organisation still exists, and the Zionist Congress continues to meet, now in Jerusalem. Basel remains linked with this history, and plaques mark the Stadtcasino and the Hotel Les Trois Rois, where Herzl was photographed leaning on a balcony in a picture that became famous.

Kishinev pogrom.background: Kishinev, today Chișinău, the capital of Moldova, was then the capital of the Russian province of Bessarabia. Around a third of its population was Jewish. A local newspaper, Bessarabets, edited by Pavel Krushevan, published a steady stream of attacks on Jews. In February 1903 a Christian boy was found murdered in the nearby town of Dubossary. Although he had been killed by a relative, the newspaper spread the claim that Jews had killed him for his blood before Passover.
Kishinev pogrom.happened:
The violence began on 19 April 1903, which was both Easter Sunday and the last day of Passover, and continued into the next day. Groups of rioters, some organised, attacked Jewish homes and shops, looted, beat and murdered. Police and soldiers largely stood by until the authorities finally intervened on the second evening. Forty-nine Jews were killed, many women were raped and hundreds of homes and businesses were destroyed. Many people suspected that officials, including the Interior Minister Vyacheslav von Plehve, had at least allowed it to happen.

Soon after, a Jewish historical commission in Odessa sent the young poet Hayim Nahman Bialik to interview survivors. His long Hebrew poem, In the City of Slaughter, published in 1904, described the horrors and attacked Jewish passivity and the silence of heaven. The pogrom caused protests around the world. Mass meetings were held in American cities, a petition to the Tsar was organised with the support of President Theodore Roosevelt's government, and the writer Leo Tolstoy condemned it.
Kishinev pogrom.matters:
Kishinev became a turning point. Young Jews in Russia formed self-defence groups, which fought back during later pogroms such as Gomel in 1903, and some of these activists later helped found Hashomer in the Land of Israel. The shock also lent urgency to Zionism. At the Sixth Zionist Congress in 1903, Herzl presented a British offer of land in East Africa, the Uganda Scheme, as a temporary refuge, a proposal that bitterly divided the movement.

A second pogrom struck Kishinev in 1905. Bialik's poem remains one of the most studied works of modern Hebrew literature, and the word Kishinev came to stand for state-tolerated violence against Jews.

Second Aliyah.background: After the Kishinev pogrom of 1903 and the failed Russian revolution of 1905, which was followed by more pogroms, many young Jews in the Russian Empire were searching for a new way of life. Some were influenced by socialist ideas, others by the Zionist dream. They saw the First Aliyah villages, where Jewish farmers often hired Arab workers and depended on Baron Rothschild, as a betrayal of the ideal of Jews working their own land.
Second Aliyah.happened:
Between 1904 and the outbreak of the First World War in 1914, around 35,000 Jews came to the Land of Israel, though many could not cope with the hardship and left again. The newcomers took on hard labour in orchards and vineyards, often earning little and suffering from malaria. They were guided by the ideas of Aaron David Gordon, an older thinker who believed physical work on the land would heal the Jewish people.

The Second Aliyah created many new institutions. In 1907 a small group formed Bar Giora, a secret defence group, which in 1909 grew into Hashomer, "The Guard", protecting Jewish villages. Workers' parties such as Poale Zion and Hapoel Hatzair were founded, along with the training farm at Kinneret and, in 1910, Degania, the first kibbutz. In Jaffa the Herzliya Gymnasium became the first Hebrew high school, in Jerusalem the Bezalel art school opened in 1906, and in 1909 Tel Aviv was founded. Members included David Ben-Gurion, who arrived in 1906, Yitzhak Ben-Zvi, Berl Katznelson, Yosef Trumpeldor and the poet Rachel.
Second Aliyah.matters:
Although relatively few in number, the people of the Second Aliyah shaped Israel more than almost any other group. Their commitment to Hebrew, manual labour, self-defence and collective farming became the core values of the Labour Zionist movement that led the Jewish community and the early state. Ben-Gurion became Israel's first prime minister and Ben-Zvi its second president.

Many of them are buried in the small cemetery of Kinneret on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, including Rachel and Berl Katznelson, and it remains a place of pilgrimage. Their story is taught in Israeli schools as the heroic age of the pioneers.

Tel Aviv founded.background: By the early 1900s Jaffa, the main port of the region, was crowded, noisy and expensive for its growing Jewish population. Many Jews lived in narrow alleys with high rents. In 1906 a group led by Akiva Aryeh Weiss formed a society called Ahuzat Bayit, "Homestead", to build a modern, clean Jewish garden suburb with wide streets, gardens and proper sanitation, away from the old town. The Jewish National Fund provided a loan to help buy land.
Tel Aviv founded.happened:
The society bought an area of sand dunes north of Jaffa known as Karm al-Jabali. On 11 April 1909 the 66 families met on the dunes to divide the land. Weiss collected 66 white shells and 66 grey ones, wrote family names on the white shells and plot numbers on the grey ones, and drew them in pairs. The photographer Avraham Soskin captured the scene in what became one of the most famous images in Israeli history. Building began soon afterwards, with Herzl Street as the main road and the Herzliya Gymnasium, a Hebrew high school, at its end.

In May 1910 residents chose the name Tel Aviv. It came from Nahum Sokolow's Hebrew title for Herzl's novel Altneuland, "Old New Land". Sokolow had borrowed it from a place named in the Book of Ezekiel. A tel is an ancient mound built up over ages and aviv means spring, combining the old and the new. Meir Dizengoff led the town committee from 1911 and later became its first mayor.
Tel Aviv founded.matters:
Tel Aviv grew rapidly, especially in the 1920s and 1930s, and became the first city where daily life was conducted in Hebrew. Its many white buildings in the Bauhaus and International style, built largely by architects who had trained in Europe, earned the White City recognition as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003.

On 14 May 1948 Israel's independence was declared in Dizengoff's former home on Rothschild Boulevard, now Independence Hall. Today the city of Tel Aviv-Yafo, which absorbed Jaffa in 1950, has around 470,000 residents and is Israel's economic and cultural centre. The lottery photograph is still reproduced widely, and the founding is celebrated in the city's anniversaries.

First kibbutz, Degania.background: The young pioneers of the Second Aliyah wanted to build a new kind of Jewish society based on equality and their own labour. In 1909 a group of workers who had met in Hadera was sent to farm land at Umm Juni, at the southern tip of the Sea of Galilee, owned by the Jewish National Fund. They found that working as a self-run group gave better results than working under a manager.
First kibbutz, Degania.happened:
In October 1910 the group settled at Umm Juni as a permanent commune, and soon called it Degania, after the cereal grain that grew in the area. The founders, ten men and two women, included Joseph Baratz, Miriam Baratz and Joseph Bussel, who shaped its ideas. They lived in simple huts, worked the fields together, shared all property and income and made decisions in a general meeting. Heat, malaria and attacks by raiders made life very hard.

The community soon faced new questions, such as whether women should work in the fields as equals, and how to raise children. Over time Degania and later kibbutzim developed collective child-rearing, with children living together in children's houses. In 1912 the community moved to a permanent site nearby. The second child born at Degania, in 1915, was Moshe Dayan, later Israel's chief of staff and defence minister. The thinker Aaron David Gordon spent his last years there and died there in 1922.
First kibbutz, Degania.matters:
Degania became known as the mother of the kibbutzim. The movement spread to hundreds of communities that played a central role in farming, settlement, defence and politics, and produced many military officers and leaders. Since the 1980s many kibbutzim have changed, with private salaries and housing, but more than 250 still exist.

During the War of Independence in May 1948, the members of Degania, with Haganah forces, stopped an advancing Syrian armoured column at the kibbutz gates. A Syrian tank stopped near the fence still stands there as a memorial. The original courtyard and buildings of Degania Alef are preserved, and the kibbutz remains a symbol of the pioneering era.

Beilis trial.background: In the early 1900s the Russian Empire was shaken by revolution and unrest. Nationalist groups known as the Black Hundreds blamed Jews for the country's problems, and they had friends in government. The blood libel, the false claim that Jews murder Christians for ritual purposes, had been repeatedly condemned by Popes and scholars, yet it still circulated.
Beilis trial.happened:
In March 1911 the body of 13-year-old Andrei Yushchinsky was found stabbed in a cave on the edge of Kyiv. Police evidence pointed to a criminal gang linked to a woman named Vera Cheberyak, whose home the boy had visited. But right-wing activists insisted it was a Jewish ritual murder, and the Minister of Justice, Ivan Shcheglovitov, pushed for a Jewish suspect. In July 1911 police arrested Menahem Mendel Beilis, a father of five who worked as a clerk at a brick factory near where the body was found.

Beilis was held in prison for over two years while the state prepared its case. Detectives who pointed to the real killers were removed. The trial opened in Kyiv in September 1913 and lasted more than a month. The prosecution called a Catholic priest, Justinas Pranaitis, who claimed Jewish texts required ritual murder. Defence experts, including Rabbi Jacob Mazeh of Moscow and leading Christian scholars, exposed his ignorance. On 28 October the jury, mostly peasants and townspeople, found Beilis not guilty.
Beilis trial.matters:
The trial became an international embarrassment for the Russian government, which had tried to put Judaism itself on trial. Writers, scientists and politicians around the world protested. After his release Beilis moved to Palestine and then to the United States, where he published a memoir in 1926 and died in 1934.

The case inspired Bernard Malamud's novel The Fixer, which won the Pulitzer Prize in 1967. In the same year as the Beilis trial, Leo Frank, a Jewish factory manager in Atlanta, was convicted of murder in a trial marked by antisemitism. In October 1913 B'nai B'rith founded the Anti-Defamation League in response. Frank was lynched by a mob in 1915, and in 1986 the state of Georgia granted him a posthumous pardon.

Balfour Declaration.background: During the First World War, Britain fought the Ottoman Empire, which ruled Palestine. British leaders made several promises about the region. Letters between Sir Henry McMahon and Sharif Hussein of Mecca in 1915 and 1916 discussed Arab independence, and the secret Sykes-Picot Agreement of 1916 divided the area between Britain and France. Meanwhile Zionist leaders, especially the chemist Chaim Weizmann in Manchester and Nahum Sokolow, worked to win British support. Some British politicians were sympathetic for religious reasons, and some hoped the move would win Jewish support for the war in America and Russia.
Balfour Declaration.happened:
