After months of drafts and debate in the War Cabinet, Foreign Secretary Arthur James Balfour signed a letter dated 2 November 1917 to Lionel Walter, Lord Rothschild, a leader of British Jewry, asking him to pass it to the Zionist Federation. The only Jewish member of the cabinet, Edwin Montagu, strongly opposed it, fearing it would undermine the position of Jews in Britain. The final text of 67 words added two conditions: nothing should prejudice the civil and religious rights of existing non-Jewish communities in Palestine, or the rights and status of Jews in other countries.

British forces under General Edmund Allenby had taken Beersheba days before, and Allenby entered Jerusalem in December 1917. In 1920 the San Remo conference gave Britain the mandate for Palestine, and in 1922 the League of Nations approved it with the declaration written into its text.
Balfour Declaration.matters:
For Zionists the declaration was the first time a great power had recognised Jewish national aspirations in the Land of Israel, and it opened the way to large-scale immigration under British rule. For Palestinian Arabs, who were then the large majority of the population, it was seen as a promise made without their consent and as the start of their dispossession. The tension between its two commitments shaped the conflict that followed.

The original letter is kept at the British Library. Its centenary in 2017 was marked by celebrations in Israel and Britain and by protests among Palestinians, showing how differently it is still remembered.

Haganah founded.background: Before the First World War, small groups such as Hashomer guarded Jewish villages. After the war, under British rule, tension between Jews and Arabs grew. In March 1920 Yosef Trumpeldor, a one-armed veteran of the Russian army, was killed with seven others defending the isolated settlement of Tel Hai in the Upper Galilee during fighting in the area. In April 1920, during the Nebi Musa festival in Jerusalem, riots broke out in which five Jews were killed and over 200 injured. Ze'ev Jabotinsky, who organised a defence group, was arrested and jailed by the British. Jewish leaders concluded that they could not rely on the British for protection.
Haganah founded.happened:
In June 1920 the Ahdut HaAvoda labour party decided to create a single defence organisation for the whole Jewish community. It was called the Haganah, Hebrew for "defence", and soon came under the Histadrut, the general federation of Jewish workers, and later the Jewish Agency. It was illegal under British law, so its members trained in secret and hid weapons in caches known as slicks. The 1921 Jaffa riots and the 1929 riots showed its early weakness, but it grew steadily.

During the Arab revolt of 1936 to 1939 it cooperated with the British, and some members trained with Captain Orde Wingate's Special Night Squads. In 1941 it formed an elite strike force, the Palmach. After the Second World War it organised the illegal immigration of Holocaust survivors, known as Aliyah Bet, and led armed resistance against British restrictions. A group that disagreed with its policy of restraint split away in 1931 and became the Irgun.
Haganah founded.matters:
On 26 May 1948, shortly after independence, the new government of Israel ordered the creation of the Israel Defense Forces, built mainly on the Haganah, and other armed groups were absorbed into it. Many Haganah commanders became the IDF's first generals.

The Haganah Museum is in the Tel Aviv house of Eliyahu Golomb, one of its founders, on Rothschild Boulevard. Trumpeldor's death made Tel Hai a symbol of determination, and the Roaring Lion statue at his grave at Kfar Giladi is still visited, especially on Tel Hai Day, the eleventh of the Hebrew month of Adar.

Hebrew University opens.background: The idea of a Jewish university in the Land of Israel had been discussed for decades. Jewish students in Eastern Europe faced strict quotas at universities, and Zionist leaders believed that a national revival needed a centre of learning in Hebrew. At the Eleventh Zionist Congress in 1913 the movement formally decided to build one. In July 1918, even before the First World War had ended, Chaim Weizmann laid foundation stones on Mount Scopus, a hill overlooking Jerusalem.
Hebrew University opens.happened:
On 1 April 1925 the university was formally opened in an outdoor amphitheatre on Mount Scopus. Arthur Balfour, the former British Foreign Secretary, gave the main address, alongside Weizmann, the High Commissioner Sir Herbert Samuel and other leaders. Thousands attended, and the event was celebrated in Jewish communities around the world.

The university began with a small number of research institutes, in Jewish studies, chemistry and microbiology, and soon added teaching. Its early board of governors included Albert Einstein and Sigmund Freud. Einstein had already visited in February 1923 and given a lecture on relativity on the site. Judah Magnes, an American rabbi, became its first chancellor and later its president. The Jewish National and University Library, today the National Library of Israel, became part of the campus.
Hebrew University opens.matters:
The Hebrew University became a cornerstone of Israeli science and culture, and its graduates include prime ministers, judges and Nobel Prize winners such as the economists Daniel Kahneman and Robert Aumann. From 1948 to 1967 Mount Scopus was cut off as an Israeli enclave in Jordanian territory, and the university moved to a new campus at Givat Ram. In April 1948 a convoy of doctors, nurses and staff on the way to Hadassah Hospital and the university was attacked, and 78 people were killed. After 1967 the Mount Scopus campus was rebuilt.

Einstein left his personal papers and literary rights to the university, which holds the Albert Einstein Archives. The university today has several campuses and is regularly ranked among the leading universities in the world.

Hebron massacre.background:
Hebron is home to the Cave of the Patriarchs, revered by Jews as the burial place of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and their wives, and also holy to Muslims. Jews had lived in the city for centuries, and by the 1920s the community numbered several hundred, mostly long-established Sephardi families and Ashkenazi residents. In 1924 part of the famous Slabodka yeshiva, a religious academy, moved from Lithuania to Hebron.

In 1928 and 1929 tension grew in Jerusalem over Jewish prayer at the Western Wall, which Muslims feared was a step towards taking over the Haram al-Sharif, the Temple Mount. A Jewish demonstration at the Wall on 15 August 1929 was followed by Arab counter-protests, and false rumours spread that Jews planned to attack the al-Aqsa mosque.
Hebron massacre.happened:
On 23 August 1929 riots broke out in Jerusalem. The next morning, Saturday 24 August, a crowd attacked Jewish homes in Hebron. The single British police officer in charge, Raymond Cafferata, had only a small force of local police, and reinforcements took hours to arrive. Sixty-seven Jews were murdered, including men, women and children, and many of the yeshiva's students. Eliezer Dan Slonim, a bank manager with close ties to Arab leaders, was killed with members of his family. The Beit Hadassah clinic, which served Arabs and Jews alike, was ransacked.

At the same time, a number of Arab families sheltered Jewish neighbours in their homes, saving many lives. In the days that followed, the British evacuated the surviving Jews to Jerusalem. Across Palestine 133 Jews were killed during the week of riots, including 18 in Safed, and 116 Arabs were killed, mostly by British forces.
Hebron massacre.matters:
The massacre ended continuous Jewish life in Hebron. A few families returned in 1931 but were evacuated again during the riots of 1936. The Slabodka yeshiva re-established itself in Jerusalem as the Hevron yeshiva, which still exists today. A British inquiry, the Shaw Commission, blamed the violence on Arab fears about Jewish immigration and land purchase, leading to tighter limits that Jews strongly opposed.

The victims are buried in Hebron's old Jewish cemetery, and Beit Hadassah now houses a museum about the community. Since 1967 Jews have again lived in Hebron, an issue that remains deeply disputed. The stories of Arab families who saved Jews are also part of how the massacre is remembered.

Nazis take power.background: Germany emerged from the First World War defeated and humiliated. The Weimar Republic that followed suffered from hyperinflation in 1923 and mass unemployment after the crash of 1929. Adolf Hitler's National Socialist German Workers' Party, the Nazis, blamed Jews and communists for Germany's troubles and promised national rebirth. In the July 1932 elections the Nazis became the largest party in the Reichstag, the German parliament. Around 500,000 Jews lived in Germany, less than one percent of the population.
Nazis take power.happened:
On 30 January 1933 President Paul von Hindenburg appointed Hitler chancellor, after conservative politicians believed they could control him. After the Reichstag building burned on 27 February, an emergency decree suspended civil rights. On 23 March the Enabling Act gave Hitler power to pass laws without parliament. Dachau, near Munich, opened in March as the first regular concentration camp, at first mainly for political opponents.

On 1 April 1933 the Nazis held a national boycott of Jewish shops, doctors and lawyers. Storm troopers of the SA stood outside with signs telling Germans not to buy from Jews. On 7 April a new civil service law removed most Jews from government jobs, including teachers and university staff, although at Hindenburg's insistence First World War veterans were at first exempted. Further laws limited Jewish lawyers, doctors and students. On 10 May students burned books by Jewish and other banned authors in Berlin and other university towns. About 37,000 Jews left Germany in 1933.
Nazis take power.matters:
In just a few months a modern democracy had become a dictatorship, and Jews had been turned into outsiders by law. Each step tested how far the regime could go without resistance, and the world's limited response encouraged it. Albert Einstein, who was abroad, never returned to Germany.

Today the book burning is remembered at Bebelplatz in Berlin, where a glass window in the ground looks down on empty bookshelves. The Dachau Concentration Camp Memorial Site stands on the former camp. Across Europe, small brass Stolpersteine, "stumbling stones", set in pavements outside homes, record the names of individual victims of Nazi persecution.

Nuremberg Laws.background: From 1933 the Nazi regime removed Jews from public life step by step, but there was still no legal definition of who was a Jew. Party radicals demanded laws against marriage and relationships between Jews and other Germans, and in 1935 there were new waves of local violence and boycotts. Nuremberg hosted the Nazi Party's huge annual rallies, and in September 1935 Hitler called the Reichstag to meet there.
Nuremberg Laws.happened:
On 15 September 1935 the Reichstag passed two laws, drafted in haste. The Reich Citizenship Law said only people of "German or related blood" could be citizens with full political rights, making Jews mere "subjects". The Law for the Protection of German Blood and German Honour banned marriage and sexual relations between Jews and non-Jewish Germans, banned Jews from employing non-Jewish German women under 45 as household staff, and forbade Jews from flying the national flag. A third law made the swastika flag the national flag.

On 14 November a decree defined who counted as a Jew. A person with three or four Jewish grandparents was a Jew. Those with one or two Jewish grandparents were classed as Mischlinge, "mixed", with partial rights depending on their religion and marriage. Because there was no biological test, the grandparents' status was decided by their religious membership, so even Christians whose grandparents had been Jewish were caught by the laws. Officials published charts with circles to explain the categories.
Nuremberg Laws.matters:
The Nuremberg Laws turned antisemitism into the formal law of the state and gave the regime a system for identifying Jews, which was later used for confiscation, deportation and murder. They were soon applied to Roma and Black Germans as well. Some foreign observers mistakenly believed the laws would bring stability, and persecution was eased slightly during the 1936 Berlin Olympics.

The original signed copies were found by American forces in 1945 and given to General George Patton, who placed them in the Huntington Library in California. In 2010 they were transferred to the US National Archives. Nuremberg was chosen as the site of the postwar trials of Nazi leaders partly because of its symbolism, and the former rally grounds now house a documentation centre.

Peel Commission.background: Under the British mandate the Jewish population of Palestine grew quickly, especially after 1933 as Jews fled Nazi Germany. By 1936 Jews made up around 30 percent of the population. Arab leaders feared they would become a minority in their own land. In April 1936 the Arab Higher Committee, led by the Mufti of Jerusalem, Haj Amin al-Husseini, called a general strike, which grew into an armed revolt against British rule and Jewish immigration.
Peel Commission.happened:
In 1936 the British government appointed a Royal Commission led by Lord Robert Peel, a former Secretary of State for India. It arrived in November 1936 and heard evidence from many witnesses, including Chaim Weizmann, David Ben-Gurion and, later in its visit, Arab leaders including Haj Amin al-Husseini. Its report, published on 7 July 1937, concluded that the mandate could not work because the aims of the two peoples could not be reconciled.

It proposed dividing the country. A Jewish state would cover about a fifth of the land, including the Galilee and much of the coastal plain. An Arab state, joined with Transjordan, would cover most of the rest. Britain would keep a zone including Jerusalem, Bethlehem and a corridor to the sea at Jaffa. The report also suggested exchanging populations, moving around 225,000 Arabs and 1,250 Jews. The Arab Higher Committee rejected the plan outright, and the revolt resumed with greater force. The Zionist Congress in Zurich rejected the proposed borders but allowed its leaders to negotiate, with Weizmann and Ben-Gurion seeing a state, even a small one, as a chance to save Jews.
Peel Commission.matters:
In 1938 a second body, the Woodhead Commission, judged partition unworkable, and Britain abandoned it. In 1939 Britain turned instead to the White Paper, which sharply limited Jewish immigration.

The Peel report was the first official proposal to divide the land into two states. Its ideas of partition and of a special status for Jerusalem shaped the United Nations partition plan of 1947 and continue to influence discussions of the conflict today.

Kristallnacht.background: By 1938 Jews in Germany had already lost their citizenship and most of their livelihoods. That year Nazi Germany annexed Austria, where Jews were publicly humiliated and attacked. In late October 1938 Germany expelled around 17,000 Polish Jews living in Germany, dumping many at the Polish border. Among them were the parents of 17-year-old Herschel Grynszpan, who was living in Paris. On 7 November he shot a German diplomat, Ernst vom Rath, who died on 9 November.
Kristallnacht.happened:
That evening, Nazi leaders were gathered in Munich to mark the anniversary of Hitler's failed coup of 1923. Propaganda Minister Joseph Goebbels gave a speech that was understood as a signal to unleash violence while presenting it as spontaneous public anger. Through the night of 9 to 10 November and into the next day, SA storm troopers, SS men and Hitler Youth, often in civilian clothes, attacked Jews across Germany, Austria and the Sudetenland. Fire brigades were told to protect only neighbouring non-Jewish buildings.

More than 1,400 synagogues and prayer rooms were burned or damaged, around 7,500 Jewish shops were destroyed, homes, schools and cemeteries were attacked, and at least 91 Jews were murdered. About 30,000 Jewish men were arrested and sent to Dachau, Buchenwald and Sachsenhausen, where hundreds more died. On 12 November Hermann Göring ordered the Jewish community to pay a collective fine of one billion Reichsmarks, while insurance payments for the damage were seized by the state. Jews were then barred from running businesses, attending schools and entering many public places.
Kristallnacht.matters:
Kristallnacht showed that the Nazis were ready to use open, organised violence against Jews, and that the German public would largely stand aside. It drove a desperate rush to emigrate, but many countries kept their doors closed, although Britain agreed to the Kindertransport for children.

In Germany today the events are often called the November Pogrom, because the Nazi-era name "night of broken glass" can make the violence sound minor. Each year on 9 November ceremonies are held across Germany and Austria, names of victims are read, and many cities have memorials on the sites of destroyed synagogues.

Kindertransport.background: After Kristallnacht in November 1938, Jewish families in Germany and Austria were desperate to escape. Britain, like most countries, limited refugees. Jewish and Quaker groups lobbied the government, and on 21 November 1938 the House of Commons debated the crisis. The government agreed to admit unaccompanied children under 17 on temporary travel documents, without visas, as long as private organisations guaranteed £50 for each child to pay for their eventual return.
Kindertransport.happened:
The newly formed Movement for the Care of Children from Germany, later the Refugee Children's Movement, organised the transports with volunteers in Germany, Austria, Czechoslovakia and Poland. The first transport, carrying around 200 children from Berlin, many from a Jewish orphanage destroyed on Kristallnacht, arrived at Harwich on 2 December 1938. Children travelled by train to the Netherlands and by ferry to England, each with a small suitcase and a numbered tag. Parents said goodbye on station platforms. In Amsterdam, the Dutch campaigner Geertruida Wijsmuller-Meijer helped many transports cross the border.

In Prague, the young London stockbroker Nicholas Winton, with colleagues on the ground, organised eight transports carrying 669 children. The last train from Germany left as war began on 1 September 1939, and a final ship sailed from the Netherlands in May 1940. In Britain the children went to foster families, hostels and farms. Some older boys were later interned as "enemy aliens", and some were deported to Canada and Australia.
Kindertransport.matters:
Around 10,000 children were saved. Most of their parents were later murdered in the Holocaust, and many children grew up with little knowledge of what had happened to their families. Some later served in the British armed forces, and many built careers in Britain, Israel and the United States. Among them is Alf Dubs, later a member of the House of Lords, who came on one of Winton's trains.

Winton's role was little known until 1988, when it was revealed on the BBC programme That's Life. He was knighted in 2003 and died in 2015 aged 106, and his story is told in the 2023 film One Life. Statues by the sculptor Frank Meisler, himself a Kindertransport child, stand at Liverpool Street station in London and at Friedrichstrasse station in Berlin.

White Paper.background: By the late 1930s Britain was trying to calm the Arab revolt in Palestine and secure Arab support in a coming war with Germany. The Peel partition plan had been abandoned, and a conference in London in early 1939 with Jewish and Arab delegations failed to reach any agreement. At the same time, Jews in Germany, Austria and Czechoslovakia were trying to flee, and at the Évian Conference of July 1938 nearly every country had refused to take in significantly more refugees.
White Paper.happened:
On 17 May 1939 the government published a policy paper, known after the Colonial Secretary as the MacDonald White Paper. It stated that Britain did not intend Palestine to become a Jewish state. Jewish immigration would be limited to 75,000 over five years, after which it would depend on Arab consent. Within ten years an independent Palestine would be established, governed jointly by Arabs and Jews in proportion to their population.

Jews in Palestine protested in the streets, and the League of Nations Permanent Mandates Commission found the policy did not fit the terms of the mandate. During the war, the Jewish underground organised illegal immigration, known as Aliyah Bet, but British forces intercepted many ships. In November 1940 the Patria sank in Haifa harbour after a bomb planted by the Haganah to stop its deportation went wrong, killing more than 250 people. In February 1942 the Struma, stranded off Istanbul after being refused entry, was towed to sea and sunk by a Soviet submarine, and nearly 800 refugees died, with only one survivor.
White Paper.matters:
The White Paper closed one of the few escape routes for European Jews at the moment they needed it most. It turned the Zionist movement firmly against British rule, and in 1944 the Irgun and Lehi underground groups began an armed revolt. Despite this, around 30,000 Jews from Palestine volunteered for the British forces, and a Jewish Brigade fought in Italy in 1945.

After the war Britain kept the limits in place, and tens of thousands of Holocaust survivors were held in camps in Cyprus. The struggle over immigration helped bring the Palestine question to the United Nations in 1947. The Struma and the Patria are remembered with memorials in Israel, including at Haifa.

The Holocaust.background: The Holocaust, called the Shoah in Hebrew, meaning "catastrophe", grew out of the Nazis' racial ideology, which portrayed Jews as a deadly enemy of the German people. From 1933 Jews in Germany were stripped of rights, property and livelihoods. When Germany invaded Poland in September 1939, nearly two million more Jews came under its control. Jews were forced to wear identifying badges and crowded into ghettos such as Łódź and Warsaw, where hunger and disease killed tens of thousands.
The Holocaust.happened:
In June 1941 Germany invaded the Soviet Union. Mobile killing units, the Einsatzgruppen, together with police battalions, local collaborators and the army, began shooting Jewish men, women and children in pits and ravines near their homes. At Babyn Yar outside Kyiv, 33,771 Jews were murdered in two days in September 1941. By the end of the war around two million Jews had been killed in such shootings.

From December 1941 the Nazis began murdering Jews with poison gas. Killing centres were built in occupied Poland at Chełmno, Bełżec, Sobibór, Treblinka, Majdanek and Auschwitz-Birkenau. Jews were deported there by train from ghettos and from across Europe, from France and the Netherlands to Greece and, in 1944, Hungary, from where around 430,000 Jews were sent to Auschwitz in less than two months. Most were murdered on arrival. Others were worked to death in camps, and in the last months of the war tens of thousands died on forced marches. The Nazis also murdered Roma, disabled people, Soviet prisoners of war, Polish civilians and others. Some resisted, in ghetto revolts and with the partisans.
The Holocaust.matters:
Six million Jews were murdered, and the centuries-old Jewish civilisations of Poland, Lithuania, Ukraine, Greece and many other countries were largely destroyed, along with the Yiddish-speaking world of Eastern Europe. The Holocaust led to new international laws on genocide and human rights and gave urgency to the creation of a Jewish state.

It is remembered in many ways. Yad Vashem in Jerusalem, founded in 1953, records the names of victims and honours over 28,000 non-Jews as Righteous Among the Nations for saving Jews. Israel marks Yom HaShoah, Holocaust Remembrance Day, in spring with a two-minute siren, and the world marks International Holocaust Remembrance Day on 27 January. Survivors' testimonies, museums and memorials keep the memory alive.

Wannsee Conference.background: By late 1941 the mass murder of Jews was already under way. Mobile killing squads had shot hundreds of thousands of Jews in the occupied Soviet Union, and deportations of German Jews to the east had begun. In July 1941 Hermann Göring had authorised Reinhard Heydrich, head of the Reich Security Main Office, to prepare a "total solution of the Jewish question" across German-controlled Europe. Heydrich needed the cooperation of different government ministries and party offices, and called a meeting to make sure they would follow his lead. It was first planned for December 1941 but postponed.
Wannsee Conference.happened:
On 20 January 1942 fifteen officials gathered at a villa on the shore of Lake Wannsee in Berlin, used as an SS guest house. They included senior civil servants from the ministries of the interior, justice and foreign affairs, officials responsible for occupied Poland and the eastern territories, and SS officers. Adolf Eichmann, head of the Gestapo's Jewish affairs office, organised the meeting and drafted the minutes.

Heydrich explained that Jews would be deported to the east. A list counted 11 million Jews in Europe, including in countries not under German control such as Britain, Ireland, Sweden and Switzerland. The minutes used careful language, speaking of "evacuation" and of Jews who survived forced labour being "treated accordingly", but the meaning was murder. The officials also discussed what to do with people of mixed descent and Jews married to non-Jews. The meeting lasted about 90 minutes. Gas killings had already begun at Chełmno in December 1941, and Bełżec began operating in March 1942.
Wannsee Conference.matters:
Wannsee did not decide to begin the Holocaust, but it shows how the state's bureaucracy willingly joined in planning genocide. Of the 30 copies of the minutes, only one, the sixteenth, survived. The American prosecutor Robert Kempner found it in German Foreign Office files in 1947, and it became key evidence. At his trial in Jerusalem in 1961, Eichmann described the relaxed atmosphere after the meeting.

The villa has been the House of the Wannsee Conference, a memorial and education centre, since 1992. The meeting has been dramatised in films such as Conspiracy (2001) and The Conference (2022).

Warsaw Ghetto Uprising.background:
Before the war Warsaw had the largest Jewish community in Europe, around 350,000 people, about a third of the city. In November 1940 the Germans sealed more than 400,000 Jews inside a small walled ghetto. Starvation and disease killed tens of thousands. The historian Emanuel Ringelblum and his group, Oneg Shabbat, secretly gathered documents and buried them in milk cans and metal boxes.

Between July and September 1942, in what became known as the Great Deportation, more than a quarter of a million Jews were sent from the ghetto to be murdered at Treblinka. Around 55,000 to 60,000 remained. Young people from Zionist, socialist and Bundist youth movements formed the Jewish Combat Organisation, known by its Polish initials ŻOB, led by Mordechai Anielewicz, aged 23.
Warsaw Ghetto Uprising.happened:
In January 1943 fighters opened fire during a new round of deportations, and the Germans withdrew after several days. On 19 April 1943, the eve of Passover, German forces under SS General Jürgen Stroop entered the ghetto to destroy it. Fighters attacked them with pistols, a few rifles, grenades and petrol bombs, and drove them back.

The Germans then set the ghetto on fire, building by building, and used smoke and gas to force people from bunkers. On 8 May Anielewicz and many fighters died in the command bunker at 18 Mila Street. On 16 May Stroop blew up the Great Synagogue on Tłomackie Street and declared the ghetto destroyed. His report counted about 56,000 Jews captured or killed. A small number of fighters, including Marek Edelman and Zivia Lubetkin, escaped through the sewers.
Warsaw Ghetto Uprising.matters:
The uprising was the first large urban revolt against the Germans in occupied Europe and inspired resistance in other ghettos and camps. It became a central symbol of Jewish courage, and the date of Israel's Yom HaShoah was chosen to fall near its anniversary. Part of Ringelblum's archive was dug up after the war and is now held at the Jewish Historical Institute in Warsaw.

The Monument to the Ghetto Heroes by Nathan Rapoport was unveiled in 1948, and in 1970 the West German chancellor Willy Brandt knelt before it. The POLIN Museum of the History of Polish Jews stands opposite. Each 19 April Warsaw residents wear paper daffodils in memory, a tradition linked to Marek Edelman. In Israel survivors founded the Ghetto Fighters' House at Kibbutz Lohamei HaGeta'ot.

Auschwitz liberated.background: Auschwitz was opened by the Germans in 1940 in the Polish town of Oświęcim, at first as a prison camp for Polish political prisoners. It grew into a vast complex of camps. Auschwitz-Birkenau, built from 1941, became the largest killing centre of the Holocaust, with gas chambers and crematoria. At nearby Monowitz, prisoners worked as slave labour for the chemical company IG Farben. From 1942 trains brought Jews from all over Europe. Most were sent directly to the gas chambers after a selection on arrival, while others were registered, tattooed with a number and forced to work.
Auschwitz liberated.happened:
As the Red Army approached in late 1944, the SS tried to hide their crimes. They burned records and blew up the gas chambers and crematoria at Birkenau. Between 17 and 21 January 1945 they forced about 58,000 prisoners to march west in freezing weather, shooting those who fell behind. Many thousands died on these marches.

On the afternoon of Saturday 27 January 1945, soldiers of the Soviet 60th Army reached the camp. They found about 7,000 sick and starving prisoners, including several hundred children, as well as hundreds of bodies and huge stores of victims' clothing, shoes and human hair. Among those liberated were the Italian chemist and writer Primo Levi, who had been left behind ill in the Monowitz infirmary, and Otto Frank, father of Anne Frank. Many survivors were too weak to recover and died in the following weeks despite medical care.

About 1.1 million people were murdered at Auschwitz. Around one million were Jews, along with tens of thousands of Poles, about 21,000 Roma and Sinti and some 15,000 Soviet prisoners of war.
Auschwitz liberated.matters:
Auschwitz became the best-known symbol of the Holocaust. In 1947 Poland created the Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum on the site, and in 1979 it was made a UNESCO World Heritage Site. More than a million people visit each year, passing under the gate with the words Arbeit macht frei, "work makes you free".

In 2005 the United Nations chose 27 January, the day of liberation, as International Holocaust Remembrance Day. Each year survivors, leaders and young people gather at Birkenau, and the annual March of the Living takes Jewish students from Auschwitz to Birkenau on Yom HaShoah.

Dead Sea Scrolls found.background: Before 1947 the oldest known complete Hebrew Bible manuscripts dated from around the 900s to 1000s CE, such as the Aleppo Codex and the Leningrad Codex. Scholars knew from ancient writers such as Josephus that in the late Second Temple period there were many Jewish groups, including Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes, but had few writings from that time in Hebrew or Aramaic.
Dead Sea Scrolls found.happened:
In late 1946 or early 1947 a young Bedouin shepherd, Muhammad edh-Dhib, and his cousins found a cave in the cliffs at Qumran, on the north-western shore of the Dead Sea, containing jars with seven scrolls. Four were sold to the Syrian Orthodox Metropolitan of Jerusalem, Mar Athanasius Samuel. Three were bought by the archaeologist Eleazar Sukenik of the Hebrew University, who completed the purchase on 29 November 1947, the same day as the United Nations vote on partition. In 1954 the Metropolitan advertised his four scrolls in the Wall Street Journal, and Sukenik's son, the archaeologist Yigael Yadin, secretly bought them for the State of Israel.

From 1949 to 1956 archaeologists and Bedouin searched the area and found eleven caves with fragments of about 900 manuscripts. Most are written in Hebrew, some in Aramaic and Greek, and they date from about the 200s BCE to the 1st century CE. They include biblical books, commentaries, prayers, laws and the rules of a strict community, which many scholars link with the Essenes, though this is debated. The Great Isaiah Scroll is over seven metres long. One unusual text, the Copper Scroll, lists hidden treasures.
Dead Sea Scrolls found.matters:
The scrolls showed that the text of the Hebrew Bible had been copied with remarkable care for over a thousand years, while also revealing variant versions. They gave a window into Jewish life and belief at the time of the Second Temple and the rise of Christianity.

The seven original scrolls are displayed in the Shrine of the Book at the Israel Museum in Jerusalem, opened in 1965, whose white dome is shaped like the lids of the jars in which they were found. Most fragments are held by the Israel Antiquities Authority, and high-resolution images can now be viewed online through the Leon Levy Dead Sea Scrolls Digital Library.

UN partition vote.background:
After the Second World War Britain faced an armed Jewish revolt, growing international pressure to let Holocaust survivors into Palestine, and fierce Arab opposition to further immigration. In February 1947 Britain handed the question to the newly founded United Nations. The UN set up a Special Committee on Palestine, UNSCOP, with members from eleven countries, which toured the country that summer. Arab leaders boycotted it.

In July 1947 the ship Exodus 1947 arrived off Haifa with about 4,500 Holocaust survivors. British forces stormed it, and the passengers were sent back to France and then to Hamburg in Germany. Some UNSCOP members watched the passengers being forced off in Haifa.
UN partition vote.happened:
UNSCOP's majority recommended dividing Palestine into a Jewish state and an Arab state, linked in an economic union, with Jerusalem and Bethlehem as an international zone run by the UN. The Jewish state would cover about 56 percent of the land, much of it the Negev desert, and would have a large Arab minority. A minority proposed one federal state.

On 29 November 1947 the General Assembly, meeting at Flushing Meadows in New York, voted on Resolution 181. It passed with 33 votes in favour, 13 against and 10 abstentions, including Britain. Both the United States and the Soviet Union voted in favour. Across the Jewish community in Palestine people listened to the vote on the radio and celebrated through the night. The Jewish Agency accepted the plan. The Arab Higher Committee and the Arab states rejected it as unjust to the Arab majority. The next day fighting broke out, beginning a civil war between Jews and Arabs that lasted until the end of the British mandate.
UN partition vote.matters:
The vote gave international legitimacy to a Jewish state and set out, for the first time in UN terms, a two-state solution, an idea still at the centre of diplomacy. The Arab state it proposed was never created.

Many Israeli towns have a street named Kaf-Tet BeNovember, Hebrew for "29 November". The novelist Amos Oz described the night of the vote in Jerusalem in his memoir A Tale of Love and Darkness. In 1977 the UN chose 29 November as the International Day of Solidarity with the Palestinian People, so the date carries very different meanings for Israelis and Palestinians.

State of Israel.background: After the United Nations partition vote in November 1947, fighting spread across Palestine between Jewish and Arab forces. Jerusalem's Jewish neighbourhoods were besieged, and convoys to the city were attacked. Britain announced that its mandate would end at midnight on 14 to 15 May 1948. The United States, worried about war, suggested delaying statehood, and Jewish leaders debated whether to declare independence at once. On 12 May the People's Administration, the provisional leadership, narrowly voted to go ahead.
State of Israel.happened:
On Friday 14 May 1948, the fifth of the Hebrew month of Iyar, invited guests gathered in the hall of the Tel Aviv Museum on Rothschild Boulevard, the former home of Meir Dizengoff. To keep the event secret from British forces and to finish before the Sabbath, invitations were sent only that morning. Under a portrait of Theodor Herzl, David Ben-Gurion read the Declaration of Independence. It announced the establishment of a Jewish state in the Land of Israel, to be called the State of Israel, promised equality for all citizens regardless of religion, race or sex, and appealed to Arab inhabitants to take part in building the state. The members of the People's Council signed it, and the audience sang Hatikvah.

Within minutes the United States recognised Israel, and the Soviet Union followed days later. On 15 May armies from Egypt, Transjordan, Syria, Lebanon and Iraq entered the country. After months of fighting and several truces, armistice agreements were signed in 1949. Around 700,000 Palestinian Arabs fled or were expelled from their homes during the war, which Palestinians call the Nakba, "catastrophe".
State of Israel.matters:
After nearly 2,000 years, a Jewish state existed again. Israel's Law of Return in 1950 gave every Jew the right to settle there, and in its first years its population doubled as Holocaust survivors and Jews from Arab and Muslim countries arrived. Chaim Weizmann became its first president and Ben-Gurion its first prime minister.

Israel celebrates Yom Ha'atzmaut, Independence Day, on 5 Iyar, immediately after Yom HaZikaron, the day of remembrance for fallen soldiers and victims of terror. The hall where independence was declared is preserved as Independence Hall. Palestinians mark Nakba Day on 15 May, a reminder that the same events are remembered very differently.

Operation Magic Carpet.background:
Jews had lived in Yemen, in the south of the Arabian Peninsula, since ancient times, with traditions tracing their arrival to the days of the First Temple. They developed their own customs, a distinctive way of pronouncing Hebrew and rich religious poetry, especially that of the 17th-century poet Rabbi Shalom Shabazi. Under the rule of the Imams they were a protected but inferior minority. Under the Orphans' Decree, Jewish children who lost their fathers could be taken to be raised as Muslims.

Small groups of Yemenite Jews had moved to the Land of Israel since 1881. After the UN partition vote in 1947, riots in Aden, then a British colony, killed more than 80 Jews, and tension grew across the region.
Operation Magic Carpet.happened:
In 1949 Imam Ahmad allowed Jews to leave Yemen, provided they gave up their property. Families travelled for weeks on foot or by donkey through the mountains and desert, often robbed or taxed along the way, to reach Aden. There the American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee ran a camp called Hashed, where many arrived exhausted, malnourished and sick.

From June 1949 to September 1950, aircraft chartered by the Joint and the Jewish Agency, including planes from Alaska Airlines and other companies, flew from Aden to Lydda airport in Israel, a long flight with a refuelling stop. The airlift was officially called On Wings of Eagles, recalling God's promise in the Book of Exodus to carry the Israelites on eagles' wings. Some passengers, seeing planes for the first time, saw the flights as the fulfilment of that promise.
Operation Magic Carpet.matters:
The airlift brought almost the entire Jewish population of Yemen to Israel, one of the first great rescue operations of the new state. The newcomers faced a hard start in tents and transit camps called ma'abarot, and the loss of their traditional way of life. A painful chapter in this period is the Yemenite children affair: many families say their babies disappeared from hospitals and camps in the early 1950s, and the issue was investigated by several state inquiries and is still debated.

Yemenite Jews have greatly enriched Israeli culture, through music, food, crafts and religious traditions such as the henna ceremony before weddings. Today only a handful of Jews, if any, remain in Yemen.

Law of Return.background:
When Israel declared independence in May 1948, its founding declaration promised that the new state would be open to Jewish immigration. This was a direct answer to the years before, when Britain's 1939 White Paper had tightly limited Jewish entry to Palestine.

At independence there were only about 650,000 Jews in the country. At the same time, Jewish communities across the Arab world were facing growing hostility, and hundreds of thousands of survivors were still living in displaced persons camps in Europe.
Law of Return.happened:
The Knesset passed the Law of Return on 5 July 1950. The date was chosen on purpose: it fell on the Hebrew anniversary of the death of Theodor Herzl, the founder of political Zionism. The law was short. It said that every Jew had the right to come to Israel as an oleh, an immigrant, and a 1952 nationality law then made such immigrants citizens.

The arrivals were overwhelming. Operation On Wings of Eagles flew almost the entire Jewish community of Yemen, around 49,000 people, to Israel in 1949 and 1950. Most of Libya's Jews came, followed by the great airlift from Iraq, and later large waves from Morocco. By the end of 1951 the Jewish population had roughly doubled. There were not enough homes, so newcomers were placed in ma'abarot, transit camps of tents and tin huts. At their peak around a quarter of a million people lived in them, and the last ones did not close until the early 1960s.
Law of Return.matters:
The Law of Return is often called the heart of Israel's identity as a Jewish state. It turned the country into a refuge for any Jew in danger, a direct lesson from the years when Jews fleeing Nazi Europe had nowhere to go. It has since brought millions of people to Israel, from Ethiopia, the former Soviet Union, France, the Americas and beyond.

The law has also been a source of lasting debate. A 1970 amendment defined a Jew as someone born to a Jewish mother or who has converted, and extended the right to children, grandchildren and spouses of Jews. Questions about who counts as a Jew, which conversions are recognised, and whether the grandchild clause should stay are still argued over in the Knesset today. The hardship of the ma'abarot, felt most by immigrants from Arab countries, also left a long mark on Israeli society and politics.

Exodus from Iraq.background:
Jews had lived in Mesopotamia since the Babylonian exile in the 6th century BCE. It was there that the Babylonian Talmud was written, and great academies such as Sura and Pumbedita led the Jewish world for centuries. By the 1940s around 130,000 Jews lived in Iraq, most of them in Baghdad, where they made up a large part of the city's population and were prominent in trade, banking, music and government service.

Their position grew dangerous in the 1930s and 1940s. In June 1941, during the Shavuot holiday, mobs attacked Jews in Baghdad in the Farhud, killing around 180 people and looting homes and shops. After Israel's creation in 1948, Zionism became a crime in Iraq.
Exodus from Iraq.happened:
In March 1950 the Iraqi parliament passed a law allowing Jews to leave the country, but only if they gave up their Iraqi citizenship. Many hesitated at first, but numbers grew quickly, helped by fear after a series of bombings against Jewish targets in Baghdad, including one at the Masuda Shemtov synagogue in January 1951. Who was behind the bombings is still disputed. In March 1951, just as registration closed, Iraq froze the property of all Jews who had signed up to leave.

Israel organised the airlift, called Operation Ezra and Nehemiah after the leaders who brought Jews back from Babylon in the Bible. Planes flew people out, often by way of Cyprus, between 1950 and 1952. Around 120,000 Jews left, most taking only a suitcase and a small sum of money.
Exodus from Iraq.matters:
In just two years one of the oldest Jewish communities in the world almost vanished. Those who stayed faced harsh treatment, and in January 1969 nine Jews were among those publicly hanged in Baghdad after being accused of spying. Most of the remaining Jews then fled. Today only a tiny handful are thought to live in Iraq, and ancient sites such as the tombs of the prophet Ezekiel and the scribe Ezra are no longer cared for by a local community.

Iraqi Jews and their descendants became a major part of Israeli society, in politics, literature, music and the army. Their history is preserved at the Babylonian Jewry Heritage Centre in Or Yehuda. The exodus is also part of the wider story of the roughly 850,000 Jews who left or were forced out of Arab countries and Iran in the decades after 1948, a story now marked in Israel each year on 30 November.

Yad Vashem founded.background:
Even before the Second World War ended, people in the Jewish community of Palestine were talking about how to remember the victims. In 1942 Mordecai Shenhavi, a member of a kibbutz, proposed a national memorial. After the war, survivors arriving in Israel carried the memory of families and whole towns that had been wiped out, often with no grave and sometimes with no one left to say their names.

The young state was poor and busy absorbing hundreds of thousands of immigrants, but there was a strong feeling that remembrance could not wait.
Yad Vashem founded.happened:
On 19 August 1953 the Knesset passed the Yad Vashem Law, creating a national authority for the remembrance of the Holocaust. The name comes from Isaiah 56:5, a promise to give those with no descendants a memorial and a name that will not be cut off. The site was built on the Mount of Remembrance in western Jerusalem, next to Mount Herzl.

Yad Vashem began collecting Pages of Testimony, forms on which survivors and relatives recorded the name and details of each person murdered. Its database now holds almost five million names. From 1963 a public commission, first led by Supreme Court justice Moshe Landau, began formally recognising Righteous Among the Nations. Each is honoured with a medal and certificate, and their names are carved in the Garden of the Righteous. They include Oskar Schindler, Irena Sendler in Poland, Raoul Wallenberg in Hungary and Chiune Sugihara, a Japanese diplomat in Lithuania.
Yad Vashem founded.matters:
Yad Vashem has become one of the world's leading centres for Holocaust research, education and documentation. Its Holocaust History Museum, designed by the architect Moshe Safdie, opened in 2005. The Children's Memorial, a dark hall where a single candle is reflected into countless points of light while the names of murdered children are read aloud, is remembered by many visitors as the most moving part of the site.

Visiting Yad Vashem is a standard part of official visits to Israel, and world leaders lay wreaths in the Hall of Remembrance, where an eternal flame burns beside the names of camps and killing sites. The national ceremony for Yom HaShoah opens there each year. As the last survivors pass away, its archive of testimonies, photographs and names has become even more important as a lasting record of the six million and of those who risked everything to save lives.

Suez Crisis.background:
In the early 1950s Israel's southern border with Egypt was tense. Armed Palestinian fighters known as fedayeen crossed from Egyptian-ruled Gaza to attack Israeli villages and roads, and Israel answered with reprisal raids. Egypt barred Israeli ships from the Suez Canal and blocked the Straits of Tiran, cutting off Israel's southern port of Eilat. In 1955 Egypt signed a large arms deal with Czechoslovakia, backed by the Soviet Union, which alarmed Israeli leaders.

In July 1956, after the United States and Britain withdrew funding for the Aswan Dam, President Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal Company, which was largely owned by British and French shareholders. Britain and France wanted to take the canal back and weaken Nasser.
Suez Crisis.happened:
In October 1956, at a secret meeting at Sèvres near Paris, Israeli Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion, army chief Moshe Dayan and Shimon Peres agreed a plan with French and British officials. On 29 October Israeli paratroopers, led by Ariel Sharon's brigade, dropped near the Mitla Pass deep in the Sinai. Britain and France then issued an ultimatum to both sides to pull back from the canal, and when Egypt refused they bombed Egyptian airfields and landed troops at Port Said.

Within about a week Israel had taken almost the whole Sinai Peninsula and the Gaza Strip, reaching Sharm el-Sheikh at the southern tip. But the United States under President Eisenhower was furious at not being told, and the Soviet Union threatened the invaders. Under this pressure Britain and France withdrew, and Israel pulled out of the Sinai and Gaza by March 1957.
Suez Crisis.matters:
For Britain and France, Suez was a humiliation that marked the end of their era as great powers in the Middle East, and British Prime Minister Anthony Eden resigned soon after. Nasser emerged as a hero across the Arab world despite his military defeat.

For Israel the gains were real. A new United Nations Emergency Force, the first major UN peacekeeping force, proposed by Canada's Lester Pearson, was stationed in Sinai and Gaza. Fedayeen raids largely stopped, and the Straits of Tiran reopened, allowing Eilat to grow as a port for trade with Asia and Africa. The southern border stayed mostly quiet for ten years. When Nasser ordered the UN force out and closed the straits again in May 1967, it set off the crisis that led to the Six-Day War.

Eichmann trial.background:
Adolf Eichmann was an SS officer who headed the Gestapo office in charge of Jewish affairs. He helped organise the Wannsee Conference of January 1942, where Nazi officials coordinated the murder of Europe's Jews, and he managed the trains that carried Jews from across Europe to ghettos and death camps. In 1944 he went to Hungary and oversaw the deportation of around 437,000 Jews, most of whom were sent to Auschwitz.

After the war Eichmann escaped from an American camp, hid in Germany, and in 1950 reached Argentina. He lived in a suburb of Buenos Aires under the name Ricardo Klement and worked at a Mercedes-Benz factory. A tip passed to Israel by Fritz Bauer, a Jewish prosecutor in West Germany, helped confirm his identity.
Eichmann trial.happened:
On 11 May 1960 a team of Mossad agents seized Eichmann near his home as he got off a bus. They held him in a safe house for nine days, then smuggled him out on an El Al plane. On 23 May Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion told a stunned Knesset that Eichmann was in Israeli custody.

The trial opened in Jerusalem on 11 April 1961, before three judges led by Moshe Landau. Eichmann sat in a bulletproof glass booth. The prosecutor, Gideon Hausner, called more than 100 witnesses, many of them survivors, and the hearings were filmed and broadcast around the world. Eichmann argued that he was a minor official following orders. In December 1961 he was found guilty on all counts, including crimes against the Jewish people and crimes against humanity. He was hanged at Ramla prison just after midnight on 1 June 1962, and his ashes were scattered at sea outside Israel's waters.
Eichmann trial.matters:
The trial changed how the Holocaust was understood, in Israel and around the world. Before it, many survivors in Israel had kept silent, and some felt their suffering was not fully heard. Hearing story after story in court, often on the radio in their own homes, Israelis began to grasp the scale of what had happened and to treat survivors with new respect.

The philosopher Hannah Arendt covered the trial and wrote about the banality of evil, the idea that terrible crimes can be carried out by ordinary bureaucrats. The trial also set an example for later cases against Nazi criminals and helped establish that crimes against humanity can be tried long after they took place. Eichmann's execution remains the only time the State of Israel has carried out a death sentence imposed by a civilian court.

Agnon wins the Nobel.background:
Shmuel Yosef Agnon was born Shmuel Yosef Czaczkes in 1888 in Buczacz, a small town in Galicia, then part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire and now in Ukraine. He grew up steeped in religious texts and Hasidic stories. In 1908 he moved to Jaffa in Ottoman Palestine, and his first story there, Agunot, gave him his pen name.

He spent the years from 1912 to 1924 in Germany, where the businessman Salman Schocken became his patron and publisher. In 1924 a fire at his home in Bad Homburg destroyed his library and unpublished manuscripts. He returned to Jerusalem and settled in the Talpiot neighbourhood, where his house was damaged again in the riots of 1929.
Agnon wins the Nobel.happened:
Over five decades Agnon wrote novels and stories that blended the old language of the Talmud and prayer book with modern Hebrew. His major works include The Bridal Canopy, a comic journey through the world of Galician Jews; A Guest for the Night, about a visit to his ruined home town after the First World War; and Only Yesterday, set among the early Zionist pioneers in Jaffa and Jerusalem.

On 10 December 1966 he received the Nobel Prize in Literature in Stockholm, wearing a skullcap. He shared it with Nelly Sachs, a poet born in Berlin in 1891 who fled to Sweden in 1940 with the help of the Swedish novelist Selma Lagerlöf. Her poems mourned the Jewish dead of the Holocaust. At the royal ceremony Agnon recited in Hebrew the traditional blessing said on seeing a king.
Agnon wins the Nobel.matters:
Agnon is still the only writer in Hebrew to win the Nobel Prize in Literature. His prize was seen as recognition of modern Hebrew itself, a language that had been revived for everyday speech only a few generations earlier. It showed that Hebrew literature could stand among the great literatures of the world.

Agnon died in 1970, the same year as Nelly Sachs. His portrait appeared on Israel's 50-shekel banknote for many years, and his home in Talpiot is now a museum and cultural centre. His books are still studied in Israeli schools and universities. They are valued as a bridge between the lost world of East European Jewish towns and the new life being built in the Land of Israel, and as a record of how that change felt to the people who lived through it.

Six-Day War.background:
In the mid-1960s tension grew on all of Israel's borders. Syria shelled Israeli farms below the Golan Heights and tried to divert the sources of the Jordan River. Palestinian fighters from the new Fatah movement carried out raids, and Israel struck back, including a large raid on the West Bank village of Samu in November 1966.

In May 1967 the Soviet Union falsely told Egypt that Israel was massing troops against Syria. President Nasser moved large forces into Sinai, ordered the UN peacekeepers out, and on 22 May closed the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping. Jordan signed a defence pact with Egypt on 30 May. Arab leaders spoke openly of destroying Israel, and many Israelis feared a second Holocaust.
Six-Day War.happened:
On the morning of 5 June 1967 the Israeli air force launched Operation Focus, destroying most of Egypt's air force on the ground within hours. Israeli ground forces then swept through Gaza and Sinai and reached the Suez Canal.

Jordan began shelling West Jerusalem, and Israel moved into the West Bank. On 7 June paratroopers under Mordechai Gur fought their way into the Old City and reached the Western Wall, where the army's chief rabbi, Shlomo Goren, blew the shofar. On 9 and 10 June Israeli forces climbed the Golan Heights under heavy fire and took them from Syria. Around 800 Israeli soldiers were killed. Arab losses were far higher, running into many thousands. According to UN estimates, around 300,000 Palestinians fled or were displaced, many for the second time since 1948.
Six-Day War.matters:
In less than a week Israel more than tripled the land under its control. Jews could again pray at the Western Wall and visit sites such as the Cave of the Patriarchs in Hebron, and Jerusalem Day is still celebrated in Israel each year. The victory brought a wave of pride across the Jewish world, and it helped spark the movement of Soviet Jews demanding the right to leave.

The war also created questions that remain unresolved. UN Security Council Resolution 242 set out the idea of land for peace, while an Arab summit in Khartoum rejected peace, recognition and negotiations with Israel. Israel's rule over the West Bank and Gaza, with their large Palestinian populations, and the building of settlements there, became the centre of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Sinai was later returned to Egypt in exchange for peace, but the status of the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan is still bitterly disputed.

Soviet Jewry movement.background:
The Soviet Union was home to one of the largest Jewish populations in the world, but Jewish life there was heavily restricted. Teaching Hebrew was banned, almost all synagogues were closed, and religious practice was discouraged. Yet internal passports listed Jewish as a nationality, and Jews faced quotas at universities and barriers in many careers. Most were not allowed to leave.

Israel's victory in 1967 stirred a new sense of identity among many Soviet Jews. In the West, groups such as the Student Struggle for Soviet Jewry, founded in New York in 1964, had already begun campaigning.
Soviet Jewry movement.happened:
In June 1970 a group of Jews and two non-Jewish friends planned to buy every seat on a small 12-seat plane at an airfield near Leningrad, posing as guests travelling to a wedding, then take it over and fly to Sweden. The KGB knew of the plan and arrested them before they reached the plane. At their trial in December 1970, the former pilot Mark Dymshits and Eduard Kuznetsov were sentenced to death, and others received long prison terms. After protests from around the world, the death sentences were reduced to 15 years.

The case turned a small movement into a global cause. Activists marched, held vigils and adopted individual refuseniks, people who had been refused permission to leave and often lost their jobs as a result. In 1974 the US Congress passed the Jackson-Vanik amendment, linking trade with the Soviet Union to freedom of emigration. Natan Sharansky, a young computer scientist and campaigner, was arrested in 1977 on false charges of spying for the United States and sentenced to 13 years. He was freed in February 1986 in an exchange on the Glienicke Bridge in Berlin.
Soviet Jewry movement.matters:
The campaign was one of the largest human rights movements of the Cold War. In December 1987 around 250,000 people rallied in Washington on the eve of a summit between President Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev. Emigration rose and fell with the politics of the time, with around 250,000 Jews leaving during the 1970s, before the gates opened fully at the end of the 1980s.

The movement united Jews across many countries around a single goal, and it helped put human rights at the heart of relations with the Soviet Union. Sharansky went on to become an Israeli government minister and head of the Jewish Agency. Many of the refuseniks became leading figures in Israel, and the mass aliyah that followed reshaped the country.

Munich massacre.background:
The 1972 Summer Olympics in Munich were meant to show a new, peaceful West Germany, 36 years after the Nazi-era Berlin Games of 1936. Security in the athletes' village was deliberately light. The Israeli team, many of them children of Holocaust survivors, stayed in apartments at Connollystrasse 31.

Black September was a Palestinian militant group linked to Fatah. It took its name from the conflict of September 1970, when Jordan's army drove Palestinian armed groups out of the country.
Munich massacre.happened:
Before dawn on 5 September 1972, eight armed members of Black September climbed the fence of the village and forced their way into the Israeli apartments. The wrestling coach Moshe Weinberg and the weightlifter Yossef Romano fought back and were killed. Some athletes escaped, but nine were taken hostage. The attackers demanded the release of more than 200 Palestinian prisoners held in Israel, as well as two German left-wing militants. Prime Minister Golda Meir refused to negotiate.

Late that evening the hostage-takers and their captives were flown by helicopter to the Fürstenfeldbruck air base, where German police had planned an ambush. The plan was badly prepared, with too few snipers and no proper equipment. In the gunfight that followed, all nine hostages were killed, along with a German police officer, Anton Fliegerbauer. Five of the attackers died and three were captured. They were freed only weeks later, in October 1972, after the hijacking of a Lufthansa plane.
Munich massacre.matters:
The Games were halted for a memorial service in the Olympic stadium, then continued, which many Israelis found deeply painful. Israel launched a long covert campaign, often called Operation Wrath of God, to kill those it held responsible. In 1973 its agents mistakenly killed an innocent Moroccan waiter in Lillehammer, Norway.

For decades the widows, especially Ankie Spitzer and Ilana Romano, campaigned for official remembrance and for the truth about the failed rescue. A minute of silence for the Israeli victims was finally held at an Olympic opening ceremony in Tokyo in 2021. At the 50th anniversary in 2022, Germany's president apologised and Germany reached a compensation agreement with the families. A memorial now stands in Munich's Olympic Park, and the massacre is remembered as a turning point in the history of international terrorism and security at major events.

Yom Kippur War.background:
After the Six-Day War, Egypt and Israel fought a long War of Attrition along the Suez Canal until 1970. Israel built a line of forts on the canal known as the Bar Lev Line. Anwar Sadat, who became Egypt's president in 1970, wanted to recover the Sinai and break the deadlock, and he prepared a joint attack with Syria.

Israeli military intelligence held a firm belief, later called the conception, that Egypt would not go to war until it could match Israel's air force. Warning signs in the days before the war were played down. Only on the morning of 6 October did Prime Minister Golda Meir receive clear warning, and she decided against a pre-emptive strike so that Israel would not be seen as the aggressor.
Yom Kippur War.happened:
At 2pm on 6 October 1973, on Yom Kippur, when most Israelis were fasting and in synagogue, Egypt and Syria attacked. Egyptian troops crossed the Suez Canal, used water cannons to break through the sand banks, and overran most of the Bar Lev Line. On the Golan Heights, around 1,400 Syrian tanks faced a small Israeli force that held on at great cost in places such as the Valley of Tears.

After the first terrible days, Israel stopped the Syrians and pushed towards Damascus. From 14 October a large American airlift brought weapons and supplies. On 15 and 16 October forces led by Ariel Sharon crossed the canal into Egypt, and Israel encircled Egypt's Third Army. UN-backed ceasefires took hold by late October, amid tension between the US and the Soviet Union. Around 2,650 Israeli soldiers were killed. Egyptian and Syrian losses were much higher, with estimates running from about 8,000 to well over 15,000.
Yom Kippur War.matters:
Israel ended the war in a strong military position, but the shock was immense. The Agranat Commission investigated the failures, and Golda Meir resigned in 1974, followed by defence minister Moshe Dayan. Public anger helped end decades of Labour Party rule, and in 1977 Menachem Begin's Likud came to power.

In Egypt the crossing of the canal is still celebrated as a great victory, and 6 October is a national holiday. Having restored national pride, Sadat felt able to seek peace, and the war led directly to his visit to Jerusalem and the 1979 peace treaty. In Israel the war is remembered with deep grief and as a warning about overconfidence, and on 7 October 2023 many Israelis immediately compared the surprise attack to 1973.

\"Zionism is racism\" resolution.background:
By the mid-1970s the balance of power at the United Nations had shifted. Dozens of newly independent states had joined, and many voted together in the Non-Aligned Movement, often alongside the Soviet bloc and the Arab states. In 1974 PLO leader Yasser Arafat addressed the General Assembly, and the PLO was given observer status.

After the 1973 war and the Arab oil embargo, pressure on Israel at the UN grew. Earlier in 1975, conferences in Mexico City and elsewhere had already linked Zionism with racism in their declarations, setting the stage for a vote in the General Assembly.
\"Zionism is racism\" resolution.happened:
On 10 November 1975 the General Assembly adopted Resolution 3379, which stated that Zionism is a form of racism and racial discrimination. It passed by 72 votes to 35, with 32 countries abstaining. Supporters included the Arab states, the Soviet Union and its allies, and many countries in Africa and Asia. Most Western democracies voted against.

Israel's ambassador, Chaim Herzog, gave a powerful speech in reply. He noted that the vote fell on the anniversary of Kristallnacht, the Nazi pogrom of 9 and 10 November 1938, and at the end he tore the resolution in half at the podium. The US ambassador, Daniel Patrick Moynihan, declared that the United States would never accept the resolution, calling it an infamous act. Jewish communities around the world held protests, and many people who were not Jewish also spoke out against it.
\"Zionism is racism\" resolution.matters:
For many Jews the resolution felt like an attack on the very idea of a Jewish homeland, and on the right of Jews to define themselves as a people. It damaged Israel's trust in the United Nations for years. Herzog's speech made him a national figure in Israel, and he later served as the country's sixth president. His son, Isaac Herzog, became president in 2021.

After the end of the Cold War, the resolution lost much of its support. Israel made its repeal a condition for taking part in the Madrid peace conference, and on 16 December 1991 the General Assembly revoked it by 111 votes to 25. It is one of very few General Assembly resolutions ever to be withdrawn. The debate it started did not end, however. Similar language returned at the UN conference against racism in Durban in 2001, and arguments over Zionism and racism remain part of discussions about Israel today.

Entebbe raid.background: In the 1970s Palestinian and European militant groups carried out a series of plane hijackings to draw attention to their causes and to demand the release of prisoners. Israel's policy was generally not to give in to such demands. Uganda was ruled by Idi Amin, a military dictator who had once been friendly with Israel but had broken off ties and turned openly hostile.
Entebbe raid.happened:
On 27 June 1976 Air France Flight 139, flying from Tel Aviv to Paris, was hijacked after a stop in Athens. The hijackers were two members of a breakaway faction of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine and two Germans from a left-wing group, the Revolutionary Cells. After refuelling in Libya, the plane landed at Entebbe airport in Uganda, where more hijackers joined them and Ugandan troops protected them. They demanded the release of dozens of prisoners, most of them held in Israel.

The hijackers separated the Israeli and Jewish passengers from the rest, which reminded many of the Nazi selections, and freed most of the others. The Air France captain, Michel Bacos, and his crew chose to stay with the remaining hostages. On the night of 3 to 4 July, four Israeli Hercules transport planes flew low over the Red Sea to Entebbe. Commandos drove out in a black Mercedes made to look like Amin's car, stormed the old terminal and killed the hijackers in minutes. Around 45 Ugandan soldiers were killed and Ugandan fighter jets were destroyed on the ground. The planes refuelled in Nairobi, Kenya, on the way home.
Entebbe raid.matters:
Three hostages were killed during the raid, and Lieutenant Colonel Yoni Netanyahu, the commander of the assault force, was shot and killed. An elderly hostage, Dora Bloch, who had been taken to a hospital in Kampala, was murdered afterwards on Amin's orders. The rest, more than 100 people, landed safely in Israel to huge celebrations.

The operation was renamed Operation Jonathan in Yoni Netanyahu's memory. His younger brother Benjamin later became Israel's prime minister. The raid, which took place on the day the United States marked 200 years of independence, became a model for hostage rescue around the world and a symbol of Israel's determination to protect Jews in danger anywhere. It has been the subject of several films and is still taught in military academies.

Sadat visits Jerusalem.background:
Israel and Egypt had fought four wars since 1948. After the Yom Kippur War, Egypt's President Anwar Sadat felt that Egyptian pride had been restored, and his country was struggling with deep economic problems. Agreements to separate the two armies, negotiated by US Secretary of State Henry Kissinger in 1974 and 1975, had started a cautious process.

In May 1977 Menachem Begin of the Likud party became Israel's prime minister. Many expected him to be a hardliner, but secret contacts soon began, including a meeting in Morocco between Israel's foreign minister Moshe Dayan and a senior Egyptian official.
Sadat visits Jerusalem.happened:
On 9 November 1977 Sadat told the Egyptian parliament that he was ready to go to the Knesset itself in search of peace. Begin quickly sent an invitation. On the evening of Saturday 19 November, just after Shabbat ended, Sadat's plane landed at Ben Gurion Airport. He was greeted by Begin, President Ephraim Katzir and figures such as Golda Meir and Ariel Sharon, while millions watched on television.

The next day Sadat prayed at the al-Aqsa Mosque, which fell on the Muslim festival of Eid al-Adha, and visited Yad Vashem. He then spoke to the Knesset in Arabic. He called for an end to war and for Israel to withdraw from land taken in 1967 and to recognise Palestinian rights. Begin replied with his own speech. The two leaders disagreed on much, but the meeting itself broke a barrier that had seemed permanent.
Sadat visits Jerusalem.matters:
The visit changed what people in the region believed was possible. Until then no Arab leader had publicly recognised Israel by setting foot there. In Israel Sadat was received with enormous warmth. In much of the Arab world he was called a traitor, and several states cut ties with Egypt.

Talks moved slowly at first, so US President Jimmy Carter invited both leaders to Camp David, the presidential retreat in Maryland. After 13 days of tense negotiations, the Camp David Accords were signed on 17 September 1978. They led to the peace treaty of 1979. Sadat and Begin shared the 1978 Nobel Peace Prize. The visit is still remembered as one of the most dramatic moments in the history of the Middle East, an example of how a single bold act of leadership can open a door.

Peace with Egypt.background: The Camp David Accords of September 1978 contained two frameworks. The first set out the terms for peace between Egypt and Israel. The second proposed self-government for Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, leading to talks on their final status. Turning the first framework into a full treaty took six more months of hard bargaining, and US President Jimmy Carter flew to both Cairo and Jerusalem in March 1979 to close the remaining gaps.
Peace with Egypt.happened:
On 26 March 1979, on the North Lawn of the White House, Menachem Begin and Anwar Sadat signed the Egypt-Israel peace treaty, with Carter signing as witness. Egypt recognised Israel, the two countries opened embassies, and Israeli ships gained free passage through the Suez Canal. Israel agreed to withdraw completely from the Sinai Peninsula, including its air bases, oil fields and settlements. A Multinational Force and Observers was set up to monitor the border, and it is still there today.

Israel withdrew in stages and handed over the last of the Sinai in April 1982. The town of Yamit was evacuated, sometimes by force, and then demolished. A dispute over the small resort area of Taba near Eilat went to international arbitration and was returned to Egypt in 1989. The autonomy talks for the Palestinians made little progress.
Peace with Egypt.matters:
Egypt was the largest and most powerful Arab state, so its decision to make peace meant that a full Arab war against Israel became far less likely. The Arab League suspended Egypt and moved its headquarters from Cairo to Tunis, though Egypt was readmitted in 1989. On 6 October 1981, during a military parade marking the anniversary of the 1973 war, Sadat was shot dead by members of an Islamist group opposed to the peace. His successor, Hosni Mubarak, kept the treaty in place.

The peace has lasted for more than four decades through wars, uprisings and changes of government. It is often described as a cold peace, with close security cooperation but limited tourism and trade and little warmth between ordinary people. Still, it set the pattern of land for peace and paved the way for later agreements with Jordan and other Arab states.

Osirak strike.background:
In the 1970s Iraq bought a research reactor from France, along with nuclear fuel of weapons-grade enriched uranium. The reactor, called Osirak by the French and Tammuz by the Iraqis, was built at the al-Tuwaitha nuclear centre south-east of Baghdad. Iraq said it was for peaceful research, but Israeli leaders believed Saddam Hussein intended to build a nuclear bomb, and Iraq was openly hostile to Israel.

Israel tried diplomacy to stop the project, and there were also acts of sabotage against the programme in France. In September 1980, soon after the Iran-Iraq War began, Iranian jets attacked the site but caused only limited damage.
Osirak strike.happened:
On the afternoon of 7 June 1981, eight Israeli F-16 fighter-bombers, escorted by F-15s, took off from the Etzion air base in Sinai, which Israel still held at the time. They flew low over Jordanian and Saudi territory to avoid radar, then climbed and dived on the reactor, dropping their bombs in less than two minutes. All the planes returned safely. The reactor was destroyed before it had been loaded with fuel. Ten Iraqi soldiers and a French engineer were killed.

One of the youngest pilots was Ilan Ramon, who later became Israel's first astronaut and died in the Columbia space shuttle disaster in 2003. Prime Minister Menachem Begin defended the strike, saying Israel would not allow an enemy to develop weapons that could be used to destroy it.
Osirak strike.matters:
At the time the strike was widely condemned. The UN Security Council unanimously passed Resolution 487 against it, with the United States voting in favour. Critics said it broke international law and might push Iraq to pursue weapons more secretly, and historians still debate how far it slowed Iraq's programme.

After the 1991 Gulf War, when inspectors found how advanced Iraq's secret nuclear work had become, many came to see the raid differently. The policy that Israel will act to stop hostile states in the region from getting nuclear weapons became known as the Begin Doctrine. Israel followed it again in 2007 with a strike on a suspected reactor in Syria, and it has shaped Israel's approach to Iran's nuclear programme.

First Lebanon War.background:
After being driven out of Jordan in 1970 and 1971, the Palestine Liberation Organization moved its main base to Lebanon. When Lebanon's civil war broke out in 1975, the PLO became a powerful armed force in the south and in Beirut. From there its fighters fired rockets and launched raids into northern Israel. In 1978, after an attack on a bus on Israel's coastal road killed dozens of Israelis, Israel briefly invaded southern Lebanon, and UN peacekeepers were sent to the area.

A US-brokered ceasefire in July 1981 brought some quiet. Then on 3 June 1982 gunmen from the Abu Nidal group, a rival of the PLO, shot and badly wounded Israel's ambassador in London, Shlomo Argov. Israel used the attack as the trigger for a long-planned operation.
First Lebanon War.happened:
On 6 June 1982 Israel launched Operation Peace for Galilee. The government's stated aim was to push the PLO about 40 kilometres back from the border, but forces under Defence Minister Ariel Sharon pressed on to the outskirts of Beirut. During the summer Israel besieged and bombarded West Beirut, causing heavy civilian casualties. In August, under a US-led agreement, thousands of PLO fighters and Yasser Arafat himself left Lebanon, with the leadership moving to Tunisia.

Israel's Lebanese ally Bashir Gemayel was elected president but was assassinated on 14 September. Over the next days, Christian Phalangist militiamen entered the Sabra and Shatila refugee camps, in an area under Israeli army control, and killed hundreds of Palestinian and Lebanese civilians. Estimates of the dead range widely, from several hundred to a few thousand. On 25 September a huge crowd, often estimated at 400,000, protested in Tel Aviv and demanded an inquiry.
First Lebanon War.matters:
Israel's Kahan Commission found that while the militia carried out the killings, Israeli leaders bore indirect responsibility for failing to foresee and prevent them. Sharon was forced to resign as defence minister. Prime Minister Menachem Begin, worn down by the war and the death of his wife, resigned in 1983. The war was the first in Israel's history to cause deep public division while it was being fought, and it gave new strength to the Peace Now movement.

Israel pulled back to a security zone in southern Lebanon in 1985 and stayed there until May 2000, losing hundreds more soldiers over the years. The war also helped give rise to Hezbollah, a Shiite militia backed by Iran, which became Israel's most powerful enemy on its northern border. For Lebanese and Palestinians, the siege of Beirut and Sabra and Shatila remain painful memories.

Operation Moses.background:
The Beta Israel lived for centuries in villages in northern Ethiopia, mainly around Gondar and in Tigray. They kept a form of Judaism based on the Bible, with their own priests and holy books, but they had been cut off from other Jews for so long that they did not know the Talmud or later customs. Many outsiders called them Falasha, a word meaning strangers, which they found insulting.

In 1973 Israel's Sephardi Chief Rabbi, Ovadia Yosef, ruled that they were Jews, and in 1975 the Israeli government accepted that the Law of Return applied to them. But Ethiopia's communist military regime would not let them leave. In the early 1980s war and a terrible famine struck, and thousands of Beta Israel set out on foot for Sudan, hoping to reach Israel from there.
Operation Moses.happened:
