The journey was extremely dangerous. People walked for weeks through mountains and desert, facing bandits, hunger and disease. In crowded refugee camps in Sudan they often had to hide their Jewish identity. Around 4,000 are believed to have died on the way or in the camps.

Between November 1984 and January 1985, Israel carried out a secret airlift with the help of the United States and quiet cooperation from Sudanese officials, even though Sudan was a member of the Arab League. Planes chartered from a Belgian company flew people from Khartoum, often by way of Europe, to Israel. About 8,000 were brought out. When Israeli officials and newspapers began to talk about the operation, Arab governments protested, and Sudan stopped it at once. Many families were left split between Israel and Sudan. In March 1985 a US-led follow-up, sometimes called Operation Joshua, flew out around 500 more.
Operation Moses.matters:
Operation Moses was the first large airlift of Ethiopian Jews, and it began the ingathering of a community that had dreamed of Jerusalem for generations. Their arrival also brought challenges. Many immigrants faced poverty, racism and painful questions over their religious status, and Ethiopian Israelis have protested for equal treatment at several points since.

The journey through Sudan has become a central part of Ethiopian Israeli memory. A national memorial on Mount Herzl honours those who died on the way to Israel, and a state ceremony is held there every year. The community's own festival, Sigd, which celebrates the longing for Jerusalem, became an Israeli national holiday in 2008.

First Intifada.background: After the 1967 war, the West Bank and Gaza came under Israeli military rule. By the late 1980s a whole generation of Palestinians had grown up under occupation, facing checkpoints, restrictions, land taken for settlements and few economic chances. Many worked as day labourers in Israel. The PLO leadership was far away in Tunis, and young people in the territories felt their cause was being ignored, including by Arab leaders.
First Intifada.happened:
On 8 December 1987 an Israeli truck crashed into cars carrying Palestinian workers near the Erez crossing in Gaza, killing four. Rumours spread that it was deliberate, and the funerals turned into mass protests, beginning in the Jabalia refugee camp. Within days the unrest spread across Gaza and the West Bank. A local Unified National Leadership organised strikes, boycotts of Israeli goods and refusals to pay taxes. Young people threw stones and petrol bombs at soldiers, and later attacks included stabbings and shootings.

Israel responded with mass arrests, curfews, closures and the use of live ammunition, rubber bullets and beatings, which drew wide international criticism. According to the Israeli rights group B'Tselem, more than 1,000 Palestinians were killed by Israeli forces and about 160 Israelis were killed by Palestinians before the uprising wound down in 1993. Hundreds of Palestinians were also killed by other Palestinians as suspected collaborators. In December 1987 Sheikh Ahmed Yassin and others founded Hamas, an Islamist movement opposed to any compromise with Israel.
First Intifada.matters:
The intifada showed Israelis that ruling millions of Palestinians had a heavy cost, and it put the Palestinian cause back at the centre of world attention. In 1988 Jordan gave up its claim to the West Bank, and the PLO declared a Palestinian state and soon afterwards accepted UN resolutions that implied recognition of Israel.

These shifts led to the Madrid peace conference of 1991 and then to the Oslo Accords of 1993. At the same time, the rise of Hamas created a powerful rival to the PLO that would shape the conflict for decades. For Palestinians the first intifada is remembered as a popular uprising, while for many Israeli soldiers who served in it, policing civilians left lasting and difficult memories.

Soviet aliyah.background:
Through the 1970s around a quarter of a million Jews had left the Soviet Union, but in the early 1980s emigration almost stopped, and refuseniks faced arrest and harassment. When Mikhail Gorbachev came to power in 1985, his policies of glasnost, meaning openness, and perestroika, meaning restructuring, slowly loosened controls. By 1989 permission to leave was being granted in large numbers.

In earlier years many Soviet Jews who left on Israeli visas had gone instead to the United States. In 1989 the US tightened its rules on accepting Soviet Jews as refugees, so far more of those leaving now went to Israel.
Soviet aliyah.happened:
In 1990 alone, around 185,000 people from the Soviet Union arrived in Israel, and around 150,000 more came in 1991, the year the Soviet Union collapsed. Some landed during the Gulf War as Iraqi Scud missiles hit Israeli cities, and were handed gas masks at the airport. Over the decade around a million people arrived from the former Soviet Union. Israel used a system called direct absorption, giving newcomers a package of money and letting them choose where to live, but housing ran short and many lived in caravan sites at first.

The new immigrants were highly educated. Doctors, engineers and scientists often had to start in low-paid jobs while they learned Hebrew and retrained. A sizeable minority were not Jewish under religious law, but qualified under the Law of Return as children, grandchildren or spouses of Jews.
Soviet aliyah.matters:
The aliyah changed Israel more than almost any event since 1948. The influx of skilled workers helped power the country's high-tech boom in the 1990s and 2000s. Immigrants filled orchestras, hospitals, universities and sports teams, and Russian became one of the most widely spoken languages in the country, with its own newspapers and television.

The newcomers also reshaped politics, forming parties such as Natan Sharansky's Yisrael BaAliyah and Avigdor Lieberman's Yisrael Beiteinu. Questions about the religious status of those not considered Jewish by the rabbinate, including marriage and burial, are still unresolved. Today the immigrants and their children are a major part of Israeli life in every field.

Operation Solomon.background:
After Operation Moses in 1984 and 1985, many Beta Israel were still in Ethiopia, and families had been split. In the following years thousands moved to the capital, Addis Ababa, to wait for permission to leave, living in difficult conditions. Israel negotiated with the government of Mengistu Haile Mariam, who allowed only small numbers to go.

By May 1991 Ethiopia's long civil war was ending. Rebel forces were closing in on Addis Ababa, and Mengistu fled the country on 21 May. Israel feared the Jews waiting in the city could be caught up in the chaos.
Operation Solomon.happened:
With help from the United States, Israel reached an agreement with what remained of the Ethiopian government, reportedly including a payment of millions of dollars, and the rebels agreed not to interfere. Israel's envoy Uri Lubrani played a leading role. Beginning on Friday 24 May 1991, a fleet of Israeli air force and El Al planes flew non-stop between Addis Ababa and Israel, even though it was Shabbat. Seats were removed so that more people could fit, and many passengers carried nothing but the clothes they wore.

In about 36 hours more than 14,000 people were flown to Israel. One El Al Boeing 747 carried over 1,000 people, the largest number ever flown on a single plane. Several babies were born during the flights. At Ben Gurion Airport families who had been separated for years were reunited.
Operation Solomon.matters:
Operation Solomon brought almost all of the remaining Beta Israel to Israel in one dramatic weekend, and it is remembered as one of the great rescue missions in Jewish history. It showed the state using all of its resources to bring an endangered Jewish community home.

Afterwards a further question arose over the Falash Mura, descendants of Beta Israel who had converted to Christianity, often under pressure, generations earlier. Many have since been allowed to come to Israel in stages after returning to Judaism, though families remain divided and waiting. Today more than 160,000 Ethiopian Israelis live in Israel, many born there. They serve in the army, sit in the Knesset and work in every field, while still campaigning against discrimination.

Oslo Accords.background:
After the Gulf War of 1991, the United States and the Soviet Union brought Israel, its Arab neighbours and a Palestinian delegation together at the Madrid peace conference. Formal talks in Washington followed but made little progress. Israeli law still banned contact with the PLO, which Israel regarded as a terrorist organisation.

In 1992 Yitzhak Rabin of the Labour Party was elected prime minister, promising to pursue peace. The first intifada and the rise of Hamas had convinced many on both sides that the status quo could not last.
Oslo Accords.happened:
In January 1993 two Israeli academics, Yair Hirschfeld and Ron Pundak, began secret meetings near Oslo with PLO officials led by Ahmed Qurei. The talks were hosted by the Norwegian researcher Terje Rød-Larsen, his wife, the diplomat Mona Juul, and Norway's foreign minister Johan Jørgen Holst. With backing from Foreign Minister Shimon Peres and his deputy Yossi Beilin, senior Israeli officials soon took over. On 9 September 1993 Arafat and Rabin exchanged letters: the PLO recognised Israel's right to exist in peace and renounced terrorism, and Israel recognised the PLO as the representative of the Palestinian people.

On 13 September 1993 Peres and the PLO's Mahmoud Abbas signed the Declaration of Principles at the White House. Rabin and Arafat then shook hands, with President Clinton gently guiding them together. Under the agreement and later deals, the new Palestinian Authority took control of Gaza and Jericho in 1994. The 1995 interim agreement, known as Oslo II, divided the West Bank into Areas A, B and C with different levels of Palestinian and Israeli control. The hardest issues, including Jerusalem, refugees, borders and settlements, were left for final talks within five years.
Oslo Accords.matters:
Oslo was the first time Israelis and Palestinians formally recognised each other, and it created Palestinian self-government for the first time. Rabin, Peres and Arafat shared the 1994 Nobel Peace Prize. Yet the process was fiercely opposed on both sides. In February 1994 a Jewish extremist, Baruch Goldstein, murdered 29 Palestinian worshippers in Hebron, and Hamas and Islamic Jihad carried out suicide bombings that killed scores of Israelis.

A final agreement was never reached, and the Camp David summit of 2000 failed. Still, the structures Oslo created remain in place today, including the Palestinian Authority and the division of the West Bank into areas A, B and C. Whether Oslo was a missed opportunity or a flawed idea from the start is still debated by Israelis, Palestinians and historians.

Peace with Jordan.background:
Israel and Jordan had been formally at war since 1948, and Jordan ruled the West Bank and East Jerusalem until 1967. Yet behind the scenes King Hussein had met Israeli leaders secretly for decades, from the 1960s onwards, and the two countries shared interests, including stability along their long border. Jordan had stayed out of the 1973 war's main fighting and was cautious about openly making peace while the Palestinian question was unresolved.

The Oslo Accords of 1993 changed this. Once the PLO had recognised Israel, King Hussein felt free to act.
Peace with Jordan.happened:
In July 1994 King Hussein and Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin met publicly in Washington and signed a declaration ending the state of war. On 26 October 1994 they signed a full peace treaty at the Arava crossing in the desert between Eilat and Aqaba, with President Clinton present and thousands of guests watching. Balloons were released into the desert sky.

The treaty fixed the international border and dealt with the sharing of water from the Jordan and Yarmouk rivers, with Israel agreeing to supply Jordan with a set amount each year. Two small areas, Naharayim and Tzofar, were recognised as Jordanian but leased to Israeli farmers. The treaty also recognised Jordan's special role at the Muslim holy sites in Jerusalem. Embassies opened, and Israelis began visiting Petra.
Peace with Jordan.matters:
The peace with Jordan was warmer at the top than many expected. King Hussein and Rabin had a genuine friendship, and when Rabin was assassinated a year later, Hussein's grief at the funeral moved many Israelis. In 1997, after a Jordanian soldier shot dead seven Israeli schoolgirls at Naharayim, the king travelled to Israel and knelt to comfort the bereaved families in their homes.

The treaty has lasted for three decades and is vital to the security of both countries, with close cooperation on borders, water and energy. Public opinion in Jordan, where many citizens are of Palestinian origin, has often been hostile to Israel, and relations have cooled during times of conflict. In 2019 Jordan ended the lease of Naharayim and Tzofar. Even so, the treaty remains one of the most important pillars of stability in the region.

Rabin assassinated.background: Yitzhak Rabin was a former army chief of staff who had led Israel's forces in the Six-Day War. As prime minister for a second time from 1992, he signed the Oslo Accords and the peace treaty with Jordan. These moves split Israeli society deeply, especially after a wave of Hamas suicide bombings. Opponents held angry protests, some calling Rabin a traitor, and at one rally in Jerusalem posters showed him in a Nazi SS uniform. Some extremist rabbis were reported to have discussed religious justifications for harming him.
Rabin assassinated.happened:
On the evening of Saturday 4 November 1995, around 100,000 people filled the Kings of Israel Square in Tel Aviv for a rally in support of peace and against violence. Rabin, who was usually reserved, appeared moved by the crowd and joined in singing Shir LaShalom, the Song for Peace. As he walked down the steps to his car at around 9.40pm, Yigal Amir, a 25-year-old law student from Bar-Ilan University, shot him in the back. Rabin was rushed to Ichilov Hospital, where he died on the operating table. His aide Eitan Haber announced the death to the waiting crowd. A blood-stained sheet with the song's words was later found in his pocket.

Amir said he had acted to stop the peace process. He was sentenced to life in prison. His funeral on Mount Herzl in Jerusalem was attended by leaders from dozens of countries, including President Clinton, King Hussein of Jordan and President Hosni Mubarak of Egypt, on his first visit to Israel.
Rabin assassinated.matters:
The murder of a prime minister by a fellow Jew shocked Israel to its core. Young people gathered for weeks in the square, lighting candles, singing and writing messages on the walls, and became known as the candle generation. The square was renamed Rabin Square, and a memorial marks the spot where he fell.

Shimon Peres took over as prime minister, but after a series of bus bombings Benjamin Netanyahu, an opponent of Oslo, narrowly won the election in May 1996. Many believe the assassination did lasting damage to the peace process. Every year Israel holds an official memorial on the Hebrew date of his death, and a large rally takes place in Rabin Square. Arguments about incitement, political violence and what might have happened had Rabin lived continue to this day.

Second Intifada.background:
In July 2000 US President Bill Clinton hosted Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat at Camp David to try to reach a final peace deal. After two weeks the summit ended without agreement, and each side blamed the other. The biggest gaps were over Jerusalem and its holy sites, and the future of Palestinian refugees.

On 28 September 2000, opposition leader Ariel Sharon visited the Temple Mount, known to Muslims as the Haram al-Sharif. Palestinians saw the visit as a provocation, and the next day protests at the site turned deadly.
Second Intifada.happened:
The violence quickly spread across the West Bank, Gaza and Arab towns inside Israel. Palestinian armed groups, including Hamas, Islamic Jihad and the al-Aqsa Martyrs' Brigades linked to Fatah, launched waves of attacks. Suicide bombings hit Israeli cities, including the Dolphinarium nightclub in Tel Aviv in June 2001, where 21 people, mostly teenagers, were killed, the Sbarro pizzeria in Jerusalem in August 2001, and the Park Hotel in Netanya during a Passover meal in March 2002, where 30 people died.

After that attack Israel launched Operation Defensive Shield, re-entering Palestinian cities in the West Bank, with heavy fighting in the Jenin refugee camp. Arafat was confined to his compound in Ramallah. Israel also carried out targeted killings and imposed widespread closures and curfews, causing great hardship for Palestinians. In 2002 Israel began building a barrier of fences and walls along and inside the West Bank. Arafat died in November 2004, and the violence gradually faded after a summit at Sharm el-Sheikh in February 2005.
Second Intifada.matters:
The second intifada had a deep and lasting effect on both societies. For Israelis, the bombings of buses, cafés and restaurants created a time of constant fear and pushed politics sharply to the right. Many lost faith in the idea that a peace deal was possible. For Palestinians, Israeli military operations, closures and the barrier brought heavy loss of life, damage and economic collapse.

The barrier remains highly controversial. Israel credits it with a sharp drop in suicide bombings, while Palestinians see it as taking land and dividing communities, and in 2004 the International Court of Justice gave an advisory opinion that the parts built in the West Bank were contrary to international law. The trust broken in these years has never been restored, and the period still shapes how each side views the other.

Pope at the Western Wall.background:
For much of history, Christian teaching blamed the Jewish people for the death of Jesus. This belief fuelled persecution, expulsions and violence against Jews for centuries. After the Holocaust, the Catholic Church began to rethink its attitude. In 1965 the Second Vatican Council issued Nostra Aetate, a declaration rejecting the charge that Jews as a people were guilty of Jesus's death and condemning antisemitism.

Pope John Paul II, born Karol Wojtyła in Wadowice, Poland, had grown up with Jewish friends and neighbours, many of whom were murdered in the Holocaust. In 1986 he became the first pope to visit a synagogue, the Great Synagogue of Rome, and in 1993 the Vatican and Israel agreed to establish full diplomatic relations.
Pope at the Western Wall.happened:
In March 2000, during a pilgrimage to the Holy Land marking the Christian jubilee year, the pope spent several days in Israel and the Palestinian territories. On 23 March he visited Yad Vashem, where he spoke of the Holocaust and met survivors, including some from his home town. He also met Israel's chief rabbis, Yisrael Meir Lau and Eliyahu Bakshi-Doron, and visited the Palestinian Dheisheh refugee camp near Bethlehem.

On 26 March, his last day, the frail 79-year-old pope stood at the Western Wall and, following Jewish custom, placed a folded note between its stones. Signed by him, it asked God's forgiveness for those who had caused the children of Abraham to suffer, and committed the Church to genuine brotherhood with the people of the covenant. The note was later given to Yad Vashem.
Pope at the Western Wall.matters:
The image of the head of the Catholic Church praying at Judaism's holiest accessible site went around the world. For many Jews, especially Holocaust survivors, it was a moment they had never imagined they would see. It built on the Church's day of pardon a few weeks earlier, when the pope had asked forgiveness for past sins of Christians, including those against Jews.

The visit is widely seen as a high point of John Paul II's efforts to transform Catholic-Jewish relations. His successors Benedict XVI, in 2009, and Francis, in 2014, also visited Israel and the Western Wall, continuing the tradition. Dialogue between Catholics and Jews continues today, though differences remain on some issues.

Gaza disengagement.background:
After 1967 Israel built settlements in the Gaza Strip, most of them in a bloc called Gush Katif in the south. By 2005 around 8,000 Israelis lived in 21 settlements there, surrounded by well over a million Palestinians and protected by large numbers of soldiers. The settlements were frequent targets of attacks during the second intifada.

Ariel Sharon had long been one of the strongest supporters of settlements. But in December 2003, as prime minister, he announced a plan to withdraw from Gaza without waiting for an agreement with the Palestinians. He argued it would improve Israel's security and preserve a Jewish majority. Members of his own Likud party rejected the plan in an internal vote in 2004, but the Knesset approved it.
Gaza disengagement.happened:
The plan divided the country. Opponents wore orange ribbons and held huge protests, while supporters adopted blue. In August 2005, after the deadline for leaving had passed, tens of thousands of soldiers and police went house to house. Many residents left in tears, some were carried out, and some protesters barricaded themselves in synagogues. The evacuation of Gaza took about a week, and four small settlements in the northern West Bank were cleared soon after.

The homes were demolished. The last Israeli soldiers left Gaza on 12 September 2005, ending 38 years of Israeli presence inside the strip. Israel kept control of Gaza's airspace, coastline and most of its border crossings.
Gaza disengagement.matters:
Many evacuees spent years in temporary housing, and some struggled to rebuild their communities and livelihoods. Sharon left Likud and founded a new party, Kadima, but suffered a massive stroke in January 2006 and never recovered. Hamas won Palestinian parliamentary elections that month, and in June 2007 it seized full control of Gaza after fighting with Fatah. Israel and Egypt then imposed a blockade on the strip.

Rocket fire from Gaza increased, leading to repeated wars. Supporters of the withdrawal say it was right to leave and that Hamas, not the pullout, caused what followed. Critics say it showed that giving up land without agreement brings more danger. The disengagement still shapes Israeli debate about any future withdrawal from the West Bank.

Holocaust Remembrance Day.background:
Soviet soldiers liberated Auschwitz-Birkenau, the largest Nazi death camp, on 27 January 1945. About 1.1 million people were murdered there, around a million of them Jews. In the decades after the war, countries remembered the Holocaust in different ways and at different times, and some hardly at all.

In Israel, the Knesset set Yom HaShoah in 1951 on the 27th day of the Hebrew month of Nisan, close to the anniversary of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, and a 1959 law made it official. In Europe, Germany began marking 27 January in 1996, and the United Kingdom held its first Holocaust Memorial Day in 2001. In 2000 leaders from dozens of countries signed the Stockholm Declaration, committing to Holocaust education and remembrance.
Holocaust Remembrance Day.happened:
In January 2005 the UN General Assembly held a special session to mark 60 years since the liberation of the camps, the first time it had done so. Later that year, on 1 November 2005, it adopted a resolution, put forward by Israel and co-sponsored by more than 100 countries, naming 27 January as International Holocaust Remembrance Day. It was the first resolution initiated by Israel to be adopted by the General Assembly.

The resolution rejected any denial of the Holocaust, in full or in part, and urged member states to develop education programmes so that future generations would learn its lessons. It also led the UN to set up an outreach programme on the Holocaust. In 2007 the General Assembly passed a further resolution condemning Holocaust denial.
Holocaust Remembrance Day.matters:
Today 27 January is marked in many countries with ceremonies, lessons in schools and the lighting of candles. Survivors, world leaders and young people gather at Auschwitz on major anniversaries, and parliaments and city halls hold readings of names.

In Israel, Yom HaShoah remains the central day of memory. It begins with a state ceremony at Yad Vashem, where six survivors light six torches for the six million. The next morning, a siren sounds across the country for two minutes. Drivers stop their cars on the motorways and step out, and people in shops, offices and streets stand still in silence. As the number of living survivors grows smaller each year, both days have taken on new urgency as a way to pass on their testimony and to confront denial and distortion.

Second Lebanon War.background:
Israel withdrew its forces from southern Lebanon in May 2000, ending 18 years in its security zone. Hezbollah, the Shiite militia backed by Iran, took over much of the border area and built up a large arsenal of rockets. It also carried out cross-border raids, including one in October 2000 in which three Israeli soldiers were captured and killed.

In June 2006, Hamas fighters from Gaza had captured the Israeli soldier Gilad Shalit, and Israel was already fighting in Gaza when trouble broke out in the north.
Second Lebanon War.happened:
On the morning of 12 July 2006, Hezbollah fighters crossed the border and ambushed an Israeli army patrol, killing three soldiers and capturing two reservists, Ehud Goldwasser and Eldad Regev. Five more soldiers were killed when an Israeli tank chasing the attackers hit a mine. Prime Minister Ehud Olmert's government launched a massive air campaign, striking Hezbollah positions, its strongholds in the southern suburbs of Beirut, as well as roads, bridges and Beirut airport. Later Israel sent in ground troops.

Hezbollah fired around 4,000 rockets at northern Israel, reaching as far as Haifa, where a strike on a train depot killed eight workers. According to official figures, around 160 Israelis were killed, 121 of them soldiers and the rest civilians. Lebanese authorities reported around 1,200 people killed in Lebanon, many of them civilians, and around a million Lebanese were displaced. UN Security Council Resolution 1701 brought a ceasefire on 14 August, and expanded the UN force in southern Lebanon.
Second Lebanon War.matters:
In Israel, the war was widely seen as a failure. It did not bring back the captured soldiers or stop the rockets, and reservists complained of poor planning and supplies. The Winograd Commission sharply criticised the political and military leadership, and the army chief of staff, Dan Halutz, resigned. Hezbollah claimed victory simply for surviving.

In July 2008 the bodies of Goldwasser and Regev were returned in exchange for Lebanese prisoners, including Samir Kuntar, who had been convicted of a deadly 1979 attack in Nahariya. The northern border then stayed mostly quiet for 17 years, but Hezbollah rebuilt and greatly enlarged its rocket arsenal. The lessons of 2006 shaped Israel's preparations for the much larger conflict with Hezbollah that began in October 2023.

Gilad Shalit freed.background:
Before dawn on 25 June 2006, Palestinian fighters from Hamas and other groups dug a tunnel under the Gaza border and attacked an Israeli army post near Kerem Shalom. Two soldiers, Hanan Barak and Pavel Slutzker, were killed. Corporal Gilad Shalit, a tank gunner, was wounded and dragged back into Gaza.

Hamas demanded the release of large numbers of Palestinian prisoners in exchange for him. Israel launched military operations in Gaza, but could not find him, and talks dragged on for years through Egyptian and German mediators.
Gilad Shalit freed.happened:
Shalit was kept in hiding for more than five years. The International Committee of the Red Cross was never allowed to see him. Apart from a few letters, an audio message and a short video released in 2009 in return for the freeing of 20 Palestinian women prisoners, his family had almost no sign that he was alive. His parents, Noam and Aviva Shalit, led a huge public campaign. In 2010 they marched across the country from their home in northern Israel to Jerusalem, and set up a protest tent near the prime minister's residence, where they stayed until his release.

In October 2011 Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government approved a deal brokered by Egypt. On 18 October Shalit, thin and pale, was handed over through Egypt and flown home. Israel released 1,027 prisoners in two stages, many of them serving life sentences for attacks that had killed Israelis.
Gilad Shalit freed.matters:
Shalit's return brought scenes of national joy, and it reflected a deeply held Israeli value: that the state will do almost anything to bring its soldiers home. But the price caused painful debate. Families of victims protested the release of those who had killed their loved ones, and some freed prisoners returned to violence.

Among those released was Yahya Sinwar, who had served more than 20 years for murdering Palestinians he accused of collaborating with Israel. He rose to lead Hamas in Gaza and is regarded as the main planner of the 7 October 2023 attack, in which 251 people were taken hostage. Since then the Shalit deal has been widely re-examined in Israel as a warning about the long-term cost of large prisoner exchanges.

Gaza war.background:
After Hamas took control of Gaza in 2007, Israel and Egypt kept a tight blockade on the strip. Rocket fire into Israel led to rounds of fighting in 2008 to 2009 and 2012. In 2011 Israel deployed Iron Dome, a new system designed to shoot down short-range rockets heading for populated areas.

On 12 June 2014, three Israeli teenagers, Eyal Yifrach, Gilad Shaer and Naftali Fraenkel, were kidnapped while hitchhiking near Gush Etzion in the West Bank. Israel blamed Hamas and arrested hundreds of its members during a large search. On 30 June their bodies were found. Two days later, Jewish extremists kidnapped a 16-year-old Palestinian, Mohammed Abu Khdeir, in Jerusalem and burned him to death. Rocket fire from Gaza grew heavier.
Gaza war.happened:
On 8 July 2014 Israel launched Operation Protective Edge with air strikes across Gaza. Hamas and other groups fired around 4,500 rockets and mortars at Israel over the course of the war, reaching Tel Aviv, Jerusalem and beyond. Iron Dome intercepted most of those heading for cities, and air raid sirens sent millions of Israelis into shelters.

On 17 July Israeli ground forces entered Gaza, focusing on a network of tunnels that Hamas had dug under the border to carry out attacks inside Israel. Fighting in crowded neighbourhoods was intense. According to UN figures, more than 2,200 Palestinians were killed, many of them civilians, including hundreds of children, and thousands of homes were destroyed. On the Israeli side, 67 soldiers and six civilians in Israel were killed, among them a four-year-old boy, Daniel Tregerman. An Egyptian-brokered ceasefire ended the fighting on 26 August.
Gaza war.matters:
The war left much of Gaza in ruins and its people facing a long struggle to rebuild under the blockade. It also left deep trauma in Israeli communities near the border, which had lived under constant rocket fire and the threat of tunnel attacks.

Hamas held the bodies of two Israeli soldiers, Hadar Goldin and Oron Shaul, as well as two Israeli civilians who later crossed into Gaza, for years, and their families campaigned for their return. Iron Dome became a symbol of Israeli technology and is credited with saving many lives. The war did not resolve the underlying conflict, and both sides prepared for the next round. Many of the tunnels destroyed in 2014 were rebuilt, and the threat they posed returned with terrible force in October 2023.

Pittsburgh synagogue attack.background:
Squirrel Hill is the heart of Jewish life in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, a neighbourhood of synagogues, kosher shops and Jewish schools. The Tree of Life building was home to three congregations that shared the space: Tree of Life Or L'Simcha, Dor Hadash and New Light.

In the years before the attack, antisemitic conspiracy theories had been spreading online. The gunman had posted hateful messages on a social media site, attacking HIAS, a Jewish charity that helps refugees settle in the United States, and repeating the false claim that Jews were bringing in immigrants to harm the country.
Pittsburgh synagogue attack.happened:
On Saturday 27 October 2018, as the congregations gathered for Shabbat morning services, a 46-year-old man armed with an assault rifle and handguns entered the building. He moved through the synagogue, shooting worshippers and shouting antisemitic slurs. Eleven people were murdered. They included the brothers Cecil and David Rosenthal, the married couple Bernice and Sylvan Simon, and Rose Mallinger, who was 97. Several others were wounded, including police officers who exchanged fire with the gunman before he was wounded and arrested.

In 2023 a federal jury convicted him of 63 charges, including hate crimes, and he was sentenced to death.
Pittsburgh synagogue attack.matters:
The attack is the deadliest act of antisemitic violence in American history. It shook Jewish communities across the United States and around the world. In the days after, thousands of people of all faiths gathered for vigils, and local Muslim groups raised money for the victims' families.

The massacre led to major changes in how synagogues and Jewish schools protect themselves, with more armed guards, locked doors and government grants for security. It was followed by another deadly synagogue attack in Poway, California, in 2019. The original Tree of Life building has been demolished, and a new building designed by the architect Daniel Libeskind is planned, including a memorial to the victims and spaces for education about antisemitism.

US embassy in Jerusalem.background:
Israel has treated Jerusalem as its capital since 1949, and the Knesset, the Supreme Court and the prime minister's office are all there. But the UN partition plan of 1947 had proposed that Jerusalem be an international city, and after 1967 most countries did not recognise Israel's rule over East Jerusalem, which Palestinians want as the capital of a future state. For this reason almost all embassies were in or near Tel Aviv.

In 1995 the US Congress passed the Jerusalem Embassy Act, requiring the embassy to move. However, Presidents Clinton, Bush and Obama each signed waivers every six months to delay the move, citing national security and the peace process.
US embassy in Jerusalem.happened:
On 6 December 2017 President Donald Trump announced that the United States recognised Jerusalem as Israel's capital and would move its embassy there. He said the final borders of Israeli sovereignty in the city were still a matter for negotiation. Later that month the UN General Assembly voted by 128 to 9 to call on countries not to move their embassies to Jerusalem.

On 14 May 2018 the embassy opened in an existing US consular building in the Arnona neighbourhood of southern Jerusalem, with Trump's daughter Ivanka and son-in-law Jared Kushner attending. On the same day, mass protests took place along the Gaza border as part of the Great March of Return, and around 60 Palestinians were killed by Israeli fire, according to Gaza's health ministry. Guatemala moved its embassy two days later. Paraguay moved and then moved back, and later Honduras, Kosovo and Papua New Guinea opened embassies in Jerusalem.
US embassy in Jerusalem.matters:
For many Israelis the move was a long-awaited recognition of a historical fact and of Jerusalem's central place in Jewish history. Palestinian leaders saw it as the United States taking Israel's side on one of the most sensitive issues in the conflict, and Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas cut off contact with the Trump administration for a time.

The embassy has stayed in Jerusalem under later US administrations. Most countries still keep their embassies in the Tel Aviv area, saying the city's status should be settled in negotiations. Jerusalem remains one of the most emotional and contested questions in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

Abraham Accords.background:
For decades most Arab states refused to recognise Israel until the Palestinian question was solved, a position written into the Arab Peace Initiative of 2002. Only Egypt and Jordan had signed peace treaties. Yet in the 2010s quiet ties grew between Israel and several Gulf states, driven by shared concern about Iran, interest in technology and trade, and frustration with the stalled peace process.

In 2020 Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was planning to annex parts of the West Bank. The United Arab Emirates offered normal relations in return for dropping the plan, and the Trump administration brokered the talks.
Abraham Accords.happened:
On 13 August 2020 Israel and the UAE announced they would establish full relations, and Israel suspended its annexation plans. On 31 August the first direct commercial flight from Israel to Abu Dhabi crossed Saudi airspace, carrying Israeli and American officials. On 15 September 2020, at the White House, Netanyahu signed agreements with the foreign ministers of the UAE, Abdullah bin Zayed, and Bahrain, Abdullatif Al Zayani, with President Trump hosting.

Sudan agreed to join in October 2020, linked to its removal from the US list of state sponsors of terrorism, and Morocco followed in December, as the United States recognised Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara. Embassies opened, flights began, and hundreds of thousands of Israeli tourists visited Dubai. Trade agreements and military cooperation followed quickly.
Abraham Accords.matters:
The accords broke the long-standing pattern that Arab normalisation with Israel would come only after a Palestinian state. They opened up visible, everyday relations: kosher restaurants in Dubai, business deals, student exchanges and joint air defence planning. In 2023 the Abrahamic Family House opened in Abu Dhabi, with a mosque, a church and a synagogue side by side.

Palestinian leaders condemned the accords as a betrayal. Sudan's participation stalled amid its civil war. The agreements have survived the war in Gaza that began in 2023, though public relations cooled sharply. Expanding the accords, especially to Saudi Arabia, remains a major goal of Israeli and American diplomacy.

7 October attack.background:
Hamas had ruled Gaza since 2007, and Israel and Egypt kept a blockade on the strip. Several rounds of war had followed, the last major one in May 2021. In 2023 Israel was deeply divided over the government's plans to overhaul the judiciary, with months of mass protests, and many reservists had threatened to stop volunteering.

Israeli security officials believed Hamas was focused on governing Gaza and was deterred. Warnings from soldiers watching the border, many of them young women serving as surveillance spotters, were not acted on. The attack was planned by Hamas's leader in Gaza, Yahya Sinwar, and its military commander, Mohammed Deif.
7 October attack.happened:
At around 6.30am on Saturday 7 October 2023, the holiday of Simchat Torah, Hamas fired thousands of rockets at Israel. At the same time, fighters broke through the border fence at dozens of points, some using paragliders and boats. They overran army bases and attacked more than 20 communities, including Be'eri, Kfar Aza, Nir Oz and Nahal Oz, and the town of Sderot. At the Nova music festival near Re'im, more than 360 people were murdered.

Families were killed in their homes and safe rooms, and houses were set on fire. Around 1,200 people were killed, most of them civilians, including children and elderly people, as well as many foreign workers. A total of 251 people were taken into Gaza as hostages, from babies to people in their eighties. It took the army days to regain full control of the area. A UN report later found reasonable grounds to believe that sexual violence had taken place during the attack.
7 October attack.matters:
7 October was the deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust, and it left Israel in deep trauma and grief. Almost everyone knew someone who was killed, taken or displaced. Tens of thousands of people from the border communities were evacuated, and the nation's sense of security was shattered. The failure to prevent the attack led to the resignation of senior security officials and to demands for a full state inquiry.

The attack started a long war in Gaza and on other fronts. It was followed by a sharp rise in antisemitic incidents around the world. The Nova festival site and the damaged kibbutzim have become places of remembrance, visited by Israelis and foreign leaders.

War in Gaza.background: In response to the 7 October attack, Israel declared war on Hamas with the stated aims of destroying its military and governing power and bringing back all the hostages. It called up around 360,000 reservists, one of the largest mobilisations in its history. On 8 October Hezbollah began firing rockets and missiles at northern Israel in support of Hamas.
War in Gaza.happened:
After weeks of air strikes, Israeli ground forces entered Gaza in late October 2023. A week-long truce in November 2023 saw 105 hostages freed in exchange for 240 Palestinian prisoners. Fighting then moved through Gaza City, Khan Younis and Rafah. Israeli forces rescued some hostages in military operations, including four freed from Nuseirat in June 2024, an operation in which many Palestinians were also killed. Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was killed in Rafah in October 2024.

On the northern front, around 60,000 Israelis had to leave their homes. In September 2024 Israel struck Hezbollah hard, including the killing of its leader Hassan Nasrallah, and sent troops into southern Lebanon before a ceasefire in November 2024. A ceasefire in Gaza in early 2025 freed more hostages, but fighting resumed in March. According to Gaza's health ministry, more than 67,000 Palestinians had been killed by October 2025, a figure that does not distinguish between civilians and fighters. Most of Gaza's population of about two million was displaced, much of the territory was destroyed, and UN agencies warned of famine. Hundreds of Israeli soldiers were also killed.
War in Gaza.matters:
The war caused immense suffering. For Palestinians in Gaza it brought loss of life, hunger and destruction on a scale not seen before in the conflict. For Israelis it brought grief for fallen soldiers, long displacement and the agony of hostages held in tunnels for months and years.

The war also had major international effects. South Africa brought a genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice, which Israel strongly rejects, and the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Israeli and Hamas leaders. Protests took place across the world, and Jewish communities faced a sharp rise in antisemitism. A US-brokered ceasefire took effect in October 2025, and its long-term future, including who will govern Gaza, remains uncertain.

Twelve-Day War with Iran.background: Iran's leaders had long called for Israel's destruction, and Iran supported Hamas, Hezbollah and other armed groups. For years Israel had tried to slow Iran's nuclear programme through sabotage and covert action. In April and October 2024 Iran fired hundreds of missiles and drones directly at Israel for the first time, and Israel struck back. By 2025 Hezbollah had been badly weakened and Iran was enriching uranium to levels close to weapons grade. On 12 June 2025 the board of the International Atomic Energy Agency found Iran in breach of its obligations.
Twelve-Day War with Iran.happened:
In the early hours of 13 June 2025, Israel launched a large air campaign against Iran. It struck nuclear sites such as Natanz, missile bases and air defences, and killed senior military commanders and nuclear scientists. Iran responded with waves of ballistic missiles and drones. Most were intercepted, but some struck Israeli cities, hitting homes in Tel Aviv, Bat Yam and Rishon LeZion, the Soroka hospital in Beersheba and the Weizmann Institute of Science. Millions of Israelis spent nights in shelters.

On 22 June the United States bombed Iran's nuclear sites at Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan. Iran fired missiles at a US base in Qatar, and on 24 June a ceasefire announced by President Trump took effect. In Israel around 30 people were killed. Iranian authorities reported hundreds of deaths in Iran.
Twelve-Day War with Iran.matters: The war was the first open, sustained conflict between Israel and Iran after decades of fighting through proxies and covert operations. Israel described it as a necessary step to stop Iran from getting a nuclear weapon. How much it set back Iran's programme is still debated. For Israelis, the direct missile strikes on cities brought the dangers of the conflict home in a new way.

Hostages come home.background:
Of the 251 people taken into Gaza on 7 October 2023, many were freed in a truce in November 2023, in a ceasefire in early 2025, and in a small number of rescue operations. Others were killed or died in captivity. Throughout, families of the hostages led a huge public campaign, and Hostages Square, the plaza outside the Tel Aviv Museum of Art, became the centre of weekly rallies and vigils.

In late September 2025 US President Donald Trump put forward a plan to end the war. After talks in Egypt, Israel and Hamas agreed to its first phase, and a ceasefire took effect on 10 October 2025.
Hostages come home.happened:
On 13 October 2025 Hamas handed the last 20 living hostages to the Red Cross, which brought them to Israeli forces. All of them were men, held for more than two years. Huge crowds filled Hostages Square and cheered as the releases were shown on giant screens, while families were reunited at army bases and hospitals. The same day Trump addressed the Knesset in Jerusalem.

In return, Israel released nearly 2,000 Palestinian prisoners and detainees, including around 250 serving long or life sentences and many people held from Gaza during the war.
Hostages come home.matters: The return of the living hostages was a moment of enormous relief and emotion across Israel after more than two years of anguish. Their freedom was also tied to the ceasefire in Gaza and to hopes for an end to the war. The work of returning the bodies of hostages who died continued after the release, and families of the dead waited to bring them home for burial.
